11762-the-american-missionary-volume-42-:
Published in New York by the American Missionary Association, this January 1888 issue opens the forty-second volume of the association's monthly magazine. Its pages mix editorial notes on finance and prohibition with reports from the association's schools and missions across the American South.

Articles describe work among freedpeople in the South, Native American pupils at the Santee Normal Training School, and Chinese immigrants facing restriction laws. A closing section prints donation receipts, so readers could see exactly where their fifty-cent yearly subscriptions and gifts were going. A later passage describes the Santee school's industrial exhibit for the New Orleans Exposition, with chains and wheels from the blacksmith shop, brackets and step-ladders from the carpenter shop. Cups and coffee-pots from the tin shop also appear.
11763-the-american-missionary-volume-42-:
The American Missionary for February 1888, volume 42, number 2, is the monthly journal of the American Missionary Association, published in New York at 56 Reade Street for fifty cents a year. Its contents list editorial matter, the death of Rev. James Powell, and a word to workers.

Field reports follow, with a list of missionaries and teachers, notes from the South, and notes in the saddle by Superintendent Ryder. Indian work, a bureau of woman's work, paragraphs for children, and a story of how Susy went to Tougaloo complete the number. Receipts close the issue, as a missionary journal's accounts should.
11764-the-american-missionary-volume-42-:
New York's American Missionary Association issued this March 1888 number as the third issue of its forty-second volume. Editorial paragraphs on finance sit beside a debate over whether Christ or Mohammed would win Africa, and an argument for teaching Native pupils in their own languages.

Field reports cover the Lewis Normal Institute, Tougaloo University. A gathering of Black residents at Macon, alongside a letter from Grand River, Dakota, and a Chinese Christian's account from China. The issue closes with women's bureau notes, a children's page, and the month's receipts. The children's page carries a story of bullets, and the issue closes with the month's donation receipts.
12087-the-american-missionary-volume-42-:
Volume 42, number 4 of The American Missionary, dated April 1888, opens its contents with editorial and financial paragraphs, mountain work, Atlanta University, and an Indian order from George W. Cable. The death of Hon. A. S. Barnes is noted, with paragraphs, specimens of school endeavor, and a serious alarm in Georgia.

Educational work in the South, a letter from an evangelist. A Chinese section on results that elude the statistician follow, with the bureau of woman's work. One report quotes a man teaching a colored class who lost a white pupil. AChinese evangelist's impassioned address, with expressive gestures, draws upturned faces in a schoolroom, giving the issue its human detail.
12118-the-american-missionary-volume-42-:
The May 1888 number of The American Missionary, volume forty-two, number five, reports the work of the American Missionary Association. Published in New York at fifty cents a year, the monthly served Congregational supporters of schools and churches for freed people, Native Americans, and Chinese immigrants.

Editorials discuss the vernacular in Indian schools and the time factor in the Southern problem, while field letters describe Fisk University graduates, Talladega fruit growing, and Le Moyne School classrooms. Reports from the South, the Chinese missions, and the Bureau of Woman Work sit beside receipts and officer lists. The issue gives a frank, if partisan, view of Reconstruction-era mission work from inside the organization.
12134-the-american-missionary-volume-42-:
Volume 42, number 6 of The American Missionary, dated June 1888, opens with editorial and financial paragraphs, a noble word from the Ohio Congregational Association, and facts and figures. The color-line question, what is it, follows, with paragraphs from an address by Rev. E. T. Fleming of Georgia and a striking statement on misapplied benefactions.

In memoriam notices and a piece on the radical forces of Christianity frame the issue. A passage on the Congregational Union shows the association defending its own standards of giving. The Union began at Albany thirty-five years earlier to protect eastern friends from miscellaneous solicitation, while its workers are praised as heroes and heroines answering a roll-call.
13584-the-american-missionary-volume-42-:
The American Missionary for November 1888, volume forty-two, number eleven, reports the American Missionary Association from rooms at 56 Reade Street, New York, at fifty cents a year. Editorials cover not quite free, encouraging responses to appeal, the Mohonk Conference, ordination, yellow fever, and the Samaritan woman.

A general survey follows schools, church work, mountain work, Indians, Chinese, woman's bureau, and finances, with a student's letter on struggles in the Lone Star State and a review of the year. Christian schools, the editors say, are missionary schools bearing a torch into darkness and teaching industries as well as faith. Receipts from Maine towns, from Kennebunkport to Presque Isle, close the number with small gifts carefully listed.
13641-the-american-missionary-volume-42-:
The October 1888 number of The American Missionary, organ of the American Missionary Association, reports on the group's work among freed people, Native Americans, and Chinese immigrants. Notes cover the annual meeting, qualifications for mission workers, the expulsion of Black residents from Marion, Arkansas, and school echoes from the South.

Longer pieces praise missionaries whose self-denying endurance, the editors say, helped atone for the wrongs done to slaves. They report on Dwight Moody's meetings for Indian missions, addressed by the association's financial secretary. The issue gives a frank view of late nineteenth-century missionary thinking, with its mix of charity, paternalism, and genuine devotion.
13907-the-american-missionary-volume-42-:
The American Missionary Association published this July 1888 number from rooms at 56 Reade Street, New York. It cost fifty cents a year and served mission supporters. Editorial notes cover the association president, the Indian problem, Wade Hampton, and Mr. Cable's pamphlet. Southern reports include Notes in the Saddle and a day at Tougaloo.

Sections treat the Chinese mission, woman's temperance work in the South, and children's day at Talladega. Receipts close the number, listing gifts for the cause. The issue shows post-Reconstruction mission work among freed people and immigrants. Its tone is earnest and reforming. Historians of religion and race will find it revealing.
14102-the-american-missionary-volume-42-:
August 1888 brought this number of the American Missionary, the monthly organ of the American Missionary Association in New York. Editorials open on money, language work, and a London missionary conference. Reports follow from Atlanta University, Fisk University, Straight University, and Tillotson, where commencements and closing exercises mark the school year. Student teachers fan out to country schools each summer.

Missions widen the view. Notes from Oahe and Fort Berthold describe Indian churches, sewing women, and social gatherings. Chinese work and a bureau of woman's work add further fields. A children's card scheme invites small collectors to prick squares for five-cent gifts toward a life membership. Read as a whole, the issue records a network of schools and churches built after emancipation, funded coin by coin and sustained by teachers in the field.
14383-the-american-missionary-volume-42-:
The American Missionary Association printed this December 1888 number of its monthly journal. It reports the annual meeting, with the treasurer's summary, committee reports, and a memorial service. A gift for colored people takes pride of place: the Daniel Hand Educational Fund, with a sketch of Hand's life and the deed of trust. Secretaries Strieby and Beard write on African missions and Indian missions. The number speaks to donors and church workers.

Strieby asks whether American freedmen can serve as missionaries in Africa, where Muslim schools already train many. The Old University of Cairo, the number notes, at times holds ten thousand students of the Koran. Their pupils run where Protestants halt and win where Protestants fail, the writer warns. A second piece praises Indian missions in the light of history. The journal mixes reports, appeals, and mission strategy for its readers.
16671-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
This April 28, 1888 number of the Scientific American Supplement, volume twenty-five, number 643, gathers short pieces across many fields. Archaeology leads with the cave temples of India, then lives of General Perrier and the German crown prince follow. Biology gives poisons and rot germs, and chemistry and other fields fill the rest.

Each piece is brief, plain, and rich in pictures, tables, and shop talk, aimed at makers, workers, and keen readers. The issue shows 1888 science as a mix of wonder and use: old temples, new germs, and fresh tools side by side. Readers can dip in by topic or read through for a snapshot of late Victorian technical life.
17167-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
This February 18, 1888 Scientific American Supplement opens with Statham's lectures on architectural design, tracing styles and their makers with thirty-four pictures. Astronomy adds a fivefold comet, split by the sun into five parts. Biography gives Linnaeus, with portrait and birthplace, while chemistry covers fluorine's isolation, gas apparatus, and atoms in space.

Electricity notes on air and a thermo-magnetic generator round out a packed number. The mix shows the magazine's range: art, sky, life, lab, and machine in one weekly bundle. Readers keen on Victorian science will find a clear, pictured snap of what skilled minds studied and built in 1888.
24322-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
This number of the Scientific American Supplement, volume twenty-six, number 664, is dated New York, September 22, 1888. The Supplement cost five dollars a year, or seven with the parent paper, founded in 1845. Its table of contents shows the range of late Victorian popular science, from architecture and the art of war to biology, chemistry, civil engineering, electricity, and ethnology.

Articles include the Commercial Exchange in Paris, the new Central Railway Station at Frankfort-on-the-Main, gun practice in the French navy, modern cavalry by Colonel Liddell, subterraneous flora and fauna by Dr. Zacharias, pepsin by Percy Smith, timber diseases by Marshall Ward, electric motor charges, and a Chinese imperial cemetery of the Ming dynasty. Readers get a packed weekly of science and craft.
27667-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
Dated May 26, 1888, this weekly supplement to Scientific American collects illustrated articles on architecture, chemistry, civil and naval engineering, electricity, and photography. Its contents include a lecture on influence machines by James Wimshurst and a study of the Lachine railway bridge.

Other pieces cover mill design, steam-engine trials, the care of the eyes, and a new observatory on Mount Santis in Switzerland. The issue shows the supplement's wide net, catching new machines, buildings, and scientific methods for readers outside the professions. A photography section describes how sensitive plates are made.
30284-virginia-under-the-stuarts-1607-16:
Thomas J. Wertenbaker traces Virginia under the Stuarts from 1607 to 1688. A Russell and Russell volume from New York in 1959 carries it, under a 1914 copyright by Princeton University Press and 1958 and 1959 copyrights by Wertenbaker. Dedicated to his mother and dated from Princeton, New Jersey, in August 1957, the book opens with the founding of Virginia and the establishment of representative government.

The expulsion of Sir John Harvey follows, with Governor Berkeley and the Commonwealth. The causes of Bacon's Rebellion, Bacon's Rebellion itself, a period of confusion, and a critical period follow, closed by an index. Notes draw on Smith through Arber, Brown, Force, Tyler, Neill, and Hening, among others. Wertenbaker writes colonial Virginia as a Stuart story of charter, assembly, governor, and rebellion.
32105-belford-s-magazine-vol-2-december-:
Volume II of Belford's Magazine covers December 1888 to May 1889. It is a bound half-year of the periodical, published in Chicago, New York, and San Francisco by Belford, Clarke and Company, with a London agent. Its contents page runs for pages, mixing stories, essays, and serial fiction in the general magazine manner of the late 1880s. Readers who open the volume get a cross-section of American magazine writing from a single season.

The fiction includes John W. Bell's America, the King of, Henry C. Wood's America's Romance, T. C. De Leon's Andy's Gift, and a complete novel, A Covenant with Death, by the author of An Unlaid Ghost. Nonfiction ranges from James A. MacKnight on the American consular service to pieces on the decline of the farmer and the cost of things. Christmas writing appears too, with Rose Eytinge's Christmas in Egypt and Celia Logan's Christmas Round-Robin.
32141-garden-and-forest-weekly-volume-1-:
Garden and Forest, a journal of horticulture, landscape art, and forestry, began with this first issue on February 29, 1888. Published weekly in New York by the Garden and Forest Publishing Company, it cost ten cents a copy or four dollars a year in advance. Its masthead and table of contents promise a working journal for gardeners, landscape artists, and foresters, with departments and book reviews.

The issue opens with notices of important new books, including William Dean Howells's April Hopes and his Modern Italian Poets, essays and versions with portraits. Later notices cover the conclusion of Kinglake's Crimean War, T. Adolphus Trollope's autobiography, a book by the author of Self-Help, and Thomas W. Higginson's new book. Other items treat the navies of the United States and Europe, Negro troops in the Rebellion, and five hundred dollars a year for a family.
32848-speeches-and-addresses-of-h-r-h-th:
James Macaulay edits the speeches and addresses of the Prince of Wales from 1863 to 1888, published in London by John Murray in 1889. The volume carries a portrait and is dedicated to the memory of the Prince Consort. Its preface marks 1888 as both the Prince's silver wedding year and the twenty-fifth anniversary of his first public appearances.

Macaulay argues that the speeches themselves best record a quarter century of royal service. Some are widely known, on international exhibitions, the Royal College of Music, and the Imperial Institute. Others survive only here, from occasions of which there is no adequate record. The Prince gave his sanction to the collection, hoping it might prove useful to the objects he had publicly advocated. Later speeches praise railway guards, their widows and orphans fund, and an asylum near Slough for children of once-prosperous parents.
6823-army-letters-from-an-officer-s-wife:
Frances Roe insists her army letters are not imaginary. Every event came into her own life with the army in the far west. Whether of Indians, desperadoes, or hunting, not one little thing has been stolen. All flowery description is left out, she says, for a simple, concise tale suits that life best. The buffalo, antelope, and log and adobe quarters have all passed.

Her first letter, from Kit Carson, Colorado Territory, in October 1871, is only a late note to say they arrived safe and will take the stage onward. Seventeen years of frontier posts follow. Army Letters from an Officer's Wife is a vivid, honest record of a woman's army life in the west.
7163-the-history-of-australian-explorati:
Ernest Favenc compiles the history of Australian exploration from 1788 to 1888 from state documents, private papers, and the most authentic sources of information. Issued under the auspices of the government of the Australian colonies, it was published by Turner and Henderson of Sydney in 1888. It is dedicated to Sir Henry Parkes, oldest ruling statesman in Australia and, in the centenary year, premier of New South Wales, the mother colony.

From that colony first started explorations by land and sea that threw open a new continent to the nations of the world. That continent now rapidly develops under free constitutions into a prosperous, contented, and self governing community. Favenc warns a complete history will never be written, since settlement's story mixes inextricably with private travels and adventures. His volume gathers a century of opening a continent.
appletons-cyclopaedia-american-biography:
Volume Two of Appletons' Cyclopaedia of American Biography came out in 1888, running from Crane to Grimshaw. Editors Wilson and Fiske kept the pace of a life for nearly every notable name. The set was sold by subscription across the country.

This volume's span covers many founders, Civil War officers, and men of letters of the young republic. Each entry gives birth, career, works, and death in tight, factual prose. Steel portraits mark the most famous names. Read across the six volumes, Appletons' forms a portrait gallery of the nation as the Victorian age wished to remember it.

Volume Three of Appletons' Cyclopaedia, also from 1888, continues the alphabet from Grinnell to Lockwood. Wilson and Fiske's dictionary was halfway done, with thousands of American lives already in print. The work's scale was unmatched in its day.

Governors, judges, explorers, and divines fill these pages, each weighed in a column or two. The editors include Canadians and Latin Americans whose lives touched the United States. Family details and lists of writings make the entries useful for tracing kin and careers. The volume carries the national biography through the middle letters with steady, encyclopedic calm. The print is dense, but the facts are laid out in a steady, clear order.

Volume Four of Appletons' Cyclopaedia of American Biography appeared in 1888, covering Lodge to Pickens. The dictionary had become a fixture in American libraries. Wilson and Fiske drew on family papers and earlier collections for their facts.

This stretch of the alphabet holds many Revolutionary officers, senators, and college presidents. Entries balance public deeds with private character sketches drawn from obituaries and memoirs. A few lives were polished by the families themselves, a flaw later readers learned to discount. Even so, the volume preserves facts about hundreds of figures that survive nowhere else in print. Many entries rest on obituaries clipped from the newspapers of the day.

Volume Five of Appletons' Cyclopaedia came out in 1888, running from Pickering to Sumter. The set was nearing its end, and the editors' net had caught most of the nation's notable dead and living. Subscribers received the volumes year by year.

Revolutionary statesmen, Civil War generals, and leading clergy crowd this part of the alphabet. The entries keep the house style: dates, posts, battles, books, and a closing judgment. Charles Sumter's contemporaries and Charles Sumner both appear in these pages. For students of nineteenth-century America, the volume is a dense quarry of names, dates, and careers.
army-letters-from-an-officer-s-wife-1871:
Frances M. A. Roe insists in her preface that nothing in her letters is imaginary or stolen. They are truthful accounts of her own life with the army in the far West. Indians, desperadoes, and hunting all figure in them. She has left out flowery description, she says, for simple narration. The first letter is dated at Kit Carson, Colorado Territory, in October 1871.

From there the letters follow her officer husband's postings across the frontier for seventeen years: stage rides to Fort Lyon, quarters of log and adobe, marches, hunts, and alarms. She writes of a life already passing, as the buffalo and antelope passed. Her book is among the best women's records of the peacetime frontier army.
arxiv-2509-00088:
Ting-Chun Liu, Ching-Yu Hsu, Kuan-Yi Lee, Chi-An Fu, and Hung-yi Lee present AEGIS in 2025, a framework that hardens language models against prompt injection. In such attacks, hidden text in input tricks a model into ignoring its true task. Prompt-based guards are light and clear, but they rely on hand-tuned wording that soon goes stale.

AEGIS pits attack and defense prompts against each other so both evolve on their own. A textual gradient method, which rewrites prompts based on feedback phrased in words, drives each round. An evaluator model scores the clash and feeds the loop. On a real grading data set full of injection tries, the method beats prior baselines. Evolved guards could keep pace as attack styles shift.
arxiv-2509-00188:
Ruojing Jiang and Franco Vargas Pallete prove stability of Ricci flow on hyperbolic three-manifolds of finite volume in 2025. Ricci flow deforms a shape's metric over time to even out curvature, like heat spreading. A hyperbolic manifold has constant negative curvature, and finite volume allows cusp ends that stretch to infinity.

If the starting metric sits close enough to the hyperbolic one, the normalized Ricci-DeTurck flow exists for all time. It converges to the hyperbolic metric exponentially fast in a weighted norm that handles the cusps. Interpolation theory is a key tool in the proof. The result also serves as a tool for minimal surface entropy, a growth rate for closed minimal surfaces by genus.
arxiv-2509-00288:
Viktor G. Czinner and Hideo Iguchi study the Hawking-Rényi thermodynamics of rotating black holes in 2025. Rényi entropy is a generalized measure of disorder. The Hawking-Rényi model demands that the temperature from Rényi entropy match the Hawking temperature set by surface gravity at the horizon, a match that needs proof for spinning holes.

The authors show that a locally Kiselev-type behavior near the horizon, tied to an anisotropic fluid, suffices to solve the match. Rotation also forces a shift in the effective mass, set by the spin and the Rényi parameter. The solution's form is the same with or without electric charge. The letter derives and interprets the solution, leaving full thermodynamic analysis for later work.
arxiv-2509-01588:
Naming the chords in a recording is a core task in music analysis, yet systems have hit a ceiling that better models alone have not broken. Andrea Poltronieri, Xavier Serra, and Martin Rocamora trace part of that ceiling to the labels themselves. Annotators disagree about chords, and chord data sets over-represent some chord classes while starving others.

Their first contribution measures agreement between annotators with richer tools than simple match counts. They also propose a distance metric informed by consonance, how pleasant two chords sound together, so near misses count for less than wild ones. Analysis suggests that metric tracks musical meaning better. On that base the team builds consonance-based training, using the perceptual distance to teach models. The work aims to unstick chord estimation by fixing how harmony is judged, not only how it is predicted.
arxiv-2509-01788:
Leonid V Pourovskii leads five co-authors in a review of hidden order in materials that entangle spin and orbit. Hidden order is a phase change with clear heat signs but no easy signal of what has ordered. Spin-orbit coupling, the link between electron spin and motion, mixes exchange, magnetic, and lattice effects. Standard probes often miss the order that results.

The review surveys theory and computation built to catch these phases. The key actors are high rank multipole moments, patterns of charge and magnetism with complex shapes, on heavy atoms. Authors weigh direct first principle counts against simpler effective models. Case studies cover layered perovskite compounds and actinide oxides, where theory helped read experiments.
arxiv-2509-01888:
Yong Yuan leads four co-authors on spotting bent gravitational waves from merging giant black holes with a space detector. Gravitational waves are ripples in space from massive events, and a mass in the path can bend them like a lens. In wave optics, the bending leaves wavy marks that simple ray views miss. The team uses Bayesian methods, which weigh evidence for lensed versus plain models.

They vary lens mass, path offset, source distance, and source mass for equal mass mergers. Bigger lens mass widens the waveform gap and lifts the signal strength, aiding detection. Wide offsets wash the marks out beyond reach. Distance and lens mass confusion breaks for close offsets, and marks stay visible to the far sources tested. Taiji, the planned detector, anchors the study.
arxiv-2509-02288:
Daniel Hoonhout, Richard Loscher, and Carolina Urzua-Torres take a first step to a T-coercive way for the wave equation in space and time. Weak forms of the wave equation can lack the firm grip that coercivity gives. A change map T can bring that grip back when built with care. Their test case is a plain swing equation tied to the wave case by Fourier growth in space.

For each rate term, a fit change map sets coercivity of the paired form. The build that comes out is firm with no terms and error bounds free of that rate. Just the test space shifts, while trial spaces stay as standard Sobolev spaces. Clear rate links are the new bit, which point to a full space time map. Worked numeric cases back the theory in the text.
arxiv-2509-02488:
Nabil Jabareen and four co-authors wrote a 2025 medical imaging paper. It covers positional encodings. These codes tell a transformer model where each image patch sits. Medical scans are often anisotropic. That means the spacing differs by direction. Standard codes ignore that fact.

Sine-based codes fail to keep distances true in higher dimensions. Isotropic Fourier codes fix distances but assume equal spacing in all directions. The new code adapts to direction, class, and domain. Tests cover chest X-ray labelling, organ sorting in CT scans, and heart pump readings from sound-based video. The choice of code changed results a lot. The new code beat top rivals in each test with uneven spacing. The authors say the code should fit the shape of the scan.
arxiv-2509-02788:
Patrick Bennett, Alan Frieze, and Wesley Pegden wrote a 2025 combinatorics paper on biased Maker-Breaker games played on hypergraphs, where edges can join more than two vertices. Two players claim edges in turns; Breaker claims several per round, while Maker races to build a structure with a target property.

The board starts as the complete uniform hypergraph on many vertices. Maker's goals vary across the results: reaching a minimum degree everywhere, building an incidence matrix of full rank, or completing structures such as a perfect matching or Hamilton-type cycles. Biased games model an adversary with more resources, so thresholds found here mark where Maker's aim stays achievable. The paper treats several classic targets inside one hypergraph game framework.
arxiv-2509-02988:
Yan Xu and 4 co-authors studied in 2025 how hyperons affect a fast cooling process inside neutron stars. Hyperons are heavier cousins of protons and neutrons that may appear in a star's dense core. The process under study lets neutrinos, nearly massless particles, carry energy straight out of the star.

The team ran models with two parameter sets and two symmetry schemes for how particle types relate. They compared outcomes with mass and size estimates for three pulsars, which are spinning neutron stars. One pulsar showed no such cooling because momentum rules block it. In the other two, cooling strength shifted with the hyperon share, inferred mass, and chosen model. Those links could someday help astronomers test whether hyperons really exist in cores.
arxiv-2509-03188:
Hania Ghouse and Muzammil Behzad proposed a 2025 framework for outlining the adrenal glands in CT scans. These small glands sit above the kidneys with irregular shapes, so automated segmentation is hard. Scarcity of labeled scans and a huge imbalance between gland and background pixels add to the difficulty.

Their design joins three parts: a variational autoencoder that rebuilds image patches, a U-Net style segmenter, and an adversarial critic that judges realism patch by patch. Training mixes in synthetic patches drawn from the model's own learned space, at ratios the authors vary systematically. A perceptual loss based on features from a standard vision network sharpens output quality. On a public abdominal dataset, accuracy improved most near organ boundaries.
arxiv-2509-03588:
Entanglement in the Haldane phase of a quantum spin ladder is what Yu-Chin Tzeng and one co-author examine in a 2025 research paper. Entanglement, the deep linking of quantum states, can reveal phases of matter that ordinary measurements miss. Their system is a two-leg ladder of spin-half particles with XXZ interactions.

Using exact diagonalisation of ladders up to forty spins, they resolve the entanglement spectrum, a fingerprint of how a system splits into two halves. Where earlier work saw one branch for fifteen years, they find two modes crossing to form a sharp cusp. Adding anisotropy, which favours one spin direction, triggers an entanglement transition well before the bulk material changes phase. Between those points the expected edge signature vanishes, breaking a widely used correspondence. The work establishes entanglement-only criticality as a distinct kind of transition.
arxiv-2509-03688:
Reverse mathematics, the study of exactly which axioms a theorem needs, is the setting for a 2025 mathematics paper by Quentin Le Houérou and one co-author. Their target is a weakened two-colour form of Ramsey's theorem about pairs. In that theorem, one colour's homogeneous sets, sets where every pair shares that colour, are required to have bounded size.

Every such colouring still admits an endless homogeneous set for the other colour, a statement called bounded Ramsey's theorem for pairs. The statement is computably true: every computable colouring has a computable solution. Known proofs, though, lean on a strong induction principle. The authors prove the statement using the Erdős-Moser theorem, a related combinatorial principle, while showing it is not a consequence of the Ascending Descending sequence principle. Its computable version turns out to be exactly equivalent to that induction principle over a weak base theory.
arxiv-2509-03988:
Alberto Carta and seven co-authors study the correlated material Nb3Cl8 in a 2025 research paper, combining computation and experiment. Its niobium atoms group into trimers, triangles of three, arranged in clusters. On cooling it undergoes a magnetostructural transition, and several rival explanations compete for what drives it.

Earlier proposals include charge disproportionation, where identical sites split into different charge states, magnetic quenching, and singlet formation between layers. The authors test each against the reported low-temperature structures. That charge-splitting picture is ruled out by their findings. Instead, an intricate interplay emerges: Mott physics meets the formation of singlets pairing spins across layers. Their results also hint why the observed scissoring distortion sits inside each trimer. The suggested framing treats the material as weakly coupled Hubbard dimers, pairs whose electrons repel strongly on site. That lens reframes the transition.
arxiv-2509-04088:
Farah Baracat and four co-authors decode finger movements from muscle signals using spiking neural networks in a 2025 research paper. Spiking networks are software modeled on real nerve cells, which fire in brief pulses. Restoring natural hand control for assistive devices needs fast, accurate reading of what each finger intends. The team recorded motor units, small groups of muscle fibers driven by one nerve cell, through dense needle-like sensor arrays inside the muscle.

Volunteers held steady finger pushes at a modest effort level. Shallow spiking networks read the pulse trains and recovered each finger's force reliably. Using true motor-unit pulses beat converted muscle signals on some measures and saved memory. The results offer a practical design path for responsive prosthetic hands.
arxiv-2509-04288:
Rudi Coppola and three co-authors design battery charging rules that balance speed against ageing, with formal safety checks, in a 2025 research paper. Lithium-ion cells lose capacity as they age, and fast charging can hasten that loss. Battery management systems must walk that trade-off carefully. The team starts from a detailed physics-based cell model, then lets reinforcement learning agents draft controllers for different starting conditions.

A data-driven abstraction divides starting measurements into zones, each served by its own learned controller, forming a switched hybrid system. Counterexamples guide repeated redesign until criteria are met. When a design passes, the abstraction supplies probability-based guarantees for the closed loop. Safer fast-charging protocols could follow from this recipe.
arxiv-2509-04588:
Siyu Zhang and one co-author, Kenneth Mcmillan, argue that explanations of neural networks must preserve the network's actual computation, not just its output, in a 2025 research paper. Faithfulness scores usually insert or delete features and watch the answer change. The authors show rival pathways can game those scores: perturbations reroute computation through different feature detectors while the output looks unchanged. Activation preservation, keeping internal activity close to the original, serves as a workable stand-in for pathway preservation.

Their method, FEI, optimizes both external scores and internal closeness together, using ensemble quantile tuning and selective gradient clipping. On image benchmarks with VGG and ResNet models, it topped insertion and deletion scores while deviating far less inside.
arxiv-2509-04788:
Calibrating a continuum model of crystal deformation from smaller-scale simulations usually needs long expert effort. The team automate much of that work. Nicholas Huebner Julian, lead author with four co-authors, present the method in a 2025 materials paper. They cast a crystal plasticity flow rule as a Gaussian process model, which carries its own uncertainty estimates.

Bayesian optimisation uses that uncertainty to choose new discrete dislocation dynamics runs on its own. The semi-autonomous loop builds a dataset and a fitted flow rule efficiently. A check against a separate dataset four times larger tests error, uncertainty, and physical sensitivities. The authors present the pipeline as a reusable active learning method.
arxiv-2509-05188:
Sign language videos contain stretches that carry little meaning for recognising the sign. Ariel Basso Madjoukeng, lead author with four co-authors, design a self-supervised learning framework for that problem in a 2025 paper. Only some frames of a sign video carry the sign itself. Contrastive learning usually treats all video parts equally. It struggles because different signs share movements, making negative pairs confusingly similar.

Their framework adds a free-negative pair approach and a new data augmentation technique. Both parts target the two problems above. The two parts work together to learn more discriminative representations without annotated data. Experiments show a considerable accuracy gain over earlier self-supervised approaches in their tests. The field is limited by scarce labelled sign data, which the method is built to work around.
arxiv-2509-05488:
A modern sequence model family is squeezed onto tiny microcontrollers by Hongjun Xu and four co-authors in a 2025 embedded systems paper. Mamba models process long sequences efficiently, but chips in small devices have little memory, few built-in operations, and no friendly deployment tools.

Their engine, MambaLite-Micro, is to their knowledge the first Mamba deployment on such a chip, written fully in C with no runtime. Weights are exported in a light format and the core layer is hand-built with fused operations and careful memory layout, cutting peak memory sharply while matching the reference implementation closely. Keyword spotting and activity recognition tasks kept full accuracy, on two different microcontroller families.
arxiv-2509-05688:
Running image networks on small edge devices in real time is the target of a chip design from Kuan-Ting Lin and four co-authors in a 2025 computer engineering paper. Deep convolutional networks are too heavy in computation and data movement for such hardware, making state-of-the-art models too slow in practice.

Their accelerator builds its computing units from the smallest convolution kernel size and tailors units to each model's needs. Feature data are kept on chip in a reuse buffer, and output reuse plus a ring-shaped data flow cut transfers to external memory drastically. Pooling is done on the fly inside the chip. The design reports very high utilisation, large data access savings, and real-time runs of standard classifiers.
arxiv-2509-05788:
How electricity moves across the surface of the crystal FeSb2 at very low temperature is the question behind a 2025 study led by Jarryd A. Horn with six co-authors. FeSb2 belongs to a family of Kondo insulators, materials that resist flow inside yet can conduct on their faces. The team probes whether magnetism shapes that surface conduction.

Using disk-shaped contacts that isolate a single face, the authors measure each natural crystal face on its own. The response depends on crystal direction, with an easy axis along one edge, pointing to scattering from local magnetic moments rather than a simple two-dimensional flow. Below the crossover to surface control, charge moves by hopping through a thin three-dimensional channel, which sits uneasily with a strong topological insulator picture.
arxiv-2509-06088:
Heat racing through a plasma too fast for local rules is modeled by a time-aware neural network in a 2025 paper led by Mufei Luo with seven co-authors. Under strongly nonlocal conditions, heat flux depends on the plasma's wider state and history, and the team's earlier model gave physically inconsistent kernels when conditions changed quickly. Their new time-embedded convolutional network predicts heat flux and a nonlocality measure together.

Trained on fully kinetic particle-in-cell simulations, the network tracks nonlocal dynamics across a broad range of collisionality. Time modulation, coupled prediction, and convolutional depth each add accuracy, by the authors' tests. The result is a data-driven yet physically consistent tool for multiscale plasma transport, a step toward fast surrogates for fusion and space plasma studies.
arxiv-2509-06588:
Power generators that cannot change output too fast are handled in a distributed control scheme by Mohammadreza Doostmohammadian and one co-author in a 2025 power systems paper. Automatic generation control balances supply and demand across a network of generators that share information. Most optimization methods ignore ramp-rate limits, so their instructions may be impossible to follow in practice.

The proposed method respects ramp limits, output bounds, and the supply-demand balance at every step of the algorithm, not just at the end. That anytime feasibility means stopping early still leaves a valid operating point. A signum-based nonlinearity speeds convergence, and the design tolerates lost communication links as long as the network stays connected over time. The result is a control scheme whose promised optimum generators can actually reach.
arxiv-2509-06688:
A design language for evacuation scenes, with a drawing editor, is built by Heerok Banerjee in a solo 2025 software engineering paper. Such special languages help firms model their own work, but building editors with canvases, palettes, and layered forms takes heavy effort. Novice users often face a steep gap.

The language, called Bmod, is built with the Eclipse Modeling Framework and its drawing companion. Users can draw evacuation scenarios rather than write code. Banerjee also weighs the Eclipse tools against other model platforms, including AToMPM, metaDepth, and Sirius, judging how much they can express, how fast they are learned, and how well they run. The weighing is meant to guide builders of like tools. The paper's contribution is practical: a working evacuation model tool plus proof of what it costs to build one this way.
arxiv-2509-06888:
A multilingual encoder model covering more than eighteen hundred languages is introduced by Marc Marone and five co-authors in a 2025 language technology paper. Encoder-only models power classification and retrieval, but recent research has neglected them, especially multilingual ones. The new model, mmBERT, was pretrained on three trillion tokens of multilingual text.

Several training choices are new. The masking ratio and the sampling temperature both follow inverse schedules, changing direction compared with common practice. Over seventeen hundred low-resource languages enter the data mix only during the final decay phase, yet that short exposure lifts their performance dramatically. On classification tests for low-resource languages, mmBERT rivals far larger proprietary systems named in the paper. Across classification and retrieval tasks, in both rich and poor resource settings, it significantly outperforms the previous generation of encoder models.
arxiv-2509-07488:
Xiao Li and 8 co-authors fine-tune a vision-language model in 2025 to guide visually impaired people indoors. Indoor navigation lacks the precise location data that outdoor systems rely on, so satellite guidance fails inside buildings. Their approach joins image understanding with natural language to produce step-by-step spoken-style directions toward a target room or point.

The team fine-tunes the BLIP-2 model with LoRA, a low-rank adaptation method that adjusts a small set of added weights, on a hand-annotated indoor navigation dataset. They also propose an evaluation metric that refines the BERT F1 score by weighting directional and sequential details, which matter most in directions. After adaptation, the model gives much better directional instructions than the base model. The work targets greater accessibility and independence for blind and low-vision users.
arxiv-2509-07588:
Andrey Sakhovskiy's 2025 paper, joined by 1 co-author, aligns language models with a biomedical knowledge graph. Biomedical language models read medical text well but grasp complex concept structures and graph-encoded facts poorly. Knowledge graphs store facts as linked concepts, and the Unified Medical Language System is the field's central example. The proposed method, BALI, trains the two kinds of model together.

During pre-training, concept mentions in text are linked to the medical knowledge graph, and the local subgraph around each concept serves as a matching partner for the mention. A dedicated graph encoder learns alongside the language model, and their representations are aligned. Applied to leading models such as PubMedBERT and BioLinkBERT, BALI improved language understanding scores and entity representation quality. Notably, gains came from minimal pre-training on a small alignment dataset drawn from PubMed abstracts.
arxiv-2509-07788:
Christopher Hughes and 1 co-author conjecture formulas in 2025 for the complex moments of the derivative of the Riemann zeta function at its zeros. The zeta function sits at the heart of number theory, and its nontrivial zeros encode the distribution of prime numbers. Moments, averages of powers, of its derivative sampled at those zeros are expected to follow patterns first seen in random matrix theory.

Two computations support the conjecture. The first finds an exact formula for the matching moments of characteristic polynomials of unitary matrices, averaged over the Haar measure, using Selberg's integral. The second follows the hybrid approach for zeta proposed by Gonek, Hughes, and Keating. Agreement between independent routes is the standard evidence offered for such conjectures, which guide later attempts at proof. The results are presented as conjectures, not theorems.
arxiv-2509-08088:
Open-source code sits in repositories waiting for someone to wire it up by hand, which wastes its value. Linyao Chen and 6 co-authors present EnvX in a 2025 research paper. EnvX turns GitHub repositories into autonomous agents that users can talk to in plain language. The agents can also collaborate with each other.

The framework works in three phases. It first initializes each repository's environment, guided by task lists. It then lets the agent perform real tasks in a human-aligned way. Finally, an agent-to-agent protocol supports joint work across repositories. On a benchmark of eighteen repositories, EnvX completed and passed tasks at rates above rival frameworks. Case studies show several repository agents solving problems together. The authors see software reuse shifting from passive code to active, conversable agents.
arxiv-2509-08188:
Brainwave recordings are polluted by muscle movement, blinks, and chewing, and tagging those artifacts by hand is costly. Hritik Arasu and Faisal R Jahangiri ask whether generative models can fake them well, in a 2025 research paper. They compare two model families on a public corpus of EEG artifacts. One is an adversarial network variant; the other is a diffusion model.

Both models were trained to produce label-aware artifact segments for data augmentation and stress testing. The team judged fidelity with spectral and statistical checks. They also tested whether simple classifiers could recover the intended class, and whether added fake data improved recognition. The adversarial model matched real spectral patterns more closely. Both models recovered classes weakly, limiting gains from added data. The authors release their full pipeline as a baseline, with failure modes written down for the next attempt.
arxiv-2509-08288:
Sijie Chen and 3 co-authors protect a precise clock method with symmetry in a 2025 quantum physics paper. The method is Ramsey spectroscopy. It reads a frequency by letting atoms evolve and watching how they answer. Particle interactions, noise, and decay all shift the read frequency. Those shifts cap how sharp the method can be.

The fix matches the symmetry of the input states to the symmetry of the system. The measured spectrum is then forced into a mirror shape. Its centre point marks the true frequency, free of the usual shifts. Clocks and sensors set the pace for navigation, timing networks, and basic physics tests. A guard built on symmetry beats one built on endless calibration.
arxiv-2509-08588:
Yao Wan asks when a shape problem has just one answer in a 2025 paper. The problem is the Lp Minkowski problem, which seeks a convex body from data about its surface. Wan looks at cases where the body has a high degree of turn based symmetry.

The proof uses a tool called the Hilbert-Brunn-Minkowski operator. Its key values show how a shape reacts to small shifts. From them, Wan gets bounds that make some known shape laws more stable. Under stated limits on those values, the symmetric answer is the only one. A wider range also works if the body is centered at the origin.
arxiv-2509-08688:
Truong Thi Hien and 3 co-authors study depth and regularity for powers of edge ideals of weighted trees in a 2025 paper. In algebra, depth and regularity measure how complex an ideal and its powers are. A weighted tree assigns numbers to edges of a tree graph.

For increasing weighted trees, the authors find an asymptotic value and a sharp bound for when depth stabilizes. For strictly increasing trees, they give the minimal free resolution of the edge ideal. That resolution yields an exact formula for regularity of all powers. The results are theoretical. They show how weight order on a tree controls algebraic behavior over many powers.
arxiv-2509-08988:
Brendan Young and 6 co-authors combine active learning and explainable AI to optimize spin coated polymers in a 2025 paper. Spin coating makes thin polymer films, and users want several properties at once, such as hardness and elasticity. That is a multi-objective problem.

A Pareto front learning algorithm uses Gaussian process models to predict properties from spin speed, dilution, and mixture. It picks new samples in promising regions adaptively. UMAP maps the front to two dimensions for viewing. Fuzzy linguistic summaries turn learned links into plain statements experts can read. Results efficiently find promising designs while supporting expert analysis and knowledge discovery.
arxiv-2509-09388:
Dependency graphs can be turned into plain sequences, and Ana Ezquerro and 2 co-authors test whether a hierarchical bracketing code does that job well in 2025. Graph parsing handles sentence structures where words may link back, form cycles, or leave empty nodes. Older linear forms, the team notes, often need a very large label set.

Their encoding keeps those hard cases while cutting the label space sharply, and parsing then needs only a linear number of tagging steps. On a benchmark spanning several languages and formalisms, results were competitive throughout. Exact match scores improved consistently over rival linear methods, making the approach attractive for practical multilingual parsing.
arxiv-2509-09588:
F. Boivin and 5 co-authors measure how heat moves through the bulk of two fractional quantum Hall states in a 2025 experiment. They work in a Corbino layout, warming a two-dimensional electron gas in place with Joule heating and watching the response over time. Electron temperatures ran from twenty to one hundred fifty thousandths of a kelvin, covering the five-halves and seven-thirds states.

Their conductance values largely agree with a recent study that used a very different setup and a much different sample size. Both point the same way: the bulk carries heat and breaks the Wiedemann-Franz law, and not by a little. Small gaps between the studies are discussed through particle-hole symmetry near the two states.
arxiv-2509-09688:
A quarter-century of heavy-ion collisions ends with an exabyte of data and the risk that the knowledge inside it retires with its scientists. Mohammad Atif and 5 co-authors describe an AI preservation assistant in a 2025 research paper. The Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider at Brookhaven is concluding operations after twenty-five years. Its preservation plan pairs the archive with an AI-powered guide.

The assistant answers natural language questions over documentation, workflows, and software from the collider's experiments. It is built on large language models with retrieval-augmented generation and a standard context protocol. The authors report deployment experience, computing performance, and the ongoing integration of several experiments. The design targets sustainable, explainable access over decades. The lesson reaches beyond one laboratory: legacy science stays alive when future researchers can interrogate it conversationally, not just download it.
arxiv-2509-10188:
Étienne Grandjean and Louis Jachiet define a new complexity class in this 2025 theory paper. The class collects operations on numbers. A RAM machine may first spend linear time preparing tables. After that, it must answer each query in constant time. They call the class cstPP, for constant time with minimal preprocessing.

The class turns out to be sturdy and broad. It does not change if the machine's basic tools are just addition. A richer arithmetic set gives the same class. The class is closed under composition. For fast-growing functions, it is closed under taking inverses as well. Stranger still, the constant-time step can shrink to a single return instruction. Widening or narrowing the prep time within wide limits changes nothing. Push the prep time too low, though, and the class collapses.
arxiv-2509-10588:
Hendrik Wladimir Albrecht Edwin Kuipers presents a claimed new equivalent of the Riemann Hypothesis. He does so in this solo-authored 2025 paper. The hypothesis concerns the zeros of the zeta function. It is among the most famous open problems in mathematics. Any claimed equivalence must be read as the author's own result. It awaits wider scrutiny.

Kuipers defines a walk on the integers. Composite numbers jump forward by a prime-counting step. Primes step back to the previous prime. He argues that the trajectories' contraction behavior mirrors the distribution of primes. He proves unconditional bounds for related error terms. He claims the hypothesis equals one sharp contraction condition, placed on the trajectory error. The converse direction leans on classical oscillation results. Landau and Littlewood proved those. If the argument holds, the conjecture becomes a stability property. A simple deterministic system would carry it.
arxiv-2509-10688: Xiao Shan Chen and Hongguo Xu present combined perturbation bounds in this 2025 paper. The bounds cover Hermitian matrices and their eigenstructure. They also cover the singular structure of general matrices. Such bounds answer a practical question. When a matrix is slightly disturbed, how far can its eigenvalues and eigenspaces move? How far can its singular values and subspaces move? The authors derive the bounds from smooth decompositions. They use basic calculus tools, not heavy machinery.
arxiv-2509-10788:
Zachary Van Oosten and Ruodu Wang give axioms for a decision model in this 2025 paper. The model covers choices under ambiguity. It is the Choquet rank-dependent utility model, set in the Savage framework. It assumes one clean source of pure risk that the decision maker fully understands. Views on risk and on ambiguity are unified in it. With only pure risks in play, it falls back to plain rank-dependent utility.

Two main axioms on biseparable preferences do the foundational work, with weak regularity conditions beside them. Those mild assumptions already guarantee that matching probabilities exist. The authors then describe ambiguity attitudes through properties of those probabilities. Supermodularity gives a robust representation, they show. Under one extra property, a second representation appears, using act-dependent distortion functions. Two lenses thus view the same preferences.
arxiv-2509-11088:
Alexandros Grosdos, Elina Robeva, and Maksym Zubkov wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on rational neural networks, networks whose activations are fractions of polynomials rather than the usual smooth curves. They ask exactly which functions a given network design can express.

The set of all functions a design can produce forms a geometric object the authors call the neuromanifold. For networks with one hidden layer they compute its dimension and find equations defining it in some cases, along with algorithms that test whether a given function belongs to it. For deep networks built from binary layers, they classify when the neuromanifold fills its whole ambient space and bound its dimension otherwise. The work gives network design a firmer algebraic footing.
arxiv-2509-11288:
Anindita Nandi, Biswajit Pandey, and Prakash Sarkar study the cosmic web in this 2025 astronomy paper. A galaxy's address may shape its traits. Galaxies live in dense knots, in filaments, in sheets, or in voids. Their traits may link up in unlike ways in each place.

The team used galaxies from the IllustrisTNG simulation. They matched the sample by star mass across all four settings. They then gauged how strongly the traits move together. The traits were color, mass, star birth rate, and metal share. A shared-information score gauged each link. Tests showed the gaps between settings were real, not chance. In each case the web's shape changed how galaxy traits hang together.
arxiv-2509-11388:
Romerik Lokossou and three co-authors bring quantum computing into robot training in this 2025 robotics paper. Classical reinforcement learning for humanoid walking takes many parameters and steps. The authors try a hybrid quantum-classical Soft Actor-Critic instead.

Parameterized quantum circuits handle the policy. The observation and action spaces are large. Tests ran in the MuJoCo Humanoid and Walker2d simulators. These environments dwarf those of earlier quantum reinforcement learning work. That work covered wheeled robots and arms. The quantum version reached a slightly higher average return. It used dramatically fewer training steps. The authors present this as early evidence. Quantum assistance may speed learning for complex embodied agents.
arxiv-2509-11588:
Mirco Felske and Stefan Stiene argue the recipe matters as much as the model. This 2025 machine learning paper treats multi-class image classification. Class counts in training data are usually set evenly, or by what is on hand. In safety-critical work, some classes matter far more. A person matters more than a dog.

Their framework is BiCDO. It searches for class mixes on the Pareto frontier. Overall reliability is balanced against priority for chosen classes. Bias and variance in the goal are cut too. The tool drops into live training pipelines. Code changes stay minimal. Any labeled multi-class dataset works. Tests used three network families on CIFAR-10 and iNaturalist21. The tuned mixes gave more balanced, dependable models.
arxiv-2509-11888:
Two schools of noncommutative geometry define torsion and metric compatibility for connections in different ways, and Jyotishman Bhowmick with two co-authors set out in 2025 to reconcile them. The frameworks under comparison come from Beggs and Majid on one side and Mesland and Rennie on the other.

For connections that respect the star structure, the authors show, compatibility with a real metric in the first framework amounts to being Hermitian in the second. When the calculus is quasi-tame, the two torsion-free conditions also match. Combining these bridges settles a concrete prize. Levi-Civita connections in the Mesland-Rennie sense exist and are unique for a large class of deformed Riemannian manifolds. The same holds for the calculi on all quantized irreducible flag manifolds.
arxiv-2509-12188:
Event sequences become geometry in a solo 2025 paper by Antonin Sulc. Sentences, system logs, and other chains of events all fit the frame. His method, Event2Vec, learns a vector for each event. The vector for a whole sequence is just the sum of its event vectors. He calls that rule the linear additive hypothesis.

A simple additive recurrent model does the learning. Theory shows the result clearly. Under the right training goals, the learned Euclidean vectors converge to that ideal sum. Trees and hierarchies strain flat geometry, though. So a hyperbolic variant embeds them with low distortion. On the Brown Corpus, sequence clusters scored higher than a Word2Vec baseline on a silhouette measure. That is evidence the model picks up structure with no supervision. The additive design keeps the vectors composable and easy to read.
arxiv-2509-12788:
Y. Q. Guo and 4 co-authors model how rod-shaped particles steer the self-assembly of mixed polymers in a 2025 paper. Their system combines diblock copolymers, chains made of two joined blocks, homopolymers, and Janus nanorods, rods whose two sides behave differently. Such mixtures can form layered patterns useful for new materials.

Using cell dynamics model run, the team varied the component ratios and the number of nanorods. At one homopolymer share, the system moved from disorder to parallel layers, then tilted layers, and finally perpendicular layers as rods increased. They also analyzed domain sizes and tested how repulsion strength, wetting strength, rod length, and asymmetry changed the behavior. The work offers guidance for preparing structured polymer materials.
arxiv-2509-12988:
Franklin Cho, Y. Cho and two co-authors widen the Ginzburg and Landau theory in 2025 for triplet pairing and spin waves. Triplet pairs carry spin, unlike plain pairs. Magnon spin tools need the same spin gauge at their core.

The broad theory holds a heavy photon, a light neutral wave, a heavy spin wave, and a Higgs field for pair density. Long-range links flow via the light wave. Two saved flows run: charge and spin. Two vortex types and two monopole types appear. Three length scales set the whole. Uses span paired matter and spin tech.
arxiv-2509-13088:
Rose Berry builds in 2025 a plain maker for the derived class of unipotent forms of a p-adic general linear group. The field has residue size a prime power, and forms are taken over a closed field of a second prime. Prior makers in the plain setting were far more complex.

The new maker is far simpler to state. It yields a match between the derived class and perfect complexes over a derived endomorphism algebra. That algebra acts as a derived Schur algebra. A finite-field twin result is proved on the way. The case of size two was known before in a narrow form.
arxiv-2509-13588:
Xuan Liu, Haoyang Shang, and Haojian Jin introduce CoBRA in 2025, a toolkit for giving simulated social agents controlled cognitive biases. Social simulations built on language models usually describe agent behavior in loose prose, which different models interpret inconsistently and without fine detail.

CoBRA replaces prose with measurement and control. A Cognitive Bias Index scores how much bias an agent shows by running it through classic, validated social science experiments. A Behavioral Regulation Engine then adjusts the agent until the measured bias hits the target level. The approach is model-agnostic and treats famous experiments as reusable gyms for training agent behavior, a pattern the authors suggest could extend to richer social and emotional simulation.
arxiv-2509-13788:
Giovanni Giuseppe Grimaldi surveys homomorphic encryption in a solo 2025 cryptography paper. Such encryption lets a cloud server compute on data it cannot read. Adding or multiplying ciphertexts yields the encryption of the same operation on the hidden plaintexts. Private data stays protected even if the server is breached.

Schemes come in three grades: partially, somewhat, and fully homomorphic. The grade depends on which operations they support, and how many. Grimaldi reviews the state of the art for two families. One is built on coding theory, the other on polynomials. Both differ sharply from the lattice methods that dominate headlines. The survey organizes what is known about their constructions and capabilities. It is written for readers entering this branch of the field.
arxiv-2509-13888:
Mariano Barone and four co-authors extend their biomedical fact-checking work in a 2025 paper. The focus here is claim detection across multiple modes of content. Health misinformation spreads as text, images, and mixed posts. Spotting the checkable claims inside that flow is the first step. No verdict can be trusted until that step is done.

The verification side uses their CER framework. It retrieves high-quality scientific evidence and reasons over it with a large language model. A supervised classifier then predicts veracity. Generated text stays anchored to verifiable sources. Evaluated on the expert-annotated HealthFC, BioASQ-7b, and SciFact collections, the approach reached the best reported results. It also carried across datasets well. Code and data are public for scrutiny and reuse.
arxiv-2509-14588:
Keerti Choudhary, Amit Kumar and Lakshay Saggi give a faster algorithm in 2025 for the two disjoint shortest paths problem. Given two start and target pairs in a directed weighted graph, decide whether each pair can be joined by a shortest path, with the two paths sharing no vertex.

Their algorithm runs far faster than the previously known bound for graphs without negative or zero weight cycles. The method exploits polynomials that enumerate shortest paths between terminal pairs, turning counting structure into a decision tool. Extensions of the basic problem are also treated. Disjoint shortest routing matters for resilient networks, where backup routes must be both optimal and truly separate.
arxiv-2509-15288:
Yu-qing Zhao and ten co-authors search for Majorana marks in a squeezed superconductor and do not find them, in a 2025 paper. The stuff, PbTaSe2, has no center of symmetry and hosts odd electronic states. That makes it a prime pick for topological superconductivity. A zero-bias peak in Andreev spectra would be the telltale mark of Majorana states.

Under high pressure the team pairs Andreev spectra with resistance gauges. A surface-like superconducting state splits from the bulk one at a key pressure. Its pairing looks standard and strongly linked. Across magnetic fields, the hoped-for zero-bias peak stays absent in the squeezed runs. The null result disciplines the hunt: this pick, in these states, shows no Majorana proof.
arxiv-2509-15488:
Preethi Basani, Varsha Subramanyan, and Smitha Vishveshwara study pairs of exotic particles called anyons. Anyons arise in flat quantum Hall systems, where electrons move in a strong magnetic field. The pair use smooth states that describe two such particles in the lowest energy band. They ask how these pairs bunch and move when a curved trap holds them.

Drawing on quantum optics and symmetry, they work out a bunching score tied to the particles' quantum statistics. In open saddle shaped traps, pair paths split apart fast, at a rate the score controls. In closed oval traps, the score swings up and down, with a peak set by the trap's shape. The results link to lab efforts to spot anyons.
arxiv-2509-15688:
Johann Schmidt leads a team that sorts photos into fine classes, like bird species that look near alike. The clues are small and local, while members of one class can vary a lot. Part based tools often need complex nets to find the parts, and their sampled points can cluster in one spot. The team borrow from how human eyes jump between fixations.

Their method first takes a coarse view of the whole image and builds a sample map. Patches at chosen fixations are then read in parallel by a shared encoder. A selective attention step weighs each patch before the coarse and fine views merge. A thinning rule stops patches from piling up. Tests span birds, food, and dogs.
arxiv-2509-15788:
Haotian Zhang leads a team that spots land changes in satellite photos with meaning attached. Change spotting should say not just where land changed, but what it changed from and to. Past data sets held few change types and coarse classes. Past methods also used change facts weakly, as a late cleanup step.

They build a new data set over Beijing with many change classes and fine subtypes, down to paved versus unpaved roads. Their method, FoBa, lets foreground regions of interest and background context guide each other. That joint guidance cuts mix ups and sharpens subtle changes. The task needs the two photo times to interact well and the map to stay consistent.
arxiv-2509-15888:
Senkang Hu leads a large team that adapts a big language model at decoding time instead of by retraining. Even light fine tuning of huge models costs much. Their view recasts adaptation as aligning outputs: steer what the model says toward what the task needs, directly as it writes. A short warm up fine tune comes first.

From that warm up they extract a steering vector, a direction in output space tied to the task. Decoding then leans along that vector. They prove the method matches a full fine tuning step to first order, and solve for the best steering strength. Across three tasks and nine test sets, accuracy and truthfulness both rise. The method pairs with standard light tuning tools.
arxiv-2509-16188:
As chat models spread across the world, judging how well they grasp each culture has become a test of trust. Jinghao Zhang and nine co-authors build CultureScope, a test frame based on a theory that compares culture to an iceberg, with deep layers below the surface. Their scheme sorts cultural knowledge into three layers and one hundred forty dimensions, which lets them build test sets for any language or culture by machine.

Tests show the frame can grade cultural grasp in a useful way. Current large models show clear gaps, and adding more languages alone did not close them. All code and data are shared in public.
arxiv-2509-16388:
Exceptional collections are ordered sets of objects that organize a derived category, a deep tool in modern algebra and geometry. Kiyoshi Igusa and Ray Maresca study a diagram that records maps and extensions between such objects, and they recast it as a kind of superquiver. In one key type, the diagram matches the tiling algebra of a geometric model of the collection.

There, twists of the surface sort the collections, and those twists come from functors that act as symmetries of the category. The authors give generators for those symmetries and pose open questions. Superquivers extend the picture to all finite acyclic cases.
arxiv-2509-17788:
Xingyu Fan and 3 co-authors built WeStar, a chat aide for huge sets of official accounts. Their 2025 paper faces a hard mix: replies must fit the facts at hand and match each account's style. Slow step-by-step prompts lag, and one tuned model per account costs too much.

WeStar pairs search-based facts with small style units that switch on by style group. A new training step tunes each style group for better replies. Tests on a large work data set show the plan is fast and works well at scale. One shared aide can thus serve many accounts.
arxiv-2509-18488:
Classic price models treat investors as if they react at once, with no hesitation. Diego da Silva Santos and Luiz Gustavo Bastos Pinho build inertia into price dynamics in this 2025 paper. Their frame has two stages. First, they ground a known drift-and-spread model in a simple walk where the log price can step up, step down, or stay put.

That first model gives drift and volatility a clear behavioral origin. But its bell-shaped returns miss the heavy tails seen in real markets, where extreme moves happen too often. So the team adds a fourth-order extension drawn from retention models, where inertia takes a richer form. On Brazilian stock data for Petrobras shares, the extended model fit the real return spread far better. The authors read inertia as a dual force. It can explain both calm trends and sudden extremes.
arxiv-2509-19088:
Tianyi Peng and twenty-two co-authors put digital twins, language-model stand-ins trained to answer as a specific person would, to a hard test. Across 19 pre-registered studies and 164 outcomes, they compared each twin's answers with its real person's. The twins were trained on each person's answers to more than 500 questions. Even so, their predictions beat a generic model only modestly, and the link to real answers was weak.

The authors name five systematic distortions. Twins blur personal differences, lean on stereotypes, under-represent some groups, tilt ideologically, and act hyper-rational compared with real people. Like a funhouse mirror, the twin reflects a person with warped proportions. The team releases its data and code as a standard testbed for the field. Their findings warn against deploying twins too soon in social science and policy work.
arxiv-2509-19488:
Simulating fluids that resist flow in odd ways, such as thick pastes, needs numerical pieces that stay stable. Charles Parker and Endre Süli study Scott-Vogelius elements, a high-order tool for two-dimensional flow that cannot be compressed. They focus on elements of degree four and above. The core task is to undo the divergence operation in a way that stays controlled as the degree grows.

The authors build that inverse and bound its strength, with only a mild loss as degree rises. They also build local correction tools with explicit bounds. Numerical examples suggest that raising the degree can beat refining the mesh, even for these tricky fluids. Stable high-order tools matter for engineers who model polymers, slurries, and biological fluids. The proofs give users a firmer base for trusting such simulations.
arxiv-2509-19688:
Learned motion planners can invent smooth routes, but proving those routes safe is hard when the planner holds millions of weights. Devesh Nath, Haoran Yin, and Glen Chou verify safety by imitation at small scale. A compact tracking controller follows routes sampled from the big planner. Standard neural verification tools can then handle the small closed loop.

The reachable sets from that check certify safety with rigor. Verified routes form a library used at run time, mimicking the big planner whenever doing so is safe. No retraining of the planner is needed. Tests span several planner types, including diffusion models. The approach trades a bit of freedom for proof, a bargain that matters for robots near people. It also keeps the planner's expressiveness where safety allows.
arxiv-2509-19888:
Designing a material layout under physics constraints mixes yes-no choices with smooth laws, a notoriously hard blend. Harsh Choudhary, Sven Leyffer, and Dominic Yang attack it with ADMM, a method that splits one hard problem into easier alternating steps. Total variation regularization keeps the designs crisp rather than fuzzy. An augmented Lagrangian keeps the split pieces in agreement.

Topology optimization with integer choices, nonsmooth penalties, and a non-convex goal resists direct solvers. The split turns each subproblem into something tractable. Convergence holds under stated conditions. Such optimization designs lightweight parts for aircraft, implants, and heat exchangers. A solver that handles discrete choices honestly widens what designers can ask for. The paper contributes method rather than a single design.
arxiv-2509-19988:
Designing gene perturbation experiments means choosing a few tests from a genome-sized menu. Yanke Li and four co-authors inform that choice with biology itself. Their method, BioBO, wraps Bayesian optimization with gene embeddings from several data types and enrichment analysis, the standard gene prioritization tool. Priors grounded in biology steer the surrogate model and the acquisition rule together.

The search leans toward promising genes while still exploring. Exhaustive perturbation is impossible, so each chosen experiment must earn its place. Drug discovery and target identification both ride on such choices. Generic optimizers waste budget in biologically dead regions. The authors argue domain knowledge belongs inside the optimization loop, not as an afterthought. BioBO is their principled version of that argument.
arxiv-2509-20088:
Oscar Lithgow-Serrano, Vani Kanjirangat, and Alessandro Antonucci wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on language models and causation. Recent studies find that these models classify causal relations in text at near-random levels. The authors ask whether the failure comes from too little exposure in training or from a deeper gap. They test the question with an uncertainty-based evaluation.

They tested seven models on more than eighteen thousand medical sentences. Half the sentences came from a known training corpus and half were newer. Models sorted relations into direct, conditional, correlational, or none. Accuracy was nearly the same on seen and unseen sentences, and models showed no bias toward text they had memorized. Output choices were almost flat, a sign of random guessing. One instruction-tuned model was highly confident yet often wrong. The authors conclude the gap lies in missing causal structure, not missing exposure.
arxiv-2509-20288:
Satellite knots tie a pattern knot around a companion knot, and Daren Chen, Ian Zemke, and Hugo Zhou compute a key invariant for them in a 2025 arXiv paper. The invariant, called tau, comes from knot Floer homology. Their formula covers satellites built by L-space operators, a well-behaved family of patterns. It applies most cleanly when the companion has a certain sign invariant.

The engine behind the formula is an algorithm from their earlier work that computes the Floer complex of such satellites. The tau formula recovers many known special cases, including cable knots. The authors apply it to the slice genus, a measure of how simply a knot bounds a surface. Satellites of knots whose tau equals their slice genus keep that property, they show. They also settle a conjecture about which L-space operators act as homomorphisms on the concordance group: only three trivial ones do.
arxiv-2509-20488:
Formal proof methods promise robot behavior that can be verified, not just tested. Atef Azaiez and three co-authors survey how those methods have been applied to autonomous robots in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their structured review complements an earlier survey and tracks how the field matured. The authors describe their database choices, search strings, filters, and shared screening process in detail.

The review catalogs which formalisms and approaches have been used to specify and verify robotic systems. It also examines formal methods for robots whose behavior comes from learned, sub-symbolic components. Some trends from the earlier survey persisted. New ones appeared as well, including a clear rise in formal synthesis and in probabilistic verification. The paper maps a field moving from proving hand-built controllers toward assuring learning-enabled machines.
arxiv-2509-21588:
Morning and evening edges of a hot Jupiter can now be observed separately with JWST. Maria Steinrueck leads a large team comparing models of WASP-39b in a 2025 paper. The evening terminator showed a larger transit radius and a stronger carbon dioxide trait than the morning side. Temperature differences, chemistry, clouds, and hazes could each cause such asymmetry. Forward models are needed to interpret the data.

Five general circulation models are matched against the limb records. One simulates disequilibrium chemistry, another includes cloud radiative feedback. Temperature forms from all model runs are post processed into spectra. The multi model comparison tests which processes reproduce the observed morning evening contrast. Results guide interpretation of limb asymmetry on other exoplanets.
arxiv-2509-21988:
Ilia Ryzov, Faedi Loulidi, and David Elkouss build a rulebook for using quantum entanglement when computing power is limited. Entanglement is a resource for quantum devices, but it only helps if the parties can actually manipulate it with the tools they have. Two recent measures count how much entanglement is usable under such limits, one for extraction and one for creation cost. Their 2025 paper studies both.

The authors first adapt the standard properties of entanglement measures to settings where only bounds on the values are known. They then trace how the two measures behave under mixing of states, pairing of systems, and local operations. A geometric link to families of states built from projective nets yields a proven gap between computational and ideal distillable entanglement. They also prove the first continuity bound for the computational measure, showing it cannot jump wildly under small noise.
arxiv-2509-22188:
A geodetic graph is one where any two points are joined by exactly one shortest path, a rare and rigid property. Joshua Abraham, Murray Elder, Adam Piggott, and Kane Townsend present a systematic way to build new examples in this 2025 paper. Their objects are Cayley graphs, which picture a group's structure as a network whose shape depends on a chosen generating set.
