Salvatore Capozziello, Maurizio Capriolo, and Gaetano Lambiase derive an energy-momentum form for a modified gravity theory. The theory, called f(Q) gravity, extends a flat, torsion-free form of general relativity. It is based on non-metricity, a measure of how lengths change under transport.

They build the affine tensor for the energy and momentum of both gravity and matter fields. That joined form is the complex pseudo-tensor for this theory. Such forms are needed to track energy flow in cosmology. The work puts energy bookkeeping for f(Q) on a firm base.
arxiv-2601-12188:
Aditi Singh, Bogumiła Jezierska, Subrata Jana, and Szymon Śmiga give a simpler way to tune range separation for many-body calculations. One-shot GW and Bethe-Salpeter runs rest much on their start point, got from mean-field theory. A range-separated hybrid start can lift skill a lot if tuned well.

Full tuning is costly, so a simple start helps. Their method gives a practical first tune with less work. Better starts mean better spectra and gaps at the same cost. The work aims at real use in materials and molecule codes.  A cheap first tune can save days of compute time.
arxiv-2601-12388:
Amartya Goswami and Joseph Israel Zelezniak study ideals in commutative rings. Their focus is on strongly hollow ideals and a stricter class that adds the word completely. They work with no finiteness assumptions, which keeps the results broad. Ideals are core objects in ring theory, so new classes draw close study.

The pair set out basic structural facts about these ideals. They look at maximality and at what holds under quotients and surjective maps. They give several ways to test when an ideal is completely strongly hollow. One key result links the two classes through the Jacobson radical. If a strongly hollow ideal is not inside that radical, it must be of the stricter kind.
arxiv-2601-13088:
Harry Huang, Talia Xu, and Marco Zuniga Zamalloa look at how light can aid tiny flying craft. Small air craft now do tasks from stock checks to air sensing. Their short flight time and weak sense of place in GPS free zones hold them back.

Craft that are lighter than air offer a swap. A helium skin gives lift, so hover takes near zero power and flights can run far longer. The snag is how to steer and stay on course with so light a craft. The team tests how light can be used both to boost flight length and to guide the craft. For indoor and calm air tasks, the work points to a low power path.
arxiv-2601-13188:
Patrick Yung Kang Lee and a large team study how people form ties with ChatGPT as a companion. Folks now turn to broad chat bots for company, not just to play apps built for that role. Yet little is known about how they see and run such ties.

The team asks how outer forces shape those ties. Friends, press, and norms may push how a tie is kept or hid. They also ask what tricks users use to keep the tie as they want it. The study fills a gap in how AI company is lived day to day. For teams that build chat bots, the finds show care points for health and trust.
arxiv-2601-13288:
Gonzalo Ariel Meyoyan and Luciano Del Corro reuse a live model's own maths to tag text in the same pass. Big served models often call split small models for safety and tag tasks. Each split call adds lag, memory load, and ops bulk.

Their swap is to train light probes on the served model's hid states. The probes read states the model has paid to make for its main text task. Tags then come out in the same pass as the text, with no split call. The probes can pick which tokens and which layers to read. For teams that serve models at scale, the trick cuts cost while it keeps the tag step.
arxiv-2601-13388:
Sasha Ronaghi, Prerit Choudhary, David H. Rehkopf, and Bryant Lin pull diabetes risk clues from free text in health files. Social facts of health, such as home, food, and work strain, sway type two diabetes care. Yet they are oft absent from the neat fields of a health file. Most such facts are caught by fixed forms, which miss the nuance of each clinic's crowd.

Free text in notes holds a rich store of such facts. The team uses large language models to draw them out in a firm form. That form then feeds a risk guess for each patient. For clinics, the route may catch risks that fixed forms leave blank.
arxiv-2601-13488:
Peter J. Forrester and Fei Wei note a set of results on high order equations for unitary matrix sums. The note gives the back tale and spur for a joint paper. It then maps the main finds of that work for a fast read.

The finds link matrix and scalar equations of high order. The sums at stake are Hankel and Toeplitz determinants built from I-Bessel functions. Such sums are the same as set unitary matrix sums. The note puts that link in a wider frame. For maths physics readers, a short map of a dense work plus its wider place has clear worth.
arxiv-2601-13988:
Laura Monk and Frédéric Naud review progress on spectral gaps of large hyperbolic surfaces in 2026. This expository paper surveys the history and recent breakthroughs in the field. The focus is the first non-trivial eigenvalue, called lambda-one. That value sets the spectral gap, a key trait of the surface's vibrations.

They ask how lambda-one can behave as surface volume grows large. The story runs from Selberg to Mirzakhani, two giants of the field. Spectral gaps link geometry, number theory, and quantum chaos. A clear review helps new researchers enter a fast-moving area.
arxiv-2601-14088:
Maria Abu-Sini and Reinhard Heckel build codes for data torn into pieces with typos in 2026. The adversarial torn paper channel models a word that is first edited, then broken. At most a set number of edit errors hit the word: insertions, deletions, and substitutions. The word then breaks into fragments at arbitrary positions.

DNA storage systems and 3D fingerprinting motivate this channel. The team studies near optimal code construction for it. A good code lets the receiver rebuild the message from torn, flawed pieces. Such codes guard data stored in fragile physical media.
arxiv-2601-14688:
Timothy D. Brandt derives statistical formulas for companion hunting in this 2026 paper. Astronomers often detect a companion only through a trend: a radial velocity or astrometric acceleration of its host star. Brandt derives the statistical relationship between that trend, a companion's mass, and its projected separation. The relationships are expressed as probability density functions.

The formulas are analytic and hold independent of all Keplerian orbital elements, so long as orbits are randomly oriented in space. In plain terms, a measured drift can be turned into odds on mass and distance without knowing the orbit's shape. The math is short and closed. No large code run is used, which makes the tool fast to use at a desk. Readers get closed-form relations for a common detection problem in exoplanet and binary star work.
arxiv-2601-14788:
Yifei Liu, Changxing Ding, Ling Guo, Huaiguang Jiang, and Qiong Cao generate human motion from text in this 2026 paper. Diffusion models have seen widespread adoption for text-driven human motion generation. Their generative capabilities and flexibility are impressive. Current motion diffusion models face two major limitations, though.

One is a representational gap. Pre-trained text encoders lack motion-specific information, so prompts are read with the wrong nuance. The other is error propagation during the iterative denoising process. Small slips compound across steps. Their model is reconstruction-anchored, using reconstruction to hold the motion on track. The aim is faith. A wave of an arm should look like the words asked for it, start to end. Readers get a text-to-motion design that fights drift in both meaning and movement.
arxiv-2601-15088:
Arnab Priya Saha and Aninda Sinha study how five particles scatter, one piece at a time. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with five-point tree amplitudes, the basic terms in a scattering process. All five external particles are identical scalars.

The team expands the residues of the amplitude in partial waves. They check the build in two ways. One uses massive spinor-helicity building blocks. The other matches the five-point Veneziano amplitude at fixed mass levels. The work also brings in splitting constraints and the hidden zeros of the full five-point scattering amplitude.
arxiv-2601-15588:
A team signing as Alibaba-AAIG presents a safety guardrail model in a 2026 arXiv paper. The model is called YuFeng-XGuard. As language models spread into real products, guardrails must do more than coarse filtering. They need to judge risk in fine detail. They also need to explain their calls and adapt to new policies. Existing tools often fall short on one of these counts.

Many current guards classify fast but stay opaque. Others rely on fixed rules added after the fact. Inference cost can also block deployment at scale. XGuard is described as reasoning-centric, interpretable, and flexible. It reasons about risk rather than just matching patterns. For builders, a guard that shows its reasoning is easier to audit. That matters when a wrong block or a missed risk carries real cost.
arxiv-2601-15688:
Zhixuan Liang, Xingyu Zeng, Rui Zhao, and Ping Luo improve active learning for object detection in a 2026 arXiv paper. Active learning trains strong models with minimal labeling effort. It picks the most informative examples for humans to annotate. Most methods judge informativeness by data distribution or content alone. That judgment does not directly track downstream performance. In detection, the score that matters is mean average precision.

The authors propose performance-guided reinforced active learning, per the title. The guide is the task metric itself, not a proxy. Reinforcement learning steers which images get picked for labeling. If picks track real gains, annotation budgets stretch further. Labeling images for detection is slow and costly. A smarter picker saves money on every training round.
arxiv-2601-15888:
An unsigned 2026 arXiv paper asks why vision foundation models transfer unevenly. Foundation models pretrain on huge data to capture broad knowledge. In language tasks, that pretraining generalizes well. Vision foundation models behave differently. Despite heavy compute, their gains vary sharply across downstream tasks. One task leaps forward while another barely moves.

The authors postulate a cause: a mismatch between pretraining objectives and what downstream vision tasks demand. Pretraining may teach features the tasks cannot use well. The paper studies these transfer limits directly. For labs spending heavily on vision pretraining, knowing the limits guides where the next dollar of compute should go.
arxiv-2601-15988:
Kalyan Banerjee links two classic objects in number theory in a 2026 arXiv paper. On one side stand elliptic curves, whose rank counts independent rational points. On the other stand class groups of real quadratic fields. Class groups measure how badly unique factorization fails in those fields. Banerjee proves a relation between the two. The link ties curve ranks to the nontriviality of class groups. The connection runs across infinitely many real quadratic fields, he states.

Bridges like this are prized in arithmetic geometry. A fact about curves becomes a fact about fields, and back. Each side has its own tools, so a bridge doubles the attack on hard questions. The abstract states the claim in brief terms. Specialists will look to the proof for the exact shape of the relation.
arxiv-2601-16088:
Abhinav Jangir and Anees Ahmed study how pulse form shapes pair birth in strong fields. Their 2026 preprint looks at birth of electron and positron pairs from void space. A time based field that is not the same on each side drives the birth. The team solves the quantum Vlasov maths for this case. They vary both the phase at the pulse heart and the pulse shape.

The pair track how each change shifts the yield of new pairs. Shape and phase can raise or cut the count in clear ways. Such links help labs plan strong laser tests of pair birth. They also test if maths matches what labs will see. The work stays close to the field maths and its terms.
arxiv-2601-16188:
Sebastián Donoso, Sovanlal Mondal and Vicente Saavedra-Araya extend mean sum results along return times. Their 2026 preprint sits in the maths of long run means. Return times are the times a path comes back to a small mark. Means can be taken along those sparse times in their place of all times. Past work showed such means settle in fast mix systems.

The team widens those results to groups of acts that commute. They also use marks that shrink as time grows. The work part fills gaps left by the first author, Maass and the third author. Sparse means that still settle have use in chance and flow maths. The proof joins mix speed to mean acts.
arxiv-2601-16288:
Van Weeren and coauthors share new MeerKAT views of two star groups, Abell 1775 and Abell 1795. Their 2026 preprint deals with huge radio glows in such groups. Big glows mark groups in clash, while small glows mark cool core groups. Both trace fast grains in the thin gas in the group. Late views hint the two glow types may not split clean.

The new views span a wide band from the MeerKAT scopes. They test if the small glow in one group is of the big type. Glow type tells of past clashes and gas acts in the group. Clear views help sort glow birth tales. The work adds fine radio maps of two key groups.
arxiv-2601-16388:
Hironori Yamaguchi and coauthors find magnet order that Kondo acts help to build. Their 2026 preprint deals with a chain model called the Kondo necklace. Kondo acts pair a free spin with a held spin in a singlet. Such pairs were long thought to kill magnet order. Late work hints Kondo acts can in some cases aid order.

The team shows Néel order, a flip flop spin line, can grow with Kondo aid. That growth flips the old tale for this model class. It widens where teams should look for such order. Real stuff may show the same aid in its spin acts. The work joins two themes long set as foes.
arxiv-2601-16788:
Xuewei Li, Xinghan Bao, Zhimin Chen, and Xi Li sort wide-view street shots into named zones. A full round view shows roads, cars, folks, and sky at once. Tools must tag each point in that wide span. Depth cues help split near from far in the shot. Past tools used depth in raw or plain forms. Their 2026 preprint builds a depth code fit for round views.

Their code reshapes depth to match the round warp of the shot. A fusion step then joins depth with the color view. Sharper tags aid self-drive cars and guide bots. Such tools need the full round scene read right.
arxiv-2601-17488:
Quinn M. Gallagher and four co-authors seek a local key to sort amorphous ices. Amorphous solids lack the neat unit cells of crystals. Yet ice phases with unlike traits must differ in local structure. The authors look for a structural basis at that local scale. Such a basis would do for glasses what space groups do for crystals.

A clear basis lets labs name and sort ice forms with proof. It can show which local motifs drive trait shifts. Water ice is a model for glasses at large. Its lessons reach drugs, foods, and planetary science. The work builds a language for forms that look alike at first glance. That language is a step to control them.
arxiv-2601-17588:
Marcus Ma and Shrikanth Narayanan argue that intelligence needs grounding, not embodiment. Recent language model gains revived an old debate. Must a mind have a body to be intelligent? The authors define intelligence by four properties. They list motivation, predictive ability, and understanding among them. Grounding links symbols to the world they mean.

Embodiment entails grounding, they argue, but grounding can arise without a body. That split reshapes what builders must give AI systems. It shifts focus from robot bodies to world linkage. The debate guides research funds and design choices. A clear stance helps labs test claims about machine minds. The paper stakes that stance with care.
arxiv-2601-17688:
Sudhanva Joshi and Sunil Kumar Mishra study traversability in a wormhole-inspired teleportation protocol. The protocol uses coupled Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev systems. They are prepared in a thermofield double state with a bath. The authors add PT-symmetric non-unitary deformations. PT symmetry pairs parity and time reversal. They ask how those deformations change traversability dynamics.

Traversability marks if a signal can pass through the wormhole analogue. SYK models are a lab for holography ideas. Deformations test how robust the effect is. Results guide both theory and quantum simulation design. Teams can build SYK-like systems on quantum hardware. Knowing which knobs help or harm passage matters for those builds.
arxiv-2601-17988:
Nachi Avraham-Re'em and Emmanuel Roy prove a mixing result for a broad class of random processes. Their 2026 preprint studies infinitely divisible stationary processes indexed by a group. Stationary means the statistics do not shift over the index. Infinitely divisible means each piece can be split into like parts. The authors show that if such a process is ergodic and separable in probability, then it is weakly mixing.

Weak mixing is a stronger form of long-run independence. The result holds for any indexing group at all. It removes group assumptions that older work needed. As with Gaussian processes, ergodicity alone forces mixing here. Clean results like this anchor the theory of random processes.
arxiv-2601-18188:
Weiye Zhu and co-authors present NaVIDA, a navigation agent that learns how its own actions change the world. Their 2026 preprint deals with vision-and-language navigation. An agent reads a natural language instruction and acts on it inside a rich visual scene. Most methods learn reactive links from state to action. They do not model how an action causally reshapes the scene, so errors can compound step by step.

NaVIDA adds inverse dynamics augmentation to the training. Inverse dynamics asks which action could have caused a seen change. That signal teaches cause and effect, not just correlation. Agents that grasp it should follow routes with fewer wrong turns.
arxiv-2601-18288:
S.C. İnan probes the electromagnetic traits of the tau lepton in lead-lead collisions at a future collider. His 2026 preprint studies pairs of tau leptons made in PbPb collisions at the FCC-hh. Two numbers are in view: the anomalous magnetic moment of the tau, and its electric dipole moment. The authors report 95 percent confidence exclusion limits, plus sensitivity limits at three and five sigma. Such limits say how small a deviation the collider could detect or rule out.

The tau is the heaviest lepton, so its moments are prized probes of new physics. A dipole moment would signal a deep asymmetry in nature. Future collider studies of this kind set targets for machine design.
arxiv-2601-18488:
Alice Bernard and five colleagues study how the split of an atom's core can vary from split to split. When a heavy core splits, the two parts fly off with traits that can be counted, such as spin and mass. Math based on energy maps can give the odds for each trait. New tools add those odds up with care.

Still, a mean count can hide how wide the spread runs. The team use a dice-roll math trick to chart that spread in full. Each roll picks a split by the odds, and many rolls build the whole range. That range tells labs what a real test should see, miss by miss. It also shows which counts are firm and which ones swing a lot. Such maps help plan tests on cores that are hard to make.
arxiv-2601-19088:
Saba Alimadadi and Golnaz Gharachorlu blend two styles of mutation testing for Python code. Mutation testing grades a test suite by seeding small fake faults and seeing how many the tests catch. Old tools miss many fault types that are common in a loose typed language like Python.

Their hybrid method is driven by real fault patterns, not just simple code swaps. Python's dynamic typing breeds faults that stiff mutation rules never plant. A suite graded against realistic faults gives a truer read on whether the tests would catch the bugs that truly slip into Python projects.
arxiv-2601-19388:
Yimin Tang, Sven Koenig, and Erdem Bıyık tidy the paths of robot fleets after a planner has done its job. Multi agent path finding is a hard problem with uses in warehouses and robot coordination. Learning based solvers are fast and scale well, but their feasible plans often include wasteful or wobbly moves.

Their layer, Judgelight, post optimizes each trajectory by collapsing closed subwalks, loops that return to their start. Cutting dead loops keeps the plan valid while making it shorter and cleaner. A cheap cleanup step can lift any solver's output, which makes it a handy add on.
arxiv-2601-19488:
Yizhao Han and nine co-authors sample video frames with an eye on entropy to keep long clips coherent. Autoregressive models build video step by step, as language models build text. In language, picking from a small top candidate set works well because tokens are dense with meaning and low in redundancy.

Video tokens behave otherwise, so fixed candidate sets falter over long horizons. Their entropy guided k-guard sampling adjusts the guard by how unsure the model is at each step. Long, stable video generation is the prize, since drift and decay grow with every extra second.
arxiv-2601-19988:
Xuankai Zhou and colleagues build quantum sensors that sit directly on a material's surface. Optically addressable spins can sense magnetic fields with atomic resolution and quantum-limited sensitivity. Realising them at surfaces has been a long-standing ambition. The obstacle is depth: stable quantum spins usually must sit some distance below the surface, blunting their sensitivity to what lies above.

The team demonstrates a hybrid molecular and two-dimensional architecture. It places working spin sensors right on top of the surface. Surface placement maximises contact with the sample being measured. Such sensors could image magnetism and currents in new materials at the smallest scales. The work removes a depth limit that constrained the field.
arxiv-2601-20088:
Meng Xin and colleagues distil large models into aggressively compressed versions. Their technical report presents quantization-aware distillation for models squeezed to the NVFP4 format, a four-bit number format. Quantization alone usually costs accuracy. Distillation trains the compressed student to imitate a full-precision teacher, recovering much of the loss.

The report covers both language models and vision-language models. It shares best practices the team found for the recovery process. The distillation loss is a KL divergence between teacher and student outputs. Four-bit inference slashes memory and energy costs for serving models. A reliable recipe for recovering accuracy makes such deployment realistic. The report is written for practitioners facing the same squeeze.
arxiv-2601-20988:
Gabor Lippner and Arturo Ortiz San Miguel ask which regular graphs hold the most copies of a given pattern. Their 2026 paper studies subgraph counts in regular graphs. A regular graph gives every vertex the same number of edges. For a fixed pattern graph H, some regular graphs pack in more H-shaped copies than others. The authors seek the graphs with the highest H-density.

They reframe the hunt as a continuous optimization problem. The new frame runs through the eigenvalues of the graph. Counts of injective homomorphisms link to counts from quotient graphs of H. That link turns a discrete search into smooth math. The result gives extremal graph theory a fresh handle. It may help design networks with chosen pattern densities.
arxiv-2601-21088:
Thomas Blommel and four co-authors compare rival ways to simulate driven quantum systems. Their 2026 paper benchmarks the real-time Dyson expansion against Green's function approaches. Driven, interacting quantum systems are hard to simulate. The team focuses on density matrix dynamics and time-off-diagonal Green's functions. They also study time-resolved photoemission spectra. Those spectra show how a material responds right after a pulse.

Two themes run through the comparison. One is Markovianity: how much the system remembers its past. The other is self-consistency in the calculation. The rivals include Kadanoff-Baym equations, their generalized ansatz, and exact diagonalization for small systems. Second-order perturbation theory supplies the interaction treatment. The study tells simulators which tool to trust for driven materials. It is a careful methods audit for non-equilibrium physics.
arxiv-2601-21388:
Mingyi Wang and Dongling Wang build high-order numerical schemes for a fractional diffusion operator. The tempered fractional Laplacian models spread that is heavier-tailed than normal diffusion but still fades at long range. Accurate schemes for it are hard to design.

The authors base their framework on new generating functions drawn from the discrete symbols. For smooth functions, the schemes reach high orders of accuracy. A general frame matters because each new application otherwise needs its own scheme. Their approach gives later work a ready path to accurate, fast solvers for this class of problems.
arxiv-2601-21788:
C. J. K. Larkin and co-authors ask how one unusual pair of massive stars came to be. Wolf-Rayet stars are hot, stripped stars, and how they form at the Sun's metal content is still unclear. Simple single-star paths are hard to square with the orbit patterns seen in different Wolf-Rayet pairs.

Their 2026 study focuses on Wd1-72, a Wolf-Rayet plus O-star binary inside the young massive cluster Westerlund 1. The pair sits inside the shared wind of the whole cluster. The title poses the question the evidence must answer: is this system a recent case where the two stars interacted and exchanged material? The answer would help pin down how often binary interaction, not solo aging, makes Wolf-Rayet stars.
arxiv-2601-21888:
Alexander Fel'shtyn and Mateusz Slomiany introduce a new object in dynamical systems: the synchronization zeta function. It is attached to a pair of self-maps of a topological space, functions that send the space into itself. Zeta functions in dynamics package counting data about repeating behavior into one analytic object.

The authors also define the growth rate of synchronization points, places where the two maps agree in step. And derive an explicit formula for it in the setting of endomorphisms of compact, connected Abelian groups. Their 2026 preprint then studies congruences and asymptotics tied to the new function. Work like this extends a classic toolkit, Reidemeister theory and dynamical zeta functions, into two-map territory.
arxiv-2601-22088:
Levin Maier puts a young set of equations on firm ground. The set is called the magnetic two-part Hunter-Saxton system. It was first drawn from a path law on a space with no end. That first work sketched the shape of the set and a flow that lasts for all time.

What was missed was a proof from the side of hard sums. Maier gives that proof. He studies weak forms of the law: forms that may grow sharp points yet still hold in a mean sense. Such ground work counts, since kin of this set model liquid glass, thin seas, and magnets. Those fields need laws that can be shown to hold, not just laws that look right on a screen.
arxiv-2601-22288:
Mario Truss presents PersonaCite, a tool that ties fake research users to real proof. Their 2026 work notes that model-made personas can sound sure yet hide where their claims come from. Design teams use such personas to test products and plans.

PersonaCite lets a user ask the persona direct questions in a chat. Each reply stays bound to source proof that can be checked. The tool frames personas as research aids, not as stand-ins for real people. That bound can make fake-user tests more honest and more safe to use. It also shows its work on demand.
arxiv-2601-22388:
Monica Rincon-Ramirez and five co-authors ask if a simple heat rule picks the black hole left after two black holes merge. Their 2026 preprint notes that big simulations predict the final hole with great care. Yet a plain rule from within relativity may do the same job.

They test a maximum entropy claim: the merger settles on the state with the most disorder allowed. If true, the rule would give a fast way to call the outcome. It would also tie black hole physics to heat physics in a deep way. The work checks the claim against known cases.
arxiv-2601-22588:
Zhuochun Li and a large team ask if a small model can judge as well as a large one by reading inner states. Large models are widely used as scorers, but they are costly, opaque, and prompt-sensitive. Their 2026 preprint tests small models that judge from internal representations, not from written verdicts.

The claim rests on a gap in semantic capacity between judge and judged. If it holds, judging gets cheaper and more stable. It could also make scores easier to audit. The work rethinks a costly habit of the field. Small, sharp judges would change many pipelines.
arxiv-2601-22688:
Doyoung Kim, Jaehyeok Doo, and Minjoon Seo let a language model branch its reasoning like a tree, in one pass. Models now reason in a single line, which traps dead-end paths inside the chain. Their 2026 preprint, TSLM, uses special tokens to mark branches in the text itself.

The model can grow several paths and expand only the live ones. Tree search in one pass saves the cost of many full runs. It suits puzzles where the first path often fails. The work rethinks the shape of machine thought. Branches, pruned well, beat a single line.
arxiv-2601-22788:
Jana Gonnermann-Müller and a team built FACET, a multi-agent AI that helps teachers tailor lessons to a mixed class. Classrooms now span wide gaps in skill, drive, language, and learning needs such as dyslexia and ADHD. Their 2026 preprint notes that teachers back tailored teaching, yet workload blocks it.

FACET's agents draft varied materials at scale, under the teacher's hand. That help could make tailored learning a daily fact, not an ideal. The work targets a kind bottleneck in schools. It keeps the teacher as the judge. Scale serves care, here.
arxiv-2601-22988:
Di Zhang and a team at Tongji University teach robots to see scenes in three dimensions. Real manipulation needs a steady grasp of space, even when cameras move to new viewpoints. Policies trained from one angle often fail when the view changes.

Their method learns visual representations grounded in geometry, so scenes read consistently across views. A robot that understands shape, not just pixels, can pick and place objects more reliably. View-proof vision is a step toward helpers that work in messy, real rooms. Robust spatial understanding is the stated requirement, because a manipulation policy must know where things are, not just what they look like.
arxiv-2601-23088:
Zhixiang Zhang and four co-authors attack the semantic caches that speed up language model services. Big providers cache answers by meaning, using embedding vectors as fuzzy keys for similar queries. That saves latency and compute on repeated questions.

Treating cache keys as fuzzy hashes, the authors craft collisions that make the cache serve wrong answers. A poisoned cache can mislead many users from a single planted entry. The work tells providers to harden a component many treated as harmless plumbing. Major providers already deploy semantic caching widely, so a key collision weakness reaches production systems, not just prototypes.
arxiv-2601-23188:
Zhongxiang Sun and five co-authors give deep search agents a way to watch their own thinking. These agents handle multi-step retrieval and long tasks well. Their failures often come from having no mechanism to monitor reasoning and retrieval as the job evolves.

Drawing on cognitive neuroscience, the authors add hierarchical meta-cognitive monitoring. Higher levels check the state of lower-level search and correct course when it drifts. Self-monitoring agents should be more reliable for research, law, and other long-horizon work. Meta-cognitive monitoring is hierarchical, so oversight itself is layered rather than a single checker watching a single process.
arxiv-2602-00188: Srividhya Sethuraman and Chandrashekar Lakshminarayanan make dynamic pricing interpretable at the level of product traits. Low rank bandit methods learn well but hide how single traits move price, since they rely on latent traits. Their AFDLD model writes price as a sum of trait level parts, with substitution effects modeled in the open. Their ADEPT algorithm learns online in trait space without projections or gradients, with sublinear regret. Synthetic tests and real data show it learns near best prices under shifting market conditions.
arxiv-2602-00288: Baiqi Li and team present TimeBlind, a benchmark for spatio-temporal understanding in video language models. Fine grained temporal understanding matters for video reasoning, yet models that master static semantics stay brittle on dynamics. It sorts temporal understanding into three levels: atomic event recognition, event property characterization, and reasoning about links between events. Its minimal pairs design uses video pairs with identical static content but different temporal structure, with paired questions to offset language priors. Tests on over 20 models across 600 instances reveal that instance scores lag far behind static recognition.
arxiv-2602-00488: Dongbin Jiao and colleagues address large capacitated vehicle routing, where classic heuristics grow complex and neural solvers generalise poorly. Their OD-Gear scheme joins hybrid genetic search with online barycentre clustering and group-relative optimisation, distilling expert heuristics into a graph attention network policy. Adversarial training turns divide-and-conquer tactics into dense reward signals, while group sampling uses relative gains to protect both diversity and quality. Inference needs no clustering step, runs fast, and stays near the front at the 10,000-node scale, giving heuristic-quality routes for massive graphs.
arxiv-2602-00588: Thiago Dumont Oliveira tracks French drama from 1700 to 1900 with Latent Dirichlet Allocation and Jensen-Shannon Divergence. Topic patterns shift profoundly after the French Revolution, especially between 1789 and 1850, with bourgeois themes rising among the most prevalent topics from the late 18th century. Plotting yearly topic prevalence against French GDP over the same span, he reads these changes against the political and economic shifts of the Revolution and industrialisation.
arxiv-2602-00788: Md Abir Hossen and colleagues propose RESCUE, a multi-goal multi-fidelity Bayesian optimisation method using causal priors. Multi-fidelity optimisation speeds search for black-box optima with cheap low-fidelity approximations, weighing their low cost against reduced accuracy. A causal hypervolume knowledge-gradient plan then picks input-fidelity pairs weighing likely multi-goal gain against cost. On test and real problems in robot work, AutoML, and healthcare, RESCUE beats leading multi-fidelity methods on sample efficiency.
arxiv-2602-00888: Yingjie Niu and colleagues introduce GAPNet, which jointly learns task topology and representations end to end as a Graph Adaptation Plug-in Network. Current methods fix graphs for inter-stock relations, but noisy, out-of-sync web signals misalign those graphs with downstream tasks and hurt results. GAPNet attaches to graph or hypergraph backbones and dynamically rewires edges. A Spatial Perception Layer tracks short-term moves across assets, while a Temporal Perception Layer keeps long-term links under data shift.
arxiv-2602-01088: Fernando Zhapa-Camacho and Robert Hoehndorf build INDIGENA, a gene-disease ranker for brand-new diseases. Old trait scores use only the trait tree, while trait-vector plans need the disease at train time, so they fail on fresh diseases. INDIGENA turns trait rules into a graph, vectors traits, and pools them into gene and disease forms for fresh trait sets. A signal from known gene-disease links tunes the vectors to the job. On mouse models of human disease, it beat trait-score baselines and matched vector plans.
arxiv-2602-01288: Chenghua Zhu and co-authors read language-model thought through the path of doubt over time, not just its mean. Past doubt scores sum token doubt into one flat number, wasting doubt's shape as words unfold. Their read of token doubt paths finds wrong answers marked by wild swings: burst spikes of rising doubt and peak-valley spikes after brief calm. Those marks hold across models and train stages, hinting at deep failure traits. Their EDIS score sums path wobble and lifts pick accuracy at run time.
arxiv-2602-01988: James Boran Yu and colleagues build a strict framework for stochastic interpolants in infinite Hilbert spaces, bridging distributions for function data. Diffusion models already handle function data, but stochastic interpolants, a flex bridge between distributions, stayed finite. The team proves well posedness and error bounds, giving theory bases. They demonstrate conditional sampling on complex PDE benchmarks, with top results. By enabling bridges between function distributions, the approach offers a general tool for science.
arxiv-2602-02088: Daniel Plummer and colleagues build a statistical account of the degrees of freedom for electrons in wave packet molecular dynamics. Widths of Gaussian packets get their own spread laws, worked out for both round (isotropic) and stretched (anisotropic) setups. Under warm dense matter, the new spread laws match molecular dynamics runs well, giving hands-on help for pinning down the confining potential, a model knob set by hand. The authors also trace how these spreads shape the effective Coulomb forces that result.
arxiv-2602-02388:
Rajalaxmi Rajagopalan and 3 co-authors help a person steer image generation toward a picture held only in memory, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Words often cannot close the last gap between a generated image and the imagined one. Yet a person can still tell which of two new images looks closer to the target.

Their system, MultiBO, uses that comparative judgment. It generates a small set of candidate images, asks the user to pick favorites, and feeds those choices into a Bayesian optimization loop, which plans the next candidates from past feedback. Round by round, the images move closer to the remembered scene. Tests with thirty users and five rival methods show clear gains. The work points to preference clicks, not longer prompts, as the missing control.
arxiv-2602-02588:
Alan Maciel and 2 co-authors prove that matter trapping surfaces act as true boundaries between independent regions of an inhomogeneous cosmos, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The setting restricts to spherical dust plus a cosmological constant. A matter trapping surface marks where gravity's pull on light and matter balances cosmic expansion.

The authors show the surface is a characteristic surface of the Cauchy problem, generated by its own characteristic curves. That property opens the possibility of infinitely many solutions stitched across it. In effect, collapsing and expanding regions on either side can evolve arbitrarily independently, echoing Birkhoff-theorem behavior. Three example models illustrate the claim, combining the standard cosmology with Schwarzschild-de Sitter and inhomogeneous Lemaître-Tolman-Bondi-de Sitter spacetimes. The inhomogeneous example displays a static, stable trapping surface for the first time.
arxiv-2602-02788:
Benjamin D. Shaffer and 4 co-authors teach neural PDE solvers the structure of finite element methods so answers survive new geometries, in a 2026 paper. Physics foundation models promise real-time answers to partial differential equations, but quality usually collapses on shapes the model never saw. Conservation laws must hold exactly, not roughly, for engineering trust.

Their approach, Geo-NeW, jointly learns a differential operator and compatible reduced finite element spaces defined on the geometry itself. Finite element exterior calculus guarantees physical conservation laws hold exactly. Geometry enters twice: through a transformer encoding of the mesh and as the basis of the learned spaces, tying boundary conditions straight to solutions. A novel parameterization ensures the solution exists and is unique. Steady-state benchmarks reached state-of-the-art accuracy, with significant gains over conventional rivals on geometries far from the training set.
arxiv-2602-02888:
Spotting made-up answers from language models is the aim of Ahmad Shapiro and 2 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Their detector, HALT, reads only the top token probabilities produced during generation, treated as a time series. It needs no access to hidden states, attention maps, or model weights.

A small recurrent model plus entropy-based features learns each model's calibration bias. The authors also built HUB, a unified benchmark covering ten abilities from math to summarization. HALT beat a fine-tuned encoder baseline while being far smaller. It also ran many times faster. Because it uses only output probabilities, HALT can work with closed commercial models too.
arxiv-2602-02988:
Nonlinear operations slow down language model inference, and Jiangyong Yu and 5 co-authors propose a cheaper replacement in a 2026 paper. Functions like SiLU, RMSNorm, and Softmax still need high-precision floating-point math. Linear layers have been compressed heavily, but these nonlinear layers remain a cost in memory and computation for deployment.

Their framework, NLI, approximates nonlinear functions with non-uniform linear interpolation. Choosing the interpolation cutpoints becomes a dynamic programming problem with a globally minimal error guarantee. The method needs no calibration and suits hardware. The team also built a plug-and-play computation unit implementing it. Hardware experiments showed more than four times the computational efficiency of leading designs, with almost no accuracy loss in integrated models.
arxiv-2602-03088:
Star formation shutting down in galaxy clusters is mapped by Oğuzhan Çakır and 17 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Cluster environments curtail star formation, notably through ram-pressure stripping, where a galaxy's gas is swept back as it moves through hot cluster material. The authors use spatially resolved spectroscopy from the SAMI Galaxy Survey in eight nearby clusters.

Galaxies are classified by their ionized gas shapes as unperturbed, asymmetric, or truncated. Asymmetric galaxies occupy a narrow range of cluster distances and show larger velocity spread. Star formation in affected galaxies is suppressed in their outskirts, most strongly for truncated systems. Centers, by contrast, match unperturbed and field galaxies. The pattern favors outside-in quenching, with the classes forming an evolutionary sequence from freshly arrived to post-stripping systems.
arxiv-2602-03488:
Maria Chiara Angelini and 3 co-authors compute critical exponents for a spin glass transition at zero temperature. Their 2026 paper studies a one-dimensional long-range spin glass in a magnetic field, a model that stands in for harder higher-dimensional systems. Critical exponents are the numbers that describe how the system behaves exactly at its transition.

The method is a new loop expansion inside the Bethe M-layer formalism, adapted here to the zero-temperature field case. The resulting exponent estimates matter beyond the model itself. Numerical simulations can reach much larger sizes in one dimension, so these values give simulators a sharp benchmark. They also serve as a key test of the theory of spin glasses in a field.
arxiv-2602-03588:
Compiler optimizations often assign values across a program's control-flow graph so that as many constraints as possible hold. Xuran Cai and Amir Goharshady study that problem class in a 2026 paper. It is partial constraint satisfaction over control-flow graphs, where violated constraints cost money and the goal is the cheapest assignment. Register allocation is a classic example.

Control-flow graphs of structured programs decompose neatly into series, parallel, and loop pieces. The authors give a general algorithm over such decompositions whose running time is linear for any fixed value domain. It unifies earlier specialized methods for register allocation and redundancy elimination. On the bank selection task, experiments run about four times faster than the best previous method.
arxiv-2602-03688:
A team of language model agents that always talks in the same pattern wastes tokens and adapts poorly when conditions change. Wenzhe Fan and 5 co-authors propose TodyComm in a 2026 paper, a task-oriented dynamic communication algorithm for multi-round multi-agent systems. Roles shift across rounds under adversaries, task progress, and bandwidth limits, so the topology should shift too.

TodyComm builds behavior-driven collaboration topologies that adapt each round, tuned by policy gradient toward task utility. Experiments on five benchmarks cover dynamic adversarial settings and tight communication budgets. The method achieves better task performance than fixed-topology rivals while staying token-efficient. It also scales and generalizes across different adversarial conditions, the authors report.
arxiv-2602-04188:
One model that turns text into motion and motion back into text is Ning Zhang and 9 co-authors' goal. Their 2026 framework, DiMo, uses discrete diffusion over motion tokens instead of left-to-right generation. Iterative masked refinement unifies text-to-motion, motion-to-text, and motion completion in a single system.

Residual vector quantization raises token fidelity. A group-relative policy optimization step improves alignment and controllability. More refinement steps trade latency for quality at inference time. On standard human motion benchmarks, DiMo showed strong generation quality and competitive understanding both ways. Editors could caption, complete, and correct motion with one model.
arxiv-2602-04388:
Testing tools that verify neural networks requires networks to test on. Nadia Daoudi and 1 co-author use language models to generate a benchmark dataset of neural networks in a 2026 paper. Diverse public datasets of networks are scarce, which blocks systematic evaluation of verification, refactoring, and migration tools.

Their generated collection holds six hundred eight networks following precise design choices. Architectures vary across components, input types, and tasks. Language models thus manufacture the test fixtures that the tooling community lacked. Such synthetic benchmarks let researchers measure whether verification tools actually catch broken networks before those networks support real decisions.
arxiv-2602-04588:
Francisco Ferreira da Silva and Stephanie Wehner show that quantum entanglement can help distant servers work together, in a 2026 paper on spread-out systems. Message delay normally limits such teamwork, while entangled particles show instant links when measured, however far apart they are.

Their system runs a background task that can be paused, plus user requests that arrive in pairs. Scores trade background throughput against user waiting time. Using queueing theory, a non-local game framing, and computer-checked classic bounds, the authors prove an edge. Entanglement-assisted routing beats every message-free classic strategy when longer unbroken work periods pay off more than in proportion. The result names scheduling as a fresh use for quantum networks.
arxiv-2602-04688:
Seonjae Lee and 10 co-authors map the jet and outflow of a young star called EC 53 in a 2026 astronomy paper. EC 53 is a Class I protostar, still wrapped in material, with nearly periodic brightness changes. The study combines two major observatories, JWST in space and ALMA on the ground.

ALMA resolved a compact disk around the star. JWST instruments saw scattered light from the outflow cavity and many hydrogen emission lines tracing a narrow cone. A fast ionized jet appeared in forbidden atomic lines, with a tight opening angle. Mid-infrared carbon monoxide lines traced hot gas in the cavity walls. Slower, colder components appeared in other molecular lines. The layered structure broadly matches magnetized disk wind models.
arxiv-2602-04788:
Louise Alamichel and 3 co-authors rework a standard ecological risk tool in a 2026 study. Species sensitivity curves estimate what share of species a pollutant level might harm, and regulators worldwide mandate them. Critics have long attacked their use of rigid parametric assumptions.

The authors recast the method in a Bayesian nonparametric scheme using mixture models that let the data shape the curve. The approach handles small and censored datasets, common in ecotoxicology, while putting uncertainty on a firm footing. It also estimates density and clusters species at once. Runs on simulated and real data showed it beat classical methods. A free web app makes the method open to practitioners.
arxiv-2602-04888:
Bowen Zhao, a physics researcher, wrote this 2026 paper on holographic entropy, a way of measuring how quantum information is spread out in theories that link gravity with quantum mechanics. Earlier work built graph models for still, unchanging spacetimes. Zhao asks whether the same approach works when the spacetime itself changes over time.

Zhao finds a geometric condition, called exposed regions, under which the graph model still gives the right answers. He proves that any shortcut built from partial surfaces is beaten by a surface made of complete pieces. Where the condition fails, grouping surfaces into clusters partly fixes the problem. The result supports the idea that the changing and static versions of the entropy cone match.
arxiv-2602-05688:
The small nonlinear function inside each neural network layer, the activation function, shapes both training speed and what the network tends to learn. Alex Vitvitskyi and 5 co-authors use evolutionary search to mine new activation functions, with a modern twist. Pipelines such as AlphaEvolve use frontier language models as the mutation operator, so the search can range over arbitrary short programs within a computing budget.

That wider space removes the need to hand build a search grammar, and model bias steers mutations toward sensible candidates. The team also shows fitness can target a chosen inductive bias directly, by rewarding performance on out of distribution data. Early experiments support both claims: searched functions can improve performance, and they can encode biases that survive distribution shift. The paper is an empirical exploration rather than a finished catalogue. It should interest researchers who design network components by search instead of by hand.
arxiv-2602-05788:
Products over prime numbers obey elegant formulas, and Hwanyup Jung proves one over function fields, where polynomials over a finite field play the role of integers. The target is a Mertens style formula for Euler products over prime polynomials that lie in a fixed arithmetic progression. 

An elementary argument first handles the full product: up to degree n it equals a simple exponential of a harmonic number, with exponentially small error. Combining that with the Riemann hypothesis for Dirichlet L functions over function fields, which is a theorem in this setting, gives the progression result. The right normalizing function turns out to be a specific quantity built from harmonic numbers, not the naive analogue of log x. Using the wrong one creates an expansion whose leading correction is combinatorial rather than arithmetic.
arxiv-2602-05988:
Fine-tuning a large language model for a new task costs a fortune in trainable weights. Low-rank adaptation, or LoRA, cuts that cost by freezing the base model and training only small add-on weights, often trimming trainable weights by over ninety-nine percent. Keith Ando Ogawa and seven co-authors argue even that may not be enough as models grow, and that not every layer pulls equal weight.

Their fix tunes only a few layers, chosen by how much each layer shifts the model's inner representations. The choice works beside standard LoRA methods and cuts LoRA trainable weights by up to half, while holding performance steady. Encoder models stay near par on a standard benchmark, decoder models hold or gain on math and coding tasks, and multimodal models stay competitive. The method lets teams tune big models with far fewer moving parts.
arxiv-2602-06588:
Jakob G. R. von Saldern and four co-authors present a new way to break down unsteady flow data into its main patterns at each frequency. Their method, called band-ensemble spectral proper orthogonal decomposition, builds on an older tool used to study turbulence and noise in moving fluids. It aims to give cleaner results from a single long record of measurements.

Instead of chopping the record into short segments, the method works from one full transform of the whole signal and groups nearby frequencies together. Tests on made-up data and on lab measurements of air flowing over a cavity show less leakage between frequencies and sharper detail than the standard approach. The authors say it suits flows that mix steady tones with broad, noisy motion.
arxiv-2602-06788:
Idan Pipano, Shoham Sabach, Kavosh Asadi, and Mohammad Ghavamzadeh generalize the theory behind direct preference optimization, the method that aligns language models with human preferences without a separate reward model. Earlier work showed the method stays tractable when the closeness penalty uses any convex f-divergence, not just the usual KL divergence. This paper asks what really makes the trick work, and what else a good penalty needs.

The authors show convexity is not essential: they identify a precise condition, called DPO-inducing, that determines tractability. They then add a second condition that prevents probability displacement, the odd effect in which both the winning and losing answers lose probability. A specific function satisfying both yields their SquaredPO loss, which keeps DPO's practical performance while carrying stronger theoretical guarantees.
arxiv-2602-07088:
Muhammad Zafar Iqbal and three co-authors offer a focus-led system for non-rigid medical image matching. Deformable matching aligns images that differ by large, body-constrained warps, serving diagnosis, treatment planning, and image-guided interventions. Yet aligning large warps while keeping anatomy plausible stays hard, even as deep learning matching has advanced. Their system, AD-RegNet, steers matching with focus mechanisms.

A 3D UNet backbone pairs with two-way cross-focus, linking moving and fixed images at many scales. A regional adaptive focus step spotlights body-relevant structures, and a multi-scale warp synthesis step yields accurate matching. Tests on DIRLab thoracic 4D CT scans and IXI brain MRI scans show versatility across body parts and scan types. Scores match top methods on both sets, with a favorable balance of score and compute cost for clinical use.
arxiv-2602-07188:
Comet C/2022 E3 (ZTF) swept past Earth in early 2023, offering a rare close look at an Oort cloud comet.  Nathan X.  Roth and eleven co-authors observed it with the NASA Infrared Telescope Facility days after closest approach, measuring the gases streaming from its coma.

Their spectra securely detect water, carbon monoxide, methanol, methane, ethane, acetylene, hydrogen cyanide. Carbonyl sulfide, and they report temperatures, production rates, and abundance ratios for each, with slit angles chosen to test how each gas spreads around the nucleus.  Comet experts get a detailed chemical snapshot of a pristine visitor, useful for comparing comets and tracing the solar system's icy origins.
arxiv-2602-07288:
Identifying a dynamical system from one trajectory is hard when the data carries usual noise, adversarial attacks, or both at once.  Jihun Kim and one co-author develop robust identification frameworks for linearly parametrized non-linear systems that handle each regime.

For the agnostic case, where the regime is unknown, the Huber estimator achieves a fast error rate under noise and a bounded error under attack. It acts as a bridge between mean- and median-based methods.  For concurrent noise and attacks, the paper shows no convex one-stage estimator suffices and builds a two-stage option.  Control theorists get robustness guarantees matched to the corruption they face.
arxiv-2602-07388:
In long robot tasks, the same view can recur at other stages demanding other actions, confusing policies that look only at the present moment.  Yuxuan Hu and six co-authors address this multi-modal action ambiguity with a Trace-Focused Diffusion Policy that conditions action generation on execution history.

Past motion is represented as an explicit trace projected into the visual observation space, supplying stage-aware context, while a trace-focused field emphasizes regions tied to that history.  The policy thus knows not just what it sees but where it is in the task.  Imitation learning teams get a simple, effective fix for ambiguity that plagues long-horizon manipulation.
arxiv-2602-07488:
Neural scaling laws guide how much data and compute to throw at models, but no theory predicted their exponents for real language data.  Francesco Cagnetta and three co-authors supply the first such theory for data-limited scaling, built from two statistical properties of natural language alone.

The decay of token correlations with separation, plus the decay of next-token entropy with context length, feed a formula with no tunable values for scaling exponents. That formula matches tests from training GPT-style models.  Machine learning theorists get a first-principles account of why scaling curves bend as they do, grounded in language statistics rather than fitted curves.
arxiv-2602-08188:
The Fermi paradox asks why a universe that should teem with life shows no sign of other intelligences, and the Great Filter hypothesis answers with obstacles that weed out most species. Darren J. Dougan proposes a new filter: depopulation driven by success itself.

His argument runs from evolution to economics: a species freed from predation breeds less, then intelligence brings medicine and contraception that cut infant mortality while controlling births. Social, economic, and educational factors further discourage reproduction. The author claims modeling of these exponential trends points to a human population peak mid-century followed by collapse within five hundred years, with extinction thresholds in view. Readers should treat this as a speculative hypothesis, not an shown forecast.
arxiv-2602-08288:
Carbon-12's internal structure, whether its nucleons arrange as a smooth distribution or as triangular clusters of alpha particles, should leave traces in low-energy nuclear collisions. Subhash Singha tests that sensitivity with the Jet AA transport model for carbon-carbon and carbon-lead collisions at 2.36 GeV per nucleon pair, relevant to tests at Lanzhou's Cooling Storage Ring and the forthcoming HIAF facility.

Comparing Woods-Saxon and triangular alpha-clustered configurations, he finds clustering yields a more compact participant zone, while size and eccentricity fluctuations barely respond. Radial observables stay sensitive to compactness at this energy. Nuclear physics teams gain guidance on which collision observables can actually reveal alpha clustering in carbon, and which cannot.
arxiv-2602-08488:
The High-Luminosity LHC upgrade will replace ATLAS's inner detector, and its control system must be checked before production. Lukas Flad and two co-authors define a test rig and a check method for the MOPS readout, which watches voltages and temperatures of pixel modules. Their arXiv paper compares two controller designs: an early Raspberry Pi mock-up and the final FPGA-based hub.

The method sets out checks of total delay, timing wobble, and data soundness across CAN and UART links. It uses one shared clock scheme, taps that do not disturb signals, and one logging pipeline. Load tests cover normal use, full-crate stress, and channel isolation, with pass marks and error analysis. Readers get a repeatable check procedure; a companion paper will report the actual head-to-head results.
arxiv-2602-08588:
Time series drive finance, health care, and cloud systems, yet benchmarks for language models on temporal tasks remain scattered. Yao Yin and nine co-authors introduce MMTS-BENCH, a multimodal benchmark organized by a hierarchy of time-series tasks. Their arXiv paper spans structure, features, temporal reasoning, matching, and cross-modal links.

The set holds 2,424 question-answer pairs across four subsets, built through a progressive real-world framework plus modular synthetic construction. Evaluations reveal four patterns: specialized time-series models lag general models on cross-domain transfer, local tasks are weaker than global ones, chain-of-thought and multimodal input help markedly, and backbone capability dominates encoder design. Readers get both a rigorous yardstick and clear directions for better temporal reasoning.
arxiv-2602-09288:
Fake money data must weigh use against privacy under strict rule risk and sharp class skew. Michael Zuo and three co-authors rate typical table makers, including self-coders, AI-made rival nets, spread models, and copula fakers, on money data sets. They add new privacy-saving builds of GAN and self-coder makers for this field.

The study tests whether and how well makers jointly hit data quality, later use, and privacy, weighing even and skewed inputs. Results light up the special snags of mixed-type traits and rare classes in money work, where naive making can leak or mislead. For workers picking a faker under rule watch, the side-by-side maps trade-offs that plain tests miss.
arxiv-2602-09588:
Tangled grain chains behave more like sticky solids than loose grains, thanks to reduced freedom and contact friction. Palash Sarate and three co-authors shear such chain groups head-on in their 2026 paper, asking how classic grain habits, shear clumping and plastic flow, change when shape itself binds the system together. The answer differs sharply from plain rubbing grains.

Chains longer than four beads harden markedly under shear, nearly no matter the applied normal stress, while shear clumping dies fully. Volume swelling in long-chain groups also persists into steady state rather than fading. Sim runs trace tensile forces to locally jammed grains with high coordination, giving a diffuse clumping zone and stronger strength gain. The study shows links steering flow and stiffness in order.
arxiv-2602-09688:
Germanium selenide has drawn strong eyes as a rare one-dim van der Waals matter. Seoung-Hun Kang and three co-authors study the solar promise of bulk-stacked GeSe chains using first-rules math with the GW guess and the Bethe-Salpeter rule to capture quasi and exciton effects. Their 2026 paper compares two stacking types, with the wider-gap type-I and smaller-gap type-II showing distinct ways.

Optical math shows much stronger visible-light uptake in type-II, yielding a spectrally limited maximum yield near a quarter at half a micron thickness. Phonon and room-heat atom moves tests show type-II is stable in motion, whereas type-I shows fake phonon modes hinting at shape warp. Type-II thus emerges as a hopeful stable soaker for thin-film solar cells, with better bend against typical two-dim van der Waals systems.
arxiv-2602-09888:
Mobile manipulators widen what robots can do, but whole-body teleoperation forces one operator to coordinate a wheeled base and two arms while watching obstacles and contact. Zihao Li and five co-authors present TriPilot-FF, an open-source whole-body teleoperation system for a bimanual mobile manipulator, in their 2026 paper. Its channel is a foot-operated pedal with lidar-driven haptics, paired with upper bimanual leader-follower control.

From proximity-to-obstacle signals along the commanded direction, a resistive pedal cue is rendered by the system using only a cheap mounted lidar. Commands steer toward safer behavior with no avoidance controller in play. Arm-side force reflection adds contact awareness, and live force and visual guidance of bimanual manipulability prompts base repositioning for better reach. The team also feeds teleoperation signals into an Action Chunking with Transformers policy with improved results, and releases the pedal design and software stack.
arxiv-2602-09988:
Kolmogorov-Arnold networks promise efficient recovery of unknown terms in physics models, but their record in constrained recurrent settings was still open. A 2026 paper led by Enzo Nicolas Spotorno, with two co-authors, plugs these networks into hard-constrained recurrent physics-informed architectures and checks the learned residual manifolds in oscillatory systems.

Small networks compete with standard multilayer perceptrons on simple polynomial residuals, the authors find, but they prove fragile. Deeper setups turn unstable, multiplicative terms fail, and standard networks usually win. The study points to limits of the original additive design for coupled states and offers early evidence for future hybrid models.
arxiv-2602-10088:
Confinement, the force that locks quarks inside hadrons, still lacks a simple order parameter in quantum chromodynamics. A 2026 paper led by Xavier Crean, with two co-authors, introduces a new observable called simplicity, built from Abelian monopole currents under a maximal Abelian gauge choice in SU(3) Yang-Mills theory. Simplicity is the zeroth Betti number divided by the first Betti number for a given current graph.

A lattice numerical study of its expectation value pins down the deconfinement temperature more accurately than conventional methods at comparable cost. The results tie Abelian current loops closely to the degrees of freedom that determine confinement. The work opens a path toward an order parameter exposing the theory's rich phase structure.
arxiv-2602-10488:
Khai-Hoan Nguyen-Dang studies when number fields admit a power integral basis in a 2026 paper. Earlier work showed that even a strengthened local setting does not force such a basis in general cubic and quartic fields. A positive proportion pass the local test yet fail globally. The paper asks whether the same failure persists inside tightly constrained one-parameter families.

For pure fields generated by a root of a square-free integer, the answer is no. The author proves that the set of cases passing the local obstruction test while failing monogenicity has density zero. In this family, monogenicity and making by the natural root share the same density. The proof isolates a reusable sieve process built on Eisenstein primes.
arxiv-2602-11188:
A radiating solution that works in general relativity may also work elsewhere. Olivier Minazzoli and Maxime Wavasseur embed the Mineur-Vaidya radiating solution in a magnet or electric field within Entangled Relativity. In that theory, a scalar field defined from a ratio becomes ill-defined for the bare solution.

The embedded solution shows Mineur-Vaidya as the limit where the field vanishes. That code also shows that naked singularities can form dynamically in Entangled Relativity, as in general relativity. The conclusion extends to any Einstein-Maxwell-dilaton theory, though the authors note it is not widely noted in the literature.
arxiv-2602-11388:
Theory says huge language models should overfit, yet they generalize. Dibyanayan Bandyopadhyay and Asif Ekbal propose that effective capacity lives in form shape, not setting count. Signal states lie on a small, sparse manifold, formalized as Sparse Semantic Dimension from a sparse autoencoder's active trait vocabulary.

Tests on two models show the bound gives non-vacuous certificates at realistic sample sizes. Counterintuitively, the larger model needs far fewer tuning samples to identify its active manifold, suggesting larger models learn more compressible semantic structures. Out-of-spread inputs trigger a trait explosion that signals knowledge doubt, making the frame a practical safety monitor as well as a transfer account.
arxiv-2602-11688:
Language-model services now route requests to engine replicas around the world, and routing must weigh cache locality, replica load, and shifting network delay at once. Existing systems score only part of that mix, piling load and cache unevenly across replicas. Alessio Ricci Toniolo and two co-authors present GORGO, a proxy design that factors network delay, prefill cost, and queueing delay through tunable parameters.

Because public chat datasets lack long-context, high-reuse data, the team also releases a synthetic dataset built from long-context production metadata. Evolutionary tuning on that data sets the policy parameters to optimize tail response time. On held-out windows the tuned policy improves tail time-to-first-token by about 7 to 16 percent and tail end-to-end delay by about 14 to 31 percent over simple baselines.
arxiv-2602-11888:
Measurements of the electron electric dipole moment have grown remarkably sensitive, opening prospects to probe new physics that first shows up at three-loop order. Tatsuya Banno and four co-authors calculate the full three-loop effect from additional weak-isospin multiplets with CP-violating Yukawa interactions. Here the dipole moment arises from two sources: a CP-odd three-way W-boson coupling and a CP-odd dipole operator. The two are generated at two-loop and three-loop levels respectively, after integrating them out.

Earlier work found the W-boson coupling could be probed in future tests, but its one-loop matching condition gains no large logarithmic boost because its anomalous dimension vanishes. The dipole term contributes at the same three-loop order. A central result is that the full three-loop calculation is three times the W-boson coupling alone, a difference future tests must reckon with.
arxiv-2602-11988:
Toolmakers strongly push tuning coding agents with repository context files like AGENTS.md, but no careful study had tested whether those files actually help. Thibaud Gloaguen and four co-authors evaluate task success in two settings: standard SWE-bench tasks with model-generated context files, and a novel collection of issues from repositories with developer-written context files. Surprisingly, providing context files does not generally raise task success rates, while lifting inference cost by over 20 percent on average.

The pattern holds across different language models, coding agents, and both machine-made and hand-written files. File instructions are well followed, the authors find, but project overviews, though popular and provider-recommended, do not help. Context files remain useful for setting non-standard practices, they conclude, but performance claims should be put to the test before deployment.
arxiv-2602-12088:
Rare heavy-flavor hadrons are hard to study because they appear seldom and decay in tangled patterns. Anisa Khatun studies one benchmark case, the Xi-c-plus baryon, in lead-lead collisions at the ALICE experiment, where full simulation of rare signals is costly and statistically thin.

This feasibility study explores generative adversarial networks trained on reconstructed quantities such as momenta, positions, and decay-vertex coordinates from augmented ALICE simulations. The networks aim to produce statistically useful synthetic signal samples without further full simulations. While the benchmark is one particle, the broader goal is to open searches for exotic heavy-flavor states with complex decays.
arxiv-2602-12188:
Degree counts alone cannot explain why postdoctoral posts keep growing while faculty posts stay flat in maths. Oluwatosin Babasola led this work with eight co-authors, building a discrete-time model of the United States maths pipeline from student to professor. Undergraduate and graduate numbers are rebuilt from national degree data, then postdoctoral and faculty flows are tracked through completion, exit, and hiring.

Faculty entry in the model is limited by vacancies, so rivalry for permanent posts grows with the queue below. Simulations show that more degrees do not yield more professors when turnover is low; surplus instead piles up at the postdoctoral stage. Long-run outcomes hinge most on exit rates and hiring capacity, not on degree production alone.
arxiv-2602-12488:
Ammonia gas harms ecosystems and human health, yet tracking it has relied on thermal IR sensors limited by thermal contrast, coarse space resolution, and infrequent aerial surveys. Nicholas Balasus led this work with five co-authors, showing that ammonia can be measured with shortwave IR imaging spectra instead. Reflected sunlight replaces thermal glow as the signal source, dodging thermal contrast limits.

That switch opens a large class of current and future imaging sensors to ammonia watching. As proof of concept, the team uses Tanager-1 data to measure gas from factory point sources in Pakistan and Uzbekistan. The newly shown power could widen ammonia tracking to many more sensors, giving fresher, finer maps of a harmful gas.
arxiv-2602-12588:
Key points hosting discrete nonlocal order values and twin edge modes have moved guarded topo phases into gapless regions. Longwen Zhou works alone here, revealing gapless topo phases in systems driven out of rest by regular drivings and open couplings. The focus is one-dimensional models with lattice balance, where topo can survive at edge cases.

Winding numbers are given by applying Cauchy's argument rule to the general Brillouin zone. That yields unified topo labels and bulk-edge links in both gapped phases and at gapless edge cases. The theory is shown in a broad class of Floquet two-part grids, unveiling unique topo edge cases of open Floquet origin. Findings identify gapless topo phases in driven open systems and uncover robust topo edge modes at phase changes beyond rest.
arxiv-2602-12788:
Sound waves that grow steep and spawn overtones need number methods that stay cheap and stable. Daniele Corallo, Pascal Lehner, and Christian Wieners present a space-time Galerkin scheme with a degree that adapts to the local flow, built for sound with strong non-linear effects. The model uses only first-order time rates of change, and its grid pairs a balanced Friedrichs scheme for wave parts with an inner penalty scheme for damping.

Newton's method solves the final non-linear set of formulas. The authors prove that answers exist, act sanely, and come with error bounds, starting from a linear calm result and building on it with a fixed-point proof. Number tests back the expected rates at which errors shrink and show that adapting the degree cuts the unknowns needed for target outputs. The model also shows hallmark non-linear effects like overtone creation, backing the approach.
arxiv-2602-12988:
The Dickman spread appears across number theory, combinatorics, physics, and biology, and a many-way version has lately been defined. Anastasiia Kovtun, Nikolai Leonenko, and Andrey Pepelyshev extend that definition to vector-valued random elements more broadly. They describe the new distributions as fixed points of an affine change built from a random matrix, itself from the matrix fast of a uniform random variable.

The authors prove the new distributions are infinitely divisible and operator selfdecomposable, two key structural traits. They also spot cases where the spread arises as a limiting law. The extension matters because many-way Lévy processes, whose small jumps the Dickman law helps approximate, need vector-valued tools, and this paper supplies them with proven traits.
arxiv-2602-13388:
Binary stars are gravitational two-body systems, and studying whole populations of them needs both orbit mechanics and statistics. Dyad is a Python library for that job. It is built around a TwoBody class that captures a binary from its two stellar masses plus the secondary's six orbital elements in a frame moving with the primary. A companion statistics module then treats each of those eight parameters as a random variable with a chosen distribution.

Included distributions cover stellar masses from Kroupa and Salpeter, plus mass ratios and orbital elements from Duquennoy and Mayor and from Moe and Di Stefano. The library is published in the Journal of Open Source Software, with its repository public for reuse. Amery Gration is the sole author.
arxiv-2602-13488:
Pilot studies are everywhere in human-computer interaction research, cited to justify designs, check procedures, or motivate methods, yet what counts as a pilot study remains vague and rarely examined. Medicine, nursing, and education have settled definitions, guidelines, reporting standards, and even a dedicated journal. The CHI community, by contrast, lacks a shared account of what pilots are, why they run, or how they should be reported. Many papers mention pilots only in passing, with no design, outcome, or link to the main study.

This meta-review offers early findings on how pilot studies are reported at CHI, exposing a methodological blind spot where a ubiquitous practice escapes scrutiny. Clarifying the role of pilots could tighten how HCI studies are designed, justified, and judged. Belu Ticona leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14288:
Gurkirat Wadhwa, writing alone, models a 2026 arXiv supply-chain game with two rival makers and two rival shops. Makers sell through shops while running take-back plans to get back used goods for reuse. Price and take-back choices mix, and buyers differ in wish to return goods.

Makers act as Stackelberg leaders, setting bulk prices and buyer take-back bonuses jointly, while shops vie in Nash style over shop prices. The model joins split linear demand with cross-price effects, set returns, and an inertia-based rule for splitting returned goods between makers. Closed-form Nash answers for the shop sub-game and symmetric Stackelberg outcomes anchor the study.
arxiv-2602-14588:
Alexander Freiszlinger and three co-authors derive a 2026 arXiv set of a posteriori error estimates for full-space transmission problems. Working upper bounds are proved for possible error in finite-element boundary-element linking forms for a non-linear Poisson-type flow problem. The bounds are free of the precise split plan and give assured upper bounds for possible error.

Working out those bounds leans on local helper finite element problems on patches in the inner zone and in a strip along the linking edge. Number tests show the worth of the error bound plan for a tuned mesh-refinement plan. They show how assured bounds can steer refinement where error piles up, rather than leaning on hunch gauges alone.
arxiv-2602-14688:
Measuring two couplings at once in a quantum device tests the limits of precision. Adnan Naimy, with three co-authors, enhances multiparameter estimation in cavity magnomechanics with a coherent feedback loop. The targets are the photon-magnon and magnon-mechanical coupling strengths.

A coherent drive plus tuned feedback cuts the error on both couplings at once. Performance is judged by the quantum Cramér-Rao bound under two formalisms. The right-logarithmic-derivative bound sits systematically below the symmetric one in this noncommutative setting. The scheme is presented as effective and experimentally feasible for hybrid quantum platforms.
arxiv-2602-14788:
