Yubin Cho and colleagues propose VIPA, a visual informative part attention framework for referring image segmentation, the task of cutting out an object named in natural language. Older methods push vision into language tokens, but VIPA exploits informative parts of visual context, called a visual expression, to hand the network structural and semantic target information directly.

That design cuts high-variance cross-modal projection and strengthens semantic consistency inside attention, helping fine-grained segmentation follow the words more faithfully. A visual expression module supports the attention mechanism throughout. Language-guided cutting gains a steadier visual anchor.
arxiv-2602-15088:
Franch and colleagues release IT-DPC-SRI, the first public long-term archive of Italian weather radar rainfall estimates, spanning 16 years from 2010 to 2025. It holds surface rainfall intensity observations from the Italian Civil Protection radar mosaic, harmonized into a coherent cloud-optimized Zarr datacube. The archive holds over one million timesteps at resolutions between 5 and 15 minutes, covering a kilometer domain at 1 kilometer resolution, compressed from 7 terabytes to 51 gigabytes.

The release repairs years of fragmentation, as Italian radar data had sat scattered across mixed formats, domains, and projections. Users can reach a static versioned snapshot on Zenodo, cloud-native access on the ECMWF European Weather Cloud, or a live version on ArcoDataHub. The archive fills a notable gap, since Italy does not join the EUMETNET OPERA pan-European radar composite, and it ships under a CC BY-SA license.
arxiv-2602-15188:
Feintzeig shows that quantization acts as a categorical equivalence for Hilbert bimodules and Lagrangian relations. Classical and quantum theories carry distinct representation types, each matching possible values of broad charges in its context. The paper shows a sense in which the structure of these theories is kept from classical to quantum physics.

To show this, Feintzeig covers morphisms keeping representations in both contexts: Lagrangian relations in the old world and Hilbert bimodules in the quantum world. Such morphisms matter because they induce representations in both worlds. The quantum step and the limit back are treated as functors between these groups, via strict warping of a Poisson algebra and via spread of an evenly smooth bundle of C-star algebras. With those tools, he proves the two functors are almost-inverse to each other, establishing the match.
arxiv-2602-15488:
Yu and colleagues tackle a search task common in modern AI and data systems. The task is to find near neighbours for a high-dimensional vector among items passing limits on several numeric traits. Older indexes handle one trait at a time, and stretching them tends to work poorly. The team answers with KHI, an index pairing a tree over attribute space with fast graph search at each node.

A skew-aware split rule keeps the tree shallow. A query walks the tree, then a greedy search runs on the graphs it meets. Tests on four real data sets show high throughput and high recall. KHI beats the best prior method by about two and a half times on average in queries per second, and far more on the hardest set. Gains grow when few items pass the filter, when more neighbours are sought, and when more traits are used.
arxiv-2602-15788:
Csörnyei and Gutiérrez investigate whether Type II supernovae split into distinct groups or form a smooth range. But whether those reflect distinct progenitors or a smooth spread remains debated. Growing evidence suggests smoothness between slow-fading IIP and fast-fading IIL blasts. The team tests that smoothness with a stats analysis of spectral time series, linking spectral shapes to light-curve decline rates.

They introduce a new standard method for Type II spectra. After flattening spectra via continuum scaling, they fill in feature spectra onto a fixed epoch grid using Gaussian process fit and principal component analysis. Results show IIP and IIL forming a spectroscopic smooth range. Variety is driven mainly by two parts: a smooth group with well-defined P-Cygni shapes and a less-regular group with stronger near-star matter mixing. Variety shrinks over time, and steeper declines match weaker spectral marks.
arxiv-2602-15988:
Li and colleagues build a training phantom that grades kidney ureteroscopy without an expert standing by. Navigating a ureteroscope through the kidney is hard to learn, and current training leans on one to one expert feedback inside the operating room, which limits practice opportunities.

Their system needs only scope video. A slow, thorough prior pass builds a reference reconstruction of the phantom kidney, against which any trainee pass can be localized to flag missed calyces. Across fifteen exploration videos, sixty nine of seventy four calyces were classified correctly. Camera pose error stayed under four millimetres, and a typical one to two minute exploration took ten minutes to grade. The result is automated, out of theatre feedback for a steep skill.
arxiv-2602-16088:
Alexei Morozov and Kazumi Okuyama find a short cut through a hard sum from the Gaussian matrix model. The sum at issue is an average of an exponential trace, a group character that extends the Schur polynomial. Here time variables are swapped for traces of products of matrices that do not commute. Matrix entries made from extended Laguerre polynomials make the sums harder still.

The authors set out generic sum rules that spell out any such trace in terms of convolutions of just one Laguerre polynomial. That is a big simplification. A web of matrix entries collapses to repeat use of one known function. For readers who work with matrix models and symmetric functions, the paper gives a clean path through sums that once looked daunting, with one Laguerre polynomial doing most of the work.
arxiv-2602-16288:
Inigo Asiain and coauthors ask whether the Standard Model Effective Field Theory suffices for Higgs pair production. They study Higgs-boson pair production in that theory up to dimension six, and in the Higgs Effective Field Theory at leading order. The goal is to assess which description fits concrete ultraviolet scenarios. Motivated by Loryon-inspired models, they compare cross sections predicted by full models against their effective counterparts.

They identify regimes where the two effective theories provide comparable descriptions, and clarify the limits required for their couplings to match. They also find that, for parts of parameter space in some models, the Higgs effective theory can reproduce Higgs pair production more accurately than the Standard Model effective theory. That finding highlights di-Higgs measurements as a potential probe of non-linear electroweak dynamics.
arxiv-2602-16488:
Jonathan Cook leads four coauthors on teaching large language models to learn from language feedback. Such models often fail to learn from corrections in conversation and rarely ask for feedback when unsure, leaving dialogues static and one-sided. The authors draw on social meta-learning in humans, or learning how to learn from others, and turn it into a fine-tuning method.

Models train in simulated teaching dialogues, where fixed tasks become interactive social learning problems. The method teaches models to use conversation to solve problems they cannot solve in one turn, and the skill transfers across domains: training on math helps coding, and vice versa. Trained only on fully stated problems, the models still handle vague tasks better, asking for missing facts instead of guessing early. The paper offers a scalable route to systems that learn from language feedback.
arxiv-2602-16688:
Suhas Thejaswi settles the hardness of approximation for the fair k-center problem. Data points in a metric space are split into groups. Centers must be chosen with a set number from each group. The goal is to minimize the worst distance from any point to its nearest center. A factor-three approximation was known. It was open whether that bound was tight. Plain k-center admits a factor-two approximation, so doubt lingered.

Assuming P differs from NP, the author proves no fast algorithm can beat a factor just below three, for any small margin. The result holds even with only two disjoint groups and at least one center from each. It extends to the one-per-group setting with any number of groups. The factor-three barrier is thus inherent, and existing three-approximation algorithms are optimal.
arxiv-2602-16788:
Fabian Ballar Trigueros and Markus Heyl show that quantum circuits can learn nonequilibrium states with long-range order that equilibrium forbids. Equilibrium ensembles tightly constrain quantum matter: the Mermin-Wagner theorem bars long-range order in low-dimensional systems beyond the ground state. Coherent circuits, by contrast, can engineer states outside equilibrium reach.

Variational quantum circuits are built to generate symmetry-broken and symmetry-protected topological states with long-range order in one-dimensional systems at finite energy density, where equilibrium states are typically featureless. The learned states can show enhanced metrological traits, with quantum Fisher information near a GHZ state yet robust against local measures. Quantum engineers get a dynamical route to phases of matter beyond equilibrium limits.
arxiv-2602-16888:
A. C. Burgess, P. H. Danziger, and A. Lacaze-Masmonteil solve the directed Oberwolfach problem of order two modulo four with cycles of even lengths. The Oberwolfach problem asks for a factorization of the complete graph in which each factor is isomorphic to a specific factor. The directed version asks for a directed factorization of the complete symmetric digraph in which each directed factor is isomorphic to a specific directed factor.

Here, directed factors consist of cycles of even lengths, and the order of the complete symmetric digraph is congruent to two modulo four. The paper provides a complete solution for that case, giving combinatorial designers a finished result for a natural directed extension of a classic decomposition problem.
arxiv-2602-16988:
Xin-Ru Liu and co-authors apply the Regge trajectory approach to doubly heavy triquarks, three-quark systems with two heavy quarks. They propose Regge trajectory relations for those triquarks and use them to crudely estimate spectra for eight combinations of charm, bottom, up, down, and strange quarks. Both lambda-trajectories and rho-trajectories are investigated.

The triquark Regge trajectory becomes a new and very simple approach for estimating triquark spectra. It also provides a simple method to investigate rho-mode and sigma-mode excitations of pentaquarks and hexaquarks in the triquark picture. Spin-averaged masses of the ground states of three pentaquarks are estimated as well, consistent with other theoretical predictions. Hadron physicists get a spare, simple tool for spectra that are otherwise hard to compute.
arxiv-2602-17088:
Haoyu Wang led a six-author team on machine unlearning, the task of making a trained model forget specific data without wrecking the rest. Aggressive erasure usually damages retained knowledge, while gentle erasure leaves traces of the target behind. The paper traces that trade-off to feature entanglement: class concepts share associated features while keeping their own discriminative parts.

Their method, Machine-Guided Unlearning or MeGU, steers forgetting with concept-aware re-alignment. Multimodal large language models assign perturbing labels that set re-alignment directions, inter-class similarities feed a light transition matrix, and a positive-negative noise pair suppresses target patterns while reinforcing shared ones. The coordinated design achieves selective forgetting that curbs both under- and over-unlearning.
arxiv-2602-17288:
Anuj Gupta, writing alone, documents the practical craft of training a scientific language model from raw sources. Frontier models show strong reasoning and math skill, yet the process of building domain-focused science models from raw material stays under-documented. The paper gives a detailed case study of training a scientific model with over a billion parameters directly from raw arXiv LaTeX sources in mathematics, computer science, and theoretical physics.

The end-to-end pipeline covers metadata filtering, archive validation, LaTeX extraction, text normalization, domain-aware token splitting, and dense transformer training under constrained compute. Across two dozen experimental runs, the author analyzes stability, scaling, data yield losses, and infrastructure bottlenecks. Preprocessing choices strongly affect usable token volume, token splitting affects symbolic stability, and storage and input-output limits can rival compute as constraints. The account targets researchers with moderate budgets.
arxiv-2602-17588:
Faria Huq and team ask when a human should step into web agent work, and why. Current agents often sail past key choice points. At other times they pester users for needless approval. The gap is a missing model of human intervention in collaborative web tasks.

The team built CowCorpus: hundreds of real-user navigation paths holding thousands of interleaved human and agent acts. They sort intervention into four styles, from hands-off supervision to full user takeover. Models trained to foresee intervention from user style beat base models by a wide margin. In live tests, users rated intervention-aware agents markedly more useful. Agents that adapt to people are the payoff.
arxiv-2602-17688:
Anton Xue and team introduce AnchorTree, a frame that anchors diffusion-based code making in the rigid structure of programming languages. Diffusion language models allow global planning and step-by-step refinement, yet past versions often break programs because they ignore language structure. AnchorTree uses the abstract syntax tree to rank tokens by salience.

Keywords and identifiers get resolved first, forming a structural scaffold that guides the rest of the build. The team validates the frame through AnCoder, a family of models showing that anchored diffusion offers a lean path to high-quality code. Code that respects structure from the start fails less often at run time, a practical gain for diffusion methods in programming.
arxiv-2602-17788:
Fariha Iftikhar and Gábor Nagy enumerate nilpotent loops by orbit counting. They study central extensions of nilpotent loops by elementary abelian p-groups using normalized cocycles. An affine automorphism group acting on the full cocycle space gives a direct correspondence between affine orbits and isomorphism classes of central extensions.

That correspondence yields an efficient orbit-counting method for enumerating nilpotent loops. The method reproduces known results for orders below twenty-four. It then enumerates the nilpotent loops of order twenty-four with center of size at least three, a concrete advance in the classification of these algebraic structures. Readers gain both a counting tool and a verified census at the new order.
arxiv-2602-17888:
Sayeed Shafayet Chowdhury and team evaluate machine learning prediction of surgical outcomes in chronic rhinosinusitis from clinical data. Artificial intelligence has transformed medical forecasts. Yet predictions from pre-planned, uniform data in watching clinical trials remain underexplored, despite cost and outcome potential. Chronic rhinosinusitis is a persistent swelling disease of the sinus spaces lasting over three months, burdening quality of life and social cost.

The team tests guided models for predicting surgical benefit, using Sino-Nasal Outcome Test-22 as the outcome. Their cohort from a watching trial includes patients who all underwent surgery. The question is whether models trained only on pre-surgery data can spot patients who might not have been recommended surgery beforehand. Across algorithms including a combo, the best model reaches about eighty-five percent sorting scores. On thirty held-out cases, it reaches eighty percent scores, beating expert doctors at about seventy-six percent.
arxiv-2602-18788:
Burmese is a major language that language models still serve poorly, and until now it lacked a single broad test of how well they handle it. Thura Aung, with three co-authors, introduces BURMESE-SAN in 2026, the first holistic benchmark for Burmese across understanding, reasoning, and generation.

Seven subtasks span question answering, sentiment analysis, toxicity detection, causal reasoning, natural language inference, summarisation, and translation, several of them new for Burmese. Native speakers built the benchmark to keep the language natural and culturally authentic and to limit translation artefacts. Large-scale tests of open and commercial models show that design, representation. Tuning matter more than size alone, with regional fine-tuning and newer generations gaining most, and the benchmark is released as a public leaderboard.
arxiv-2602-18888:
Adapters let large pretrained models be fine-tuned cheaply. But do they work when medical data is extremely scarce? Ziquan Zhu, with ten co-authors, gives the first broad study of that question in 2026. The answer is sobering. Conventional adapters can harm performance under severe data limits. With under one percent of training data, they can do worse than simple linear probing.

Analysis points to a shrinking effective receptive field as a key cause. The authors therefore propose the Dual-Kernel Adapter. It widens spatial context with large-kernel convolutions. It keeps local detail with small-kernel counterparts. Across diverse classification and segmentation benchmarks, the new adapter beats existing adapter methods. It sets new leading results in both data-poor and data-rich settings.
arxiv-2602-19088:
How can performance under faults be predicted before a system is built? Ziwei Zhou, with four co-authors, offers the first formal answer in 2026. Distributed systems face faults and even adversarial behaviour. Predicting throughput and latency from designs alone has long resisted solution.

The frame centres on a fault injector with a wide fault library. Model merging joins system and tool into one unified model. Statistical analysis then yields throughput and latency numbers. Formalisation in Maude produces an automated tool, PERF, with fast stats. Tests on representative systems show accurate predictions across fault settings. Estimates from formal designs match evaluations on real deployments. Design-time prediction thus becomes practical for faulty environments.
arxiv-2602-19188:
Multi-modal models read text in images but miss where it sits. Chen Duan, with five co-authors, adds place sense in 2026 with PositionOCR. Language-model readers excel at word work yet lack place thought for text spotting and grounding. Huge weight counts also demand heavy compute and data. Text-spotting experts predict spots well but lack meaning thought.

PositionOCR merges both strengths in a weight-efficient hybrid. A text-spotting model's place skill joins a language model's contextual thought. Only around one hundred thirty million weights train. Text grounding and spotting performance excels, consistently surpassing traditional multi-modal models. Place accuracy thus becomes affordable, not an afterthought.
arxiv-2602-19488:
New ideas spread through populations, and Bass-type models have long described that spread. Nicolas Langrené and three co-authors survey research on how innovations diffuse, starting from Rogers in 1962 and the seminal Bass model of 1969. Generalizations and random extensions are covered, including counting, diffusion, and uncertain processes, along with ways to estimate model parameters.

Ways to estimate parameters range from classical statistical methods to Bayesian filtering and metaheuristic optimization. Other models, especially agent-based models, are also covered. The survey traces how Bass-type modeling has changed over past decades, giving readers a map of the field's progress and its open questions.
arxiv-2602-19788:
Meta-learning usually adapts well to new tasks that resemble its training tasks, but it can fail, even harming performance, when the target task shifts away from the source distribution. A 2026 arXiv paper by Lotta Mäkinen and two co-authors proposes a causally aware Bayesian meta-learning method for that harder setting.

The method conditions task priors on latent causal embeddings computed in advance, so transfer follows mechanistic similarity rather than spurious correlation. It also fits realistic deployment, where target data are scarce and adaptation leans on noisy expert judgments about causal similarity between tasks. Theory shows this conditioning controls prior mismatch and curbs negative transfer. Tests in simulations and in a large cross-disease clinical prediction setting show less negative transfer and better out-of-distribution adaptation.
arxiv-2602-19988:
Many-variable time series pose a classic problem: when did the underlying behaviour change? A 2026 arXiv paper by Yi Xu and Yeonwoo Rho answers with random projections, a method that sidesteps high-dimensional machinery.

Projecting a many-variable series into one dimension lets the analyst use the rich toolkit for single-variable series. The authors apply random projections repeatedly and combine the single-variable test results with standard multi-test methods. Simulations suggest the method has better size and power, and locates changes more accurately, than alternatives. Random projections can, however, make estimated locations jump around. The authors therefore advise repeating the procedure and using the most common estimated location as the final guide. An application to an Australian temperature data set shows the method at work, within a single-change-point setting.
arxiv-2602-20088:
Tissues can flow like fluids because cells push and pull on each other, yet how that fluid character shapes tissue structure remains unclear. A 2026 arXiv paper by Giulia L. Celora and three co-authors models cell clusters migrating as active droplets along chemical gradients, or chemotaxis.

The model follows an active droplet growing under a self-made chemical slope. Simulations match the experiments: droplets undergo shape shifts driven by proliferation. A multiple scales study shows droplet motion tracks moving wave patterns governed by a nonlinear eigenvalue problem tied to droplet volume growth. Shifts may be continuous or may arrive through a discontinuous bifurcation. Further study traces shifts to tiny terms from the rear and front contact lines. Two dimensionless parameters determine each shift's nature: internal stress balance and coupling strength between movement and the chemical field. The results describe the morphodynamics of migrating thin droplets.
arxiv-2602-20188:
Some Calabi-Yau threefolds are suspected to be rank-2 attractors. Their Galois representations would split into pieces coming from modular forms. A 2026 arXiv paper by Neil Dummigan, working alone, attempts to prove that the four-dimensional Galois representations attached to a certain Calabi-Yau threefold are reducible.

The two-dimensional composition factors would come from specific modular forms of weights two and four, both of level fourteen. The claim was essentially conjectured by Meyer and Verrill. Candelas, de la Ossa, Elmi, van Straten revisited it. Their computations of Euler factors across a pencil of Calabi-Yau threefolds marked this fibre as a strong rank-2 attractor candidate, one of three. The paper reports its argument honestly, including an error in Section 7, so readers gain both the modularity strategy for this fibre and a clear view of where the proof currently stands.
arxiv-2602-20288:
Yi-Ming Wu and six co-authors study superconductivity and magnetism in bilayer nickelates from an itinerant viewpoint. They start from a tight-binding fit to recent photoemission measurements on compressively strained thin films. They add the standard on-site repulsions among partly filled eg orbitals: intra-orbital and inter-orbital terms, Hund coupling, and pair hopping. Particle-hole fluctuations then dress those bare interactions into an effective pairing interaction.

When Hund coupling is strong, s-wave superconductivity and a spin-density-wave order at one wavevector emerge as the favored ground states. When it is weaker, d-wave pairing and a spin-density-wave order at a second wavevector take the lead. The pattern matches earlier density-matrix renormalization-group studies in broad outline. The central lesson is that Hund coupling plays a key role in deciding which superconducting and magnetic states win in bilayer nickelates.
arxiv-2602-20688:
Models of matter infall from a collapsing molecular cloud anchor numerical studies of protoplanetary disk formation and evolution. E. R. Redkin and E. I. Vorobyov analyze the widely used Nakamoto and Nakagawa model from nineteen ninety-four and propose modifications to complement it. Improvements include computing the outer boundary of a molecular cloud and refining the initial density distribution inside.

Because a cloud has finite size, the paper also modifies how the mass infall rate onto the disk during collapse is computed. The enhancements aim to eliminate key limitations of the initial model while keeping its advantages, such as simplicity in number work. Using the modified model, the authors investigate the duration of the early phase of young star growth and compare modeling results with sky data. Results indicate a shorter early phase, above all in star-forming regions with a high amplitude of initial density bumps in prestellar cores.
arxiv-2602-20888:
Effect algebras carry a notion of order, and the maps that preserve that order have a known general form in the complex case. Peter Semrl gives a simpler proof of that description in this 2026 arXiv paper, built on projective geometry. The new proof also works in the real case, where the older argument did not reach.

As an application, the author classifies pairs of matrix intervals that are order isomorphic, and describes the general form of order isomorphisms for any such pair. The result tightens a corner of order theory with a shorter, wider argument. Readers get both the simplified proof and a complete classification for matrix intervals.
arxiv-2602-21088:
Catalytic space lets an algorithm borrow memory that must be restored afterward. Roman Edenhofer proves a space-space trade-off for directed connectivity in that model in this 2026 arXiv paper. A tunable parameter interpolates between the classical Savitch bound and a catalytic endpoint with logarithmic workspace and much larger catalytic memory.

A catalytic variant of Savitch's algorithm supplies the endpoint as a warm-up. Up to logarithmic factors, the catalyst size matches the smallest currently known for catalytic logspace algorithms. The techniques also extend to counting walks of a given length between two vertices. Readers get a smooth spectrum of time-space options rather than two isolated results.
arxiv-2602-21288:
Matter-wave tools with massive nano-grains are keenly touchy to speed-up noise. Sneha Narasimha Moorthy, Andrew Geraci, Sougato Bose, and Anupam Mazumdar study that touchiness in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their system is a one-loop Stern-Gerlach wave tool holding a nitrogen-vacancy nano-diamond in a wave-like trap under a magnet-field gradient. Outside speed-up and tilt jitters enter as random inputs.

The authors work out the random phase gap between arms and the phase loss rate that follows, plus transfer functions for each noise channel. Stated limits on noise power spectra follow for a stacked state around one nano-meter under an order target. A working regime also emerges where speed-up noise can be cut by varying tilt or speed-up at fixed other dials. Builders get numbered noise budgets for nano-grain wave work.
arxiv-2602-21388:
Ryan O. Behunin and five co-authors derive a quantum master equation for phonon decoherence caused by two-level tunneling states in crystal resonators. Phonon modes in clean crystals now reach the quantum ground state. Surface oxides and damaged dead layers host tunneling states. Their dissipation grows worse at lower temperatures, a nasty problem for quantum devices.

Their framework couples one chosen phonon mode to a large ensemble of tunneling states. That lets decoherence be computed for realistic devices. Applied to quartz micro-resonators with a thin surface layer of tunneling states, it finds coherence time is longest at low temperatures despite higher dissipation. Coupling also drops for modes whose strain vanishes at the surfaces. The result guides design of longer-lived mechanical quantum devices.
arxiv-2602-21788:
Scaling long-context skills matters for large language models. Real data hold many strings of varied lengths, and current training toolkits rely on static split plans that suffer load skew, redundant chatter, and poor hardware use under varied data. Yifan Niu and four co-authors propose Flexible Context Parallelism, which regroups link groups and context split degrees on the fly during training. It covers flexible non-power-of-two split degrees and uses a fast method to build near-optimal plans with only tiny cost per batch.

Flexible Context Parallelism keeps high hardware speed even under wild varied data. Tests show it clearly beats Megatron-LM and DeepSpeed in both language model and mixed-media training. It reaches nearly 1.5 times speedup in average throughput while keeping near-linear scaling speed across large-scale clusters. For wild skewed batches, it more than doubles throughput.
arxiv-2602-21888:
Ankit Bhojak and one co-author prove weak type (1,1) bounds for the variation and jump operators for truncations of singular integrals with rough kernels. The finding settles a puzzle Jones, Seeger and Wright had left open since 2008. The setting is one where classical smoothness assumptions fail, since the kernels involved are rough.

As an immediate consequence of the variational estimate, they recover the weak type (1,1) boundedness of the maximal truncation operator for the same class of integrals. The result thus closes a long-standing gap for this class of rough-kernel singular integrals.
arxiv-2602-22188:
Predicting how fluid flows through rock and reacts at its surfaces means solving costly partial differential equations at high resolution. Nathalie C. Pinheiro and six co-authors build eight surrogate models that mimic those simulations cheaply, for multi-query jobs like uncertainty quantification and optimization. Four are reduced-order models pairing a compression network with a prediction network.

The other four are single neural networks with grid-size invariance: they can infer on domains larger than their training domains, a property the authors define for image-to-image models. Together the eight surrogates trade a little fidelity for large speedups where many scenarios must be run. Engineers gain fast stand-ins for simulations too expensive to repeat.
arxiv-2602-22288:
Sudden cardiac death in Chagas cardiomyopathy is hard to predict, especially for patients not already flagged as high risk. Vinícius P. Chagas and six co-authors note that AI risk models face a trust barrier: they read as black boxes, and heuristic explanations without correctness guarantees can mislead decisions. They apply a logic-based explainability method with correctness guarantees to the problem.

Applied to a classifier with over ninety-five percent accuracy and recall, the method achieves perfect explanation fidelity and beats heuristic rivals on consistency and robustness. Clinicians gain explanations they can verify, not just plausible stories. The approach strengthens trust in AI-driven risk tools for a disease where a missed warning can be fatal.
arxiv-2602-22988:
Bum Jun Kim and four co-authors predict transformer training divergence before training starts. Divergence wastes compute, yet practitioners usually learn of instability only after costly runs begin. Residual Koopman Spectral Profiling extracts spectral features from a single forward pass at initialization, using whitened dynamic mode decomposition on layer-wise residual snapshots.

The central diagnostic, near-unit spectral mass, measures the share of modes clustered near the unit circle and captures instability risk. It predicts divergence with an AUROC near one, beating the best gradient baseline. When risk runs high, Koopman Spectral Shaping reshapes spectra during training and prevents divergence. It cuts the rate from about two-thirds to about one-eighth without normalization layers at high learning rates, and allows fifty to one hundred fifty percent higher rates.
arxiv-2602-23388:
Swati Sharma and two co-authors survey Indian speech data sets through Task-Lens, a cross-task profiling study for low-resource tongues. Inclusive speech technology needs multilingual data sets, but researchers often do not know what task-specific resources exist for low-resource tongues, a problem especially acute in linguistically diverse India. Prior surveys usually catalogue data sets for a single task.

Task-Lens instead assesses the readiness of 50 Indian speech data sets spanning 26 languages for nine downstream speech tasks. The team first analyzes which data sets hold data tags and properties suited to each task. Task-aligned enhancements then unlock each data set's full downstream potential. Finally, the team identifies tasks and tongues critically underserved by current resources. Many data sets hold untapped metadata supporting several tasks, so cross-task linkages can stretch scarce resources and guide where new data sets matter most.
arxiv-2602-23488:
Tarini Kumar Dutta and three co-authors extend a dynamical system model of cancer treatment by adding virotherapy to chemotherapy and immunotherapy. The model tracks cancer spread in healthy tissue and allows computer experiments on treatment combinations that cannot be run in the laboratory.

The authors show solutions exist, stay bounded, and remain nonnegative over each finite time interval, hence biologically feasible. A time-stepping algorithm is built and implemented, and simulations cover no treatment, each treatment alone, and several combinations. Combined treatments prove more effective in the simulations, though the authors note they ignore possible limits or incompatibilities of joint use in practice. Once validated in the field, the model could help design combination treatment schedules.
arxiv-2602-23688:
Qing He and five co-authors ask whether tailored nudging wears off, in a long-run study of AI self-models for habit buy-in. Keeping habit-change tech worth its cost remains a key challenge. AI self-models, making tailored portrayals of one's ideal self, have shown promise for driving change, yet prior work largely probes short-term effects.

The team presents one of the first long-run tests of AI self-models in fitness use through a two-stage study. A one-week, three-arm trial with 28 people found visual self-models drove initial score gains, while sound self-models showed no real effects. A later four-week study with 31 people showed visual self-models kept higher scores but with fading gains after two weeks. Talks uncovered a spark effect feeding early drive through clear, doable goals, followed by habit and buy-in evening out scores.
arxiv-2602-23988:
Kristian Stølevik Olsen and two co-authors derive an information bound on how fast a smart active particle can navigate toward a distant target. The 2026 paper gives minimal information processing to an active particle model, a step beyond usual active matter, which often omits sensing and decision-making entirely.

The authors bound navigation speed across a wide range of information strategies, joining intermittent motion based on renewal with the Cramér-Rao inequality. The framework captures hallmarks of cognitive systems: a speed-accuracy trade-off balancing noise against reliability, with optimal sensing durations. Letting stored information decay before action slows navigation, yet the trade-off stays governed mainly by external orientational noise and proves remarkably insensitive to memory decay. The bound links sensing, memory, and motion in life-like systems.
arxiv-2602-24188:
Jacob Eisenstein and four co-authors present MT-PingEval, a scalable, verifiable methodology that evaluates language models in multi-turn collaboration with private information. The 2026 paper uses collaborative games that require effective communication about information each agent holds privately. They enable an interactive scaling analysis where a fixed token budget is split across a variable number of turns.

Models often fail to beat a non-interactive baseline by using interactive collaboration: in the baseline, one agent sums up its information while the other acts at once, despite substantial headroom for improvement. That gap points to significant weaknesses when models plan and execute multi-turn collaborative conversations. Linguistic analysis of sycophancy, information density, and discourse coherence finds no single explanation, but humans reach comparable task success at better token efficiency.
arxiv-2603-00088: Neumann and Singh argue AI safety evaluation must reckon with cascading effects along the algorithmic supply chain. Foundation models now sit inside chains of technical and organisational parts that mediate, adapt and augment model behaviour for particular uses. Yet most evaluations test model capabilities or single components alone, missing how parts interact, reinforce or counteract each other. The authors map cascade problems in deployed systems from component and stakeholder viewpoints, and propose research directions for treating the cascade itself as an object of analysis.
arxiv-2603-00388: Brown and three colleagues test how heat treatment changes low frequency superconducting quarter wave resonators built from bulk niobium and polished chemically. Tested near 4.3 kelvin, a two day bake at 120 degrees Celsius cuts surface resistance two to three fold by trimming one loss term. It also eases the medium field quality slope by about two fifths on average. A shorter bake at 350 degrees gives no gain, unlike results seen at higher frequencies.
arxiv-2603-00788: Russo and five colleagues build steady states centred on Lissajous figures of two dimensional oscillators, by projecting coherent states onto degenerate sets. The build maps phase kinks in each wavefunction and links laminar probability current flow to quantum interference. That work yields a clear vortex state for the two dimensional oscillator. A final check confirms the states as true coherent states through resolution, with the isotropic case giving SU(2) states.
arxiv-2603-01288: Ait Khayi offers the first Mamba-Transformer hybrid for pick-out summarization, picking key lines from long texts without cuts. An encoder captures line-level meaning, a Mamba state space model tracks links between lines, and a linear scorer scores line worth. Across news, debate, and science domains under low-resource settings, it beats BERTSUM and MATCHSUM, including a gain of 0.23 ROUGE-1 on ArXiv, with clear gains on all data sets and 24 to 27 percent faster runs on news summarization.
arxiv-2603-01388:
Graph neural networks learn from data shaped as nodes and links, but they have clear limits. Asela Hevapathige, Ahad Zehmakan, Asiri Wijesinghe, and Saman Halgamuge take up that problem in this 2026 work. Common models treat all neighbors in the same way and miss how nodes hold different roles in larger patterns.

Their fix, called ISP, groups nodes by shared traits and then passes facts along step by step in layers. A new test and a neural version both come from that one idea. Proofs show the method can tell apart graphs that older tests cannot, and it resists a known flaw where node traits blur. Tests on graph tasks, node tasks, and spread tasks beat strong prior models.
arxiv-2603-01588:
Daniel Biebert, Christian Hakert, Kay Heider, and colleagues make decision forests useful even when time runs out mid-run. Their 2026 work targets small devices where a full forest pass may not fit the time budget. An anytime method should give its best guess so far whenever it is stopped.

Older anytime forests stop between whole trees, yet each step down a tree already sharpens the guess. The team orders single steps across the whole forest to gain accuracy as fast as possible. One exact order costs too much to compute, so they offer two greedy orders that walk down or up the trees. The upward order scores near the exact best and near full runs. That makes forests safer for tight, real-time jobs.
arxiv-2603-01988:
Ilya Gorshkov links a special class of groups to graded non-associative algebras in this 2026 work. He starts from faithful odd transposition groups, where a normal set of involutions generates the group. An involution is an element that is its own inverse, and products of two here have odd order.

His subclass fixes that product order to one prime for every pair of involutions. From any such group plus a scalar parameter, he constructs a non-associative, non-commutative algebra. Each generating involution becomes a primitive semisimple idempotent inside that algebra. Those idempotents define a two-part grading of the algebra, splitting it into even and odd pieces. The construction ties group symmetry to algebra structure, in the spirit of axial algebra theory.
arxiv-2603-02188:
Songtao Liu, Hongwu Peng, Zhiwei Zhang, and colleagues cut memory traffic in large language models in this 2026 paper. During text generation, stored key and value data must be reloaded at each step. A recent design shrinks that store, but its single shared head cannot split across chips. Each chip then reloads the full store for every token, wasting bandwidth.

Their design, MLRA, uses several low-rank heads that can split across four chips. That split restores the gains of parallel decoding. In tests, the model matched top scores on language quality and downstream tasks. It also decoded text almost three times faster than the prior design. Code, weights, and data were released for others to check and build on.
arxiv-2603-02488:
Soham Nagawanshi, Shalini Panthangi, Chen Wang, and colleagues add machine learning help to streaming algorithms in this 2026 paper. Streaming algorithms summarize huge data flows in tiny memory. Learning-augmented versions use a model's predictions to beat classic space limits. Unequal weights break that progress, though, as with sliding windows where old data must expire.

Their oracle flags the heavy hitters, the most frequent items in a data set. With that help, they build algorithms for several core problems in time-decay settings. Targets include norm and moment estimation, frequency estimation, and rectangular variants. Theory is paired with tests on real and synthetic data. Results show the predicted space savings hold up in practice, even as old items fade.
arxiv-2603-02588:
Minseok Choi, Dongjin Kim, Seungbin Yang, and colleagues build a guardrail model for specialized domains in this 2026 paper. Safety filters for language models mostly cover general conversation. Finance, medicine, and law are rich in jargon where harmful content hides more easily. General guardrails leave those domains exposed to adversarial prompts.

Their model, ExpGuard, is trained for those three domains specifically. A curated data set holds tens of thousands of labeled prompts with refusal and compliant replies. Domain experts annotated the high-quality test split. On that test and eight public benchmarks, ExpGuard stayed competitive overall. Against domain-specific attacks it beat leading rivals by clear margins in prompt and response classification. Code, data, and the model are open-sourced for adaptation to more domains.
arxiv-2603-02688:
Izat Temiraliev, Diji Yang, and Yi Zhang argue that robots should look things up before they act. Their 2026 paper defines Retrieval-Augmented Robotics for cases where a robot gets no demonstrations at all. A robot facing a complex furniture kit lacks the exact steps, and its built-in knowledge cannot fill that gap.

Their system loops through three steps: retrieve, reason, and act. The robot searches visual manuals, matches flat diagrams to real three-dimensional parts, and then builds an action plan. On a hard long-horizon assembly test, planning grounded in retrieved manuals beat both unaided reasoning and example-based retrieval. The work extends search from answering questions to driving physical action.
arxiv-2603-02788:
Zhiyu Ni, Yifeng Xiao, and Zheng Liang build an agent whose job is to grade other agents fairly. Their 2026 framework tackles a practical problem: tests of reasoning agents must be repeatable, auditable, and able to survive crashes. The tested agent only needs a standard agent-to-agent interface.

An assessor agent hands out tasks, enforces time and step budgets, parses answers, and logs structured failure types. As a case study, the team graded an agent that turns plain-language logic problems into solver programs. On a cleaned, solver-checked set of first-order logic questions, that agent scored well above a chain-of-thought baseline. The setup shows how automated grading can stay rigorous without trusting the agent's own report.
arxiv-2603-02988:
Barbora Benešová, Malte Kampschulte, and Martin Kružík derive the small-strain laws of springy, flowing solids from the full nonlinear theory. Such Kelvin-Voigt solids both spring back and creep, and engineers tend to write their small-strain laws down at once. The 2026 paper starts from a nonlinear model that obeys frame indifference, the rule that response cannot hinge on how the viewer turns.

The authors show that answers of the nonlinear system tend to answers of the small-strain system as strain shrinks. They prove the same match for step-by-step time schemes on several scales. The gap matters, since codes compute with the small-strain laws while real solids obey the full ones. The proof certifies when the shortcut is safe.
arxiv-2603-03288:
Baraa Alabdulwahab and Ruzanna Chitchyan study how apples move from growers to buyers in the United Kingdom. Their 2026 paper treats the apple chain as a test case for a wider problem. Perishable food loses value fast, and poor matching of supply with demand creates waste, extra transport emissions, and needless long-distance sourcing.

The authors build a mixed-integer linear programming model that allocates supply to demand under real limits. One combined score weighs four things openly: price matching, quantity fit, freshness, and distance. Leftover supply can circulate into later allocation rounds. Tests on a realistic dataset show that changing the weights shifts outcomes in controlled ways, while also exposing trade-offs between local sourcing, freshness, and filling demand.
arxiv-2603-03988: Chunqi Wang and others propose SORT, a systematically optimized ranking Transformer for industrial-scale recommenders. SORT tackles those challenges with request-centric sampling, local focus, query pruning, making pre-training, and refinements to tokenization, focus, and feed-forward modules. Training system tuning elevates model FLOPs utilization to 45%. Online A/B testing confirms significant gains, including orders up 7.47%, while cutting latency and boosting throughput nearly sevenfold. SORT now runs in production, serving every AliExpress user.
arxiv-2603-04288: Ghatwary and colleagues test deep learning tools that spot and outline polyps in colonoscopy video. Their data span many centres and varied populations, reflecting how polyps differ in look, place, and size. Missed or incomplete removals can harm patients, so automated help matters for colorectal cancer prevention. Data scientists and gastroenterologists built the dataset together and tested methods on real time clinical tasks. The study stresses sequence data and timing across frames as keys to sharper video diagnosis.
arxiv-2603-04488: Rotman and colleagues model NASA's Pandora SmallSat for exoplanet spectra. Pandora separates stellar heterogeneity from exoplanet signals, pairing visible photometry with near infrared spectroscopy. Selected in 2021 as a Pioneers mission, its year long prime run spans 2026 to 2027. Five test cases from hot Jupiters to temperate sub-Neptunes give abundance constraints near one dex for water and methane. Pandora plus JWST near infrared data beat JWST alone on reliability, and Pandora can preview JWST targets.
arxiv-2603-04888: Yusuke Nemoto and Ken Sato build type (2, 1) cycles on a family of surfaces tied to a product of curves. The surfaces are abelian covers of degree N of the projective line, branched over n plus 2 points. For a very general member, they prove the cycles span a subgroup of the indecomposable part with rank at least n times Euler's totient function of N. The proof follows their images under the transcendental regulator map.
arxiv-2603-05088: Christian Spånslätt and team build a non-balance theory of fractional quantum Hall edges, based on a Keldysh action for bosonized chiral Luttinger liquids. For a single-mode Laughlin edge they read full counting statistics of charge, quasiparticle Green's functions. tunneling transport through a quantum point contact for generic edge excitations. Stretching the formalism to multi-mode edges featuring inter-mode contacts, they show fractionalization of anyons modifies edge dynamics, with effects visible in the Fano factor and differential Fano factor.
arxiv-2603-05188: Iman Peivaste and team present Ara, a language-model agent searching for photocatalytic covalent organic methods balancing action with durability in water. The best electronic linkages, imines, hydrolyze quickly, forcing a balance-action tradeoff across nodes, linkers, linkages, and functional groups. Ara guides the search with chemical knowledge from pretraining, donor-acceptor ideas, conjugation effects, and linkage balance rankings, screened by a fragment pipeline. It beats random search and Bayesian tuning, finding hits far earlier, with traces showing clear logic, including early settling on stable vinylene and beta-ketoenamine linkages.
arxiv-2603-05288: Luwei Wang and team offer Bayesian Supervised Causal Grouping, which uses treatment effect as the outcome guiding grouping. While most ways use unsupervised grouping, supervised methods spot operationalizable subgroups tied to a given outcome of interest. BSCC finds homogeneous subgroups of individuals similar in covariate profiles as well as treatment effects. The authors test BSCC on simulated data sets and a real-world sample from the third Global Stroke Trial. This assesses the method's real usefulness for personalized choice-making in healthcare and policy test.
arxiv-2603-05488: Boppana and colleagues present evidence of performative chain-of-thought in reasoning models, where a model grows confident in its final answer yet keeps generating tokens without revealing its belief. Across DeepSeek-R1 671B and GPT-OSS 120B, probes decode final answers from activations far earlier than a monitor can state them. Backtracking and aha moments occur almost exclusively where probes show large belief shifts, suggesting genuine uncertainty. Probe-guided early exit saves up to 80% of tokens on MMLU and 30% on GPQA-Diamond, keeping accuracy similar.
arxiv-2603-05588: Zhang and team analyze four GRMHD models of near-Eddington black hole accretion, testing field shape and spin. Two stable setups emerge: a thin thermal disk inside a magnetic envelope under enough net up-down flux, and a magnet-held high disk when that flux is weak or absent. In the thin disk, inflow runs mainly on mean-field Maxwell stress within the magnetic envelope, with heat loss packed near the midplane. In the high disk, inflow spreads through the disk body under mean-field and choppy stresses.
arxiv-2603-05788: Shukla and colleagues study robot gathering at one unannounced location despite limited sensing. Under this defected view model, an activated robot sees only part of its peers. In the fully synchronous setting they settle an open case, proving gathering completes in finite time in the adversarial (4, 2) view without extra capabilities. In the asynchronous setting they prove finite-time gathering under the general (N, K) defected view, where each robot sees at most K peers. Both results allow non-rigid motion, with the asynchronous algorithm assuming one-axis agreement.
arxiv-2603-06188: Mazanik and his team study thin films where collinear d-wave altermagnetic order sits with superconducting order under a fully penetrating magnetic field. With the Ginzburg-Landau functional, they work out how films react to fields and to in-plane supercurrent flow. They track what each push does to the films, step by step. That interplay gives fourfold anisotropies in three key things: temperature, parallel field, and current density. In superconducting films and in superconductor and altermagnetic insulator heterostructures, these patterns mark altermagnetism in ways tests can read.
arxiv-2603-06388: Heidari Soureshjani and Gorzny compare five leading token standards and frameworks for cross chain use. The five are xERC20 implementing ERC-7281, Omnichain Fungible Token, Native Token Transfers, Cross-Chain Token, and SuperchainERC20 implementing ERC-7802. Cross chain token standards let fungible tokens span multiple blockchains under a unified total supply model. Each standard's properties and technical design are examined, including architecture, message passing, interoperability scope, chain compatibility, and security features. While all share seamless cross chain fungibility as a goal, they differ across implementation approach, trust model, and target ecosystem.
arxiv-2603-06588: Ko and Chen present vLLM Hook, an open-source plug-in for programming of internal states for vLLM models, where serving limits control and blocks test-time alignment and enhancement methods. From a setup file naming states to capture, it fits smoothly and supports passive use, probing selected states for later analysis while keeping generation intact. Active use steps in output by altering set states. Version 0 shows prompt injection detection, enhanced retrieval-augmented retrieval, and activation steering, and the authors welcome user help to improve the plug-in.
arxiv-2603-06788: Alford and colleagues study neutrino distributions in a Monte Carlo transport simulation of a neutron star merger, using a snapshot shortly after merger. They ask when neutrinos act like a gas in thermal balance and when a free-streaming picture fits better. In hot, dense regions with frequent neutrino-matter interactions, distributions match a gas in thermal balance. In moderately warm regions they depart sharply, most of all for opacity and absorption rates, even when average energies look balanced. At lower temperatures results approach free streaming.
arxiv-2603-06888: Singh and colleagues test machine learning for spotting heart artery disease early, a top killer worldwide. Early detection improves outcomes and cuts costs, and recent ML work promises better diagnosis. They feed clinic data, imaging, and biomarker profiles into three models: Bi-LSTM, GRU, and a Bi-LSTM plus GRU hybrid. All three beat traditional diagnosis on hit and false-alarm rates, and the hybrid leads, giving doctors a stronger aid.
arxiv-2603-07088: Cambie and colleagues tackle an Erdős, Herzog, and Piranian problem: the largest product of distances in a point set of fixed diameter. They prove it suffices to study convex polygons and map the structure of the diameter graph. New constructions beat regular polygons by a wide margin and sketch what extremal polygons should look like. They also show that, for even orders, a full characterization of the extremal shapes cannot be hoped for in general.
arxiv-2603-07788: Tate and colleagues present spiral-hosted large double radio sources, called SDRAGNs. Radio Galaxy Zoo candidates targeted by Zoo Gems yield 15 new high-probability hosts from 36 imaged candidates. Hosts sit close to edge-on with FR II structures and optical pseudobulges. Their jet axes lie near disk poles, with angles under 30 degrees most likely and none beyond 60 degrees. Spectra show Seyfert 2, star formation and LINER signatures similar to elliptical-host radio galaxies. The sample includes FR II sources at unusually low radio power in overdensities.
arxiv-2603-07888: Kim and colleagues introduce VLM-SubtleBench, a test of whether vision-language models can spot small differences between near-identical images. It spans ten difference types, from attribute and state to viewpoint and action, and covers industrial, aerial and medical images beyond natural photos alone. Extensive tests of open and closed models reveal systematic gaps from human performance across types and domains, and pinpoint where model reasoning breaks down most sharply.
arxiv-2603-08088: Han and colleagues port tree speculative decoding to Ascend NPUs, where autoregressive decoding still bottlenecks large language model serving. Speculative decoding cuts costly teacher-model calls by verifying several candidate tokens per step, and tree-structured variants add parallelism. But porting them across backends is brittle, since attention masking, KV-cache layouts, and indexing rules differ. Their EAGLE-Pangu system brings EAGLE-3-style tree speculation to a Pangu teacher backend, with an explicit branch and commit cache manager, accelerator-safe tree tensorization, and a fused-kernel teacher verification path.
arxiv-2603-08488: Parish and colleagues propose NN-OpInf, a neural framework for reduced-order modeling of systems that keeps structure and composes. It learns latent states from snapshots, keeping operator structure: skew-symmetry, semi-positive definiteness and gradient preservation. It also combines unlike operators for complex cases. Training and cost details against linear and quadratic P-OpInf follow. Tests on nonlinear, parametric problems claim better accuracy, stability and robustness than P-OpInf and neural models, where polynomial models fit poorly, though training costs more and is non-convex.
arxiv-2603-09288: Saketh Vishnubhatla and colleagues tackle systematic measurement error in aggregate outcomes from surveys and administrative records, such as county disaster losses that drift from true damage. Their framework uses proxy variables to estimate and correct the bias. A causal graph separates latent content driving the true outcome from latent bias behind the errors, and proxies tied to the outcome but not the bias identify the distortion. A two-stage method with variational autoencoders then disentangles the two.
arxiv-2603-09488: Jinxiu Liu and colleagues propose Diagonal Distillation to make autoregressive video generation fast enough for real-time streaming. Large diffusion models make fine videos but stream poorly, and video distillation borrowed from image methods ignores temporal links, causing motion drift and error build-up. Their approach uses temporal cues across video chunks and across denoising steps alike. An asymmetric design targets two named causes: weak use of temporal context during step reduction and exposure bias in next-chunk prediction.
arxiv-2603-09588: Wladimiro Leone and colleagues report Crab pulsar timing with the HERMES instrument aboard the SpIRIT CubeSat, bringing CubeSats into the millisecond X-ray domain. HERMES is a compact X and gamma-ray spectrometer with broadband sensitivity and sub-microsecond time resolution, suited to bright transients. From one operation they collected tens of thousands of photons and detected the roughly 33 ms double-peaked pulse profile at clear significance in the low energy band. The result shows flagship-style timing accuracy from a small satellite.
arxiv-2603-09688: Denica Kjorvezir and colleagues estimate how similar two recipes are by fusing semantic, lexical, and domain views. They compare ingredients, preparation methods, and nutritional attributes for each pair, and a web interface lets domain experts validate the combined scores. Experts agreed on 255 of 318 pairs. Their judgments show which aspect weighs most when experts decide. The methods support personalized diets, better nutrition advice, and automated recipe generation for the food industry and beyond.
arxiv-2603-09888: Tung Tran, Danilo Vasconcellos Vargas and Khoat Than tackle catastrophic forgetting when a model learns task after task. Pre trained backbones adapt well, but as the backbone shifts, the task specific classifiers can drift out of line with it. Their local classifier alignment loss pulls each classifier back into step. Theory backs the gain, and a full merging based system built on it leads standard benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-10088: Zijian Zhu and coauthors speed up diffusion language models by skipping unimportant tokens in early layers. These models process the full context at every iteration, making inference costly despite parallel generation. The team finds that keys, values and hidden states barely change between successive steps. ES-dLLM estimates token importance from those small changes plus past confidence, then skips low value tokens with no retraining, gaining large speedups.
arxiv-2603-10188: Iliopoulou, Ampeliotis and Skodras present ARCHE, a learned image squeeze system that trades quality well at low cost. End to end codecs beat old ones but often run slowly with limited parallel work. ARCHE joins layered, spatial and channel priors in one probabilistic frame, with adaptive recalibration and residual refinement of the latent code. With no recurrent or transformer parts, it cuts bit rate a lot against key codecs, while keeping run time in check.
arxiv-2603-10288: Rafael Oliveira Cavalcante and Alexandre Galvão Patriota show that a widely used test for minimal sufficient statistics is false in general. Their counterexample turns on Radon-Nikodym derivatives having more than one version, and a test from Pfanzagl fails the same way without extra hypotheses. They give a version-robust method that works whenever sufficiency is known, and extend Sato's approach to wider sample spaces. Such statistics shrink data with no loss, and in complete cases point toward the best estimates a model can give.
arxiv-2603-10488: Hyun Gyu Lee, Hyeong-Chai Jeong, and Deok-Sun Lee study how wealth gaps can drive cooperation in a game on a lattice. Payoffs are scaled by the poorer player's gathered wealth, so past choices shape later games. Frequent cooperators can then out-earn defectors, even when cooperation is costly. At a high critical ratio of cost to benefit, the wealth gradient at the boundary jumps in a discontinuous transition. A stalled boundary lets that gradient build explosively, pushing cooperation to dominate below the critical ratio, and warmer noise helps.
arxiv-2603-10588: Zhaowei Zhang and co-authors ask whether LLM alignment really needs diversity-seeking methods, testing the idea on moral reasoning with MoReBench. The natural guess was that many valid answers favor distribution matching over reward maximizing. With a rubric-grounded reward pipeline built for stable training, they compared both paradigms head to head. Distribution matching showed no clear edge: high-reward moral answers cluster tightly in semantic space, unlike math answers, so mode seeking works as well or better. Standard reward-maximizing methods, they conclude, transfer fine to moral reasoning.
arxiv-2603-10988: Manuel Arnese and Daniel Lacker establish the sharp rate of propagation of chaos for McKean-Vlasov equations whose coefficients depend nonlinearly on the whole measure, not just on pairwise interactions. Their results hold both on bounded time horizons and uniformly in time. As applications they recover sharp rates for the convergence problem in mean field games and control, and for mean field Langevin dynamics, combining the BBGKY hierarchy with weak chaos techniques.
arxiv-2603-11088: Juhee Kim and coauthors present what they describe as the first systematic survey of security for AI agents. Such agents pair language models with ordinary software components in real applications. Their flexibility creates security problems unlike those of traditional software. The survey maps the design space, the attack landscape, and the defense mechanisms available. Case studies expose gaps in how current agentic systems are secured. The authors frame open challenges. These concern building agents that can be trusted in deployment.
arxiv-2603-11388: Zhiyu Xue and coauthors dissect why safety-tuned language models refuse harmless requests. They trace the failure to cues they call refusal triggers inside the training data. Alignment teaches models to link trigger phrases with refusal answers. The learned triggers sweep in benign wording alongside genuinely harmful cues. Innocent queries trip them too. Their fix makes fine-tuning account for the triggers explicitly. Tests show a better balance. The models resist jailbreaks while answering benign questions more willingly than earlier methods.
arxiv-2603-11488: Dong, Li, and Wei study charge flow through a triangular triple quantum dot tied to fermionic reservoirs. Stronger Coulomb interaction usually chokes current in dot arrays, yet here it boosts the current. The team traces that surprise with exact hierarchical equations of motion and spectral function shifts. Coulomb-driven energy shifts mix with quantum interference set by the triangular shape. Chiral current circulation and electrode coupling strength also tune the effect. A three-dimensional map shows how inter-dot tunneling and Coulomb strength jointly set the current size.
arxiv-2603-11888: Errázuriz and co-authors tackle structure-from-motion for rolling-shutter cameras from a single view. Rolling-shutter cameras are everywhere, yet their geometry has resisted a full solution. The team characterizes the single-view geometry of world points and lines seen by such cameras. From that geometry they derive which motion and scene parameters a single image can recover. They build minimal reconstruction problems and test proof-of-concept solvers on representative cases. The tests show both what is feasible and where practical limits bite.
arxiv-2603-12188: Micheli, Scala, and Valentini give a practical way to compile temporal numeric planning into discrete PDDL+. Planners have known since PDDL+ arrived that durative actions could be compiled this way. No usable compilation had appeared in print until now. Theirs keeps the full semantics while assuming only that actions do not overlap themselves. The compile step runs in polynomial time and stretches plan length by at most a constant factor. Experiments on hard temporal numeric problems show the route works in practice.
arxiv-2603-12288: Lee-St John, Lawson, and Piechowski-Jozwiak explain why messy high-dimensional data can still predict well. Modern tabular models thrive on collinear, error-prone inputs, against the garbage-in, garbage-out mantra. Their theory joins information theory, latent factor models, and psychometrics in one account. Predictor noise splits into predictor error and structural uncertainty from stochastic mappings. Large sets of flawed predictors beat both noise types in the limit, while cleaned small sets stay bounded. Informative collinearity helps too, since shared latent causes raise reliability and ease latent inference.
arxiv-2603-12488: Shiyas, Zhong, and Chamzas present CoAd, a constant-time planner for repeated manipulation tasks with moving goals. Many robot jobs repeat with only the goal object and its obstacle shifted in a fixed workspace. Prior methods lack coverage guarantees for continuous task spaces and store huge libraries. CoAd cuts the space into Task Coverage Regions and solves only representative root problems. A compressed library plus fast adaptation modules answers new goals in constant time. Tests in simulation and the real world show high success with sub-millisecond queries.
arxiv-2603-12688: Nandish Chattopadhyay and co-authors defend vision transformers against adversarial patches that hijack attention. A patch is a small, high-contrast region that can force a wrong class call. The team claims patch tokens differ in statistics from clean tokens. Their STRAP-ViT uses a divergence score to spot odd tokens, then applies random transforms to them. The block needs no training and adds little cost. Across models, datasets, and attacks, robust accuracy stayed close to clean baselines.
arxiv-2603-12888: Parsons and co-authors present a detached white dwarf and brown dwarf pair that may solve a missing population puzzle. Theory says half of cataclysmic variables should now be period bouncers with substellar partners. Yet only a few percent are seen in that phase. A late-emerging magnetic field could push the pair apart and detach it for billions of years. Their system, with an orbital period of 1.7 hours, fits that story well. Its motion hints it once accreted, despite a young white dwarf age.
arxiv-2603-12988: Aditya Parikh and Aasa Feragen build a fairness-aware system that diagnoses lung disease from chest CT scans. The task sorts scans as healthy, COVID-19, or one of two cancer types. Scores reward equal performance across genders, which the data make hard. Signal is sparse across hundreds of slices, and class and gender counts are skewed. Their attention model finds key slices with no slice labels. A gradient reversal layer strips gender cues from the scan representation.
arxiv-2603-13188: Jihyeon Park and co-authors introduce CANOE, a hybrid eigensolver that splits its basis between quantum and classical hardware. Early fault-tolerant machines have few quantum resources to spare. Quantum states add expressive power that classical states cannot cheaply copy. Classical states, though, can join the basis at near no cost. A histogram protocol measures overlaps between the two kinds on quantum gear. A Schur step then steadies the joint eigenvalue problem against near-duplicate states.
arxiv-2603-13488: Gabriel Pîrlogeanu, Adriana Stan, and Horia Cucu study the strengths and weaknesses of SSL models for audio deepfake attribution. The task names the source model behind a synthetic speech sample, which aids accountability. Self-supervised features give state-of-the-art attribution, but why they work and where they fail was unclear. The team controls parts of the generation process, like checkpoints, prompts, vocoders, and speaker identity. Small changes in each factor shift attribution in distinct ways. Their results map the robustness, biases, and limits of SSL-based attribution.
arxiv-2603-13588: Dante Kalise, Lucas M. Moschen, and Grigorios A. Pavliotis study feedback control and local convexification of Wasserstein gradient flows. They treat entropy-regularized free energies on the flat torus, where the energy may be nonconvex and nonlocal. The controlled system admits a gradient flow formulation in Wasserstein space, they show. They realize the Wasserstein Hessian at a target stationary measure as a self-adjoint operator with compact resolvent. A feedback control from an algebraic Riccati equation lifts the Hessian spectrum above a set threshold.
arxiv-2603-13688: Lezhi Tan, Naomi Sagan, Lihua Lei, and Jose Blanchet ask when humans should step in on AI-assisted decisions. AI systems give cheap factor-level assessments of complex inputs, but those can be biased or incomplete. They formulate selective human evaluation as a factor-level information-acquisition problem. Under squared loss and a linear model, the optimal dispatching reward splits into predictive relevance and residual uncertainty terms. On peer review, querying three of ten aspects under their rule matched the full ten-aspect human benchmark.
arxiv-2603-13788: You Wu and co-authors propose ST-VLA, a hierarchical VLA framework with 4D-aware spatiotemporal understanding for robot manipulation. Past VLA frameworks use 2D representations, which lack depth awareness and temporal consistency in complex 3D scenes. ST-VLA turns 2D guidance into 3D trajectories and smooth spatial masks that carry 4D context. That gives a stable interface between semantic reasoning and continuous control. The team also built ST-Human, a dataset of 14 tasks and 300k episodes with 2D, 3D, and 4D supervision.
arxiv-2603-13888: Haro and co-authors train a reinforcement learning policy for local robot navigation on long routes. Global plans can contain bad waypoints when remote sensing data are poor. Their policy reads the reference path as context but gets no direct reward for following it. It learns to use good path hints and ignore bad ones. Tests show faster navigation when paths are sound, and no loss when path data are badly degraded or missing.
arxiv-2603-13988: Afolabi and co-authors test whether closed-source language models give faithful reasons for medical answers. A fluent answer can sound right while hiding how the model reached it. Three black-box probes check causal ablation, position bias, and hint injection. Stated reasoning steps often do not drive the final prediction. Models also absorb outside hints without saying so, while position bias shows little effect. A small human study compares doctor and lay judgments of trust.
arxiv-2603-14088: Jiao and co-authors test whether a stripped moon could have made Saturn's young, icy rings. One idea says a past moon, Chrysalis, broke up after a close pass by Saturn. The team runs smoothed particle hydrodynamics simulations of that encounter. Ice from the moon's outer mantle peels off first, which yields rings of the right mass and near-pure ice mix. The closest pass must fall between the Roche limits for ice and rock. Repeated passes spin the moon up and widen the effect.
arxiv-2603-14188: Wang and co-authors propose IMO, a model that segments eye structures and grades glaucoma in one pass. Early glaucoma signs are faint, and single-image methods miss part of the picture. IMO fuses fundus photos with OCT scans at a mid level. A cross-modal alignment module trims the gap between the two data types. An iterative decoder then refines features with a diffusion-style denoising step. Tests show clean optic disc and cup outlines plus sound grading.
arxiv-2603-14488: Zhou, Tian and Zhu study an anisotropic universe in nonlocal RT gravity. The theory explains late cosmic acceleration while passing local gravity tests. Most past work assumed a smooth, isotropic background. New supernova hints suggest slight direction differences instead. The team builds a dynamical system with six dimensionless variables for a Bianchi type I cosmos. Phase-space study then tracks how the anisotropy evolves. Against most dark energy models, anisotropy grows with time here, they find. That growth challenges the cosmic no-hair idea in this theory.
arxiv-2603-14588: Bhardwaj grounds enterprise agent memory in information geometry with SuperLocalMemory V3. Agent memory tools often lean on cosine similarity and hand-set decay rules. No formal check for clashing facts exists in such tools. Three math layers fix those gaps. A Fisher-based metric drives retrieval in linear time. Langevin dynamics on a curved space govern memory lifetimes with proven steady states. A sheaf model flags clashes that no merge can fix. On LoCoMo tests, scores rise 12.7 points over baselines, Bhardwaj reports.
arxiv-2603-14788: González and Jauhari compute sequential topological complexity for symmetric products of non-orientable surfaces. A closed form gives the k-th Z2 zero-divisor cup length of SP^n(N_g). That value bounds the k-th sequential complexity from below and above. The LS-category of a related cofiber space falls out as well. As genus grows, the k=2 case breaks from the family pattern. Large k brings maximal linear growth, settling a rationality claim by Farber and Oprea.
arxiv-2603-14888: Fung demonstrates a fully reproducible AI-assisted workflow on canonical benchmark problems. One user prompt seeded the artifact stack, later reviewed by the human author. No new discovery is claimed for the results. Each test carries an exact or checkable answer by design. A quantum harmonic oscillator checks finite-difference eigenpairs against Hermite benchmarks. Heat and Poisson solvers face known and manufactured solutions. A damped-oscillation fit adds bootstrap error bars. Solver comparisons round out the demo with timing caveats.
arxiv-2603-14988: Antunes and Podobas build bitSMM, a bit-serial matrix engine for neural inference aboard spacecraft. Space missions cap power and demand reliability from their accelerators. Bit-serial multiply-accumulate units fill a systolic array in the design. Operand precision runs from 1 to 16 bits at runtime. Two unit variants face off: a Booth-style one and a corrected binary one. FPGA tests reach up to 19 GOPS with strong efficiency marks. ASIC runs in two process kits push rates far higher. Downlink savings motivate the onboard compute.
arxiv-2603-15588: Yan and co-authors design a voltage controller for power grids that feed AI training data centers. Such loads swing fast between two phases, which standard controllers treat as random noise. Their switching-reference design moves each bus reference in step with the workload phase. That cancels the phase-driven voltage shift at low control effort. Local voltage readings let each bus infer the phase with no live communication. Tests on real traces cut violations sharply, sometimes to zero, with about ten times less effort than droop control.
arxiv-2603-15688: Akbasli and Serin validate a lung-sound pipeline with patients as the split unit. Each child gives many recordings, so record-level splits can leak. They study 19,693 doctor-marked events from 736 children in the SPRSound database. A frozen HeAR encoder with small adapters feeds stacked scores. Event recognition held up, with an AUC of 0.95 for screening. Disease-group guessing failed, with an AUC of 0.58 and accuracy below the majority rate. The authors urge patient-level splits in future lung-sound work.
arxiv-2603-15788: Mendes and co-authors grade density functionals on frequency-dependent response traits. Part one of the series covered static polarizabilities and NMR traits. Part two turns to dynamic polarizabilities at five wavelengths. Some 25 functionals face HF and EOM-CCSD reference runs. TPSS0 and QTP01 led the Kohn-Sham pack on dynamic values. The team also checks pole structure in the CO molecule. For C6 dispersion coefficients, O3LYP ranked first overall. QTP01 and LC-QTP led inside the QTP family.
arxiv-2603-15888: Tupini and co-authors benchmark hands-on planning with almost no feedback. AsgardBench tests agents that revise plans while watching the scene. Input stays spare: images, action history, and success or failure pings. No navigation or fine motor control pollutes the planning signal. The set holds 108 tasks across 12 task types. Object states and placements vary by design, forcing branch points. One instruction can demand unlike action chains per scene. Top vision-language models drop sharply without image input. Weak grounding and state tracking sink plan repair.
arxiv-2603-15988: Bae and co-authors grade dysarthric speech severity with help from unlabeled data. Hand scoring of such speech costs much and scales poorly.
