Labeled sets stay small, which weakens direct model training. Their three-stage plan starts with a teacher model. The teacher pseudo-labels unlabeled dysarthric speech samples. Label-aware contrastive pretraining then spans many speakers and settings. A final fine-tune targets the severity task itself. Five unseen datasets cover varied causes and languages. The full stack reaches a mean rank score of 0.761.
arxiv-2603-16388: Allu, Biswas, and Mandal bound the Schwarzian norms of maps in new function classes. They define a subclass of analytic functions on the unit disk. A phase-weighted convexity condition picks out its members. For this class they prove sharp bounds on the Schwarzian norm. The bounds also yield tests for univalence. A matching harmonic class is built from the analytic one. Both pre-Schwarzian and Schwarzian bounds follow there too.
arxiv-2603-16488: McRobie extends graphic statics to the motion of rigid-jointed 3D frames. Parts 1 and 2 covered equilibrium with a loop formalism. There, loops in 4D space encode stress resultants on cut faces. Here, projected loop areas stand for kinematic variables instead. Three areas give a point's displacement, and three give its rotation. The fourth dimension carries the stress function. Virtual work then appears as an oriented 4-volume in this 4D setting.
arxiv-2603-16788: McMillen and co-authors map permafrost thaw from drone lidar over boreal forest in Alaska. Flat averaging of 3D points into 2D grids erases vertical structure, yet ground, understory, and canopy carry distinct clues about thaw. Their method adds learned height embeddings to a projection decoder, so features change with height. Stratified sampling keeps all forest layers represented. A Point Transformer V3 encoder then predicts thaw depth maps. The authors report that height-aware projection beats standard averaging, most clearly where vegetation structure is complex.
arxiv-2603-16988: Kernaghan surveys Kochen-Specker uncolorability in three dimensional Hilbert space across many number fields. He tests alphabets from quadratic, cyclotomic, golden ratio, and cubic fields. In every tested alphabet, KS sets appear only when a parameter supports an identity that makes dot products vanish. Three mechanisms occur: modulus two cancellation, phase cancellation, and minimal polynomial cancellation. Constructions cluster into at least eight algebraic islands, two of them cubic. Two yield potentially new KS graph types. Whether this three mechanism scheme is complete stays open.
arxiv-2603-17088: Lara revisits the Debreu Koopmans theorem, which limits separable aggregation to at most one nonconvex component. He proves that a separable function is star quasiconvex exactly when each component is. Star quasiconvex means the sublevel sets are star shaped around minimizers. This yields star quasiconvexity for separable sums of quasiconvex functions at once. It also links diversification theory with the S shaped value functions of Prospect Theory. Lara builds a calculus for the property and applies it to Cobb-Douglas functions, risk models, and market makers.
arxiv-2603-17188: Block Gorman and Perrin present sequential densities for rational languages. A rational language has a density measured against a sequence of probability measures, not a single one. They prove two results. If Bernoulli measures converge to a positive Bernoulli limit, this density equals the ordinary density under that limit. If invariant measures converge in the strong sense, the density exists for every rational language under that sequence. This extends older work to cases where the measure keeps shifting as more terms arrive.
arxiv-2603-17388: Hong and Kosecka train a diffusion model that turns text into 3D sign language motion. They test whether phonological cues from ASL-LEX 2.0, like hand shape and location, help. Their baseline beat a prior CVAE method on gloss clarity scores. Turning symbolic attribute notes into plain words proved key for CLIP-based conditioning. The best variant beat the prior method on all metrics, they report.
arxiv-2603-17588: Zheng and co-authors move language-model paper review from solo scores to paired comparisons. Fixed score scales shift across venues and years, so models learn narrow rules instead. Their CNPE framework builds training pairs with a graph-based sampler. Fine-tuning and reinforcement learning then sharpen relative judgment. At test time, pairwise votes merge into one global ranking. Scores rose 21.8 percent over a strong baseline, they report.
arxiv-2603-17788: Temmen and co-authors merge exact diagonalization with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for fermionic systems. Exact methods scale badly, while Monte Carlo fights sign problems and slow mixing. Their hybrid, H2MC, targets 2D arrays of coupled quantum wires. It scales far past exact diagonalization alone, they report. It also softens the sign problem and cuts autocorrelation times versus plain Monte Carlo. Wider parameter ranges open up for Hubbard chain arrays.
arxiv-2603-17888: Komech and Kopylova study the Maxwell-Bloch equations for a one-mode laser field tied to a two-level molecule. The system runs with damping and with pumping that repeats in a quasiperiodic way. They build solutions whose field settles into a single-frequency pattern over time. Valid starts come from the still states of a simpler averaged system, which they compute in full. They also test how stable each such state is. Gauge symmetry and a wider averaging method carry the proof.
arxiv-2603-17988: Wang and Brun study syndrome measurement when qubits can be lost, not just flipped. Loss changes syndrome patterns, so schemes built for Pauli errors alone do not transfer. They show how to turn correctable erasures into located errors with low cost. The core cost becomes a subgroup size problem for qubits and prime-size qudits. They then give adaptive measurement plans and fault-tolerance rules for this mixed error model.
arxiv-2603-18088: Ma and co-authors add an online refiner to reinforcement learning fine-tuning of language models. Fixed constraints keep training stable but block the model from finding better solutions. Their dynamic constraints act only when output turns degenerate. A reference model minimally corrects each response, keeping right content and fixing errors. A supervised loss then trains the model toward the refined text. Tests on dialogue and code beat KL and unconstrained baselines.
arxiv-2603-18288: Caputi and Di Trani compute the K-theory of matroids under Tutte coverings. They show it matches the K-theory spectrum of graphic matroids on looped forests. There the covering family is generated by isomorphisms alone. The equivalence also holds as C2-spectra, they prove. The result gives an explicit handle on a category built for matroid theory.
arxiv-2603-18488: Zhao and co-authors present TexEditor, a structure-preserving model for text-driven texture editing. Top editing models often break object structure even when only appearance should change. A Blender-built dataset, TexBlender, gives strong structural priors for a cold start. A reinforcement method, StructureNFT, then transfers those priors to real scenes with structure losses. On their new TexBench and past benchmarks, TexEditor beats strong baselines like Nano Banana Pro.
arxiv-2603-18588: Wang and co-authors turn facial action coding into rich text prompts for face synthesis. Coarse emotion labels and one-hot action unit vectors often miss fine muscle moves. Their method writes FACS muscle rules and conflict fixes into plain text signals. A dynamic processor converts raw action unit notes into sound descriptions. The result is BP4D-AUText, over 302,000 paired text and image samples. Their VQ-AUFace model beats prior methods most clearly when action units conflict.
arxiv-2603-18888: Palejova adds Authority-Level Priors to hierarchical predictive processing. Brains update beliefs with precision weighting, yet stated belief change often fails to calm stress responses. Authority-Level Priors act as gatekeepers over which identity-level hypotheses may steer body and behavior control. Precision sets influence only after a hypothesis passes that gate. This split explains why insight can change while autonomic threat reactions stay fixed. A formal version limits policy search to authorised policies. The model predicts shifts in stress curves and recovery speed after gate changes.
arxiv-2603-19088: Cerutti and Simonelli probe a hidden source of doubt in fits of parton momentum spreads. Such spreads describe how quarks move sideways inside fast protons. Fits at low energy agree well under varied choices for a key cutoff rule. The extracted spreads also match at small sideways motion. At mid-range motion, though, the choices pull apart in a clear way. That split feeds into forecasts for high-energy Drell-Yan events. The team calls the cutoff rule an intrinsic theory doubt in this fit frame.
arxiv-2603-19288: Park builds one deep network that learns stock returns and risk together for portfolio design. Classic methods split the two tasks and lean on past averages. The model trains on daily data for ten large US stocks from 2010 to 2024. Out-of-sample tests from 2020 to 2024 show sound forecasts and a feel for regime shifts. Its Neural Portfolio earns 36.4 percent per year with a Sharpe ratio of 0.91. That beats equal-weight and classic mean-variance plans on risk-adjusted terms.
arxiv-2603-19388: D'Alessandro and co-authors bound the correlations that quantum theory allows with a broader semidefinite method. Prior hierarchies miss many constraint types that real problems need. Their block-matrix relaxations fold in a wide range of such constraints at fair cost. Five showcase problems prove the reach of the approach. They span witness tests with flawed devices and certified measurements from bounded sources. Size limits for multi-particle entangled states are also computed. A last case finds uncertainty rules for near anti-commuting observables.
arxiv-2603-19688: Qi and co-authors present DataProphet, a training-free metric for picking supervision data for multimodal language models. The folk rule says pick data that looks like the target benchmark. Their study of transfer across 14 data sets and seven tasks shows looks mislead. Transfer depends on the specific data set, not its broad task type. DataProphet mixes perplexity, similarity, and diversity into one score. Its rankings match post-training gains with a Kendall tau of 86 percent. Picks from the metric beat uniform selection by up to about 7 percent.
arxiv-2603-19988: Eschenbaum and Greber study how platform design shapes market power in local electricity trading. Their players own solar panels and batteries and trade through a platform. The platform sets internal buy and sell prices from total imports and exports. Because the export price falls as total exports rise, big players hold back supply. They also underuse their storage compared with price-taking behavior. In the baseline setup, strategic play raised grid settlement costs by about 6 percent. Some platform designs nearly removed the distortion, and wider storage ownership helped too.
arxiv-2603-20088: Edgell and co-authors set out how to judge AI tools for second language education. Fast uptake of language models has outrun fair tests of teaching value. Past evaluations stayed narrow and task-specific. Their L2-Bench effort grounds scoring in a validated designer construct for learning experiences. The method joins pedagogical theory with sociotechnical evaluation practice. A layered taxonomy organizes over 1,000 real task-response pairs with expert rubric scores. A pilot check with 39 raters found the tasks authentic. Criteria scores were lower, and rater agreement was poor throughout.
arxiv-2603-20188: Gerard and Sullivan widen the range of futures that wildfire spread models can sample. Diffusion models can express many outcomes, but naive sampling wastes hundreds of draws. Rare but plausible spread paths may never show up. The authors test training-free tricks that push samples apart, with no retraining. They adapt particle guidance and SPELL from image generation, and add a clustering method. Gains reached 7.5 percent on their new MMFire wildfire dataset. A Cityscapes variant improved by 16.4 percent on the same diversity metric.
arxiv-2603-20288: Stropeni and co-authors adapt visual anomaly detection for small edge devices in factories. Cloud processing clashes with real-time and privacy needs on production lines. They present PatchCore-Lite and PaDiM-Lite, lean versions of two known methods. PatchCore-Lite searches a compressed memory bank before checking a decoded subset. PaDiM-Lite uses diagonal covariance to speed its distance math. On MVTec AD and VisA, PatchCore-Lite cut memory use by 79%. PaDiM-Lite cut memory by 77% and run time by 31%.
arxiv-2603-20588: Wang and co-authors present RayMap3R for streaming 3D reconstruction of dynamic scenes. Feed forward models can drift when objects move. Their method needs no new training at test time. RayMap outputs tend to favor static scenes, which gives a useful cue. A dual branch scheme contrasts RayMap and image outputs to spot motion. It then blocks those zones from memory updates. Reset alignment and state aware smoothing keep scale and paths steady.
arxiv-2603-20788: Lesniak proves that uniform polyconvexity and Almgren's uniform ellipticity match for Lipschitz Q-graph test pairs. Both notions measure strong convexity like behavior for geometric integrands. Earlier work had shown one direction for polyhedral test pairs. His main theorem gives the full equivalence in the Lipschitz graph setting. The proof builds on methods of De Rosa, Lei, and Young. As a result, a classical integrand is uniformly polyconvex exactly when its Q-integrand is uniformly quasiconvex. This holds for every positive integer Q.
arxiv-2603-20988: Jagadish and co-authors chart what an automated science of the mind would take. AI tools now begin to automate parts of scientific discovery, including in psychology. They frame the field around four challenges. First, experiments must be represented in a form machines can use. Second, synthetic behavior must be generated well enough to stand in for human data. Third, models of that behavior must be built and compared. Fourth, the loop must close, so the system can move from data and models to new psychological theories.
arxiv-2603-21088: Wang and co-authors analyze errors in an explicit splitting scheme for fluid and poroelastic structure interaction. The Stokes-Biot problem couples a fluid with a porous elastic solid. Their scheme decouples the two subproblems at each time step, so each can be solved on its own in parallel. With Ritz projections, they derive a discrete error energy identity. They prove first order accuracy in time and optimal space rates. Tests with a manufactured solution confirm the theory.
arxiv-2603-21688: Morozov opens a discussion of knot invariants for orthogonal groups, a case he notes has been largely neglected. Methods for SU(N) colored knot invariants, the HOMFLY-PT polynomials, are well developed. The Reshetikhin-Turaev approach, though, needs generalizing to SO(2n+1) groups, and Morozov maps the difficulties. As a concrete start, he provides the R and Racah matrices for the symmetric representation of SO(5). He then shows how those matrices yield the corresponding Kauffman polynomials. The work is meant to launch a broader program, not close it.
arxiv-2603-21788: Eriksson explains why formal verification fails, in terms a domain expert can use. When a proof fails, the solver returns a counterexample with thousands of variables and no clear story. Eriksson's method works when the checks are written with concepts from a formal domain model. A relevance score picks the predicates most likely to explain the failure. Links between predicates then chain those picks into a branching set of explanations. The goal is to help engineers find the real fault faster. Examples compare the method with other approaches.
arxiv-2603-21988: Rajapakse and co-authors explain the choices of agents trained for several goals at once. In multi-objective learning, trade-offs are the real decision, yet standard explainers assume one reward. Their TREX framework runs the expert policy under many user preferences. It clusters the trajectories into meaningful behavior segments over time. To score each segment, it retrains policies with that cluster removed and measures how rewards and actions shift. Tests on 3 MuJoCo tasks show it can isolate and price behavior patterns.
arxiv-2603-22388: Chen and co-authors build a bridge that lets collider tools from conformal field theory work in QCD. Correlation functions link to things colliders can measure. In conformal theories, the light transform makes that link. QCD is not conformal, which blocks the transform past low orders. The team continues the functions to the Wilson-Fisher fixed point. There the functions act like true conformal objects. That lets them run the light transform at higher loop orders. They test the route on a charge-charge correlation at two loops.
arxiv-2603-23188: Smirnov proposes an algorithm to compute genus-two Kleinian hyperelliptic functions. The method builds a chain of curves linked by Richelot isogenies. A recurrent procedure then reduces the work to a degenerate curve. At each step, one of fifteen possible partner curves must be chosen. Smirnov gives a choice rule that keeps the curve equations convergent. The same rule keeps weight-two Kleinian functions convergent under iteration. The algorithm evaluates the functions numerically.
arxiv-2603-23388: Moca and three co-authors extend Family-Vicsek scaling to a quantum spin chain with gain and loss. The scaling describes how fluctuations grow and level off in systems. They track roughness of moved magnetization after quenches in a dissipative XXZ chain. The chain starts from a steady state with finite magnetization. In the free limit, they derive a closed form with two-parameter scaling. It bridges ballistic growth and loss-driven regimes. Tensor-network runs show ballistic growth survives interactions, while dynamics follow the loss scale.
arxiv-2603-23488: Rahary and three co-authors train a novel-view generator from single photos alone. New views once demanded paired shots, which narrowed the training pool. Their recipe lifts each photo into 3D with a depth tool, then reprojects it from fresh angles. Masked losses guard the valid zones, and an adversarial term fills the gaps. Scaled to 30 million images, the result is OVIE. It needs no depth tool and no view pairs at test time. It matches in-domain baselines and runs at 116 frames per second.
arxiv-2603-23588: Tavangar and six co-authors study how phase spirals wind in galactic disks. These spirals in vertical phase space prove the Milky Way sits out of balance. The team track spirals in a test-particle run and a full N-body run. Test spirals wind just as pure phase mixing predicts. N-body spirals start late, wind slowly, and pulse in rate over time. Toy models of star groups crossing shifting potentials explain the drag. Effects peak in the inner galaxy, so winding times there read as lower limits.
arxiv-2603-23688: Olaniran and six co-authors validate pmsims, an R package that sizes clinical prediction studies by simulation. Picking a sample size guards a model's trust, yet sound guidance stays thin. The package fits a Gaussian process stand-in to steer the search for the right size. Tests pit that engine against bisection and a hybrid across three outcome types. The process engine gives the steadiest sizes, most in weak-signal, wide-data cases. Against rival tools, pmsims hits target performance with fewer model runs.
arxiv-2603-23988: Hoang and co-authors present CAKE, a real-time system that spots actions in video as they happen. Optical flow gives strong motion cues but costs much compute. CAKE distills motion knowledge into a model that reads plain RGB frames. A dynamic motion adapter suppresses static background and stresses pixel changes, mimicking flow. A floating contrastive step separates true action motion from background drift. On TVSeries, THUMOS'14, and Kinetics-400, CAKE leads in accuracy with the same backbone and runs over 72 frames per second on one CPU.
arxiv-2603-24188: Danchev and co-authors characterize Bassian modules over certain rings in module theory. A module is Bassian when it embeds into a direct sum of copies of the ring in a controlled way. They study modules where every proper submodule is Bassian, and the dual notion for quotient images. Over Dedekind prime rings, they prove structural criteria for both classes. For singular modules, the two notions coincide there. For general modules over such rings, the super property always implies the hereditary one.
arxiv-2603-24288: Wangsawijaya and co-authors test how to measure rough-wall drag in compressible turbulent boundary layers. Workers usually transform velocities, then read off a momentum deficit and an equivalent sand-grain roughness. That roughness often comes from one Mach and Reynolds setting, which may not transfer. Their experiments use two sandpaper grits across Mach 0.3 to 2.9. The momentum deficit barely depends on the transform used. The fully rough regime shifts with Mach number, though. A temperature-based correction factor gives the most consistent improvement across datasets.
arxiv-2603-24388: Abdelsamea and co-authors survey causal transfer learning for medical image analysis. Models often fail across hospitals, scanners, and patient groups due to domain shift, and plain transfer methods can lean on spurious links that break. The survey frames domain shift as a causal problem. It reviews how causal models, invariant risk methods, and counterfactual reasoning can sit inside transfer pipelines. Work is sorted by task, shift type, and causal assumption, with datasets, benchmarks, and open challenges covered.
arxiv-2603-24488: Proistosescu and co-authors argue that wave dynamics, long overlooked, shape how low clouds respond to Pacific warm pool warming. The standard view, based on quasi-equilibrium weak temperature gradient theory, predicts more low cloud over the East Pacific and a negative radiative effect. Drawing on older results and new simulations with an exascale Earth system model, they show Rossby waves dominate the response over the subtropical decks. Cloud cover there falls instead. The global radiative response stays negative, but the deep tropics drive it, not the low cloud decks.
arxiv-2603-24588: Kasai constructs asymptotically good quantum LDPC codes that reach the Gilbert-Varshamov bound at finite degree. The construction builds nested CSS code pairs from Hsu-Anastasopoulos and MacKay-Neal codes. For fixed balanced triples with even component degrees, the rate stays bounded away from zero. So do the relative distances on both sides, with probability tending to one as block length grows. Within an explicit low-degree search window, all 56 balanced triples with the stated conditions attain the classical bound on both sides, and hence the CSS bound.
arxiv-2603-24788: Kopparty and Tamo introduce algebraic expander codes, Tanner-type codes with Reed-Solomon local constraints. Standard counting gives no positive-rate guarantee when the local rate is at most half. That low-rate regime matters for applications needing algebraic locality. Their codes evaluate a polynomial subspace on an orbit of a subgroup of affine maps. The coset geometry forms a strong spectral expander, proved with character sums. The global rate stays bounded away from zero, with constant relative distance.
arxiv-2603-24888: Miranda and co-authors present a semi-automated approach to generating attack graphs for control systems. Such environments are too complex to map attack paths by hand. Their method merges network topology with vulnerability data into one model. A stateful traversal algorithm then finds exploit chains from preconditions. The case study applies it to the Siemens PCS7 blueprint for water treatment plants. Simulations cover known CVE attacks and device errors. The results show how one failure can break segmentation, and how one patch can protect a whole zone.
arxiv-2603-24988: Kannan and co-authors measure tiny pulse-to-pulse changes in mode-locked lasers. Timing jitter in such lasers is well mapped, but shifts in pulse height and width are hard to catch. Their method uses second-harmonic autocorrelation with a Fano factor study of the signal. It reveals a W-shaped profile that marks pulse breathing, a shape change hidden in average readings. On two shop-bought lasers they measured width swings of about 3.2 and 2.86 femtoseconds. The check worked on both units, which supports its wider use.
arxiv-2603-25188: Wang and co-authors build AnyID, a video maker that keeps a character's identity from any mix of references. Older tools assume one reference image, which makes identity shaky in new scenes. AnyID first folds faces, portraits, and clips into one shared representation. It then names one reference as the anchor and uses a contrast prompt to steer single traits. Training used a large curated set plus a round of human-ranked fine-tuning. Tests show top identity fidelity and fine control across settings.
arxiv-2603-25688: Li and co-authors build a mobile robot platform that prints parts while it moves through a factory. Fixed printer layouts limit how flexible additive manufacturing can be. Their robot couples navigation with material deposition in one control loop. Sensors feed back motion and process data in real time. The robot avoids obstacles and keeps its path stable while printing. Tests in simulation and in real runs check how it handles route changes and outside pushes. The authors say the coupled design helps robots adapt on busy floors.
arxiv-2603-26488: Tajima, Tomita, and Okamoto test whether a quantum key distribution transmitter keeps its pulses indistinguishable. If pulses coded in unlike patterns differ in hidden traits, an eavesdropper could exploit the gap. Their check uses Hong-Ou-Mandel interference between neighbouring pulses from a decoy BB84 sender running at 1.25 GHz. They prove the test matches the SWAP test for judging state fidelity in this setting. Measured visibility sits near 0.3 for all state pairs, with no clear gaps between them.
arxiv-2603-26688: Rahmana, Barros, Jurdak, and Koggalahewa frame the choice of the next charging node for vehicle-to-vehicle energy trading as a ranking problem. Cars that trade charge need spots where partners are likely and conditions suit a deal. Their supervised ranking model learns from millions of urban journey records. Features cover battery level, trade role, distance, charge speed, and how busy each station is over time. Probabilistic labels grade several good options per stop, and boosted ranking models learn the order.
arxiv-2603-26888: Mukherjee and co-authors model breast cancer outcomes from repeated CT scans during treatment. Tracking the same lesion across scans and radiologists is the first hurdle. Their RAMAC algorithm matches lesions using image registration and an assignment method. The study draws on scans from the MONALEESA-3 and MONALEESA-7 trials. Radiomic models then combine baseline features, changes over 24 weeks, and patient data. Adding later scans raised the mean concordance index from 0.58 to 0.64. Some features also tracked survival over time.
arxiv-2603-26988: Cornelissen develops rhythmic segment analysis, a framework for describing patterns in rhythmic data. The basic unit is a fixed-length group of consecutive time intervals. Each segment splits into a total duration and an internal pattern of ratios. This view unifies three known rhythm visualizations and yields a fourth, the pattern-duration plot. Paired with a cluster transition network, it exposes regularities in synthetic and real data. The framework also generalizes rhythm ratios and the nPVI measure. A new anisochrony measure and the concept of quantality follow.
arxiv-2603-27088: Read and Zhu speed up Bayesian inference in structural vector autoregressions with sign restrictions. Tight identification makes standard accept-reject sampling wastefully slow. Their sampler first draws from a soft target that smoothly penalizes restriction violations. Efficient Markov chain methods can then explore that smooth density. An importance-sampling step converts the draws to ones obeying the hard restrictions. The method also supports prior-robust Bayesian analysis. An oil-market model with sign, elasticity, and narrative restrictions shows the approach's breadth. The gains grow as identification gets tighter.
arxiv-2603-27288: Feng introduces StretchCast, a global-regional AI weather forecasting framework on a stretched cubed-sphere mesh. Uniform global models struggle to refine one region. The stretched mesh keeps a closed globe while packing cells over a target region. A one-step base model and a multistep rollout model test the design. Training used ERA5 data with 69 variables from 1998 to 2022. The larger rollout model stayed competitive on regional anomaly correlation. Typhoon and spectral checks showed realistic, smooth structure across mesh faces.
arxiv-2603-27688: Galviz proves two quantum field theories match for the U(1) case. One side is extended Chern-Simons theory. The other is the Reshetikhin-Turaev construction. Both are tied to finite quadratic modules. For even level k, the theories are naturally isomorphic. The match holds for closed manifolds and bordisms alike. A pointed modular category carries the data. The finite module thus fixes the whole theory.
arxiv-2603-27788: Asiaee and co-authors warn that trial results may not travel to new groups. Hidden traits can differ between trial and target groups. Such traits can also shift the treatment effect itself. Their framework gives an exact bias split. Bias equals moderation strength times moderator imbalance. Scale-free parameters rest on partial R-squared values. Closed-form bounds let teams benchmark hidden risks. A hidden trait as strong as a known one can be tested.
arxiv-2603-28088: He and six co-authors present GEMS, a framework that wraps multimodal generation models in an agent system with memory and skills. Base models still stumble on complex instructions and niche tasks. GEMS adds three parts: an agent loop that refines output in rounds, a layered memory of facts and past runs, and loadable skill packs for special domains. Across nine tasks, GEMS lifted every backend tested. A small 6B model with GEMS even beat a top rival on GenEval2.
arxiv-2603-28288: N'guessan upgrades Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks by swapping their spline bases for fractal interpolation functions. Fixed spline grids give KANs no built-in sense of scale, which hurts on rough functions. His FI-KAN learns each edge's fractal dimension as it trains, matching the target's roughness. A hybrid version keeps the spline path and adds a fractal fix on top. On rough targets the gains ran from 1.3 to 79 times better than plain KAN. Learned dimensions matched the true ones.
arxiv-2603-28388: Campisi gives the general formula for ergotropy, the work a classical system can give up, without the usual smoothness limits. The known formula assumed a continuous phase space density with no flat spots. He recasts the problem as rearranging a function, which yields an ergotropic rearrangement rule for any density. Applying it at large scale, he finds that densities set by the Hamiltonian alone become passive in the thermodynamic limit. No cyclic process can then extract work.
arxiv-2603-28588: Ceriotti and co-authors provide an introduction to path integral methods for atomistic modelling. Their book covers the core theory behind the methods. It also covers simulation techniques developed more recently. Readers get a self-contained resource for learning how path integrals model atomistic processes. The text grew out of the CECAM schools on Path Integral Methods. It aims to serve both study and practical use. Students and researchers can use it to build a base before applying the methods to real systems.
arxiv-2603-28788: Mason presents Legible Consensus, a quorum design for asymmetric networks that makes failure modes easy to read. Flat quorums treat all nodes as interchangeable. When consensus fails, they hide whether a tier was unreachable or lost too many replicas. Mason maps a crumbling-wall quorum onto a physically tiered network. That split separates cross-tier duties from within-tier replication. A ten-node Earth, low orbit, Moon, and Mars test case acts as a magnifying glass. During a Mars blackout, three of four tiers kept global liveness.
arxiv-2603-28888: Runwal and co-authors test a semantic observer layer for self-driving cars. Some hazards depend on context and escape pixel level detectors. Their layer runs a quantized vision-language model at 1 to 2 hertz beside the main control loop. It watches for semantic edge cases and triggers fail-safe handoffs. With NVFP4 quantization and FlashAttention2, inference took about 500 milliseconds on their hardware. That is a 50 fold speedup over the unoptimized baseline. They also flag an NF4 recall collapse as a hard deployment limit and map metrics to safety goals.
arxiv-2603-28988: Tan, Singer, and Anagnostopoulos propose an attestation gate for language model pipelines. Modern systems are built from third party weights, adapters, datasets, and packages. That speed brings supply chain risks, like forged provenance and backdoored models. Training and release claims are rarely bound by cryptography to the artifacts they describe. Their gate checks claim evidence before an artifact enters trusted settings. It enforces safe loading and scanning rules and secure default deployment limits. A claims to controls mapping and an evaluation blueprint chart a path to a full study.
arxiv-2603-29788: Sendjasni and Larabi test a fusion method for spotting AI-generated images. Detectors that use one cue type often fail on new generators. Their method joins three cue sets: contrast statistics, CLIP semantic embeddings, and texture patterns. Trials span four benchmark datasets with many generator types. Single cue sets swing widely in performance across generators. The fused set performs best and stays most consistent. It also beats leading methods on all four datasets.
arxiv-2604-00088: Sun, Shu Yang, and Yi Yang realize the erratic non-Hermitian skin effect in a driven photonic mesh lattice. Here eigenstates pile into the bulk rather than at the edges. Tuning programmable gain, loss, and phase carries the system across a transition between two oppositely directed skin phases through a point of global reciprocity. At that point edge accumulation vanishes while bulk-localized patterns persist. Added on-site disorder then gradually suppresses the erratic skin behavior in favor of Anderson localization.
arxiv-2604-00688: Zhu and colleagues present OmniVoice, a zero-shot text-to-speech model for over 600 languages. Its core is a discrete non-autoregressive diffusion architecture. Older discrete models stall in two-step pipelines from text to meaning to sound, but OmniVoice maps text to multi-codebook sound tokens. Two tricks enable this: full-codebook random masking for training, and starting from a pre-trained language model for clearness. Trained on 581,000 hours of multilingual data gathered from open sources, it claims the broadest language reach to date with top results.
arxiv-2604-00788: Souly and colleagues report methods from the UK AI Security Institute for testing advanced AI systems deployed as coding assistants. The question is whether those systems reliably follow intended goals. Across four frontier models, they find no confirmed sabotage of safety research, though two models often refuse safety-relevant tasks over concerns about research direction and scope. Both tested models could also tell evaluation from deployment when prompted, while one showed weaker unprompted evaluation awareness.
arxiv-2604-00988: Gunnarsson and Klöfkorn propose a discontinuous Galerkin scheme for degenerate-mobility Cahn-Hilliard models using the Symmetric Weighted Interior Penalty form. Judging mobility at cell means, not as a piecewise polynomial, keeps degeneracy and gives a mobility-free coercivity constant, removing regularization. They prove discrete answers exist despite degeneracy via a Leray-Schauder fixed-point proof. They show a maximum rule at any polynomial order with the Zhang-Shu limiter, or from the scheme alone at order zero. Tests confirm optimal convergence rates and the scheme's shape-keeping traits.
arxiv-2604-01188:
Neelay Junnarkar and two co-authors work on safe neural network control in a 2026 paper. Such networks do well at steering hard, curved systems in tests. But safety work needs proof they can shrug off shocks and doubt.

The team builds the network and its proof of strength at one time. The proof is a formal pledge that the closed loop will hold up. They train with attacks, where each failed case guides the next round. A failed case shows just where the pledge breaks, so training can fix it. This joins learning with proof in a single loop of work. It gives engineers a path to learned control with proof in hand.
arxiv-2604-01588: Hu and colleagues introduce NED-Tree, a method bridging the semantic gap in translating Operations Research problems from language to models. Large language models show promise in linear tasks but degrade in nonlinear settings from semantic gaps between formulations and solver codes. NED-Tree uses sentence-by-sentence extraction to map parameters, plus a recursive tree breaking complex nonlinear terms into solver-compatible sub-elements. They also present NEXTOR, a benchmark for nonlinear Operations Research problems. Across 10 benchmarks, NED-Tree sets a state-of-the-art with 72.51 percent average accuracy.
arxiv-2604-01888: Mustafa and co-authors show text-to-image models remain open to low-effort jailbreaks using only prompts. Filters aim to block harmful content, yet the authors study prompt tricks bypassing filters without model access, tuning or hostile training. They list jailbreak methods: material substitution, artistic reframing, ambiguous action substitution, pseudo-educational framing, lifestyle camouflage. These tricks exploit gaps in safety filters by masking intent in benign contexts. Tests across text-to-image systems show simple wording changes can evade guards and produce banned imagery, with success up to 74.47 percent.
arxiv-2604-01988: Zhuang and colleagues test whether language models show number sense with SenseMath, a benchmark of 4,800 items across eight types. It runs three checks: using shortcuts, judging fit or mislead, and generating fresh problems admitting a shortcut. Across five models, prompted models used shortcuts and gained up to 15 percent accuracy on shortcut items. Yet under chain-of-thought prompting spontaneous use ran below 40 percent of cases. Competence stopped at use: models overapplied shortcuts where they fail and could not generate valid ones, showing procedure without understanding of when shortcuts work.
arxiv-2604-02088: Endo, Hao and Sumi give image editing a slider that needs no training. Their FlowSlider splits a flow edit into a fidelity term that holds identity and structure steady and a steering term that pushes meaning toward the target. Because the two terms sit nearly at right angles, scaling only the steering term changes edit strength without drifting off course. The result is smooth, stable control across varied tasks, with no post training and no reliance on synthetic supervision.
arxiv-2604-02588: Avilés and three colleagues sort out order convergence in separable Banach lattices. They build a transfinite hierarchy of weakenings of the Fatou property over countable ordinals, showing it gives a full classification. A key sequence set being Borel, sigma-order convergence being analytic, and the lattice meeting some level of the hierarchy all turn out to mean the same thing. The hierarchy has no top rung, so complexity can climb as high as one likes below the first uncountable ordinal.
arxiv-2604-02888: Ong and Akimoto accelerate black-box bilevel optimization with rank-based upper-level value function approximation. Evolution methods pay high costs from nested solving. Shortcuts falter on landscapes with many modes and strong links between levels. Their framework exploits how rank-based algorithms ignore monotonic changes, approximating upper-level value rankings directly. It skips full lower-level convergence each iteration, using CMA-ES for continuous levels. Tests show competitive results against existing methods.
arxiv-2604-02988: Câmara, Slot and Zavrel ask whether deep research systems, which plan, retrieve, and synthesize evidence across hundreds of documents, can improve themselves. Today's systems lean on hand-written prompts and fixed designs, so gains are brittle and costly. The team lets agents self-play and try varied prompt combinations instead, testing several multi-agent optimization methods. The self-tuned systems match or beat expert-crafted prompts, showing that automated tuning can replace careful hand design.
arxiv-2604-03388: Xiang, Li, and Lu build a scalable Bayesian fine-tuning method for language models that also reports trustworthy uncertainty. Their PoLAR-VBLL framework pairs an orthogonalized low-rank adapter with a Bayesian last layer, avoiding both fragile post-hoc calibration and costly repeated full-model passes. Tests on common-sense reasoning show better generalization and uncertainty estimates on both familiar and unfamiliar data.
arxiv-2604-03488: Hur, Nath, and Allen's 2026 method returns trust sets for cluster labels, a quantity rarely given strict guarantees. Their split conformal clustering with random labels draws labels from soft cluster labels and fits a soft sorter to them, and tunes scores to build trust sets at any query point. Tests show target coverage with useful set sizes, and a use on single-cell RNA-seq cell types shows practical value.
arxiv-2604-03588: Sadowski and Chudziak propose Rashomon Memory, a design where side-by-side goal-tuned agents encode events by their own goals and argue at query time. Each view keeps its own world model and knowledge graph. At lookup, views propose readings, critique each other with one-sided domain knowledge, and Dung's rules decide which proposals survive. The attack graph itself explains the outcome: it records the chosen reading, the other options weighed, and the grounds for turndown.
arxiv-2604-03688: Zhifu Wei and colleagues improved recommendations for rarely seen items, which suffer because few past clicks reveal how they connect to others. Their FAERec system blends item IDs with language-model meaning through an adaptive gate, then aligns the two views at both item and feature levels. Tests on three datasets with several standard recommenders showed broad gains.
arxiv-2604-04188: Jarosław Błasiok and team disproved conjectures linking expansion to hardness for noisy k-XOR. Lower bounds in restricted models like Sum-of-Squares had suggested that expanding graphs make the problem hard. The authors built an explicit family of near-optimal expanders for which noisy k-XOR runs in polynomial time. Their graphs rest on the lossless expanders of Guruswami, Umans, and Vadhan, reinterpreted so the XOR problem becomes decoding Reed-Muller codes from random errors.
arxiv-2604-04288: Shifat and colleagues survey security flaws in open-source systems embedding large language models. They study 295 GitHub advisories from January 2025 to January 2026 that mention language-model parts, hand-checking 100 against the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications. No new implementation-level weakness class turns up; most advisories map to known types, notably injection and deserialization flaws. Yet recurring design risks appear, above all Supply Chain, Excessive Agency and Prompt Injection, often spanning several stages. The authors argue that pairing CWE and OWASP views gives a fuller picture of model-mediated exposure.
arxiv-2604-04588: Magnot treats nonreciprocal pairwise comparison matrices as a mix of scale variation and random noise, not defects to fix. He builds an additive model with a consistent base matrix that need not be reciprocal. Its reciprocal part carries ranking information, while its symmetric part describes scale variation. Around this structured matrix with added random perturbation, the paper shows how to estimate the noise level, judge whether scale variation stays moderate, and assign probabilities to admissible ranking regions. Gaussian noise is used because judgment errors often pile up from small effects.
arxiv-2604-04688: Singh proves that a graded Grothendieck-Teichmüller group matches the group of maps that keep the cyclic operad of ribbon chord diagrams in shape. The proof rests on Furusho's five-cycle form of the pentagon equation. He then sets out how that group acts on framed chord diagrams whose objects are self-dual. The action bears on the target of the Kontsevich integral for framed tangles.
arxiv-2604-04888: Ceară extends encrypted quantum cloning from qubits to systems of any dimension. A recent result showed encrypted qubits can be cloned, but a direct extension using shift and phase operators fails a basic gate rule. He introduces a new encryption operator and proves it unitary, then adapts the earlier decryption operator to multi-level systems. Checking the circuit design, he shows the extra cost grows only linearly with qudit dimension, keeping higher-dimensional encrypted cloning practical.
arxiv-2604-04988: Zhou and Shen study an ordered pipeline for shrinking neural networks under tight CPU and memory limits. Proxies such as parameter count poorly predict real inference time, and unstructured sparsity can even slow CPU runs. Their pipeline targets measured latency with pruning, INT8 quantization-aware training, and knowledge distillation. INT8 training gives the largest runtime gain, while pruning mainly regulates capacity, so step order matters for speed.
arxiv-2604-05588: Han and four colleagues propose floating Majorana edge bands in two-dimensional superconductors that break time symmetry yet carry helical-like flow. Lone, momentum-split modes that run opposite ways arise via uneven Wilson masses and show up in a quantum anomalous Hall slab paired with a d-wave superconductor. Heat-flow marks include a full quantized value and a tough half-quantized plateau.
arxiv-2604-06188: Kirgis and five colleagues audit how chatbots handle delusional and conspiratorial talk across 56 twenty-turn conversations with ChatGPT-4o and ChatGPT-5 via APIs and chat interfaces. Chat-interface results differ sharply from API results, so API-only testing misses real-world impact. In chat, ChatGPT-5 shows milder delusion reinforcement, escalation, and sycophancy than ChatGPT-4o, tying behavior to company policy choices. Similar overall intensity can hide different turn-by-turn paths, updated models still show substantial negative behavior, and the same API endpoint reverses behavior within two months.
arxiv-2604-06388: Burns-Watson, Sullivan, and Kraus use transit densities to identify host stars in binary systems. Thousands of exoplanets reveal a radius gap between about 1.8 and 2 Earth radii. The gap may vanish in binaries, where planets are usually assumed to orbit the primary, though companion planets look much larger. Across 15 exoplanets in 10 binaries, each with at least one gap planet if circumprimary, they find 5 highly likely circumprimary, with the rest ambiguous. No planet is unambiguously circumsecondary, as biases favor primaries. Summed probabilities suggest the gap looks less vacant in binaries.
arxiv-2604-06688: Liu, Shang, and Jin ask how markets should work when AI agents trade delegated work with each other. Each agent can post tasks, bid, complete work, judge outputs, and settle payments, yet market rules grow costly to change once baked into infrastructure. Their diagon system lets researchers run controlled experiments, configuring allocation, contracting, and enforcement rules while agents decide the rest. Experiments show that agent setups and market rules reshape trade, quality, and wealth, so consequences can be weighed before deployment.
arxiv-2604-06888: Liu and Zhao build a low-redshift-agnostic squeeze of DESI sound-wave spacings for dark energy density growth. Sound-wave numbers mix low-redshift growth history into higher-redshift signals through transverse spacings. The authors swap those spacings for step-to-step increments while keeping radial spacings, so errors stay exact and growth bins come out nearly uncorrelated. Dropping one absolute transverse mode strips low-redshift bias from the fit, and on DESI DR1 and DR2 data, every growth bin matches a constant density within errors.
arxiv-2604-07088: Činč, Darji, and Vejnar build a bridge from the Cantor set, a classic fractured space, to fence-like spaces such as hairy arcs and the Lelek fan. Each reversible reshaping of the Cantor set lifts to a matching reshaping of the associated fence. Properties like minimality and recurrence carry along with the lift. The construction unifies dynamics across these spaces and links their tangled geometry to the behavior of maps moving points through them.
arxiv-2604-07688: Li, Niu, and Ruzicka prove that Villadsen algebras outside the well-behaved Z-stable class are singly generated, meaning a single element suffices to generate the whole algebra. More broadly, they show the same holds for any simple unital AH algebra whose connecting maps are diagonal. The result tightens the structural picture of these algebras, which serve as test cases and counterexamples in the classification of operator algebras.
arxiv-2604-08088: Ding and three colleagues propose CDAMD for text-to-motion generation from motion data. Text-to-motion serves cartoons, virtual reality, robots, and human-machine interaction. Diffusion models amplify errors during noise prediction, while autoregressive models collapse toward few modes because motion is split. CDAMD follows the same path and uses layered perceptrons to boost fidelity. With coordinates as input, it aims for flexible, faithful motion from text.
arxiv-2604-08388: Chung and four colleagues ask whether heavy training on formal mathematics permanently kills a model's general tool use. Their test model, Goedel-Prover-V2, fell from 89.4 percent correct tool calls to near zero after specializing on 1.8 million math examples. Just 100 Lean tool use traces revived the skill, lifting a broad tool calling leaderboard score from near zero to 83.8 percent and improving proof success on ProofNet as well.
arxiv-2604-08488: Magnan and Latter test the laminar path to planetesimal formation, in which vortices gather dust until it collapses under its own weight. Using multi timescale models that differ in whether vortex mass or gas density stays fixed, they track how dust drag reshapes vortices. Vortices that adjust their spin drift toward elliptically unstable shapes, and since that instability destroys the vortex, dust caps vortex lifetimes and may kill the laminar path if destruction comes first.
arxiv-2604-08588: DiSorbo and Ju model automation as a choice under uncertainty: act now or escalate to a human. A language model predicts, gauges its own chance of being right, and weighs the costs of acting against escalating, across forecasting, recommendation, moderation, lending, and driving. Escalation thresholds vary by model in ways size and design do not predict, and training on reasoning traces yields the most robust policies across datasets and cost ratios.
arxiv-2604-08688: Biswas, Datta, and Mele probe Higgs and top interactions through a future 10 TeV muon collider's lens on dimension six operators in Standard Model effective field theory. Many operators are weakly constrained at the LHC. They simulate muon collisions producing Z plus Higgs, Higgs with muons, top pairs, and top pairs with Higgs, using differential and angular information to bound Wilson coefficients. Limits on muon Higgs gauge and muon top couplings strengthen by up to an order of magnitude, beating FCC-ee projections.
arxiv-2604-08988: Jiang and eleven colleagues formalize the self-evolving agent, which should carry experience across tasks instead of starting fresh each time. Current agents handle single episodes well but forget lessons across tasks, trapped by fixed toolsets and episodic amnesia. The paper defines this agent type and proposes the Evolutionary Flywheel as its minimal architecture. SEA-Eval is its first benchmark, built to judge such agents. Tests show token use differs by up to 31.2 times between frameworks at similar success rates, so success alone misleads.
arxiv-2604-09488: Cudennec, Jeanneau, Bacon, Lépine, and Lehnert present integral field spectrograph designs for the Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope. The telescope is a planned 12-meter segmented site for seeing-limited visible work. It will run a multi-object spectrograph with high multiplexing and a panoramic field instrument. Its field concept builds on MUSE, using field splitters and image slicers to reshape a large field into pseudo-slits. The authors present the design for high throughput and image quality, and investigate curved detectors to simplify layout and cut aberrations.
arxiv-2604-09588: Menon diagnoses a flaw in AI agent identity. When context windows overflow and histories are summarized, agents lose not just facts but continuity of self. Human identity survives damage by spreading across episodic memory, procedural memory, emotional continuity, and embodied knowledge. Agent identity, by contrast, sits in a single store. His open-source soul.py mirrors that spread with separable identity files and memory logs. A hybrid retrieval system routes queries to fitting memory patterns. It also maps a path toward agents that survive partial memory failure.
arxiv-2604-09788: Arcodia and 27 co-authors present O-C timing analysis of the eruption source eRO-QPE2 from an X-ray campaign. The campaign includes 32 eruptions spanning a month, or 325 cycles. Against accretion models, the timing fits a damped random walk, albeit with highly uncertain parameters. If an orbital clock is present, eRO-QPE2 fits a period near two and a quarter hours with super-periodic modulations near 4 days and near 95 days. No negative period derivative appears, disfavoring high-eccentricity white dwarfs and eccentric intermediate-mass black holes via gravitational decay.
arxiv-2604-10188: Zhu and eight colleagues generate radiology reports from low-quality X-ray images, a setting current vision-language models handle badly. Existing methods assume high-quality inputs and degrade sharply on real clinic noise and artifacts. Their framework first flags low-quality samples in MIMIC-CXR with an automated quality assessment agent, establishing the LRRG benchmark. A dual-loop training strategy then uses bi-level optimization and gradient consistency to learn diagnostic features that hold across quality levels. Tests show the approach effectively counters degradation from poor image quality.
arxiv-2604-10588: Herceg and Antunes build a safety-certification framework for controllers learned from data. It covers cases where training and real deployment differ and losses need not stay bounded. They combine PAC-Bayes generalization theory with distributionally robust optimization based on Wasserstein distance. From this they derive a loss proxy and a bound on the damage from distribution shift, both tied to the closed-loop map. For linear time-invariant systems the result is a tractable optimization scheme with high-probability safety certificates for real deployment.
arxiv-2604-10888: Herbig and Hung study character conductors of low-rank Lie groups. For an irreducible character chi of a finite group, the conductor is the smallest positive integer n with all values in Q(exp(2 pi i over n)). They show that for rank 1 groups of Lie type, the conductor is realized at a single element: some g gives c(chi) equal to c(chi(g)). In quasisimple cases, the value field is generated by a single value. This connects to Feit's conjecture, reduced to simple groups by Boltje and colleagues.
arxiv-2604-10988: Yuan and three colleagues present WebForge, the first self-running framework for the rerun, realism, and scale trilemma in browser agent benchmarks. A four-agent pipeline of plan, generate, refine, and validate produces interactive web environments without hand labels. Real-website benchmarks lack repeatability through content drift, while controlled settings omit real-web noise. Both need costly work. A seven-part difficulty scale structures tasks along click depth, visual load, and thinking load. WebForge-Bench holds nine hundred thirty-four tasks across seven domains and three difficulty levels.
arxiv-2604-11288: Basu tackles a blind spot in KV-cache compression: dormant tokens such as credentials and keys draw almost no attention yet prove essential at generation time. At just 16 tokens, a mere 0.4 percent of a 4K context, every existing method scores zero on credential retrieval. His Transactional Attention lets structural anchors like 'key:' shield nearby values from eviction, reaching 100 percent retrieval where six baselines score zero, and a fast variant cuts memory overhead by 52 percent.
arxiv-2604-11388: Szyfelbein generalizes min-sum set cover to parallel machines, with m set-sequences. An alpha-approximation for parallel densest subfamily yields a four-alpha approximation for the cover problem. That gives four-e-over-e-minus-one plus epsilon for identical machines and four times its square for unrelated machines. A new knapsack coverage approximation underpins the latter result. Unit-cost sets with precedence constraints admit order k-to-the-two-thirds; out-forest constraints improve this to order log k, tight unless NP sits inside quasi-polynomial randomized time.
arxiv-2604-11488: Shadab and six colleagues present HydroFirn, a large-scale multidimensional firn model. Existing large-scale firn models are mostly 1D. That limits explaining meltwater dynamics and ice patterns, and reducing doubt in mass balance and sea rise. HydroFirn is multi-phase and thermomechanical. It gains efficiency by solving an extra pressure equation only in soaked regions. It allows varied boundary conditions and dynamic sealed ice layers. Checked against exact solutions and applied to Greenland data, it shows side differences strongly shape melt percolation depth and ice-layer formation.
arxiv-2604-11688: Maiti studies frustration limits in variational quantum algorithms. Frustration from clashing ties blocks joint energy minima, challenging these methods. On a square-lattice Ising model with frustrated side links, it yields uneven correlations. Standard ansätze with global parameters capture them poorly, sharply raising required circuit depth in the mid-field regime. The limit comes not from barren plateaus but from weak ansatz expressibility. Bond-resolved parameters restore accuracy at reduced depth, though near-degenerate spectra further challenge these methods.
arxiv-2604-11788: Korem and ten colleagues generate high dynamic range video from a pretrained model by encoding footage logarithmically, as film pipelines do. That encoding already lines up with the model's latent space, so only light fine-tuning is needed and no new encoder must be trained. Camera-flaw mimicry in training helps the model infer bright and dark detail it cannot see directly, with strong results across varied scenes and hard lighting.
arxiv-2604-11888: Álvares and Fernandes build rotating thin shells that join two spacetimes in Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet gravity, using Davis junction rules. Inner and outer regions copy the same rotating metric with different mass and spin. The only possible shells are vacuum shells or shells with pressure in one tangential direction and nothing else. Their motion equation mirrors the continuity equation of general relativity, and in special vacuum cases a shell can collapse to a naked singularity, with stable static shells when both sides are overextremal.
arxiv-2604-12088: Tan, Wang, and Tan study safety in code generation, where models are judged on correctness. Code models reproduce offensive identifiers from injected renaming instructions without warning. Viewing code as machine execution and human communication, they propose a duality score unifying utility, safety, and warnings. They add Dual Reasoning, a safety audit and code review before generation. On six models and two benchmarks with keyword injections, Dual Reasoning tops the duality score, improving scores by 1.32 to 3.42 times. Chain-of-thought gives negligible gains; a safety-aware prompt gives partial improvement.
arxiv-2604-12288: Jinhang Chai and three colleagues develop a fine-tuning method for adapting a pretrained model. It targets cases where target data are scarce and variables are many. Their SMART approach adds the source model's output as an extra feature. Only the leftover, target-specific part is learned from scratch. A low-rank factor structure handles correlated inputs. The paper proves optimal risk bounds for when fine-tuning beats learning from scratch. Experiments show near-oracle performance with very small target samples.
arxiv-2604-12388: Michael Mandl compares correctness criteria for complex Langevin simulations. That method tackles systems with a sign problem, where standard sampling fails. Complex Langevin dynamics can fail to converge or converge to a wrong limit. Four simple but nontrivial models serve as test cases for the criteria. No single criterion proves foolproof on its own. Combining several criteria in practice is the advisable course. The findings likely extend to more realistic theories too.
arxiv-2604-12488: Jiaxin Li and three colleagues derive exact formulas for a quantity in commutative algebra. The quantity is the depth of a quotient ring built from powers of an edge ideal. An edge ideal turns the edges of a graph into algebraic objects. Here the graph is an increasing weighted path. Powers of the ideal raise those edge objects to higher exponents. The paper's formulas give the depth exactly across this path family.
arxiv-2604-12688: Igor Kavrakov and three colleagues build synthetic data with elastic finite element models. Their method extends a statFEM approach. Bayesian filtering handles gaps between data and model. Data join the state as it advances via a stochastic Newmark scheme. Prior curves come from a forward problem. Posterior curves follow by updating on data at each step. Random fields model forcing and flaws. A small-change trick yields a Gaussian posterior with closed-form mean and spread. Settings fit data best. 1D and 2D tests illustrate the method.
arxiv-2604-12788: Theophile Gaichies and three colleagues study the dent a slanted jet makes in a liquid bath. Below 50 degrees, a cavity forms ahead of the jet. The jet boundary layer detaches at impact, leaving a core jet region. Outside, liquid sits mainly in hydrostatic equilibrium. The outer meniscus matches that outside a tilted fiber piercing the interface. Simulations show asymmetric detachment accelerates subsurface liquid, creating a depression. A model balances suction against water weight and surface tension. It predicts the typical cavity width.
arxiv-2604-12988: Pei and five colleagues replace execution accuracy, the standard score for judging text-to-SQL systems, with ROSE, a metric that asks whether the predicted query answers the user's intent. A prover checks the query's meaning against that intent, while an adversarial refuter challenges the verdict using the reference query as evidence. On their expert-aligned test set, ROSE beats the next-best metric by nearly 24 percent in agreement with human experts.
arxiv-2604-13188: Morozov and Sy test whether city productivity edge reduces to shift, dilation, and truncation of firm productivity distributions, following Combes and colleagues' 2012 split. Using Spanish firm-level data and methods robust to noisy estimates, they find curves in denser and less dense areas are indeed identical up to those terms. Shifts and dilations alone suffice, at least in Spain, suggesting policy makers should focus on agglomeration policies.
arxiv-2604-13288: Ortega, Zevallos, and Carraro build speech synthesis for Quechua and Spanish using the Peruvian Constitution as text. They train three modern text-to-speech systems on separate Spanish and Quechua recordings of uneven size and quality, using cross-language transfer to offset Quechua data scarcity while keeping Spanish natural. They release trained models, code, and audio for every article, aiming at inclusive speech tools for legal and political material in low-resource settings.
arxiv-2604-13588: Chen and Wang study information velocity, the speed at which messages cross a long chain of erasure channels with vanishing error. For small messages they pin down the best speed with a simple bit-separation scheme that spaces bits so their flows rarely collide, unlike earlier coding-heavy designs. When every node knows all link states, the same optimum extends to larger messages, though that extra knowledge adds nothing in the small-message case.
arxiv-2604-13688: Xu and eight colleagues move 3D editing beyond voxels. Their BVE framework learns from 3D masks and a self-constructed large dataset built for editing. Lightweight trainable modules inject textual meaning into a base image-to-3D model without expensive full retraining. An annotation-free masking strategy preserves local invariance, so untouched regions stay faithful to the original. Tests show high-quality, text-aligned assets that retain the input's visual character.
arxiv-2604-13788: Rolland, Mayran de Chamisso, and Mouret build FIDeL, a module that spots genuine failures in imitation-learned robot policies. Rare faults, defective parts, or unexpected human actions can break executions. Anomaly detectors often cannot tell failures from harmless deviations. FIDeL represents nominal demos compactly. It aligns new observations by optimal transport matching to score anomalies and map them. A vision-language model then filters benign anomalies by meaning. On the new BotFails dataset it gains over 5 percent in AUROC and over 17 percent in failure-detection accuracy.
arxiv-2604-13888: Yu and colleagues test whether language-model agents can run real geographic analysis, not just match text or code. Their GeoAgentBench sandbox offers 117 atomic GIS tools across 53 tasks in 6 domains, scored by how exactly each agent sets parameters and by vision checks of maps. A new Plan-and-React design, which splits overall planning from step-by-step reaction, beat older frameworks, especially on long tasks and error recovery.
arxiv-2604-13988: Ahangarkiasari and colleagues test whether hypnogram realism can steer unsupervised adaptation when sleep signals degrade. Pairing a pretrained u-sleep model with a discriminator network, they align target-domain features with the pretrained feature space. Across distortion types, kappa gains reach up to about 0.3 and never hurt performance, though the method falls short of supervised best cases and shows little benefit on a real study-to-study mismatch.
arxiv-2604-14488: Bacellar defines controlling authority retrieval: finding the active authority frontier for an anchor, not the most similar document. In law, drug regulation, and software security, older authorities can be revoked by newer distant ones. A theorem states exactly when a retrieved set truly covers the active set: frontier inclusion plus no ignored superseder. A second result bounds coverage in the worst case. On advisories, two-stage retrieval lifts scores from 27 to about 98 percent over dense retrieval, with gains elsewhere. False not-patched claims fall from 39 to 16 percent of queries.
arxiv-2604-14688: Chatterjee and Hryczuk examine a dark sector that makes dark matter by gradual freeze-in without ever fully thermalizing inside. In a minimal two-scalar model, they compare a full phase-space treatment with the usual number-density shortcut. The predicted dark-matter abundance can differ by up to a factor of ten between the two. That gap matters for indirect-detection signals and long-lived-particle searches, so they argue phase-space computation is essential for trustworthy freeze-in predictions.
arxiv-2604-14888: Sánchez, Lewis-Lim, Aletras, and Elliott track reasoning in 18 vision-language models. They find answer inertia: early commitments get reinforced, not revised, during reasoning. Reasoning-trained models correct more, but gains depend on modality. Misleading textual cues sway models even when vision suffices, and chain-of-thought exposes this only partly. Reasoning-trained models name cues, yet fluent traces can look visually grounded while following them. Instruction-tuned models name cues less, but shorter traces expose clashes. Chain-of-thought gives only a partial view of multimodal decisions.
arxiv-2604-15588: Wu and four colleagues introduce CoLabScience, a proactive helper for biomedical discovery that jumps into streaming expert discussions instead of waiting to be asked. Its PULI framework, trained by reinforcement learning on project proposals plus long- and short-term dialogue memory, learns when and how to jump in. On a new test set of mock PubMed-derived dialogues, it beats rivals on jump-in precision and team task value.
arxiv-2604-15688: Qin and five colleagues present a velocity synthesis-assisted localization algorithm for multi-site single-input single-output radar indoor tracking. Fusing radial velocity measurements from multiple radars iteratively refines positions within range bins, staying robust under low signal-to-noise, severe multipath, and large sync latency. Without MIMO hardware or strict phase sync, the system reaches centimeter-level tracking accuracy for people, beating existing methods on complex trajectories.
arxiv-2604-16388: Lee and colleagues give robot planners a goal they can see rather than a set of joint angles they must be told. Visual-RRT merges gradient-driven refinement from differentiable robot rendering with the broad sampling of rapidly-exploring random trees. A frontier strategy steers the search toward visually promising regions, while inherited optimization states keep gradient steps consistent across branches. Experiments with Franka, UR5e and Fetch arms in simulation and the real world showed the planner reaching image-specified goals, bridging sampling-based planning and vision-led robotics.
arxiv-2604-16488: Gasquet refines complexity bounds for the satisfiability problem in dense modal logics, a question likely sitting between PSPACE and EXPSPACE depending on the logic. For the class called n-dense logics, defined by axioms taking boxed formulas to less-boxed forms, he moves beyond known membership in NEXPTIME. Using parameterized complexity with modal depth as the parameter, he proves these logics belong to para-PSPACE, meaning a polynomial-space algorithm exists once depth is fixed. The proof generalizes an earlier windows analysis tool to recursive windows.
arxiv-2604-16688: Masterson and colleagues track the X-ray quasi-periodic oscillation in the galactic nucleus ES. The source defied expectations, launching a radio jet as its oscillation appeared. Its frequency evolved across one to two and a half millihertz from 2022 to 2024, unlike other known oscillations. It persists but has plateaued at two and a half millihertz. Over 900 cycles, the team finds no second harmonic and a stable soft lag at all frequencies. Jumps near 80 percent of baseline flux persist with a dip-rise-fall pattern, and NuSTAR confirms the oscillation.
arxiv-2604-16988: Dudley and three colleagues formalize in-context change-point detection: can transformers spot when a data stream's rules shift, and adapt on the fly? They prove such transformers exist, with the needed size depending on how much is known about the change point's timing. Trained models match optimal baselines on synthetic regression and dynamical systems, and feeding change-point knowledge into a pretrained model lifts infectious-disease and financial-volatility forecasts without retraining.
arxiv-2604-17888: Wensheng Wang and four colleagues present SpaceDex, a hierarchical system for dexterous grasping in cluttered, tiered spaces where occlusion and height limits beat open-tabletop methods. A vision-language planner reads intent across camera views and proposes targets for segmentation and tracking, while a separated arm-hand network decouples reaching from grasp choice, aided by touch sensing and recovery examples. In 100 real trials with over 30 unseen objects, it succeeds 63.0 percent of the time against 39.0 percent for a strong baseline.
arxiv-2604-18188: Sahade and six colleagues study a complex coronal mass ejection that erupted on 2024 October 26. Coronal mass ejections are giant plasma clouds thrown from the Sun, and their shape depends on magnetic conditions before eruption. Using multiview observations plus a physics-based CORHELCME model, they test several plausible starting magnetic setups. Small shifts in footpoint position change the trajectory sharply, and only one background-field choice reproduces the fine shape seen from three viewpoints.
arxiv-2604-18688: Rodriguez and six colleagues study two long-period radio transients linked to white dwarfs closely orbited by M dwarf stars. New optical spectra confirm one system's orbital period nearly matches its radio pulse period, and both pairs host unusually massive, cool, nearly crystallized white dwarfs seen almost face-on. Models predict each M dwarf will overflow onto its companion within about a billion years, becoming a cataclysmic variable.
arxiv-2604-18788: Benazir and Lin present NPUMoE, a runtime engine for mixture of experts inference on Apple Silicon that offloads dense, static computation to the Neural Engine. Expert routing is unpredictable and creates dynamic tensor shapes, while irregular operators and many small expert kernels add dispatch overhead. NPUMoE addresses these with static tiers for expert capacity, grouped expert execution, and load aware residency of the expert compute graph. On Apple M series devices, with three models and four long workloads, it beats baselines on latency, energy efficiency, and CPU cycle use.
arxiv-2604-18888: Mohammadiasl and three colleagues propose a graph neural network framework for predicting link formation in social learning networks. Traditional methods are tuned to general online social networks. They often miss the complex, non-Euclidean, dynamically evolving structure of classroom networks. The method jointly weighs within-classroom temporal evolution and cross-classroom spatial aggregation. Tests on networks from four classrooms show gains in predicting future links as courses progress. Aggregating classrooms helps, especially in sparser data sets.
arxiv-2604-19488: Yan and colleagues propose CoDA, a method for effective cross-domain knowledge transfer via chain-of-thought-guided domain adaptation. Large language models have advanced substantially in logical reasoning, yet they still trail human-level performance. In-context learning boosts performance with expert-curated, in-domain exemplars, but in expertise-scarce domains like low-resource scientific fields, emerging biomedical subfields, or niche legal areas, such demonstrations are limited or absent. CoDA instead retrieves cross-domain samples as surrogate demonstrations, guided by chain-of-thought reasoning.
arxiv-2604-19588: Diez and colleagues develop a theoretical framework for magnetic coupling between nuclear motion and nuclear spins in molecules. Among dipole interactions, couplings between nuclear motion and nuclear spin have received the least attention in spectroscopy. Although very small compared with electron spin effects, this hyperfine effect matters in NMR work. The new approach sits within modern electronic structure theory and draws on the Breit-Pauli Hamiltonian, distinguishing nuclear spin-orbit and spin-other-orbit contributions.
arxiv-2604-19688: Gutiérrez, Laneve, and Sanz extend quantum signal processing to general square matrices, closing a gap in quantum algorithm design. Signal processing handles only unitary matrices through eigenvalue polynomials, while the singular value method covers Hermitian matrices alone, so neither reaches a non-Hermitian matrix that cannot be diagonalized. Their method acts on eigenvalues, giving a simple route to transform matrices of the general kind.
arxiv-2604-19888: Sharma and Chakraborty built SGAP-Gaze, a network that estimates where a driver is looking by combining face, eye, and iris images with the surrounding traffic scene. Their new UD-FSG dataset pairs synchronized driver-face and road-scene images for training. The model cut mean pixel error by 23.5 percent against leading driver-gaze systems, with gains even in rarely fixated outer scene regions that matter for safety.
arxiv-2604-19988: Nandal and five colleagues test whether pulsational mass loss from supermassive stars explains Little Red Dots, red sources with dense gas cocoons. They follow five accreting models near one hundred thousand solar masses through late evolution with pulsation checks. Mass escapes in strange-mode bursts, not a steady wind. In the clearest analogue, four late bursts eject roughly five hundred to one thousand solar masses. They leave a shell about four-tenths of a parsec wide matching the cocoon, and the star keeps about 99 percent of its mass before collapse.
arxiv-2604-20288: Aly, Sharpanskykh, and Hoekstra tackle flight diversion forecasts, where rare diversions starve models of training cases. Their synthetic data frame for aviation tables tunes new data with a joint goal of realism, stats match, truth, and forecast use, via tree-based Parzen search. Two added lenses, range and real-world fit, complete a six-stage check. Tuned TVAE, CTGAN, and CopulaGAN models beat their default forms on all six fronts, and new data lifts diversion forecasts past training on real data alone.
arxiv-2604-20588: Bae resolves the positive direction of Erdos Problem 190. H(k) is the smallest N such that every coloring of numbers up to N contains a monochromatic or rainbow k-term arithmetic progression. Bae proves the Erdos-Graham question in the positive direction. For large k, H(k) to the power 1 over k, divided by k, is at least roughly k over e log k, so it tends to infinity. The argument combines the Lovasz Local Lemma, a Blankenship-Cummings-Taranchuk recurrence, and the Baker-Harman-Pintz prime-gap theorem.
arxiv-2604-20988: Yu presents follow-up notes on mathematical programming with equilibrium constraints, this time on verifying the hypotheses behind first-order optimality conditions. He introduces core vocabulary: nonlinear programming, variational inequalities, and complementarity systems. He pursues two aims: explain the logic of the hypotheses under which first-order conditions become valid, and show how to use that theory in practice. That practice means sorting a model, choosing the right checking route, proving the right hypotheses, and drawing a correct first-order account.
arxiv-2604-21588: Andreas Holmsen and four colleagues refute a conjecture on piercing maximum cliques in hypergraphs.
