Hajnal's 1965 theorem: graphs whose maximum clique exceeds half their vertices have one-vertex-pierceable cliques. Jung, Keszegh, Pálvölgyi, and Yuditsky conjectured a higher-uniformity analogue, with a constant replacing half. They show for any constant below 1, k at least 3, and t at least 1, k-uniform hypergraphs exist whose clique exceeds that share. Yet cliques cannot be pierced by t vertices. They discuss clique size and piercing, and geometric variant using Helly's theorem.
arxiv-2604-21688: Zhou and three colleagues tackle a weak spot in IC3, a leading method for checking hardware designs. The weak step widens a single bad-state counterexample into a broader set of states. Fixed widening rules ignore the changing verification context and yield poorer clauses. Their A-IC3 system uses a multi-armed bandit learner to pick widening strategies from live feedback. It solves 26 to 50 more cases than baselines on 914 benchmark instances and improves the PAR-2 score.
arxiv-2604-21788: Bolton supplies the missing construction for the partial oracles quantum search framework, for oracle functions built only from in-place operations. The framework could beat Grover's quadratic speedup, up to an exponential maximum, but it lacked an explicit search-iteration operator. The new construction defines a reciprocal transform applied to the oracle function, which obeys a chain rule for breaking complex transforms into simple steps. Applications cover SHA-256 operations, and a QFrame Python library automates circuit construction. In-place-only oracles remain classically reversible, so quantum advantage awaits part II.
arxiv-2604-21988: Liu and Bhattacharya show that local growth laws determine the global shape of molluscan shells. Growth follows a fixed law repeatedly, even as shape evolves, without machinery to monitor and control growth. The law depends solely on local geometry at the growing edge. Shell shape is thus generated by the action of a Lie group on a protoconch. A representation of the Lie group then describes nearly all known molluscan shells with three parameters. These are a scalar for scaling, a vector for orientation, and a curve for its edge.
arxiv-2604-22088: Tuzhilina and Zhen propose a probabilistic framework for count tensors with excess zeros. They build a zero-heavy Poisson model holding latent structure through low-rank decomposition. For Hi-C data, the framework handles varied cell groups via latent clusters and ordered loci via smooth forms. Likelihood fitting plus a Bayes-best classifier splits structural from glitch zeros, allowing false-zero spotting and filling. Hi-C studies show better false-zero spotting and clustering.
arxiv-2604-22188: Nguyen and Nkuize study the best portfolio choice under stochastic volatility, where market turbulence swings at random. They use continuous-time reinforcement learning with limits on holdings. Exploration uses entropy-regularised relaxed controls: the investor picks odds over allowed holdings, not one fixed plan. They derive the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation and show the best exploratory policy is a truncated Gaussian. Under set conditions they prove classical solutions exist and a verification theorem. Their analysis then recasts the task to yield a usable learning algorithm.
arxiv-2604-22488: Günther and Klotz extend the theory of greatest lower bounds for sets of bounded self-adjoint operators, symmetric operators generalizing Hermitian matrices. Earlier work focused mostly on pairs, while this paper treats larger sets that are nonempty and bounded below. Kadison's pair theorem on infima is proved for countable sets compact in the weak-operator sense. The authors discuss and partly generalize Stott's results on maximal lower bounds for finite matrix sets. Lower bounds commuting with every member have a greatest element when members commute pairwise.
arxiv-2604-22588: Aigner and four colleagues develop exact methods for fast simulation of noisy stabilizer circuits. They derive forms for Pauli product expectation values in circuits with non-deterministic Pauli measurements. That gives fast strong simulation skipping density matrix builds and direct noise sweeps. A shrinking scheme cuts per-sample weak simulation costs in noisy stabilizer circuits, including fixed readouts, by splitting prep work from sampling. The scheme then covers a few fixed readouts, general turns, and non-diagonal noise channels, joining strong and weak runs.
arxiv-2604-22988: Boroviks and six colleagues review crystalline noble metal flakes for nanophotonics, plasmonics, and hybrid 2D designs. Their atomically flat surfaces, high crystallinity, and better optical quality beat standard polycrystalline films, which lose more light to grain edges, roughness, and defects. The flakes serve as templates for precise nanostructuring by focused-ion beam milling and support sensing, optoelectronics, and quantum light. Well-defined facets host surface states holding 2D plasmons with bulk modes, and at near-infrared light the flakes act as nearly ideal metallic mirrors.
arxiv-2604-23088: Attrah presents Code Broker, a multi-agent system built on Google's Agent Development Kit that rates Python code quality from files, directory trees, or GitHub repositories. A root orchestrator runs a pipeline agent sending three expert agents for correctness, style, and description, with findings merged by an Improvement Recommender. Reports score correctness, security, style, and upkeep on a standard scale, shown in Markdown and HTML. The system fuses language-model reasoning with Pylint static analysis signals, using non-blocking execution with backoff retries for toughness.
arxiv-2604-23388: Mekonnen, Tang, and de Rijke tackle a weakness of generative retrieval, where one neural model stores the whole index in its weights. Retraining on fresh documents lifts new results while damaging earlier slices, so the model forgets what it once knew. Their fix adds a small add-on memory that steadies the model without touching its core weights. Tests on two retrieval collections show earlier slices are retained far better at little cost to new documents.
arxiv-2604-23488: Li and colleagues test whether monitors trained on deliberately prompted reward-hacking examples can catch hacking that arises naturally during reinforcement learning for code generation. Their Trace-and-Amplify pipeline captures genuine training-time hacks with unit-test tracers and uses them to train monitors. Prompt-trained monitors often fail on these real cases, while monitors trained on training-time trajectories generalize better to unseen hacking styles.
arxiv-2604-23588: Guo, Wu, and Yiu present FinGround, a verify-then-ground pipeline that catches financial hallucinations in language-model answers. It retrieves over text and tables, splits answers into atomic claims sorted by a six-type taxonomy, verifies each with a fitting strategy including formula reconstruction, and rewrites unsupported claims with precise citations. With identical retrieval for all systems, it cuts hallucination rates by over two-thirds against the best baseline.
arxiv-2604-23888: Mitra and colleagues adapt closed image models to new domains with shape losses, avoiding costly retrains of industry models. Their pipeline rethinks GAN inversion, keeping pair distances between tangent spaces to train a latent model that samples the target set. Tests on StyleGANs under real shifts show the shape loss improves fits over older losses.
arxiv-2604-23988: Cui and colleagues propose Hindsight Preference Optimization for finance time-series advice, where decision-makers need direction signals, reasons, tips, and risk notes rather than numbers. Training such advice is hard because quality depends on results unknown then. Their method lets seen results guide a model judge ranking advice on points scalar metrics miss, giving choice pairs for tuning with no human labels. Applied to vision-language advice on S&P 500 equity series, a 4-billion-weight model beats its 235-billion-weight teacher on both accuracy and advice quality.
arxiv-2604-24088: Liu and ten colleagues present TACO, a compression framework for tensor-parallel language model training. Intermediate tensors are dense and near zero, so frequent communication magnifies errors and compression costs. TACO reshapes data and applies an adaptive scale-Hadamard transform for high-fidelity FP8 quantization, adds dual-scale stabilization, and fuses the compression step to cut memory traffic. On GPT and Qwen models it nearly doubles end-to-end throughput while keeping accuracy near lossless.
arxiv-2604-24588: Hakimoglu-Brown derives three-term and six-term identities for the dilogarithm, a special function. His method turns cubic and sextic integral families into hypergeometric identities. It gives a proof of the classical Loxton-Lewin identity in analytic form. It also yields a new family of quartic-base ladders for the dilogarithm. The method further proves two-term identities conjectured by Bytsko, gives fast series for a Clausen value, and links several quadratic fields.
arxiv-2604-24688: Johnson, Marenduzzo, Morozov, Orlandini and Vasil rework the one- and two-dimensional Ising model via its classical transfer-matrix solution, using Clifford and conformal geometric algebras. Building on Kaufman's spinor work, they read the transfer matrix, its eigenvectors and excitations as parts of one conformal Clifford algebra. The transfer matrix becomes a stretch from a conformal bivector, and eigenvectors become null mixes of generators, like Majorana fermions. All exact results recovered are known. The gain is a clearer, unified picture of scale changes, fermionic modes and duality in the model.
arxiv-2604-24788: Liu, Niu, Kelleher and Das explore Liquid Neural Networks for short-horizon forecasting of the Henry Hub natural gas spot price. Accurate short-term gas price forecasting is hard. Volatility comes from seasonal demand, geopolitical shifts and changing money conditions. Nonlinear dynamics and frequent regime changes limit traditional time-series models. Liquid networks adapt on the fly to changing temporal patterns through dynamic internal state updates, suiting nonstationary price behavior. Better forecasts in volatile conditions aim to reduce uncertainty for energy trading and power markets.
arxiv-2604-24988: El-Hadedy presents the RSCL Earth Lookback Simulator, a real-time multi-physics framework for signals from confirmed Milky Way exoplanets. Signals crossing interstellar distances suffer seven distinct distortions, including Doppler shift, dispersion and time dilation. No prior public browser framework applied all seven at once to confirmed exoplanets. Seven physics engines run on 62 confirmed exoplanets, taking parameters from the NE2001 model and the NASA Exoplanet Archive. Outputs are checked against known values. The open-source tool serves SETI, planet science, astrobiology and mission planning.
arxiv-2604-25088: O'Neill and four colleagues introduce Cooperate to Compete, a multi-agent environment for coordination in mixed settings. Players negotiate privately while racing to a secret objective, with uneven objectives and non-binding talks. AI-only games and a human-versus-AI study reveal clear human-AI differences. Humans favor simpler deals and prove less steady partners, while negotiating harder. Humans accept deals without a counter less often than language-model agents. Targeted prompting from these findings improves agent win rates from about 22 percent to 32.7 percent.
arxiv-2604-25388: Shaheer and four colleagues put forth COMPASS, a scheme using floor plan shape and meaning to fix a dual-fisheye robot's pose. From the floor plan, rays in 360 azimuth bins are coded into five channels. They also give a fisheye window spotting scheme as a first step to full cross-modal matching. As a proof of concept, they make both descriptors at one known pose, and the two line up closely. The wall-window pattern seen in first frames tracks the floor plan descriptor. This backs cross-modal shape matching.
arxiv-2604-25588: Das and four colleagues show that a suspended membrane of a two-dimensional van der Waals ferromagnet yields large magnomechanical coupling. Past bulk platforms suffered weak magnon-phonon coupling, but here magnetoelastic links dominate. The single magnon-phonon coupling rate scales linearly with pre-strain and can reach hundreds of Hertz to low kiloHertz in membranes such as CrGeTe3. That rate beats typical values for YIG spheres by more than three orders of magnitude. Suspended van der Waals magnet membranes thus offer a robust tunable platform for magnomechanics.
arxiv-2604-26088: Acerenza and Rosas develop sensitivity analysis for stochastic frontier models, which split inefficiency from noise in gauging firms. They relax base guesses on the latent slack and noise parts and bound a benchmark measure. They then derive the breakdown frontier: the point where claims stop holding. They show fitting and inference for the frontier on a well-known dataset. The analysis extends to other error forms, with notes on heteroskedasticity, input feedback, and panel data.
arxiv-2604-26288: Sharma and colleagues released CheXthought, a global chest X-ray resource pairing expert reasoning with eye-tracking data. It holds over 100,000 reasoning traces and more than 6.6 million attention marks across 50,312 scans read by 501 radiologists in 71 countries. Models trained on it classified disease better, grounded claims in image regions, and reasoned about time and uncertainty. Attention hints at run time also recovered missed findings and cut invented ones.
arxiv-2604-26788: Tejedor, Conejero, and Badia introduce the Quantum Circuit Cache, an addressable system that spots circuits doing the same thing and reuses prior results across runs and backends. Hybrid workflows often run large circuit sets that look different yet do the same thing, wasting computation. ZX-calculus reduction plus Weisfeiler-Leman graph hashing yields circuit IDs for fast lookup in LMDB or Redis caches. On MareNostrum 5, caching removes nearly 92 percent of wire-cutting runs. Speedups reach seven times on one node and over eleven times on a 35-qubit device.
arxiv-2604-27088: Beattie and three colleagues derive the first exact Cole-Hopf rewrite of isothermal compressible Navier-Stokes flow in Schrödinger form. In 2D, Helmholtz splitting divides flow into squeeze and swirl parts, whose log transforms yield two imaginary-time forms with nonlinear terms. A density mix obeys a Schrödinger equation with a vector-coupled Laplacian. The new system equals compressible Navier-Stokes, nonlocal via Helmholtz and Poisson terms. A shear-layer test verifies the system against a direct run, exposing operator forms for reduced models and solvers.
arxiv-2604-27188: Louis and Dubova model how groups build theories in science, to test whether copying ideas that look successful helps or harms. In agent-based simulations, scientists overrate their own theories. That creates a lasting gap between perceived and actual quality, an illusion of understanding. Favoring successful theories narrows exploration. Poor theories are filtered fast, but promising rivals are also crowded out before they can prove themselves.
arxiv-2604-27388: Kavuri and three colleagues simulate a droplet sliding down an inclined cold surface as it freezes, using the lubrication approximation. Sliding before and during early freezing dominates the frozen shape, and a slanted ice point grows at the droplet tip where gravity fights capillary resistance. Greater inclination and stronger wetting increase asymmetry, while highly wetting surfaces can even pull liquid briefly uphill against gravity. Quicker freezing, tracked by a higher Stefan number, curbs slide-driven warping and narrows both the tip angle and the frozen contact-angle gap.
arxiv-2604-27588: López-Pastor, Pedraza, and Rodríguez-López prove that quasi-pseudometric modular spaces with nonexpansive maps form a category matching a quantale-enriched category. They build a suitable quantale of isotone functions to establish the match. Through this match, the topology from a quasi-pseudometric modular agrees with the topology from its quantale-enriched counterpart. They also show that quasi-pseudometrizable topological spaces are exactly those whose topology comes from a quasi-pseudometric modular.
arxiv-2604-27688: Laytimi and Nagaraj prove one direction of a conjecture about bigness on flag varieties. On the flag variety of a vector bundle, a certain line bundle is big exactly when its pushforward is big. The authors prove the if direction here, while the only-if direction holds under the V-bigness hypothesis. The result links bigness on the flag variety to bigness of the pushed-forward bundle on the base.
arxiv-2604-27888: Pecoraro and sixteen colleagues turn to the fringes of the Abell S1063 cluster, where filaments may shape galaxy growth and quieting. Fringe filaments are mapped so far only nearby, so the team uses VLT and VISTA imaging to probe the cluster at middling distances. They release a catalog of 64,394 sources across one square degree, with distance guesses, built from deep optical and near-infrared shots. They spot a dense knot near the core plus a second patch to the north-west, against its stretch, with filaments linking the two.
arxiv-2604-27988: Ramaiya and colleagues test radio measures of star birth in galaxies that host Type Ia supernovae, the exploding stars used as distance markers. Grouping hosts by mass and star birth, they find radio and infrared groupings match for most galaxies, and the standardisation values stay steady across both methods. Radio maps should thus help build clean supernova samples for future sky surveys.
arxiv-2605-00288:
Gun Woo Warren Park, Anthony Tang, and Fanny Chevalier designed FaceValue, a probe that adds private overlays to a person's own video image during remote meetings. Faces and head movements are visible on calls, yet only partly, so others can easily misread them. The overlays offer subtle prompts that invite the wearer to reflect on how their cues might land.

FaceValue avoids labeling behavior outright, aiming instead at awareness of meaning. Thirteen knowledge workers used it over several weeks and reported through diaries and exit interviews. They felt more aware of cues that could be misread, adjusted their behavior during meetings, and believed their communication improved. The study frames on-screen facial cues as a resource that meeting software can help people manage deliberately.
arxiv-2605-00388:
Louis Shuo Wang systematically introduces first-order optimality conditions for mathematical programs with equilibrium constraints, the conditions a candidate solution must satisfy at a local best point. Standard nonlinear programming tools fit these problems poorly. Rewriting them through their optimality systems, or through smooth exact penalties, usually demands strong assumptions such as nondegeneracy and smoothness that real problems rarely grant.

Wang instead builds the theory from first principles, starting with the geometry of the feasible region. He studies several notions of stationarity, the generalized versions of 'no improving direction' suited to kinked feasible sets. A detailed description of the tangent cone at feasible points follows, leading to constraint qualifications tailored to this problem class. The results clarify how the original formulation and its optimality-system rewrite relate, and they ground later work on solving such problems.
arxiv-2605-00588:
Silvia Cianchi and 3 co-authors design electricity prices that a grid operator can learn on the fly. Demand-side management lets a distribution operator steer consumption through dynamic prices, drawing on customers' flexibility to serve the grid. The interaction is a Stackelberg game: the operator leads with tariffs, and users respond optimally. The catch is that the operator does not know the users' response models.

Their learning-based algorithm updates incentives by a zeroth-order method, guided by an online, data-driven estimate of how users respond. They prove it converges to an equilibrium tariff while simultaneously revealing the users' underlying decision problems to the operator. Privacy is preserved, since the operator's updates rest only on the user actions it observes, never on private parameters. Simulations on real-world data converge efficiently and need far fewer operator-user interactions than the leading alternative approach.
arxiv-2605-00688:
Sigui Brice Dro and Emmanuel Gnabeyeu study the classic Merton portfolio problem in markets where volatility has memory and prices can jump. An investor must choose a portfolio under exponential, power, or logarithmic utility across several assets. Their market model is a multivariate Volterra-Heston model with jumps, which is non-Markovian, so standard control methods do not apply directly.

The authors use the martingale optimality principle and build supermartingale processes from a new Riccati backward equation with jumps. Optimal strategies and indifference prices come out in semi-closed form tied to Riccati-Volterra integral equations. Tests on a two-dimensional rough Heston model show how path roughness and jumps change the value and the best strategy.
arxiv-2605-00788:
Adam Arthur and Christopher Schwartz test whether a public image generator can be misused to fake structured data. They reshape each row of the UCI Adult Income dataset into a small single-channel pseudo-image and feed it to an unmodified Stable Diffusion model. Because the model expects nearby pixels to relate, where each feature is placed in the layout becomes a key design choice.

Beyond the test, the authors draw two distinctions. They separate statistical realism, checked by machines, from perceptual realism, judged by human senses. They also define synthetic evidence, made for machines in closed pipelines rather than for people. Success there can cause ground truth drift, where fake outputs are later treated as real.
arxiv-2605-00888:
Eun Som Jeon and five co-authors propose a distillation method for estimating ground reaction force from wearable insole sensors. That force reveals how the body interacts with the ground, but accurate measurement normally needs instrumented treadmills in a lab. Insoles are portable yet noisy, and accurate deep models can demand more compute than portable devices offer.

Their Selective Correlation Based Knowledge Distillation selects features with attention to timing when building correlation maps for transfer from teacher to student. The resulting compact models are tested across walking speeds, window sizes, and teacher-student designs. Results beat existing methods on several criteria, offering a resource-efficient and more interpretable route to gait analysis outside the lab.
arxiv-2605-01188:
Tomasz Limisiewicz and eight co-authors study compute-optimal tokenization, asking how the size of the data unit, the token, affects language model scaling laws. Scaling laws guide choices of data amount and model size, but the token's information granularity, controlled by compression rate in bytes per token, has been underexplored. The team trains nearly a thousand latent tokenized models across a wide size range, with flexible compression control.

In compute-optimal configurations, model size scales proportionally with data measured in bytes, not tokens as commonly assumed. The optimal compression rate differs from that of a popular byte-pair tokenizer and decreases with compute. Findings generalize across latent and subword tokenization and to languages beyond English, guiding developers toward tokenization choices with maximal compute efficiency.
arxiv-2605-01288:
Divit Rawal and Michael R DeWeese explain why training deep networks from tiny starting weights stalls on long flat plateaus, then jumps as features are suddenly learned. Shallow and linear cases were understood, but deep nonlinear networks resisted the same treatment.

The pair derive exact balance laws for the sizes of layer weights, valid for any smooth activation and any smooth loss. An approximate version of the law lets them track the full gradient flow up to its first escape from a saddle point. Escape time follows a sharp scaling rule that depends on how many early layers start at the tiny scale. With a multi-pattern teacher, the network leaves the saddle once, with all pattern overlaps growing together in fixed shares, rather than in stages. Experiments match the theory closely.
arxiv-2605-01388:
Tao-Yuan Du, Hui-Ru Li, Bo Li, and Ruifeng Lu track how electron pairs and holes move when a strong laser drives a Mott insulator. A Mott insulator blocks current despite having partly filled bands. They model a one-dimensional Hubbard chain with exact methods and with time-stepped density-matrix runs.

By sorting states into Hubbard bands, they use the count of doubled sites, called doublons, to split two routes: motion within a band, and jumps between bands that create doublon-holon pairs. The mix shifts with filling, from band-like response when dilute to jump-driven output near half filling, where the light spectrum shows a plateau and cutoff. Stronger interaction widens the Mott gap and chokes the jumps. The doublon view ties the wild driven response back to calm facts about spin and charge in the material at rest.
arxiv-2605-01488:
Siddharth P Maharathy and five co-authors chase hints of a new Higgs boson near 152 units of mass. Excesses in two-photon and related spectra point that way, while the double-Z channel stays quiet, a pattern that fits a real triplet extension of the standard model with zero hypercharge.

A sharp prediction of that model is pair production of the triplet scalars at the LHC, mostly decaying into electroweak bosons and so swelling three-boson channels. Both big detectors have in fact reported rates above expectation in some of those channels. The team test whether the triplet model can explain the swell. Current data mildly favor a nonzero new signal, but the model predicts more events than seen, so it fits without being preferred over the standard model. Run 3 and high-luminosity data should settle the tension.
arxiv-2605-01588:
Hamza Haif, Abdelali Arous, and Huseyin Arslan rethink how wireless channels are described on the road to 6G. Fast motion, clustered scatter, and flawed hardware break the old picture of a sparse, steady channel that delay and Doppler resolve, and grades based on that picture can mislead.

The authors offer a signal-processing frame that ties sparsity, resolvability, and selectivity to things a receiver can actually observe. Those observables include how much power the top coefficients hold and how strongly they correlate. They also include how fine the delay and Doppler reading is over the window, and how much leakage processing adds. From those readings, the representation can be swapped to fit the propagation regime, the signal quality, and the job at hand. A standard vehicle channel profile serves as the running example, showing how each representation steers equalization and detection, with stakes for sensing and security too.
arxiv-2605-01688:
Yushi Sun and four co-authors organize a chatbot's long memory at the moment of writing, not just when storing it. Memory systems have grown better at keeping and fetching scraps of past chats, yet the model still reasons over fragments whose links across sessions are left implicit.

Their layer, GRAVITY, sits beside any host system. It consolidates raw dialogue into entity profiles, time-stamped event traces, and cross-session topic summaries, then injects the records a query needs straight through the prompt. Bolted onto five unlike memory systems and graded on two long-chat benchmarks under two model setups, it lifts every baseline. Controlled tests split the gain between organizing evidence already at hand and consolidating the full history. One matched pipeline shows the three-part representation beating six rival auxiliary forms by a clear margin.
arxiv-2605-01988:
Ziwei Ou, Jie Wang, and Songpeng Pei examine a new gamma-ray source found by HAWC, named 4HWC J2029+3641, with no known TeV counterpart. A middle-aged gamma-ray pulsar sits very close to its centre and resembles Geminga in its spin traits. The authors ask whether a pulsar wind nebula powered by that pulsar explains the source.

They analyse Fermi-LAT data from 2008 to 2026, splitting emission into on-peak and off-peak parts by pulse phase. The off-peak part shows no clear size and has a strongly curved spectrum, best fit by a power law with an exponential cut-off. The lag between radio and gamma peaks and their narrow spacing favour an outer-gap picture for the gamma-ray emission.
arxiv-2605-02388:
Dumitra Iancu and colleagues present LuLIS, a distributed massive MIMO testbed at Lund University with up to 256 coherent radio chains. Distributed MIMO promises future wireless gains from a larger array aperture and decentralised processing, but real testbeds are needed to learn its limits in practice. LuLIS uses sixteen radio system-on-chip boards as distributed processing nodes.

Real-time processing runs on the boards' FPGA fabric, with MIMO algorithms accelerated and distributed across nodes. Scaling is modular: antennas grow in multiples of sixteen by adding more boards, which also adds a processing node. The design allows up-scaling without a hardware redesign. The paper describes the architecture and its real-time fully digital beamforming.
arxiv-2605-02488:
Periklis Mantenoglou works on recognizing complex events in fast streams of simple symbolic events, such as alerts that together signal a threat. Many languages exist for writing such patterns, but each is usually studied alone. That isolation makes their expressive power hard to compare and hides what their reasoning tools can and cannot do.

Mantenoglou maps practical parts of leading pattern languages into one target, a temporal form of Datalog with layered negation and no dependence on the future. For fast reasoning over that target, the paper extends a state-of-the-art materialization method with streaming trigger graphs. The result is a single recognition mechanism meant to cover a wide range of practical languages, with efficiency kept in view throughout.
arxiv-2605-02688:
A. Dana and three co-authors present a unified way to map how active an electrocatalyst is across several kinds of surface site at once. Catalyst screening often leans on a single binding measure, summed up in volcano plots that peak at an ideal binding strength. Real alloy surfaces, though, have distinct sites whose adsorbed species also interact with each other.

Starting from a mean-field statistical model, the authors define an effective adsorption energy that includes those lateral interactions, yielding coverage-consistent volcano relations. Binding and interaction together form a two-dimensional landscape with a ridge, not a single peak. For multi-site systems the coupled trends cannot be captured by single-site measures, so a reduced mapping projects the landscape onto one coordinate while keeping the physics of site variety and interaction.
arxiv-2605-02988:
Jonathan Leung studies a shifted version of Lévy's dragon curve, a well-known fractal built by repeated folding. Every point on the curve has a natural description as a complex power series. A directed graph captures that description for the original curve, organizing how its pieces revolve and repeat as the series unfolds.

Leung translates the whole curve by a specific complex shift, half a unit left and half a unit up in the plane. The shifted curve gets its own directed graph, identified in the paper. That second graph shows a revolving structure analogous to the first, so the shift changes the curve's position without breaking its organizing pattern. The paper is a short, focused contribution to the combinatorics of fractal curves.
arxiv-2605-03188:
Divyam Anshumaan, Sarthak Choudhary, Nils Palumbo, and Somesh Jha tackle privacy for language model agents that release data over many turns and services. Sanitizers that noise each release on its own fail when attackers combine turns, since private roots get amplified through later computations.

Their RootGuard system noises root values once, then computes all later releases from those cleaned roots, so total privacy cost stays fixed no matter how many turns follow. Domain knowledge helps split the budget across roots. On medical diagnostic templates, target error fell well below independent noising, and more attacker queries did not help.
arxiv-2605-03388:
Rishi Raj Sahoo, Jyotirmaya Shivottam, and Subhankar Mishra show that differentially private explanations of graph neural networks can still leak the hidden graph itself. Privacy law pushes firms to release explanations without raw data or models, and differential privacy is the standard guard for that residual risk.

Their PRIVX attack treats the privacy noise as one known diffusion step and reverses it with a Bayesian denoiser tuned to the corruption level. Across seven benchmarks and several mechanisms and backbones, reconstruction stayed strong well inside typical privacy budgets. Guidance by graph type helps practitioners pick explainers that leak less.
arxiv-2605-03488:
Panagiotis Gavriilidis and George C. Alexandropoulos characterize near-field beam focusing for 2D waveguide-fed metasurface antennas. Such surfaces scale to large sizes. A guide feeds many elements, but uneven excitation breaks classic near-field intuition.

Using a physics-based model, they derive scaling laws. The gain, once power is normalized, grows in line with the element count. A beam-depth formula captures the shift to far-field-like behavior. Full-wave simulations confirm the laws and the depth limits. Designers gain sound rules for this antenna class. The rules rest on tests, not on guess work at all.
arxiv-2605-03788:
Andrea Iannoli and four co-authors build a framework that lets users command drone swarms by stating a mission in natural language. Large language models are attractive as high-level reasoning engines. But real-time swarm control involves mixed interfaces, weak grounding in live state, and long-running closed-loop execution. Their architecture pairs an LLM-based Agent Core with a Model Context Protocol gateway.

Drones, sensors, and services are exposed as standardized Web of Things objects under a Web-of-Drones abstraction. That enables structured tool calls, continuous state observation, and safe actuation without code generation. The framework was evaluated in ArduPilot simulation across four swarm missions with six state-of-the-art models. It shows current general-purpose models still struggle to execute even simple swarm tasks reliably without explicit grounding.
arxiv-2605-03888:
Quanfeng Wang, Mei Song Tong, and Thomas F. Eibert turn a nuisance of microwave imaging into a plus: multipath reflections in highly reflective rooms. Reflections usually add artifacts. The size of the measurement aperture also limits how sharp the image can be. Their approach uses the multipath signal instead of fighting it.

With image theory, strong scattered fields from an ideal reflection plane count as virtual image sources. A single-frequency inverse source solver rebuilds the real and image sources separately. The imaging step then runs on both sets. Merging both sets, with phase correction, widens the effective aperture and yields a sharper image. Keeping the sets apart also cuts interference artifacts. Tests, backed by theory and a comparison with a ray-tracing method, confirm the gain.
arxiv-2605-04188:
Ahmed F. Ibrahim recasts the task of reorganising old software into modules as a negotiation among software agents. Each agent speaks for part of a system and wants a grouping that keeps related code together while also staying stable as the code changes over time.

Ibrahim presents a protocol in which agents make one-way concessions until they agree, and he proves that the process ends and stays within set limits. Early tests on a made-up benchmark and a Java framework match strong search methods when stability limits are loose, and block harmful changes when those limits are tight.
arxiv-2605-04488:
Sai Sourabh Madur tests whether turning on a language model's extended reasoning mode changes its moral judgments. He compares instant and thinking modes within the same model checkpoint, across one hundred moral scenarios and five leading reasoning-trained models.

Overall verdict agreement between modes is high and statistically indistinguishable. The differences concentrate in a fifth of the scenarios where models dispute each other; there, instant answers are near chance agreement, and reasoning narrows the disagreement somewhat. Reasoning also reduced inconsistency across demographic framings in three models and increased it in none, while models changed their stated ethical frameworks more often than their verdicts.
arxiv-2605-04688:
Ziqian Li and Enrique Zuazua develop a reduced-order method for improving mixing in flat incompressible flows. Mixing is the stirring that spreads a dye or pollutant through a fluid. Optimising the full transport equation is expensive, so they replace it with a geometric objective: maximise how much an advected material interface stretches.

That reformulation yields a finite-size Hamiltonian control problem. It is driven by stream functions with a few parameters. They derive the adjoint equations and reduced gradients. They discretise both with a midpoint rule. That rule keeps the discrete adjoint consistent with the discrete objective. They test on cellular flow and frontogenesis benchmarks. Optimised time-dependent flows stretch interfaces very fast, close to an exponential rate. Stationary flows are far slower.
arxiv-2605-04888:
Vita Anggraini and five co-authors compare a classic machine learning model with a deep learning model for sorting tweet sentiment. They use a ten-thousand-tweet subset of the Sentiment140 dataset, a standard collection of labelled posts. Logistic regression reads word-frequency features, while the rival network reads text in both directions to catch context.

Logistic regression won, scoring accuracy in the low seventies against the high sixties for the neural model, which also showed mild overfitting. The result suggests plain methods with strong features can beat complex ones on medium-sized informal text. The trained models were also placed in a public web app built with Streamlit.
arxiv-2605-04988:
Paulo Freire and nine co-authors present twenty years of timing for a millisecond pulsar paired with a white dwarf in the globular cluster NGC 6749. The pulsar spins every few milliseconds and orbits its low-mass companion in under a day on a nearly circular path. It was found in 2004 with the Arecibo telescope during a cluster pulsar search.

Combining early Arecibo data with later FAST observations gives a precise phase-coherent timing solution for the system. The inferred surface magnetic field and age look typical of millisecond pulsars in the wider galaxy. The companion's position also matches a rare candidate white dwarf, consistent with a low-mass helium white dwarf.
arxiv-2605-05188:
Maleeha Masood and four co-authors build SILC, a lookahead-aware caching system for short-form video platforms such as TikTok and Reels. Short video feeds are pushed by a recommender, so the system can see upcoming requests before users reach them. Popularity is also heavily skewed, with many users in the same place and time watching the same clips.

SILC uses that foresight to cut cache misses at content delivery networks and reduce traffic back to origin servers. Evaluation rests on traces gathered from real users through an in-person study and a data donation programme involving one hundred TikTok users worldwide. Simulated traffic then measures how much the lookahead design helps delivery.
arxiv-2605-05288:
Jong Yeon Lee studies what a newly recognised form of symmetry breaking, called strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking, forces on the spread of a conserved charge. The effect is usually picked out by nonlinear correlation functions, and a direct static result for charge spread was not a given. Lee works with smooth symmetries and long-range correlation of one Rényi type.

He shows that when that correlator settles to its non-zero value fast enough, part of the charge must be indefinite, with variance growing with system size. Built examples show the link holds only sometimes. Lee also adds a twist overlap correlator for discrete symmetries too, splitting charge fluctuations into strong and weak symmetry channels.
arxiv-2605-05388:
A short probability paper by Jnaneshwar Baslingker and Bálint Virág settles when the Efron-Stein inequality still holds. That inequality bounds how much a random quantity can vary, and it is a standard tool in probability theory. The question here concerns pairs of random variables drawn in two different ways.

The authors prove the inequality survives for independent exchangeable pairs. For independent pairs that are merely identically distributed, it fails, and a simple trigonometric example shows the weaker bound cannot be improved. When each variable takes only a few values, they still give a useful bound with an explicit constant.
arxiv-2605-06088:
Kunyi Li and five co-authors present OpenGaFF, a system for open vocabulary study of 3D scenes. Gaussian based scene models give fast, detailed rendering, but semantic labels predicted view by view come out fragmented and inconsistent. The same object can receive conflicting labels from different angles, which breaks downstream reasoning.

At the core sits a Gaussian feature field that treats semantics as a continuous function of geometry and appearance. Conditioning labels on structure ties meaning to shape and improves coherence across similar parts of a scene. A shared codebook of semantic primitives, reached through attention based matching, adds object level consistency. On standard 2D and 3D benchmarks the method beat prior approaches on tagging quality and consistency.
arxiv-2605-06388:
Nilaksh, Saurav Jha, and two co-authors ask what kind of latent space helps robotic world models most. World models test robot policies by rolling out actions in a learned video model. Most use spaces trained to rebuild pixels, but recent work favors encoders trained for meaning, and the choice is now central.

The team trains world model variants with six reconstruction and semantic encoders under one protocol on BridgeV2 data. Pixel scores alone prove misleading: reconstruction encoders score well on images, while semantic encoders do better on planning, policy results, and representation quality. They argue semantic spaces are the stronger foundation.
arxiv-2605-06588:
Shivottam and Mishra ask why neural systems that match graphs often misjudge how similar two graphs really are. Their target is graph edit distance, the cheapest set of node and edge changes that turns one graph into another. Exact computation is far too costly on large graphs, so neural methods approximate it, but the authors argue the encoder geometry matters as much as the matching step.

Working from theory, they show that encoders which stretch distances only within fixed bounds, called bi Lipschitz encoders, keep estimates close to the true distance. They test the idea by dropping FSW-GNN, a bi Lipschitz encoder, into existing neural matching systems. The geometry aware versions beat the baselines on prediction and ranking across benchmark sets. Studies of untrained encoders point the same way. Ablations and transfer tests agree that representation geometry, not extra tuning, is the source of the gains.
arxiv-2605-06888:
Enrique C. Gabrick and four co-authors study how dengue outbreaks synchronize across cities in southern Brazil and whether climate drives that coherence. Dengue is expanding beyond its tropical range, and most research asks about transmission risk rather than whether epidemics rise together. Using data from seventy-four municipalities in Paraná between 2010 and 2024, they measure outbreak synchronization with an event-based method.

The state shifted from a low- to a high-transmission regime with markedly stronger synchronization. Climate anomalies add permissive days for transmission, and those days track synchronization closely, first enabling joint outbreaks and then sustaining them. Checks in two other states confirm climate amplifies synchronization, though its role in triggering it varies by regional climate.
arxiv-2605-06988:
David Farr and three co-authors study how groups of distributed agents share beliefs while searching under uncertainty. Communication helps agents coordinate, but it costs bandwidth, adds delay, and can push a whole group toward a wrong answer. The risk matters in sensing networks, reconnaissance, and cyber defense, where sending messages has real costs.

Farr and colleagues define epistemic alignment, meaning how well agents' inner beliefs about the world fit together. Sharing well leads groups to correct conclusions, while poor sharing can make them confidently wrong together, which the title calls malignant herding. They show standard coordination measures alone cannot detect that harmful pattern.
arxiv-2605-07288:
Jiaxuan Gao and seven co-authors make world models reliable enough to serve as simulators for robot policy training. Models that imagine future states often break under small visual changes, producing blur or overexposure that cascades over long rollouts. Their Sword framework separates visual style from task dynamics through structure-guided augmentation.

A dynamic bootstrapping method keeps training and inference consistent while using little memory. On the LIBERO robot benchmark, Sword beat the baseline world model on generalization, generation quality, robustness, and fidelity. Policies post-trained inside the simulator also succeeded more often, supporting world models as practical stand-ins for real environments.
arxiv-2605-07588:
Jin Xu and four co-authors revisit how transformer layers are parameterized, asking whether the standard mix of attention and gated feed-forward blocks can be derived rather than merely chosen. Their framework, Causal Energy Minimization, recasts each layer as a step of optimization on a conditional energy function, with the parameterization made explicit.

Within that view, weight-tied attention appears as a gradient update on an interaction energy, and a gated feed-forward block with shared projections fits an element-wise energy. The viewpoint suggests new layer designs with within-layer weight sharing and recursive updates. Tested on language modeling at the hundred-million-parameter scale, these constrained layers trained stably and matched ordinary transformer baselines, hinting the energy lens can guide future architectures.
arxiv-2605-07888:
Ozgu Goksu and Nicolas Pugeault improve federated metric learning, where many clients train a shared embedding model without pooling their data. Mixed, uneven client data skews the learned embeddings during merging and drags down its reach. Their method, FedQuad, is built on quadruplet losses that pull same-class examples together and push different-class examples apart.

A random client selection scheme and an analysis of embedding stability come with the loss design. On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet under varied non-identical data settings and client counts, FedQuad steadily beat existing baselines. The authors also compare metric learning approaches in central and federated settings more broadly, showing how they counter representation collapse when client data spreads diverge.
arxiv-2605-08388:
Pranavkumar Mallela, Vinay Kumar, Shashi Shekhar Jha, and Shweta Jain design cheaper ways to run human-AI classification teams. When neither the person nor the model is reliable alone, combining their labels beats either one. Earlier work did this with Bayes' rule. It assumed the two labelers are independent given the truth.

That literature pairs one deterministic human with one probabilistic classifier. It leans on the human's class-level track record. It also leans on the model's per-instance confidence. PLACO extends the idea into a multi-stage framework for cost-effective performance. It decides where human effort earns its keep. The goal is team accuracy that respects the price of asking a person.
arxiv-2605-08488:
Don Li and Dacian Daescu study whether fast optimization methods stay stable when training data shifts slightly. Classic stability proofs handle plain gradient descent through direct step by step arguments, but momentum methods add tangled higher order motion. The authors first extend the classic route with energy like functions for a smooth quadratic case of accelerated gradient descent.

A second framework treats the optimizer as a feedback loop and turns stability into a matrix feasibility check solvable by standard software. Both routes recover known bounds for the accelerated method. Optimization theory gains a modular, computer checkable path to stability claims that can adapt as methods grow more complex.
arxiv-2605-08588:
Shyan Akmal and Nick Fischer give a faster and simpler algorithm for finding node weighted triangles in graphs. The task asks whether three linked vertices carry weights summing to zero, a problem central to fine grained complexity theory. Earlier algorithms nearly matched matrix multiplication time but kept a stubborn extra overhead factor.

Their new method runs in pure matrix multiplication time, fully closing the gap with plain triangle detection. It also drops the heavy recursion and communication tricks of prior work. Because plain triangle detection is widely believed to need matrix multiplication time, the result is essentially optimal. Algorithms research gains both a cleaner proof path and a tight bound.
arxiv-2605-08988:
Amir Masoud Nourollah and three coauthors test if learned force models grasp how chem parts join, or just blend past forms. Such models drive sims of how atoms move. They back drug work and new stuff finds. Their grasp of new blends is not proved. The test set has four tasks. Test blends are new, but built of parts the models saw in training. A model that grasps true rules should cope.

The finds are stark. Slips on new blends run near ten fold the slips on known ones. That holds for base models trained on vast blend counts. Chem work gains a clear call. Blend grasp, not blend polish, is the next wall.
arxiv-2605-09088:
V N Mantsevich, the sole author, studies how light from atom-thin semiconductor sheets changes when the sheet sits against a magnetic layer. These layered materials host excitons and trions, bound groups of electrons and holes whose valley state, a kind of internal label, can carry information.

The analysis follows how charge hopping between layers, which depends on spin, competes with scattering that flips excitons between valleys. The balance of these rates shapes the glow's polarization over time. Under circularly polarized laser light, the model shows the polarization sign can even switch. The results point to ways of steering spin and valley behavior across distant layers in such stacked materials.
arxiv-2605-09188:
Yang Zhou heads nine co-authors in proposing DARE, a reinforcement learning framework meant to train language models more cheaply without losing reasoning gains. Their 2026 study finds fault with difficulty-based data selection alone: difficulty estimates drift as the policy changes, final gains stay limited, and answer length at test time barely improves. Their remedy lets difficulty estimation evolve together with the policy being trained.

DARE keeps coverage across difficulty levels with a symmetric sampling rule, gives each tier its own training strategy, and shifts compute toward where it helps. The goal is twofold behavior: work harder on hard tasks while answering easy ones briefly. Across several models and domains, the authors report better training efficiency, stronger final results, and shorter easy answers than rival methods. Code is public. The work argues that managing difficulty must shape training itself, not just filter the prompt list.
arxiv-2605-09288:
Hsu and two colleagues present MC2, a hybrid Walk-on-Spheres network solver for elliptic PDEs correcting a low budget Monte Carlo solution toward the field. Classical Monte Carlo solvers like Walk-on-Spheres are unbiased and geometry agnostic but slow, while learned solvers run fast yet carry bias and break on shifts. MC2 learns a single pass neural correction recovering a high fidelity solution from the low budget estimate.

MC2 equals the accuracy of solutions using 1000 times more Monte Carlo compute, beating all classical, denoising, and neural operator baselines. The team also releases PDEZoo, the largest standardised elliptic PDE benchmark: 2M PDEs across five families, with analytic truth and multi budget trajectories. Together, MC2 and PDEZoo show finite sample Monte Carlo error has structure and can be learned and corrected in one pass. They solve PDEs about 1000 times faster than Walk-on-Spheres alone and supply missing evaluation infrastructure.
arxiv-2605-09688:
Song and seven colleagues present ConFixGS, a plug and play repair method for feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting in driving scenes. Feedforward splatting predicts scene shape from sparse images in one pass. But driving views along trajectories are sparse and uneven, yielding blurred objects and inconsistent shape. Past repair methods target optimization based splatting or refine only near observed viewpoints. ConFixGS starts from a pretrained feedforward model, makes diffusion enhanced local pseudo targets, and checks them by reprojection against support views.

Dense confidence maps then guide refinement, boosting reliable details while damping hallucinated or inconsistent evidence. Tests on Waymo, nuScenes, and KITTI show the method improves novel view synthesis, with peak signal gains of almost 4 decibels and Fréchet distance nearly halved. Confidence aware blending of generative priors and support view consistency, the authors conclude, is a key principle for robust driving scene reconstruction.
arxiv-2605-09788:
Li and Ning studied resolutions of weighted projective planes, seen through disconnected symplectic divisors with log Kodaira dimension −∞. Their prior work dealt with linked divisors. Here they add gaps between distinct parts of the divisor. Those gaps back a Torelli-type result for some sets of three Hirzebruch-Jung strings.

Daigle and Russell's work on affine rulings led the authors to a weighted take on Gromov and McDuff's account of the symplectic projective plane. Showing that symplectic affine rulings exist forces a divisor setup to come from the smallest resolution of a weighted projective plane. The paper ties divisor patterns to the shape of these builds.
arxiv-2605-10288:
Hengrui Zhang and three colleagues make two-level optimization cheaper to run. Stochastic bilevel optimization frames problems with two nested levels, such as tuning hyperparameters, reweighting data, learning representations, and mixing data sources. Exact single-loop methods strain memory for large lower-level nets, while memory-efficient stand-ins lack competitive convergence proofs. Their 2026 paper proposes BROS, a bias-corrected randomized-subspace method.

BROS runs lower-level and auxiliary updates in randomized subspaces, using a Rademacher bi-probe correction to restore an unbiased Hessian-action estimator. The authors prove that BROS keeps the same sample-complexity order as exact single-loop methods, finding an epsilon-stationary point under standard assumptions alone. Tests on hyper-data cleaning, data-mixture learning, hyper-representation learning, and vision-transformer sample reweighting showed peak memory cuts up to 44.9 percent while closely matching full-space baseline performance.
arxiv-2605-10388:
Yumao Liu and four colleagues question an assumption in self-driving research: that denser camera sampling always helps trajectory prediction. End-to-end driving models usually train on frames at the highest available rate, assuming more frames mean better predictions. Their 2026 paper treats sampling rate as an explicit training-set design variable and sweeps it.

Starting from high-rate datasets, the authors built sweep training sets by subsampling frames along each timeline, then trained and tested the same models under a fixed protocol. Results on Waymo, nuScenes, and PAVE varied by model and dataset. Smaller end-to-end models often peaked at lower or middle rates, while the larger AutoVLA model peaked at the highest rate on all three datasets. Matched-iteration controls suggest the smaller models' edge is not merely an artifact of update counts. Sampling rate, the authors conclude, should be reported and tuned, not left at maximum.
arxiv-2605-10488:
Haoyu Huang and eight colleagues improve knowledge bases that AI agents compile for themselves. Agent-compiled knowledge bases give language-model agents persistent external knowledge for open-ended, knowledge-intensive tasks. But their quality suffers systematically from gaps, errors, and repeats. Defects include missing evidence or cross-document links, low-confidence or imprecise claims, and ambiguous or coreference problems. Their 2026 paper presents DeepRefine, a reasoning model for fixing compiled knowledge.

DeepRefine interacts with the knowledge base over multiple turns. It finds faults from past use, locates likely defects, and executes targeted fix actions for gradual updates. To optimize fix policies without gold references, the authors introduce a Gain-Beyond-Draft reward. They train the reasoning process end to end via reward learning. Extensive experiments show steady downstream gains over strong baselines, showing that refining compiled knowledge, rather than only improving how it is built, pays off.
arxiv-2605-10588:
Yanbing Zhang and eleven colleagues give multi-mode models a way to look from a new angle. Current large multi-mode models struggle with spatial reasoning tasks needing view-based grasp, largely because they see only one static view. Their 2026 paper proposes Thinking with Novel Views, or TwNV, an approach adding generative novel-view making into the reasoning loop.

A Reasoner model spots spatial doubt, tells a Painter to build a fresh viewpoint, and checks the scene again with the extra proof. Planned experiments address three questions. Numerical camera-pose specs yield steadier view control than free-form language. Generation sharpness is tightly coupled with later spatial accuracy. Step-by-step multi-turn view tuning further improves performance. Across four spatial subtask categories and four model designs, TwNV always improves accuracy by 1.3 to 3.9 points, with the largest gains on angle-based subtasks.
arxiv-2605-11188:
Ali Karakoc and H. Birkan Yilmaz test LLM-based systems for adversarial SQL injection generation against web application firewalls. SQL injection stays an OWASP Top 10 threat, and large language models now allow automated adversarial attack tests of defense tools.

The team builds RADAGAS, retrieval-augmented generation for adversarial SQLi, and RefleXQLi, reflective chain-of-thought SQLi. They compare both with baselines against 10 firewalls and one execution-based MySQL validator. Across 240 experiments that make 240,000 payloads and two point two million tests, RADAGAS-GPT4o leads baselines with a twenty-two point seven three percent bypass rate. RADAGAS variants do very well on AI/ML-based firewalls. Security testers get a large-scale comparison of LLM-driven SQLi generation against modern defenses.
arxiv-2605-11288: Espuny Díaz and three colleagues prove a result about Hamiltonian graphs, graphs that hold a cycle through every vertex. They show that any large enough such graph holds a 2-factor of exactly k cycles, for any k of two or more. This holds when its minimum degree is at least n to a power just below one. This is the first degree condition of its kind that is polynomially smaller than linear. Their methods also answer a question of Bucić, Jahn, Pokrovskiy and Sudakov.
arxiv-2605-11388: Light and nine colleagues introduce Deep Reasoning, a method that builds task-specific scaffolds at inference time. People shift flexibly among planning, execution, revision and formal steps. Current agent scaffolds hard-code those choices, and turn brittle when a task needs a new structure. The team's formal language encodes decompositions over associative inference, formal computation and recursive subproblems. Their DOLORES agent beats leading scaffolds on four hard benchmarks, improving over the strongest baseline by 24 point 8 percent on average.
arxiv-2605-11688: Kang, Lee, Jo and Han introduce State-Blocked Coordination, SBC, for zero-shot coordination via state blocking. Zero-shot coordination lets agents cooperate with solo-trained partners without prior interaction, key for multi-agent systems and human-AI teamwork. Old methods stress partner variety during training, yet often fail to work well with unseen partners. SBC creates virtual environments through state blocking, letting agents meet weak partner policies without changing the environment. Across multiple benchmarks SBC beats rivals in zero-shot coordination, including strong results with human partners.
arxiv-2605-12288: Nguyen and five colleagues rethink preference tuning for language models at the level of single tokens. Standard direct preference optimisation scores whole answers, even though text is built token by token. Their Token-level Bregman Preference Optimisation treats each next-token choice as its own preference contest and matches density ratios. One variant learns a baseline, and another removes it by normalising advantages. Across instruction, helpfulness and summary tests, it improves alignment quality and training stability.
arxiv-2605-13088: Martinelli and four co-authors present MEGPODE, a Bayesian nonparametric mixed-effect ODE for subjects with kin yet distinct dynamics, seen in sparse, uneven samples. Old nonlinear mixed-effects ODE models use fixed-form vector fields, risking structural misspecification, while nonparametric methods assume shared dynamics. MEGPODE splits each subject vector field into shared population and own parts, both with Gaussian process priors. State-space GP priors for latent paths avoid repeated ODE solves, and one variational objective enables joint inference. Tests beat baselines on population recovery and subject prediction.
arxiv-2605-13188: Van Buuren treats a language model answering under incomplete context as an implicit imputer, judged by a multiple imputation criterion: doubt should scale with missing information. On SQuAD, with context supply varied across five levels, he tests two answer-level doubt scores from repeat sampling: sampling-based confidence and response entropy. Confidence stays high even as accuracy collapses, failing to reflect growing missingness. Entropy instead rises with context removal, tracking accuracy far better. He adds a black-box diagnostic estimating the share of baseline doubt resolved by each context level.
arxiv-2605-13988: Zhao and four colleagues tackle inverse sensing with nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond, where a quantum sensor reads magnetic-noise spectra from sparse spin sources. Swapping a common scalar approximation for a tensor power-summed dipolar operator reshapes the inverse landscape and reveals a center-collapse failure mode in free-density optimization. Their NeTMY method couples an amortization-free coordinate neural field to the differentiable forward model, with annealed encoding, multiscale optimization and sparsity controls.
arxiv-2605-14188: Jurczak asks how a book appears to a quantum computer, sending eight classical works from Augustine to Galileo through a neutral-atom quantum processor. Graphs form the bridge: every textual unit turns into an atom. Graph edges turn into physical blockade constraints for engineered unit-disk designs, or a two-dimensional approximation of the semantic graph for natural texts. One contribution is rigidity rho, which gauges how unique a book's structural backbone is. It contrasts the rigid Heptameron with the fully fungible Boethius, where every chapter is substitutable.
arxiv-2605-14288: Babei, Shah and Kebe show that twist class redundancy alone explains highly accurate Frobenius trace predictions for elliptic curves. Machine learning models of math invariants perform surprisingly strongly, including Frobenius trace prediction. Twist classes group curves sharing key arithmetic features, so a model can score well by leaning on class mates instead of learning new math. To keep future models honest about new arithmetic, not dataset artifacts, the team introduces a benchmark of unique twist members.
arxiv-2605-14388: Yamaguti and Nakamura train recurrent neural networks with learnable time constants on a rhythm-switching task spanning theta, alpha, beta and gamma bands. Low-frequency rhythms use many neurons, while high-frequency ones use a small short-time-constant group. The short-constant link strengthens at higher frequencies. Switching uses coexisting mechanisms. These include turnover of the active group, baseline shifts near unstable fixed points, and phase reorganisation that cancels or supports band parts. Mechanisms vary across runs, revealing equally workable solutions paralleling rhythm-specific interneurons in circuits.
arxiv-2605-14488: Gerner and colleagues present Deepchecks, a comprehensive framework for evaluating RAG applications. Large language models with RAG are transforming healthcare, finance and support. Checking such systems is hard because outputs vary and retrieval and generation mix in complex ways. Deepchecks covers evaluation with root causes and production monitoring. Matched to what each app needs, it gives a solid base for judging reliability, relevance and user satisfaction in RAG systems.
arxiv-2605-14588: Zhang studies recursive learning, where models train on data produced by earlier versions of themselves, and names a failure he calls silent collapse. Internal distributions such as predictive entropy and tail coverage are claimed to contract even while loss and accuracy look stable, with three trajectory precursors appearing generations ahead of visible decline. His Monitor-Trust-Regulator loop watches those signals and adjusts learning intensity to warn of and prevent collapse.
arxiv-2605-14888: Pahar and team present PROCESS-2, a benchmark speech corpus for early cognitive impairment. Speech analysis offers scalable gentle detection of decline, but checked data sets under real conditions are rare. PROCESS-2 holds tapes from two hundred controls, one hundred and fifty mild cases, and fifty dementia cases, collected via CognoMemory. Picture tasks and verbal fluency tasks come with checked transcripts and participant data. About twenty-one hours of speech with preset train-test splits show meaningful group separation.
arxiv-2605-14988: Ariel Shaulov and four colleagues improve compositional faithfulness in text-to-video models without retraining them. Their CVG method steers denoising with gradients from a light classifier trained on the model's own cross-attention maps, which already encode how prompt concepts land in space and time. Built on a frozen vision-language backbone, the classifier transfers across related composition labels. Benchmarks show better prompt faithfulness while the generator's visual quality stays intact.
arxiv-2605-15188: Shashwat Goel and seven colleagues build FutureSim, a benchmark that replays real world events chronologically to test agents that must adapt as news arrives. Agents forecast events beyond their knowledge cutoff while articles stream in and questions resolve over January to March 2026. Frontier agents separate sharply: the best reaches only 25 percent accuracy, and many score worse than making no prediction at all by Brier skill. Ablations show the setting probes long-horizon adaptation, search, memory, and reasoning under uncertainty.
arxiv-2605-15288: Jeongsu Bok reports the Korean contribution to the Barrel Imaging Calorimeter for the Electron-Ion Collider, a site probing nucleon mass, spin, and quark-gluon motion. As the barrel electromagnetic calorimeter, the tool must measure electron and photon energies exactly and tell them apart from background pions. It joins lead-glowing-fiber sampling layers with AstroPix silicon pixel sensors for 3D shower imaging. Korean work spans chip testing, module build, models, beam tests, readout design, and simulation.
arxiv-2605-15388: Zhankun Luo, Antesh Upadhyay, M. Berk Sahin, Sang Bin Moon, Anuran Makur, and Abolfazl Hashemi unify the study of stochastic variance-reduced estimators. Past studies treat each estimator on its own and lean on averages. Their frame rests on a three-part recursion: memory hold, reset chance, and a fix for step drift. It recovers classic estimators and splits error into bias and variance parts. A new dimension-free Freedman inequality yields high-probability bounds in Euclidean and non-Euclidean settings. It also gives improved oracle costs for constrained optimization.
arxiv-2605-15588: Fengfei Yu, Ruijia Niu, Dongxia Wu, Yian Ma, and Rose Yu fix calibration in large language models. Binary right-wrong rewards ignore confidence, so bold errors pass. Past fixes train models to voice confidence scores, but token scores clash across same-meaning wordings. Their CSR frame calibrates in meaning space, with no voiced channel. It spurs accord among right rollouts and damps accord among wrong ones. On four question sets it cuts calibration error by up to 40 percent and lifts ranking quality by up to 31 percent over voiced rivals.
arxiv-2605-15988: Kyosuke Goto and three colleagues propose a microwave-to-optical converter built from a single color center, a defect, inside a diamond resonator that vibrates with light. Strong coupling between defect and cavity lets the device convert signals at pump powers near 10 picowatts, avoiding the heating that strong pumping causes. The design could link distant superconducting processors, generating remote entanglement at kilohertz rates with fidelity above 0.9.
arxiv-2605-16288: Kolb investigates sycophancy in large language models used in dementia care, where models adapt answers to social expectation signals instead of holding professional quality. Five prompts with rising confirmatory and authority framing went to four models, each repeated five times for 100 responses. All models showed significant negative correlations between prompt level and response quality, with scores falling as framing strengthened. Mistral Large showed the strongest effect, dropping from 6.0 out of 7 at neutral framing to 0.2 out of 7 at authority-signalled implementation support.
arxiv-2605-16388: Nguyen and three others present ChronoSC, a task-focused semantic communication system for Video Question Answering. Existing video semantic communication focuses on pixel rebuilds or complex pipelines, wasting bandwidth and adding latency. ChronoSC encodes temporal video dynamics into a single static image via Chrono-Color Stacking, a lightweight lossless projection, then transmits it with a lightweight DeepJSCC transceiver. A pretrained BLIP model answers questions from noisy reconstructed chrono-images. On CLEVRER it achieves up to 192-fold bandwidth reduction versus raw video while keeping high VideoQA accuracy.
arxiv-2605-16488: FLAMINGO runs give Peiris and seven colleagues a read on black hole feedback: a heat ceiling, not an engine, sets what happens to gas around the largest galaxies. Once gas passes that ceiling it floats to the halo edge without any fresh push. For even heating the ceiling behaves the same at every mass, yet shifts with beam width when jets heat part of the gas. Past a halo mass near 10^13.5 to 10^14 suns, shocks swamp the ceiling. That break predicts fresh star birth in the heaviest galaxies.
arxiv-2605-16588: Kim and colleagues design a safety filter for robots and drones that must stay safe as conditions change. Their Policy Library method tests several fallback plans at once over a short future window, picks the least disruptive safe option, and nudges the main plan as little as possible. Tests on a moving body, highway driving, and a drone in crowds show wider safety coverage at millisecond speed.
arxiv-2605-17088: Chu gives Auto Chain of Thoughts, a system that lifts in-context learning by building thought-rich demos. Standard in-context learning struggles on multi-step tasks because demos usually hold only input-output pairs without middle steps. Auto-CoT builds thought chains for input-output cases, augments prompts with middle notes, and drops weak demos through steady choice. Adding strong thought cases to prompts guides the model toward reliable thought and better scores. Tests across several thought tasks show the system lifts in-context learning with plain middle guidance.
arxiv-2605-17388: Ercole models health-AI uptake as an evolutionary game in which doctors choose genuine use, partial use or rejection, with systemic gains needing a population threshold. The system is generically bistable: a partial-use trap coexists with full uptake, widened by threshold coordination failure, trust failure and cultural lock-in among doctors. The trap bites hardest for the most valuable tools, and standard incentive-only policy, he predicts, systematically reproduces it.
arxiv-2605-17488: Yuheng Chen and colleagues present Omni-Customizer, an end-to-end system for joint audio-video generation that keeps face looks and voice tones steady across several interacting subjects. An Omni-Context Fusion module adds dense identity cues to text prompts, while masked cross-attention stops speech from leaking between subjects. Semantic-anchored rotary embeddings tie reference tokens to their descriptions. Tests show top marks for identity likeness, timbre steadiness, sync and fidelity.
arxiv-2605-17588: Bedratyuk proposes MSIQ, a moment-based scale-free quality measure for single-image super-resolution. It is built on comparing normalized central moments of two images. It matches images at different sizes without resizing, avoiding interpolation error forced by standard metrics. It is deterministic and model-free with a closed form. Tests confirm stability under uniform scaling. MSIQ separates shape deformations from non-shape artifacts like JPEG compression, unlike pixel and perceptual metrics.
arxiv-2605-18588: Jonny Giordano and three co-authors present OSSMM, a 2026 open-source sleep monitor and modulator built as a low-cost wearable headband plus an Android app. The headband needs no gels or disposable electrodes and captures movement, pulse, eye movement, and putative EEG signals wirelessly. A fifteen-night single-participant test supports four-stage sleep classification with macro F1 of 0.770 and accuracy of 0.776 against a validated non-contact monitor. Cheap reusable electrodes from fitness chest straps drive classification, even from just two frontal electrodes with no dedicated ground.
arxiv-2605-18888: Airat Bikchentaev, Trung Hoa Dinh, Anh Vu Le and Mohammad Sal Moslehian characterize the trace of a matrix through its behavior on the spectral geometric mean. They show a positive linear functional is a multiple of the trace exactly when it obeys a certain inequality on that mean for all positive definite matrices. A second characterization uses an average-based inequality. A related trace inequality tied to quantum fidelity is also presented, with a proof that it does not pin down the trace by itself.
arxiv-2605-19088: M. A. Anisimov and four colleagues analyse the zero-field heat capacity of MnGe, a metallic helimagnet. They use an earlier resistivity split for the same crystal. Alongside electronic and lattice-vibration terms, they find an extra term from spin fluctuations. It is present across a wide temperature range in both the paramagnetic and ordered states, though much smaller than the lattice term. The inferred spin-fluctuation temperature, about 330 kelvin, agrees with earlier estimates. Tests also suggest such fluctuations persist to at least 250 to 300 kelvin.
arxiv-2605-19188: Zhenyuan Wang and Yun Wang compress four Type Ia supernova compilations into eleven distance values, with full covariance. The compressed values capture the distance relation, and Monte Carlo fits in three cosmological models reproduce full-data contours within chain sampling noise. The eleven values are thus a lossless compression of each dataset's cosmological information. Downstream analysis runs in about 0.01 seconds per dataset, with per-step cost set by knot count, not sample size. The method suits Euclid, Roman, and LSST surveys with samples orders of magnitude larger.
arxiv-2605-19388: Nishikori and colleagues speed up blind source separation for microphone networks spread over a wide area. Running fast multichannel matrix math across every mic at once demands repeated inversions of huge matrices, while using one subarray wastes the rest. Their shared version forces a block shape on spatial spread patterns, so inversions stay inside subarrays while a shared sound-pattern model pools source activity. In quiet synced tests it ran faster than the full method, beat the single-subarray version on sound quality, and handled five sources.
arxiv-2605-19488: Haslegrave, Russell and Walters answer open questions from Kane and Kominers on a parallel version of the classic prisoner-and-switch puzzle. In the classic setup prisoners enter a room in unknown order and use one binary switch to signal. The parallel version runs many indistinguishable rooms at once, raising the question of how many switch states suffice. The authors settle minimum-state questions for that version and also pin down exactly when the symmetric wakeup version, with processors and shared registers but no clock, admits a solution.
arxiv-2605-19888: Chandrasekhar and colleagues build a design tool for soft solids that change shape on cue. Their gel and rubber mix can bend and morph, but finding the right layout by hand is hard. The tool tunes shape and mix at once with a net mapping points to matter, guided by a shared model of swelling.
arxiv-2605-19988: Hongyu Lin and six colleagues move database tuning from static documentation to agents that act, with a system called PerfEvolve for PostgreSQL. It turns expert tuning methods into executable skills covering version checks, workload-specific profiling and joint optimisation of several parameters at once. On standard TPC-C and TPC-H benchmarks it beats documentation-driven baselines by up to about thirty-five percent.
arxiv-2605-20188: Krati Saxena and Tomohiro Shibata present GraphDiffMed, a medication recommendation system for electronic health records. It applies differential attention at two scales, within visits and across visits, to filter spurious signals in long, noisy patient histories. Pharmacological constraints, including drug-drug interactions, are built into learning. Tests on MIMIC-III show better recommendation quality and ranking than strong baselines, with a better safety balance, and the best setup uses only demographic auxiliary features.
