Stationary representations keep retrieval running uninterrupted through updates and replacements, with no gallery reprocessing, at state-of-the-art accuracy.
arxiv-2606-12688:
Jha and colleagues present M*, a serving system built for composite multimodal models, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Serving means running a trained model to answer requests efficiently. Newer models combine vision encoders, language backbones, image generators, and audio codecs in varied patterns, while older frameworks assumed one fixed text-generation loop. A request may need only some components, in an order that changes by task.

M* represents each model as a dataflow graph, a map of components and data moving between them, and treats every request as a walk across that graph. Components can be placed freely across a GPU cluster, and optimisations apply regardless of model family. Across 5 representative models, M* cuts average end-to-end delay by 20 percent against vLLM-Omni on text-to-image work, delivers up to 2.7 times higher text-to-speech throughput, and speeds robotic planning rollouts by up to 12.5 times.
arxiv-2606-13188:
Abhishek and colleagues present an end-to-end framework that reconstructs cardiac surface meshes directly from 3D medical images, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Building patient-specific cardiac models for precision cardiology is bottlenecked by mesh generation. The workflow of segmentation, Marching Cubes extraction, and hours of manual cleanup is slow, inconsistent across operators, and demands specialist knowledge.

A 3D Swin Transformer encoder-decoder extracts volumetric features from CT or MRI volumes. A graph attention network head takes a template mesh and deforms it until it fits the patient's cardiac boundary. Tested on the MM-WHS 2017 benchmark, the method reached Dice scores of 0.84 on CT and 0.83 on MRI for volumetric segmentation. The authors argue mesh quality matters more for digital twins than pixel-level scores, and there the results were stronger: a mean Chamfer distance of 1.8 millimetres, with 95th-percentile surface distance below 5 millimetres.
arxiv-2606-13388:
Tenser and Queiroz connect 2D gauge theory to a many-body system in this 2026 arXiv paper. They study Yang-Mills theory, the framework behind the strong and weak nuclear forces, coupled to a particle living on a cylinder. Gauge invariance and the cylinder's compactness reduce the dynamics to a finite quantum system that can be analysed. In the Abelian case, where the gauge group is simple, the model becomes equivalent to the Landau problem, a particle in a magnetic field wrapped onto a torus. Its ground state is degenerate.

The construction generalises to non-Abelian groups, whose interactions are richer. For SU(N), the workhorse of quantum chromodynamics, the system reduces to many particles in one dimension interacting through a singular Calogero-Sutherland potential. That model is exactly solvable and studied. The bridge lets techniques from many-body physics illuminate gauge theory in a setting.
arxiv-2606-13688:
Saurabh Khanna and colleagues introduce PictoPercept in this 2026 arXiv paper, an open-source toolkit for measuring bias in humans and machines. Bias in judgement affects hiring, lending, and criminal justice, but older measurement tools have deep limits. They struggle with mixed identities, where several traits combine. They cannot evaluate artificial intelligence systems, lack grounding in demographic reality, and are vulnerable to social desirability effects, where respondents hide their true views. PictoPercept uses pictures to work around those weaknesses, letting researchers probe how people and models judge the depicted.

Because the same instrument applies to humans and machines, comparisons become direct. The toolkit is developed openly, with the stated aim of full public release. Grounding the depicted population in real distributions keeps the measures honest about who is being judged. The authors aim the tool at auditors who must judge both algorithmic and human decision-makers.
arxiv-2606-13988:
Liu argues machine societies differ from human ones because machines do not truly die. Human social life, he proposes, organizes this fact: members die taking tacit knowledge with them, newcomers start ignorant, and generations must hand things on. Kinship, inheritance, teaching, and tradition are that handover's machinery. His 2026 arXiv paper tests the claim with experiments and real genealogies.

In the experiment, shared culture built up only when death meant irreversible loss. A self-copying population was more capable per member yet culturally empty. Machine copying passed on too much status versus every human regime studied, even inherited-title nobility. The human data covered Chinese biographies, European nobility, and mathematics advisors. Storing memory outside the agents brought machine passing-on into the human range. A resettable simulated death, Liu concludes, is not finitude.
arxiv-2606-14088:
Magid, Ertem, and Suzuki show how a quantum classifier reads out its answer can matter more than adding entangling gates. Near-term hardware pays heavily for CNOT gates in error and latency, yet designers default to deeper entanglement for accuracy. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies Optimal Quantum Measurement Decoding: training a readout layer of single-qubit rotations, jointly with the circuit, to map outcomes to labels, adding no CNOTs.

On Iris, with a thirty-point test split, the best zero-CNOT circuit with the readout reached eighty-three point three three percent accuracy. Nine CNOTs hit ninety-six percent. The best eighteen-CNOT control managed fifty-six point six seven percent, and sixty-six point six seven percent even with the readout. Fifty seeds per configuration backed this. Gains were real but size-dependent: huge on minimal circuits, small on the largest. Circuit complexity is not captured by CNOT count alone.
arxiv-2606-14188:
Li and colleagues give robots a fast, cautious planner for ropes and cloth. Deformable manipulation lacks compact state descriptions; naive contact models give discontinuous gradients, blocking planning. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents CORD-SLS, built on a GPU-parallel differentiable simulator with contact smoothing, enabling gradient-based planning through contact at millisecond speed. A robust model predictive control layer plans with it under uncertainty.

Conformal prediction, a calibration method, turns perception errors into bounds the controller respects, yielding reachable tubes that keep control safe with high probability. It also speeds model-based reinforcement learning. On rope and cloth tasks (avoidance, routing, folding, smoothing), in simulation and hardware, CORD-SLS beat baselines in safety, speed, and success. One trade-off: its one-step prediction error, zero point zero one five zero meters, ran seven percent above a heavier physics simulator; a learned residual model halved it.
arxiv-2606-14288:
Gaibor, López, and Gutiérrez show a small modeling choice at each impact can rewrite the long-term fate of a rocking block. Rocking blocks, rigid bodies pivoting on corners under shaking, model statues, tanks, and masonry in earthquakes. Each impact loses energy per the coefficient of restitution; Housner's classical model derives it from geometry alone, while Mao's alternative predicts values closer to experiments. Their 2026 arXiv paper compares both under harmonic excitation, via bifurcation diagrams, Lyapunov exponents, and basins of attraction.

The alternative predicts higher restitution, less impact dissipation, and earlier, more prevalent oscillations. For stocky, low-slenderness blocks it shrinks the domain of regular bounded rocking and increases overturning. For taller blocks it instead favors multiperiodic bounded motions. As slenderness grows, the two models converge, so sensitivity to the impact law fades for tall blocks. Under identical excitation they can predict different fates: periodic rocking, chaos, or toppling.
arxiv-2606-14488:
Sarkar and Aggarwal find a sharp phase transition in two-time-scale learning algorithms in a 2026 arXiv paper. Stochastic approximation updates estimates from noisy samples, and two-time-scale versions run a fast and a slow recursion together, as in actor-critic learning. Known results gave the slow iterate a mean-square error shrinking slower than the ideal inverse-step rate unless strong linearity held.

The authors isolate a normal form where the slow drift has a linear leakage term plus a nonlinear remainder of tunable order. They prove matching upper and lower bounds showing the ideal rate holds exactly when a simple inequality on the exponents is met, so the slower term is unavoidable for the plain update. Adding an online bias estimator that tracks and subtracts the drift restores the ideal rate in every regime. Transfer theorems extend the mechanism to general nonlinear systems.
arxiv-2606-14588:
Aichner and co-authors map how helium ion bombardment changes a superconducting film in a 2026 arXiv paper. The material is YBCO, a high-temperature superconductor used in quantum devices. Focused helium beams pattern it at the nanoscale, but usable doses are squeezed between suppressing superconductivity reliably and avoiding structural damage.

The team exposed large film areas to thirty-kiloelectronvolt helium ions across a wide dose range and measured transport and structure. X-ray diffraction showed crystalline order fading and the lattice shifting shape until near-total amorphization at the highest dose. Raman spectra pointed to oxygen-related Frenkel defects rather than oxygen loss. The superconducting transition temperature fell following pair-breaking theory and vanished completely at a stated dose near the middle of the range, defining a practical window for device patterning.
arxiv-2606-14788:
Zhang, Guo, and Gong stage neurodegenerative disease from voice recordings in a 2026 arXiv paper. Voice screening is scalable and non-invasive for Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases. But staging severity is hard because the relevant data are heterogeneous. Their framework, NeurMLLM, feeds sound and text into one multimodal language model.

Spectrograms and cepstral coefficients of the audio are encoded by vision transformers. They are projected into the language model's embedding space. They join transcript and demographic tokens as one sequence. Instruction tuning with low-rank adaptation teaches the model to generate a constrained label token as its classification. On the Bridge2AI-Voice dataset, NeurMLLM beat classical machine learning methods. It also beat earlier language-model approaches. The dataset covers fine-grained staging of both diseases. The authors argue such models could make staging more accurate and accessible.
arxiv-2606-14988:
Yu and coauthors enrich computer-generated materials by upgrading simple models into layered ones in a 2026 study. Generative models for materials train on simple physically based rendering data, usually a diffuse term plus one specular lobe. Real surfaces show richer effects, such as clearcoat, dust, and peach fuzz. Hand-authoring such complex materials is too costly to build training sets.

The method procedurally expands the single specular lobe into a multi-lobe model guided by physical priors. The added lobes capture effects like layered scattering and surface coatings . The non-diffuse part is then encoded as a neural material in a shared six-dimensional latent space. Each material becomes two latent textures decoded by a pretrained network, keeping data compact. The team regularizes the latent space for generation, and fine-tunes a video diffusion model on it. The generated materials serve as a feasibility proof.
arxiv-2606-15388:
Mondal and coauthors compare two kinds of cosmic X-ray flare in a 2026 astronomy paper. A tidal disruption event, or TDE, is the flash when a star is torn apart by a supermassive black hole. Flares from active galactic nuclei can imitate that flash and contaminate TDE searches. The team cross-matched X-ray catalogs from two telescopes against quasar and TDE lists to measure the overlap.

During flares, active nuclei soften their X-ray spectrum until it resembles a TDE's, driven by a growing soft excess and a steepening continuum. A few percent of active nuclei show such soft flares, at rates far above true TDE rates, so searches using brightness changes alone will be contaminated. Requiring a twentyfold flux change over two years cuts the contamination sharply. Optical and infrared data unmask most flaring nuclei, a practical filter for surveys like eROSITA that hunt genuine disruptions.
arxiv-2606-15488:
Das and Sarkar work in geometric function theory in 2026, studying a family of analytic functions on the unit disk known as the apple-like Ma-Minda starlike class. These are univalent functions, meaning each maps the disk one-to-one onto a star-shaped region picked out by a subordination function. For such families, analysts ask how large the series coefficients can be.

The pair derive sharp bounds, meaning bounds that cannot be improved, for the first three inverse logarithmic coefficients. One concrete result caps the first coefficient at three quarters, attained by an extremal function they identify. They also pin down the second-order inverse logarithmic Hankel determinant and the full range of the generalized Fekete-Szego functional. The sharp limits of the third-order Hermitian-Toeplitz determinant complete the set. Each bound comes with the function that achieves it, so the constants are exact, not estimates.
arxiv-2606-15588:
Yang and colleagues show in 2026 that a one-dimensional quantum critical point can carry topology on top of its usual behaviour. They study the tricritical point of the cluster O'Brien-Fendley model, where tricritical Ising physics meets a symmetry-enriched topological sector. The transition shares the bulk data of the ordinary class, yet differs in its boundary physics.

With open edges the new class, TCI-star, shows a protected twofold degeneracy the plain class lacks. The criticality also admits two fixed boundary conditions, one from symmetry enrichment and one from flow at the edge, told apart by a discrete charge of the disorder field. Strikingly, the degeneracy at the topological point splits exponentially in energy, unlike the algebraic splitting at the Ising-star point. Points with identical bulk exponents can therefore still be distinct phases of matter once edges are counted.
arxiv-2606-15788:
Anifer and colleagues present GAS-Leak-LLM in 2026, a black-box jailbreaking attack that evolves attack suffixes to slip past language-model safety alignment. The attacker gets no access to model parameters or internals, matching how deployed systems are actually probed. A genetic algorithm searches the discrete prompt space, evolving candidates through selection, mutation, and crossover.

The evolved suffixes are appended to harmful prompts, scored by whether the model complies. The search finds suffixes that induce jailbreak responses across a wide range of harmful prompts, effectively yielding a universal adversarial suffix. Even instruction-tuned models with layered moderation prove vulnerable to the evolved prompts. The authors frame the work as exposing shortcomings in current safety enforcement, evidence that alignment trained against known attacks can be out-evolved by an automated search. Defences, the results argue, must be tested against adaptive black-box search, not just static prompt lists.
arxiv-2606-15988:
Choi and Mitra show in 2026 that dressed particle states in gauge theory and gravity do factorise after all, once the infrared variables are chosen correctly. Long-range interactions force asymptotic particles to wear clouds of soft photons and gravitons. Faddeev-Kulish dressings make scattering amplitudes infrared-finite, but dressed multi-particle states fail to split into one-particle products, threatening the Fock-space picture.

The failure, the authors argue, is an artefact. The genuine soft divergence is reproduced by Goldstone modes of asymptotic symmetries, the Coulomb phase by new zero modes of the radiative fields introduced here. In those variables, infrared-finite dressed multi-particle states admit the Fock-space factorisation into single-particle dressed states. Restoring factorisation matters: Fock space's tensor-product structure underlies how scattering calculations are organised. The result reframes a decades-old infrared puzzle as a poor choice of coordinates on the soft sector.
arxiv-2606-16088:
Matsumoto and colleagues report balloon-borne solar observations in 2026 that pin down the magnetic field inside a solar filament. Filaments are cool plasma ribbons held above the solar surface by magnetic fields, which are hard to measure directly. The Sunrise III observatory carried the SCIP instrument, which recorded full polarization profiles in the infrared calcium line on 15 July 2024.

The filament sat near disk center beside an active region and stayed quiet for at least two hours. Clear linear polarization signals appear inside it, above twice the noise level, with the double-lobe shape of the transverse Zeeman effect. That shape separates real magnetic signal from scattering effects. Weak-field estimates give about minus 80 gauss along the line of sight and 300 to 500 gauss across it. The authors report the first clear detection of linear polarization in this calcium line at a filament.
arxiv-2606-16288:
Ye and Zhang rebuild the error model behind quantum error correction in 2026, directly from measured syndrome data. Fault-tolerant quantum computing needs an accurate picture of circuit-level noise to decode errors well. Greedy inference methods can distort the statistics, dropping real error mechanisms and inventing false ones.

Their algorithm, CAHR, couples exact algebraic equations for correlations with a top-down pruning strategy that runs concurrently. It inverts syndrome statistics into a discrete physical hypergraph of error mechanisms. In benchmark tests, CAHR recovers the fault topology with no false positives, for both distance-5 rotated surface codes and dense 8-body two-dimensional color codes. The authors also show that exact recovery of continuous error rates in dense codes hits a variance cascade, where uncertainty piles up from high- to low-degree mechanisms. They therefore propose a two-stage approach: CAHR fixes the structure first, and rates follow.
arxiv-2606-16388:
Su and Ran show in 2026 that two small implementation choices make or break a neural tensor completion method. High-dimensional incomplete tensors, used in traffic and climate data, must be filled in from sparse observations. Neural Tucker factorization models their high-order interactions in continuous latent spaces. Yet its results hinge on how parameters are initialized and whether the final output layer carries a bias term.

Poor initialization can explode variance and saturate gradients, while a missing bias forces the interaction weights to absorb global statistics. Their variant, KaBiN, changes only two things: Kaiming uniform initialization replaces random uniform draws, and the bias in the final Tucker linear layer is switched on. On three real-world incomplete tensor datasets, KaBiN reduces mean absolute error and root mean square error against the baseline, per the report. An ablation on the PCTemp dataset confirms the bias helps most under the new initialization.
arxiv-2606-16788:
Xueluan Gong and colleagues systematize security and privacy risks in foundation-model robots in a 2026 survey. Robots driven by large foundation models can follow open-ended instructions and reason over images and text. That power also imports new risks, spreading from the model itself into the robot's body, its software ecosystem and society's governance of it.

Earlier reviews each covered one model type, one risk class or one layer of defense, leaving no shared map. The authors propose a four-layer framework running from foundation model, through embodied system and supporting ecosystem, to governance impact. Using it, they code and organize ninety-six prior studies by target, lifecycle stage, mechanism, access and effect. The synthesis exposes threat patterns that cross layers, defenses aimed at the wrong layer, and thin evaluation practice. Seven open challenges close the survey, setting an agenda for robots that are secure, private and responsibly governed.
arxiv-2606-16888:
Heidersberger, Jadav and Lee teach robots from imperfect demonstrations in a 2026 robotics paper. Human teachers are inconsistent: one demonstration mixes skilled stretches with clumsy ones, and standard learning copies both. Asking for endless fresh demonstrations burdens the user as well.

Their method, LOPAL, scores the quality of each local segment of a demonstration. A Gaussian mixture model encodes trajectories together with those local scores, letting the robot stitch the best local behaviors into a reference motion that can beat every single demonstration it learned from. Where good local data is missing, an active step asks the user to correct just those stretches through shared control. The robot runs the rest itself. Simulation plus a real pipe inspection task validate the approach. Task performance improves by up to about a quarter in the real test, while demonstration effort falls.
arxiv-2606-16988:
Oderinwale treats coding-agent trajectories as programs in a 2026 paper on agent behavior. Benchmark scores say what an agent got right, not how it worked. As models crowd the top of leaderboards, the manner of problem solving becomes the interesting difference.

Trajectories are converted into procedural representations using an induced vocabulary designed to compress away surface variation while exposing habits. Comparing ten agents, the study finds each has a recognizable behavioral fingerprint. A probe using those signatures assigns an unseen trajectory to the right agent with high accuracy, far above chance. Agents from similar release periods behave most alike, and distilled student models sit closest to their teachers by a divergence measure, at about half the typical distance. A library called ProcGrep supports auditing traces and searching past events, beating language models at episodic search on both speed and accuracy. Style, it turns out, is programmable.
arxiv-2606-17088:
Pirashvili presents a 2026 arXiv paper on deformation theory for monoid schemes. It is part one of a planned series on the subject. Monoids act like rings without addition, so schemes built from them support a form of geometry. The work generalises an approach due to Grillet and asks how such objects can deform.

Ordinary exactness fails for monoids, so Pirashvili brings in systems of abelian groups. The paper first studies monoid sheaves and proves a classification theorem for their coextensions. That theorem links the coextensions to the cohomology of certain complexes. For monoid schemes, where localisation is at hand, coextensions form a stack of symmetric categorical groups. Later papers are promised on deeper uses of stack theory in this setting.
arxiv-2606-17188:
Singh and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on whether vision-language models are truly multilingual. Most tests assume each language uses a single script. Punjabi breaks that assumption, since it is written in Gurmukhi, Shahmukhi, and Roman scripts. The team built PuMVR, a benchmark of parallel image-text items in all three.

Ten leading models were tested on the same tasks in each script. A model often solved a task in one script and failed the identical task in another. The accuracy gaps reached sixteen points in some script comparisons. Images raised scores across the board but did not close the gap. Cross-script transfer also proved brittle, and the proposed Script Consistency Rate fell as low as about a quarter.
arxiv-2606-17688:
Miao, Zhu, and Shwartz present a 2026 arXiv paper showing that language models often know a user's cultural context yet fail to use it when answering. The team built CAPRI, a set of conversations carrying graded cultural cues, and tested whether models adapt simple, checkable conventions like measurement units to the user's background. Units are standardised within countries, which makes adaptation measurable without wading into contested norms or stereotypes about how people in a culture think or behave in daily life.

Models inferred backgrounds and recalled the right conventions, but still answered with the wrong units unless told to do the steps in order. Adaptation grew as cues accumulated through a conversation, and the same gap showed for time and quantity readings. Priors were not neutral either, sometimes matching the model's country of origin. The data set gives future work a clean target for closing the gap.
arxiv-2606-17788:
Alalabi and colleagues study how to recover an unknown coefficient inside an elliptic partial differential equation, in a 2026 applied math paper. Such identification problems pair a fit to observed data with total variation regularization, which keeps the recovered coefficient sharp at edges. Past theory leaned on norms that ignore how widely a change spreads in space, a poor match for real numerical methods.

Working with finite-exponent norms instead, the authors use Sobolev regularity results to show the control-to-state map is differentiable in that setting. They derive first and second order conditions for the reduced objective, including a careful account of the nonsmooth total variation term and its multipliers. They then analyze a trust-region method built on these norms and prove it converges to points meeting the first order conditions, giving algorithms a firmer base.
arxiv-2606-18088:
Zhang and Liao calculate how the fastest cosmic rays light up the universe's oldest neutrinos, in a 2026 particle astrophysics paper. The cosmic neutrino background, relic particles from the hot early universe, is nearly impossible to detect directly at its natural energies. Ultra-high-energy cosmic rays can smash into these relics and boost some to energies telescopes can see, offering an indirect probe.

The authors build one framework covering five scattering channels. These run from elastic nucleon hits to nucleus-wide scattering, resonance production, and deep inelastic events. Each channel rules a different energy band, with coherent scattering strong at low energies for heavy cosmic ray nuclei. Feeding in mixed-composition cosmic ray spectra from propagation codes, they compare predictions with IceCube and Pierre Auger data to set upper limits on how overdense the relic background could be.
arxiv-2606-18188:
Romanov and colleagues address how to learn the full generator of an open quantum system's dynamics without assuming its structure in advance, in a 2026 quantum information paper. Reconstructing that generator, called a Lindbladian, matters for benchmarking noisy processors and designing error correction, but parts of it are fundamentally harder to measure than others.

Hamiltonian pieces that dissipation does not mask can be learned at the best possible Heisenberg scaling, while the rest face a quadratically worse limit. Earlier methods reaching those scalings needed the interaction and noise structure specified beforehand. The team gives the first algorithm that learns arbitrary sparse Lindbladians at the quantum limit with no prior knowledge. Under a regularity condition, their method also recovers a Hamiltonian part at the sharper limit. The key tool is a recursive random stabilizer-code construction that suppresses the strongest terms while keeping sensitivity to weaker unknown ones.
arxiv-2606-18388:
Fang and colleagues at Amazon introduce LLMZero, a system that uses language model agents to discover training strategies for reinforcement learning post-training, in a 2026 machine learning paper. Fixed schedules dominate this stage of model training, yet the best settings shift as training unfolds, and a preset path cannot react when dynamics go wrong.

LLMZero searches over training trajectories with tree search, letting agents inspect each checkpoint, diagnose problems such as divergence spikes or collapse, and propose coordinated changes to many parameters at once. Across four GRPO tasks, its strategies improved on the base model by wide margins and beat both grid search and random search. A pattern also emerged: capacity settings such as response length tend to grow steadily across stages, while regularization settings mostly oscillate in response to changing dynamics. The authors turn that asymmetry into design rules for multi-stage training.
arxiv-2606-18888:
Quilter and the team plan robot navigation by picturing worlds that fit what the agent has seen, in a 2026 machine learning paper. Going to a goal in a partly seen setting takes deciding under uncertainty about unseen layout. Belief-based methods compress that uncertainty into rough guesses that force a single-modal belief. That loses other options, when perceptual aliasing makes several maps plausible.

Their scheme BeliefDiffusion uses a diffusion model to show the belief as a multimodal distribution over environment configurations. The planner pictures map layouts based on what it has seen. It then runs model predictive control across the pooled configurations, to choose routes. In synthetic settings, the method beat model-free reinforcement learning baselines and other generative methods, on success rate and path efficiency. It also won on sample efficiency. That shows the worth of carrying multimodal beliefs into planning, rather than folding them.
arxiv-2606-18988:
Song and colleagues present ThinkDeception in 2026, a system that spots deception in video and audio while showing its reasons. Most past tools act as black boxes. They give a verdict with no clear trail, and they miss faint clashes between what is seen and what is heard. The new work casts the task as step-by-step reasoning for large multimodal models. A new dataset with hand-marked reasoning steps supports that shift in approach.

Training moves through four tiers, from easy cases to hard ones, in a set order. A tailored training rule rewards match between sight and sound, and rewards good process, not just the final label. Tests on main benchmarks report top results so far. Base model tests also confirm that clash between channels is a key clue. The gain is twofold. Scores improve, and each call comes with reasons a human reviewer can check.
arxiv-2606-19088:
Schwaiger and colleagues present ReSiReg in 2026, a method that makes vision-language features more spatially consistent for robots. Robots following open language instructions need dense features that tie words to the right places in three-dimensional space. Raw vision-language embeddings are noisy and shift with viewpoint, which breaks that grounding. The team first examines spatial structure across recent models to pin down the problem.

ReSiReg clusters intermediate features into visual prototypes, derives language descriptors for each, and rebuilds each patch as a soft mix of prototype-level language embeddings. Tests on open-vocabulary segmentation and three-dimensional mapping show better dense retrieval across backbones. Real manipulation scenes show more consistent target activations too. The authors also release a compact dense model far smaller than standard baselines yet competitive with them. Cleaner spatial semantics of this kind help robots find the right object, not just a similar-looking region.
arxiv-2606-19388:
Gu and colleagues ask in 2026 whether mobile agents need the phone screen at all. Recent mobile agents follow the GUI paradigm, perceiving interface elements and emitting screen interactions. Mobile platforms also expose a command-line interface with direct access to device services and data. The authors argue the command line deserves first-class consideration alongside the graphical route.

The team evaluates three coding agents across four model APIs on two mobile benchmarks, with no mobile-specific post-training. The strongest command-line setup beats every reproducible GUI baseline on both benchmarks, and other command-line setups stay competitive. Oracle command-line solutions show a high ceiling, solving most tasks in principle. A new task suite covers everyday intents beyond GUI scope, such as bulk operations, multi-condition filtering, and aggregation. The results suggest agent builders should treat the command line as a primary channel.
arxiv-2606-19488:
Tokita studies how population density rewires social networks and reshapes contagion dynamics in 2026, using a minimal agent-based model. Dense settlements coincide with bursts of productivity and change. The model isolates density. Population size and individual behavior stay fixed while only spacing varies. Agents form ties, favoring those nearby and those already well-connected.

Density alone reorganizes network structure. Sparse populations form locally clustered communities. Denser ones form globally integrated networks with shorter social distances and a tight core of popular individuals. The shift happens sharply over a narrow density range. It is governed by whether proximity or social popularity dominates tie formation. Simulated contagions then split by type. Simple contagions, like information or disease, reach a majority faster in denser populations. Complex contagions, like norms, do not spread faster but reach broader uptake. Density thus changes not just how fast things spread, but what can spread at all.
arxiv-2606-19588:
Zunchen Huang and Songgaojun Deng study the narration gap in language model and solver loops in 2026. SAT and SMT solvers give sound, checkable answers to logic questions inside model pipelines. A hybrid loop formalises a question, lets the solver decide it, then narrates the verdict to the user.

Past work covered formalising and deciding, but not narration, the step users actually read. Huang and Deng model the loop as a verified decision procedure to isolate that step. Five open-source models then face prompt injection attacks. Certificate gating keeps the solver verdict itself sound. Yet an adversary can flip the narrated conclusion across phrasings and channels. Hardened prompts cut injection sharply but cannot remove it, and adaptive attacks still bite. Robustness at the solver thus fails to reach the final answer, a warning for safety-critical pipelines.
arxiv-2606-19688:
Yunsik Kim and Yoonyoung Chung make streaming speech enhancement tunable in 2026 with LaCo-SENet. Live speech cleanup must trade delay against quality, yet designs usually force a causal or non-causal choice. One training-time setting now spans that whole range.

Asymmetric temporal padding shifts context between past and future inside the convolutions. Dual-buffer streaming pairs state buffers for past context with lookahead buffers for future context. Selective state updates stop future frames leaking into the streaming state. Training and inference thus stay consistent. One fixed backbone of modest size yields a family of models spanning low to moderate latency. Quality scores rise gently as the allowed delay grows on the VoiceBank plus DEMAND test set. Even the fully causal lowest-delay model matches or beats the prior causal best, which needed far more delay.
arxiv-2606-20088:
Martín Nava-Callejas, Stéphane Goriely, and Nicolas Chamel ask how superbursts, huge explosions on neutron star crusts, would change if carbon fused far from the classic rate. Their 2026 paper revisits the carbon fusion rate at the billion-degree temperatures where unstable carbon burning ignites these blasts in low-mass X-ray binaries. Recent work suggests the true rate could be a thousand times larger or smaller than the standard Caughlan and Fowler value.

Running the stellar code MESA with four rate variants, the team finds a faster rate shortens the wait between bursts and cuts decay time. It also lowers ignition depth, while a slower rate does the opposite. Peak temperatures shift too, altering how much alpha-element material the blast forges. These swings rival changing the heating at the envelope's base, so telescope readings of superbursts hide a dependence on one uncertain rate.
arxiv-2606-20288:
Huynh Viet Khanh characterizes when the unit group of a weighted Leavitt path algebra can contain free subgroups. His 2026 paper studies algebras built from a finite connected weighted graph over a field of characteristic zero. Khanh proves the unit group is abelian exactly when the algebra is a domain, an algebra with no zero divisors. Equivalently, the unit group contains no non-cyclic free subgroup exactly in the domain case, which the Hazrat-Preusser classification pins to three shapes: the isolated vertex, the unweighted one-petal rose, and the LV-rose.

Free subgroups inside unit groups are a classic theme, running from the Tits alternative to Lichtman's conjecture for division rings. Leavitt path algebras give the question a combinatorial home, where graph shape decides algebraic behavior. Outside the three domain cases, non-cyclic free subgroups always exist in characteristic zero.
arxiv-2606-20588:
Tobias Priesholm Gårdhus and four colleagues present AInterviewer, an open-source platform for AI-led qualitative interviews. Their 2026 paper notes that existing systems lean on closed commercial models, so studies are hard to repeat and data hard to keep safe. They also hand every interview task to the model, limiting control over wording and question order.

AInterviewer uses a multi-agent pipeline built on open models, keeping question wording and order under the researcher's control. Interviews can then be replicated exactly, and sensitive responses stay off commercial servers. Qualitative researchers gain automation without surrendering discipline. The platform shows AI interviewing can scale and still be audited.
arxiv-2606-20788:
Brian Batell, Morgan Cassidy, and Kun Cheng report a first study in 2026 of Leggett-Garg tests in muon spin precession. The Leggett-Garg inequality tests whether a system acts as if it has definite states over time. A violation points to quantum links across time. The team builds a way to recover time correlations of muon spin from decay data recorded over time.

They apply the method to public Fermilab Muon g-2 data, covering about ten billion muon decays. A simple model of detector response is used. The inequality is found violated at a strong level in a single bin. Joining nearby bins raises the strength further. Error from detector modeling limits the result. A dedicated analysis could cut that error sharply. Existing precision data may thus open a new window on quantum behavior over time, using a data set first built for a different test.
arxiv-2606-20888:
Thomas Markhorst and four colleagues propose FiGMo in 2026, a language model system for fine-grained understanding of human motion. Motion is represented as a sequence of skeletal poses. Each pose encodes body joint positions. Timestamp tokens ground each pose in time. That lets the model reason about order, duration, and rhythm, not just static posture. The team asks what supervision such reasoning needs.

A training mixture spans pose captioning, pose questions, motion captioning, and motion questions. Ablations show main gains come from diverse supervision across pose and motion levels. Staged training adds a smaller benefit. The system accepts both two-dimensional and three-dimensional skeleton data through one pose encoder. Video can be added for context. Tests on five benchmarks show strong results. Fine-grained motion understanding supports coaching, rehabilitation, and animation tools that must describe how a movement unfolds.
arxiv-2606-20988:
Haoying Niu and Xiao-Yong Yan explain a scaling law in 2026 for how people return home during daily travel. The chance of returning home after a tour of locations falls as a power law. A known model reproduces that pattern, but uses the power law as an input. The microscopic origin of its exponent stayed unresolved. Their answer starts from cognitive limits and least effort.

Activity priorities are shown to follow Zipf's law, where rank and frequency are linked. That law dictates how tour utility accumulates, more slowly than linearly. A standard choice rule then yields the return probability with an exact exponent. The exponent equals one minus the Zipf exponent. Agent simulations confirm the analytic relation. A cognitive mechanism for a travel law matters for urban models, where home-return patterns shape traffic, transit demand, and exposure estimates.
arxiv-2606-21088:
Jintao Chen and many colleagues propose MV-WAM in 2026, a world action model for robot manipulation that adds value estimation and manifold-aware training. World action models do well in-domain. Gains often fail to extend to new settings. Visual and action data live on unlike manifolds, the authors argue. Joint optimization can degrade action robustness when distributions shift.

Their framework jointly models video prediction, action generation, and value estimation. A cross-modality causal mask grounds actions in predicted video frames. Value tokens draw on both modalities. Manifold-aware optimization accounts for structural differences across data types. Video priors are leveraged in both training and inference. Stronger out-of-distribution action generalization matters for household and warehouse robots, where lighting, objects, and layouts never match the training set exactly.
arxiv-2606-21188:
Kuancheng Wang and five colleagues at UC San Diego introduce a Compressed Action Memory Policy in 2026 for robot manipulation that is only partly observable. Long, contact-rich tasks hide state: one image rarely shows prior attempts or progress. Standard vision policies and vision-language-action models then struggle for lack of memory. Their insight is that a robot's own action history is a rich, free signal.

A memory module keeps a compressed record of past actions. Training forces it to encode a latent behavioral memory of all past interactions. Future actions are then chosen with that context. Task progress is tracked implicitly, and failed attempts inform later tries, with no extra supervision. Evaluation spans four real-robot setups and two new simulation benchmarks. Cheap action memory could make robots less likely to repeat a failed grasp in a long task.
arxiv-2606-21388:
Berinyuy and four colleagues propose a theoretical scheme in 2026 to create and strengthen quantum entanglement inside a magnomechanical system. In that system, magnetic, sound, and motion modes interact in a yttrium iron garnet sphere. Such entangled states are resources for quantum communication and computing, but generating them usually demands a strong cross-Kerr coupling, a nonlinear interaction between the magnetic and sound modes.

Adding phonon hopping between the two mechanical modes, plus mechanical parametric amplification that pumps one mode, changes the picture. Entanglement then appears even when the cross-Kerr coupling is weak, and the states stay highly pure, meaning little unwanted mixing creeps in. The results show how nonlinear couplings can be combined to engineer robust quantum correlations in such devices.
arxiv-2606-21788:
Dighe and Dantu, in a 2026 robotics paper, study how a robot hand can turn an object it holds toward a target pose. The target is given as a point cloud, a set of three-dimensional points describing the object's surface in its desired orientation. Raw point clouds make poor control signals, because two samplings of the same shape rarely line up point by point.

The authors learn an embedding, a compact numeric code for each cloud, whose distance matches the true rotation error between orientations. A reinforcement learning policy then acts from current and goal embeddings, joint sensing, and centroid data, with no pose estimates or teacher demonstrations. In reorientation experiments, the setup matched baselines that used privileged state or distillation, while avoiding fragile pose computation at test time.
arxiv-2606-22088:
Zou settles, in 2026, the remaining case of a realization problem for group actions on non-positively curved three-dimensional manifolds. The setting is a closed orientable 3-manifold carrying a metric of nonpositive sectional curvature, with a finite group acting freely by orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms. Earlier results supplied a group-invariant metric of the same kind except possibly for graph manifolds.

Zou proves the invariant metric also exists when the manifold is a graph manifold. A graph manifold is one built by gluing simpler Seifert pieces along tori. The result completes the three-dimensional case of the question posed by Schoen and Yau. Their question adapts the classical Nielsen realization problem, which asks when abstract group actions can be realized by genuine symmetries of a space.
arxiv-2606-22188:
Samplawski and colleagues introduce, in 2026, the Bayesian Adaptation Gym, a benchmark for Bayesian low-rank adaptation of multimodal language models. Deployed in high-stakes domains, such models need well-calibrated uncertainty. Approximating posteriors over all weights is intractable at this scale, so recent work adapts only low-rank updates, but no standard benchmark existed to judge those methods.

Reference implementations come with the gym, covering older Bayesian baselines of the classic kind alongside adaptation methods at the current frontier. Its dataset, which is multimodal, comes with tasks that test calibration, how well methods hold up when distributions shift, and choices made under uncertainty, using active learning. The authors test extensively across model sizes, datasets, and tasks. The results map where current Bayesian adaptation approaches succeed and where they fail. The benchmark is fully open source, aiming to make future comparisons reproducible.
arxiv-2606-22288:
Dadi Ni and Kaichuan Qi wrote this 2026 paper in symplectic geometry, a branch of mathematics used to describe motion and phase spaces. Their objects are cotangent groupoids, structured spaces that pair a symmetry description with its dual space of momenta. They study affine deformations of these objects, meaning controlled changes governed by a differential one-form, which measures directed change along a space.

Ni and Qi pin down which conditions the one-form must meet for the change to be valid. They show these deformations arise from circle central extensions of Lie groupoids through symplectic reduction, a step that simplifies a system using its symmetries. The reduced form turns out to be a multiplicative magnetic form. For Kac-Moody extensions in particular, the construction yields nontrivial deformations of quotient stacks and circle gerbes.
arxiv-2606-22588:
Faruk Alpay and Barış Başaran measure a hidden unevenness inside a graphics processor in this 2026 paper. The NVIDIA L40 carries a large L2 cache, usually modelled as one uniform pool with a single hit latency. The authors test whether latency depends on which streaming multiprocessor issues the load.

A probe resolving each load's origin mapped hit latency across all one hundred forty-two multiprocessors. Latency was not constant: it spanned a range of more than fifty percent, with almost no measurement noise. A simple additive model explained most of the pattern, which was two-fold symmetric, matching the chip's two halves. The same probe on an RTX 5090 shows the effect generalizes, though each die's map is unique. As a fingerprint, one probe locates the multiprocessor accurately and separates two identical cards. Scheduling latency-bound work by the map cut makespan by up to eleven percent.
arxiv-2606-22688:
Can Savcı studies how self-play agents settle down in this 2026 game-theory paper. In two-player zero-sum games, naive gradient ascent makes the latest strategy orbit the equilibrium instead of settling. Modern fixes regularize toward a reference: a fixed one reaches only a distorted equilibrium, while snapshots power systems like DeepNash.

Savcı's method, GARIP, anchors instead to the running average of past play. The mechanism he isolates: collapse tracks the reference's peak lag. Among averages with equal mean lag, the running average minimizes that peak; a snapshot's sawtooth peaks at twice its mean. Anchoring shrinks the base rotation enough to cross the stability boundary, proving local last-iterate convergence at constant strength. On matrix games, the Coin Game, Connect Four, and Othello, GARIP matched the snapshot method's peak performance. At standard settings it collapsed in none of forty seeds, against ten of forty for a matched snapshot.
arxiv-2606-23088:
N. V. Kharuk examines background fields and cutoffs in sigma models in a 2026 theoretical physics paper. Sigma models describe fields taking values in a curved target space, and they are basic tools in quantum field theory. The background field method splits a field into a fixed classical part and a quantum fluctuation. A cutoff limits which fluctuations count, keeping calculations finite. Kharuk uses a two-dimensional nonlinear sigma model built on the Heisenberg group as the test case.

Kharuk compares two ways of splitting the chiral field into background and fluctuation parts. Only one split proves consistent with building the generating functional through a background field. The paper then renormalizes the quantum action at one loop, absorbing the simplest layer of infinities into redefined quantities. Power-law singularities are computed at two loops, and the cutoff is checked against special functional relations.
arxiv-2606-23188:
Ryo Ogawa and colleagues vary the encoding inside factorization-machine black-box optimization in a 2026 paper. Black-box optimization tackles problems whose objective has no formula and costs much to evaluate. One leading method pairs a factorization machine surrogate with an Ising machine that searches the surrogate. Integers must first be encoded as bits, and several encodings exist. Standard practice keeps one encoding for both learning the surrogate and searching it. The authors argue the best encoding may differ by stage, and propose switching deliberately.

Ogawa and colleagues derive formulas converting between one-hot and domain-wall encodings while preserving the surrogate objective up to a constant. Their mixed variant learns with one-hot encoding and searches with domain-wall encoding. On the Rastrigin test function, the learning-stage encoding dominated performance, with one-hot consistently best. The search-stage switch helped only under some size and resolution settings.
arxiv-2606-23388:
A. M. Riyas and colleagues report the first actinide detections in a class of ancient stars in a 2026 astronomy paper. CEMP-rs stars are carbon-rich, metal-poor stars enriched by both slow and rapid neutron-capture processes. Their mix of element signatures has long puzzled astronomers. The team's earlier work suggested an intermediate neutron-capture process in low-mass giant stars explains the heavy elements. Actinides like thorium and uranium usually point instead to explosive events, and their spectral lines hide under severe blending. Using high-resolution spectra from the UVES spectrograph on the Very Large Telescope, they search a sample of these stars.

Riyas and colleagues detect thorium robustly in three stars. Uranium stays marginal, giving only upper limits. Theoretical intermediate-process models reproduce the observed abundances within uncertainty. The match supports an intermediate-process origin even for the actinides.
arxiv-2606-23588:
Ranjan, Sengupta, Rangarajan, and Ranka simulate traffic at signalized intersections with a learned generative model, in a 2026 paper on transportation simulation. Standard microsimulators rely on hand-built driver models that match average flow but miss real drivers' varied behavior. Learned trajectory predictors capture richer interactions. Yet they look only a short way ahead. They also become unstable in a closed loop, feeding their own predictions back as inputs.

Their model, Enactor, focuses on vehicles and encodes actors and lane shapes in polar coordinates around the intersection center. Each vehicle also sees the rear bumper of the vehicle ahead, which helps it stop in the right place. A transformer predicts each actor's next motion. In four thousand seconds of simulation at two intersections, Enactor matches reference speed and travel-time patterns far more closely than a recent baseline. It also cuts red-light violations sharply.
arxiv-2606-24388:
Gallivanone and colleagues release a ready-made arsenal for stress-testing vision-language models. Generating adversarial attacks, inputs crafted to make a model produce harmful output, is expensive in compute. That keeps robustness research behind paywalls of compute. PHANTOM, their 2026 dataset, pre-generates tens of thousands of adversarial samples. Any team can evaluate defences immediately.

Coverage spans ten high-level categories and fifty-five subtypes of harmful intent. It merges and extends several established benchmarks into thousands of distinct intents. One additional category broadens the set. Attack strategies come from recent state-of-the-art literature, keeping the samples realistic rather than synthetic filler. Intended uses include testing model robustness and alignment, fine-tuning attack-generation models, and testing guardrails. Gallivanone's team frames the open release as lowering the barrier to adversarial research. Defenders, they argue, benefit most from shared, realistic attack data.
arxiv-2606-24788:
Arpan Mukherjee and Mourad Sini study optimal control of acoustic waves using clusters of tiny resonators as actuators. The resonators are smaller than the wavelength and contrast strongly with the surrounding medium. The goal is control over a finite band of frequencies, not just one tone. A time domain Foldy Lax approximation captures how waves and structures interact. Spectral analysis then isolates the clusters' main collective resonances.

Those resonances are weakly damped poles of a delayed transfer matrix. Projecting the point source field onto a finite spectral band gives a small coupled system. One part holds acoustic modal coefficients; the other holds the collective states of the microstructure. On this reduced model the authors pose a quadratic tracking problem. They prove the optimal control exists and is unique. An adjoint system characterises it. A resonant source lifting estimate supplies the main quantitative bound for exact control.
arxiv-2606-25288:
Harvesting the biggest fish or trees seems obviously wise, yet the population itself changes the rules as it thins or crowds. Louis Shuo Wang studies a size structured population model in 2026 where one environmental variable, generated by the population, feeds back on growth and death rates at every size. At steady state that feedback must close consistently, and Wang corrects the theory describing when it does. Crowding that slows growth piles individuals up near the entry size, breaking a naive monotonicity argument.

A second result reduces the stability calculation for threshold harvest policies to an exact adjoint formula. The same single quantity governs both closure sensitivity and how fragile the harvest threshold is. Simulations on a standard growth model show when a simple minimum size rule survives and when feedback opens extra harvest windows at smaller sizes.
arxiv-2606-25488:
Distilling a big teacher model into a small student usually trains on the full dataset, so the savings arrive only after an expensive process. Yifan Wu and colleagues ask in 2026 whether a pruned dataset can distil a better student with less data and less compute. Their framework, IF-Beta, first scores each training example's influence on distillation outcomes, then learns a sampling policy shaped like a Beta distribution that decides how likely each example is to be kept.

A two level objective trains the policy: the inner loop practises quickly inside the teacher's feature space, while the outer loop judges real distillation performance. On standard image benchmarks the method beat other pruning baselines across removal rates. Students trained on the pruned sets sometimes surpassed students distilled on everything, suggesting much full dataset training is redundant for knowledge transfer.
arxiv-2606-25788:
Phones hide their Wi-Fi hardware addresses behind random values during network discovery, supposedly defeating passive tracking. Marta Puig, Costas Michaelides, Lucia Pintor, Boris Bellalta, and Francesc Wilhelmi test that promise in 2026 and find it wanting. Probe request frames still leak unencrypted hardware capability fields, frame timing, and signal strength patterns. The team's key trick is bitwise decomposition of the high throughput capability field, splitting packed flags into individual features a clustering algorithm can exploit. Three unsupervised clusterers were tried across twenty two devices from six manufacturers, with no labelled training.

DBSCAN won, reaching global accuracy up to about ninety percent when fed the decomposed capability bits plus three signal strength measurements. Devices stayed identifiable despite fresh random addresses. Randomisation as currently standardised, the authors conclude, does not deliver its privacy promise, and the Wi-Fi standard itself needs strengthening.
arxiv-2606-26088:
Saleha Maqsood, Muhammad Kamran, and Tahir Malik simulate quantum gates on light that carries orbital angular momentum. Twisted light beams can encode qubits in their spiral structure. A spatial light modulator, a programmable device that reshapes light's phase, performs the gates through holography. Their testbed is a real commercial modulator, the HOLOEYE LC 2012. Noise figures come straight from its datasheet, with no free fitting.

Three noise channels are modelled: quantization, electronic and thermal effects, and phase-wrap clipping. The full universal gate set runs on a fine simulation grid. Single-qubit gates and entangling gates both land near ninety-nine percent fidelity. Fork grating gates suffer most from thermal and electronic noise. Phase gates do better, since they avoid clipping error entirely. A Bell state built from two modulator passes keeps the same high fidelity. Blue-to-green wavelengths emerge as the device's sweet spot.
arxiv-2606-26288:
M. S. Oey and colleagues test whether the extreme variable star AzV 493 hides a companion. The star's wild light and spectral swings suggest an unseen partner on a long, eccentric orbit, with candidate periods near seven or fifteen years. A close pass should stir the system and flash in X-rays. The team aimed the Chandra observatory at the predicted periastron of the shorter orbit, hunting that flash.

Silence came back. The observation sets only an upper limit on X-ray brightness, below what an interacting companion would likely produce. New and archival spectra hunt radial velocity wobbles instead. Their statistics cannot settle whether the star truly wobbles. One clue did flip: the violet-to-red balance of a hydrogen line recently inverted, which can signal a companion's influence. Possible companion masses are mapped for the case the variations prove real.
arxiv-2606-26488:
Pearse Jim and four colleagues ask what survives when a recursive reasoning model is compressed for small devices. Such models solve hard structured puzzles with few parameters. They update an internal state again and again instead of writing long outputs. Shrinking them for edge hardware is necessary, but compression errors compound across their reasoning cycles. Standard intuition from ordinary models does not apply.

One pattern held across every precision level, three tasks, and two designs. Aggressive compression kept single-cell predictions accurate. Whole-puzzle accuracy collapsed to zero. Quantization, pruning, distillation, and linear attention all failed the same way. The collapse hit one design family but not attention-based recursion on the same task. A per-channel calibrated low-precision format reversed the damage without retraining. The team also offers a label-free signal that tracks the reasoning path and predicts damage early.
arxiv-2606-26588:
Yiyuan Pan, Hanjiang Hu, Shangtao Li, Xusheng Luo, and Changliu Liu present ReStruct, a method for steering robot behaviour after training. Users often want a deployed robot to follow preferences nobody anticipated. Retraining is expensive. Editing symbolic plans can produce instructions that sound logical but are physically impossible. ReStruct steers behaviour at inference time, while the robot runs.

The underlying policy is split into two parts. A state-machine skeleton captures the task's structure. A continuous controller handles the physical motions and stays frozen. User preferences are written as their own automaton and merged into the skeleton. The merged structure updates the action guidance the controller receives. Steering thus stays aware of physical feasibility. Experiments in simulation and the real world covered object-based wishes and timing rules. After steering, ReStruct beat rival methods and large vision-language-action models on success and preference following.
arxiv-2606-26888:
Kazuma Igarashi and Nozomu Suzuki compute symmetry groups of prime ideal splitting using Newton polygons. When a number field extends another, prime ideals split in patterns governed by hidden Galois symmetries. Decomposition and inertia groups describe that splitting. Newton polygons, graphs built from a defining polynomial, are a classic computational tool for the job.

Earlier polygon methods determined these groups under strong assumptions due to Ore. The authors extend the method to the weaker assumptions of Montes and Nart. Their formulation runs through the index, a measure of how far a chosen generator is from generating the full ring of integers. The weaker hypotheses widen the method's reach to more extensions. Number theorists gain a more general algorithm for a fundamental computation.
arxiv-2606-26988:
Mingbo Dou and six colleagues show that an electric field can flip the magnetic spin Hall effect in a special class of matter. The spin Hall effect drives spins of opposed orientation to opposed sides. In ferroelectric altermagnets, matter both polarisable and magnetically ordered in a split way, the effect's sign ties to the polarisation.

Spin-group analysis proves the switching works beyond simple time reversal arguments. Flipping the polarisation swaps the spin-up and spin-down channels in momentum space. The spin flow, set by the gap between channels, therefore flips sign. Math on a vanadium oxyiodide monolayer confirms the mechanism. The switching needs no current and wastes no energy as heat. Programmable spin devices are the prize.
arxiv-2606-27188:
Fournier and Limonad introduce a process harness for upgrading legacy business workflows with artificial intelligence agents. Rather than replacing the workflow engine, the harness wraps an agentic layer around it. The engine keeps structural authority while agents add reasoning at chosen control points. Their Task-Decision-Flow model specifies the data schema and running semantics. Three governed agent types divide the language-model work in this design and realisation paper from 2026.

TaskAgents handle knowledge-heavy work, DecisionAgents route each case at gateways, and FlowAgents adapt the running flow through principled hooks. Every agent acts inside a stated policy taken from the process FRAME, the full rule set for model calls. A loan approval workflow demonstrates all three agent types plus a hook-driven regulatory override. The CUGA FLO system realises the design. Strict structural compliance and framed agent autonomy thus coexist in one governed platform.
arxiv-2606-27288:
Chen asks how much combining many language models can ever help, and finds a hard ceiling set by shared failure. Routers, voting, cascades, and mixtures of agents all pick one member model's answer in the end. Accuracy for any such scheme cannot exceed one minus the rate at which every model fails the same query. The field usually reports average pairwise error correlation instead. Chen proves that statistic cannot pin down the shared-failure rate, in a study published in 2026, covering sixty-seven frontier models.

 A statistical bound turns one graded held-out set into a zero-cost certificate of the largest possible gain. Across models from twenty-one providers, calibrated models still underprice the all-wrong tail, more so as pools grow. Gains come from models failing on different questions, not from adding more of them. Diverse pools beat same-model ensembles at matched quality.
arxiv-2606-27388:
Gavhale, Khlopov, Trivedi, and Krasnov ask whether nearby experiments can corner the light scalar fields that swampland conjectures discuss. Such fields are candidates for driving late-time cosmic acceleration, and quantum gravity folklore constrains their potentials. Working in a scalar-tensor framework, the team defines the swampland quantities in the canonically normalised Einstein frame. Solar System tests, lunar laser ranging, equivalence principle checks, and atomic clock bounds then translate into limits. The probes constrain products of the scalar's motion with its couplings, not the motion alone, in a cosmology paper appearing in 2026.

For coupling directions visible to local experiments, the scalar today must crawl ultra-slowly. Building a large de Sitter gradient from unscreened visible-sector couplings alone becomes severely restricted. The refined de Sitter alternative survives only in narrow corners, near a hilltop or under tuned evolution. Local precision physics thus reaches into quantum gravity's conjectured landscape.
arxiv-2606-27688:
A forecaster can be deployed in more than one way. Riku Green, Zahraa Abdallah, and Telmo Silva Filho study that choice in 2026 for multi-horizon volatility forecasting. A multi-output forecaster predicts several future steps at once. Changing the inference-time rollout rule turns one trained model into a family of predictors with different accuracy and cost.

Experiments covered twenty stock-volatility series and three forecast horizons. Architectures ranged from linear models to PatchTST. Non-default rollout rules often beat the standard deployment. The best fixed rule varied a lot across architectures and horizons, so no single static replacement is reliable. Validation-based selection worked better. Picked single rules improved accuracy at low cost. Small rule subsets captured most of that benefit at far lower inference cost. Rankings also depended on the metric used. Squared-error choices did not transfer evenly to the finance-standard QLIKE loss.
arxiv-2606-27988:
Judging fine-grained skills, like sports moves or surgical technique, needs step-by-step reasoning. Existing action quality models are black boxes that give a score without showing how it was reached. Xirui Teng, Nan Xi, and Junsong Yuan propose LVDR in 2026. Their framework models the reasoning process itself. Keypoint-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search structures the search. The output is both an assessment and the visual reasoning sequence behind it.

Reasoning is formulated as a diffusion process in a latent space. The tree search explores candidate reasoning paths. Keypoints guide which visual evidence matters at each step. Experiments span four datasets across sports and surgical domains. Accuracy is competitive with existing methods. The distinguishing gain is interpretability. The trajectories show which spatiotemporal patterns drove the final prediction. Future work targets multi-person scenarios, richer context, and real-time use in live surgical training.
arxiv-2606-28388:
Rômulo Damasclin Chaves dos Santos and Delvonei Alves de Andrade build a strict theory of Landau inequalities for rotating compressible flows at high Mach numbers. Landau inequalities are bounds that tie the size of a function to the size of its derivatives. Their version is fractional and anisotropic, meaning the derivatives are partial and depend on direction. Coriolis and centrifugal forces enter from the rotation.

Santos and Andrade define rotating fractional Sobolev spaces that encode direction, friction losses, and spin together. They split the flow by rotating frequency bands and prove sharp bounds. The constants show just how the Mach number, the spin rate, and the axis direction enter. The proof uses anisotropic maximal estimates and commutator bounds for the Coriolis term. The team then applies the bounds to stability questions for neural operators that mimic such flows, with best-possible approximation rates for physics-informed network design.
arxiv-2606-28488:
A. Gil-Ocaranza, Josue De-Santiago, Mauricio Lopez-Hernandez, and Jorge L. Cervantes-Cota generate dark energy from neutrinos. In their scenario, neutrinos interact through a light scalar field, and heat in the early universe gives them an effective mass that changes as the cosmos cools. Inside unimodular gravity, a variant of Einstein's theory, those interactions break energy conservation just enough to drive dynamical dark energy.

With one neutrino species the dark energy density climbs steadily. With two, it can peak at intermediate ages and decline today. Fitting late-time cosmological data, the team finds a preferred interaction strength at modest, two-sigma significance, weaker for heavier assumed neutrino masses, corresponding to an ultralight mediator. Adding Planck distance information shrinks the degeneracies and pushes the rebuilt history closer to a constant.
arxiv-2606-29188:
Bourin and Lee sharpen a recent matrix inequality of Teng Zhang comparing a sum of matrices with a sum of their symmetrised sizes. For matrices, size is measured by unitarily invariant norms, which depend only on singular values. Zhang's inequality bounds the norm of a sum by a constant times the norm of summed quadratic symmetric moduli, an average of a matrix and its adjoint.

The pair derive operator and eigenvalue refinements, stronger versions that compare the matrices themselves, not just their norms. Their engine is a new polar decomposition of the quadratic symmetric modulus, a factorisation that splits a matrix into a rotation-like part and a size part. One refinement bounds the modulus of the sum by an average of the summed moduli and a unitarily rotated copy. They also treat the maximal modulus tied to Olson's order, with a parallel series of estimates.
arxiv-2606-29588:
Le Fèvre reviews how heavy-ion collisions, smashing atomic nuclei together in the laboratory, constrain the nuclear equation of state at high density. That equation links pressure and density inside neutron stars, the densest objects known. Flow, the collective motion of particles produced in a collision, has proven a powerful observable for probing both symmetric and asymmetric nuclear matter.

Combining symmetry energy measurements with constraints on symmetric matter let researchers predict how pressure inside a neutron star grows with density. Those predictions agree with recent astronomical measurements from gravitational waves and pulsar observations, up to about two and a half times saturation density. A key subtlety is knowing which densities each measure actually probes. Future experiments at higher energy, such as ASY-EOS, should push the frontier further. Le Fèvre stresses that sound uncertainty estimates are essential for that progress.
arxiv-2606-29788:
Wang and Zhang show that telling a multimodal agent to forget a fact does not make the fact vanish. Current memory systems typically delete the text entry and report success. The authors find the fact may stay recoverable from retained user images, even images tagged to different facts.

Their Information Provenance Graph classifies memory forms by deletion affordance, how deletable each form is. The benchmark, MemLeak, measures leakage across a deletion cascade. Direct probing recovers almost nothing. Retained text enables substantial recovery, and retained images enable more. Content-aware semantic deletion cuts the image residual sharply. The residual appears across several vision-language models, a production memory system, and real photographs, with human validation confirming the judging.
arxiv-2606-29888:
Lee and three colleagues examine sparse autoencoders, tools that unpack the tangled internal features of vision-language models into single-concept features. Prior work quietly assumed that the same concept points in the same direction in the image and text parts of the shared space.

The authors show this assumption fails. They identify cross-modal feature heterogeneity, where one concept uses different directions for images and for text. This drives the modality split, where a concept activates different features depending on the input type. Aligning activity alone cannot fix a direction mismatch. Their remedy trains a separate model for each input type, preserving each one's shape, then aligns matching features afterwards, improving reconstruction, cross-modal retrieval, and concept steering.
arxiv-2606-29988:
Hannah McCall and colleagues report X-ray observations of the galaxy cluster A3571. Its center cools only weakly, and the cluster looks relaxed. Most earlier XRISM telescope studies targeted disturbed or merging clusters. Four XRISM pointings let this team measure gas speeds here. Measurements reach out to about one hundred twenty kiloparsecs.

The velocity dispersion stays fairly uniform across the core regions. It sits near one hundred to one hundred twenty kilometers per second. A northern sloshing feature shows a clearly lower limit. Sloshing is gas rocking slowly, like water in a bowl. The cluster's Mach number lies below the relaxed cluster A2029. It also falls below predictions from cosmological simulations. Even so, turbulent heating balances cooling losses everywhere measured. Sloshing motions therefore seem to supply much of the heat. Merging clusters show Mach numbers nearly twice the relaxed average.
arxiv-2606-30088:
Namrata Roy, Sanchayeeta Borthakur, Timothy Heckman, and Tanmay Singh search for glowing gas around radio galaxies. The gas is the circumgalactic medium, a galaxy's vast outer reservoir. Jets from central black holes may stir and light up this gas. The team looks for hydrogen-alpha emission along the jet direction. They stack spectra of background quasars taken by DESI.

A strong emission excess appears within twenty degrees of the jet axis. It clears the five sigma significance threshold comfortably. Averaging over all three hundred twenty-four sightlines instead gives no detection. The signal is therefore tightly localized along the jets. Its strength peaks just outside the galaxy's half-light radius. It rises again out near the projected radio lobes. The glow is about one hundred times brighter than normal halos. Magnesium absorption, by contrast, shows no directional difference. Jets seem to boost small, localized clouds dramatically.
arxiv-2606-30288:
Xiaoqian Shen and Mohamed Elhoseiny improve fine-grained perception in vision-language models facing very long visual inputs. High-resolution images and long videos flood such models with tokens. An attention sink effect lets irrelevant tokens absorb too much attention. Existing fixes crop regions and re-encode them in extra passes. Those passes cost time and lean on unreliable coordinate predictions.

Their framework, VisReflect, reflects on visual content inside the latent space instead. The model generates continuous visual reflections of question-relevant features. Reflections emphasize salient regions or frames in just one forward pass. No discrete intermediate predictions are decoded at any point. Evaluations span high-resolution image benchmarks up to 8K resolution. Video understanding benchmarks are included in the test suite too. Gains reach several points on image tasks and smaller ones on video. Inference runs much faster than zooming-based rivals on video.
arxiv-2606-30388:
Róisín Luo, Christian Gagné, Jonas Ngnawé, Ihsan Ullah, and Karyn Morrissey explain why neural networks sometimes generalize long after memorizing their training data. That delayed jump is called grokking. Models fit training data early, then test well much later. The mechanism behind the delay has stayed murky. The authors locate it in the geometry of solution space. Adam's dynamics with weight shrinkage create that geometry.

Reachable solutions form a shell-and-core arrangement, they argue. Random starting points sit on a thin outer spherical shell. A memorization shell encloses the core within. Generalization solutions occupy the core. Stopping-time theory analyzes when trajectories escape the memorization shell. The escape moment is the grokking transition time. Scaling laws follow for learning rate and batch size. The weight-decay scaling is derived as well. Experiments validate the predicted laws across tasks. The formulas also recover results from earlier literature.
arxiv-2606-30488:
Jaejin Shin, Seok-Jun Chang, Hee-Won Lee, and Sam Kim compare two snapshots of a symbiotic nova taken twenty years apart. RR Telescopii pairs a white dwarf with a red giant. Raman-scattered helium lines probe its neutral hydrogen gas. Those lines encode the gas's layout and motion. Spectra came from FEROS in 2004 and GHOST in 2024. The long baseline reveals how the system changed.

All three Raman helium lines are detected. They sit at wavelengths sixty-five forty-five, forty-eight fifty-one, and forty-three thirty-two angstroms. The lines show distinct relative velocities. Different depths of the neutral region are therefore being traced. Conversion efficiencies dropped between the two epochs. The neutral region's physical properties changed substantially over twenty years. Radiative transfer modeling implies a wider covering angle in 2004. No single column density describes the region. The authors argue for tomography-style modeling of such binaries.
arxiv-2606-30588:
Arpan Sadhukhan, R. B. Sandeep and Sagnik Sen prove a case of Seymour's second neighbourhood conjecture, a long-open problem about directed graphs. In an oriented graph, a vertex's second out-neighbourhood collects vertices reachable in exactly two steps but not one. The conjecture says some vertex always has a second neighbourhood at least as large as its first. Kaneko and Locke settled the conjecture in 2001 for graphs whose minimum out-degree is at most six.

Sadhukhan and his co-authors push that threshold to seven, the first improvement in two decades. Their proof is partly computer-assisted. A sequence of local reductions shrinks the problem to finitely many stubborn configurations. Those remaining cases are then eliminated by reproducible constraint-solver checks showing each one is impossible. The stronger result locates a Seymour vertex inside the closed neighbourhood of any minimum-degree vertex.
arxiv-2606-30688:
Hassan Ugail and Newton Howard derive a law for when noisy quantum neural networks stay trainable. These networks use symmetry-respecting circuits, but noise, called decoherence, can shrink their gradients until training stalls. Which physical quantity decides whether gradients survive was unclear. The pair study charge-conserving brickwork circuits with one conserved quantity, built to respect a U(1) symmetry.
