The authors combined national survey data. Sources covered adults, children, and population income. They modeled counts for each state.

About 3.4 million people had active epilepsy. That equals 1.2 percent of the population. Adults made up three million cases. Children accounted for about 470,000. State counts ranged widely by population size. Wyoming had the fewest at 5,900. California had the most at 427,700. Case numbers rose from 2010 to 2015. The authors link that rise to population growth. Planners can use the estimates for services.
europmc-pmc5695788:
Cremers and co-authors examine low statistical power in brain imaging studies. Their paper focuses on fMRI, which tracks brain activity through blood flow. Such studies test many brain measures in few subjects. Strict checks for false hits then drain power further. Weak studies can fail even when the design is sound.

The authors contrast two cases through simulation. One has weak effects spread across the brain, and the other has strong effects in one spot. Common samples of 20 to 30 subjects had very low power in the weak case. Real data from the Human Connectome Project looked more like that weak case. Fixes include larger samples, focused regions, prediction models, and meta-analysis.
europmc-pmc5724188:
Bruderer and co-authors tune a mass spectrometry method to profile proteins more deeply. Their study uses data-independent acquisition, or DIA, on an Orbitrap instrument. Standard methods pick peptide signals one by one, which limits speed and depth. DIA instead scans set slices of the ion space in parallel.

In single runs, the team found and measured 6,383 proteins in human cell lines. Mouse tissues yielded 7,739 proteins. In very complex mixes, counts passed 10,000 proteins. Missing values stayed low, between 0.3 and 2.1 percent. Variation among repeat runs stayed near five percent. The team then tracked protein networks in mouse brain across a key window for whisker-driven learning.
europmc-pmc5732288:
Fang and co-authors study how blood flow shapes the cells that line vessels. Flow drag, called shear stress, is strong in arteries. The team asked whether this drag also stops cell growth. They worked with cultured vessel cells and young mouse tissue.

They report that arterial level shear switches on Notch signaling at full strength. Notch raises Cx37, which then raises the cell cycle brake p27. Blocking any step brought excess growth and loss of artery traits. Restoring Cx37 or p27 fixed both faults. The chain links growth arrest to gaining an artery identity.
europmc-pmc5733388:
Shim and co-authors explain how to run a network meta-analysis with Stata software. Such an analysis compares three or more treatments for one condition. It mixes direct trial results with indirect ones drawn by logic. The guide works within a frequentist frame, not a Bayesian one.

The authors first set out three checks: similarity, transitivity, and consistency. They then walk through five steps of the work. Steps cover drawing the network, checking consistency, and plotting effect sizes. Ranking treatments and probing bias close the process. Worked examples with real data show each step in use.
europmc-pmc5740388:
Ito and co-authors test a new antibiotic, cefiderocol, against Gram-negative bacteria in the lab. The drug is a cephalosporin fitted with an iron grabbing part. That part lets it ride iron transport routes into the cell. Many target strains resist carbapenems, a last line drug class.

The drug killed a broad range of harmful species, including resistant Pseudomonas and Acinetobacter. It binds mainly to penicillin-binding protein 3, like ceftazidime does. Losing iron transporters raised the dose needed sixteen fold in some strains. Losing porins or adding efflux pumps had little effect, they report.
europmc-pmc5770888:
Xia and co-authors review the S100 protein family and its grip on inflammation. These calcium binding proteins work both inside and outside cells. Inside, they help steer growth, movement, energy use, and cell death. Released after damage or stress, they act as danger signals.

The review sorts the family's many jobs by member and setting. It gives special weight to macrophage inflammation, where S100 proteins can drive or shape the response. Tissue repair and injury recovery also feature. Some family members serve as markers for set diseases. The account links basic cell work to immune balance.
europmc-pmc5808288:
Liu and Nusslock review exercise, new brain cells, and BDNF. Exercise lifts memory, learning, and mood in many studies. One route may be fresh neurons in the hippocampus. That brain area builds new cells across life.

The review links running and activity to that cell birth. A growth factor called BDNF steers the process. It helps new cells mature and survive. Most firm proof comes from rodents, not humans. Human work must rely on indirect clues and gene variants. Readers get an honest map of a hopeful idea, its proof, and its limits.
europmc-pmc5815488:
Ogden and co-authors report youth obesity by family income and schooling. The CDC team used national survey data from 2011 to 2014. Children and teens aged 2 to 19 were weighed and measured. Rates were split by household traits.

Overall youth obesity stood at 17 percent. In the richest homes it was just 10.9 percent, against 19.9 and 18.9 percent in the poorer groups. Where the household head held a degree, obesity was lowest at 9.6 percent in that group. Less schooling marked higher rates, 18.3 percent and 21.6 percent in the lowest groups. The national target was under 14.5 percent for all youth. Readers get clear proof that obesity tracks family resources.
europmc-pmc5817488:
Karimkhani and co-authors measure the global burden of skin disease. The data come from the Global Burden of Disease 2013 study. Burden is counted in disability-adjusted life years, or DALYs. That yardstick lets unlike diseases be compared fairly.

Skin diseases made up 1.79 percent of all global DALYs. Dermatitis led the skin list, then acne and hives. Psoriasis, viral and fungal diseases, and scabies followed. Melanoma and other skin cancers also ranked. The ranking spans disability more than death. Readers get proof that skin disease is a major, often dismissed, source of lost healthy years.
europmc-pmc5889788:
Cipriani and co-authors compare 21 antidepressant drugs for major depression. Their network meta-analysis appeared in The Lancet. The team searched many databases and trial registers. They kept double-blind trials in adults with major depressive disorder. Both placebo and head-to-head trials were included. In all, 522 trials with 116,477 participants qualified. Main outcomes were response rate and treatment dropout.

All antidepressants beat placebo on response, the analysis found. Drugs differed in how well patients tolerated them. The network method let the team rank all 21 agents. Unpublished trials were included to reduce bias. Study quality and evidence certainty were graded formally. The rankings aim to guide first-choice prescribing.
europmc-pmc5904288:
Arce Vargas and co-authors show that Fc effector function helps anti-CTLA-4 antibodies fight cancer. Their article appeared in Cancer Cell. They used mice carrying human Fc-gamma receptors. Antibodies like ipilimumab cleared regulatory T cells inside tumours. That raised the ratio of killer cells to regulator cells. Tumours were then rejected more often.

Stronger Fc binding drove better responses and survival, they report. In melanoma patients, a high-affinity gene variant linked to ipilimumab response. The effect mattered mainly in inflamed tumours. Poorly infiltrated tumours will likely need drug combinations. Readers learn why antibody tail design matters. Patient choice may also use these markers.
europmc-pmc5997788:
Karwi and co-authors review the loss of metabolic flexibility in the failing heart. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Cardiovascular Medicine. A healthy heart burns many fuels to make ATP. Fatty acids, glucose, lactate, ketones, and amino acids all serve. Their mix shifts with supply, hormones, and demand. In heart failure that flexibility fades, the authors explain. The heart leans more on glycolysis and ketone burning. Glucose oxidation drops and insulin resistance grows.

What happens to fatty acid burning is disputed. Some studies show a fall, others show no change. Raising ATP output can still improve heart function. The review covers ways to steer fuel choice.
europmc-pmc6039488:
Griffiths and co-authors measure barcode swapping in single-cell sequencing. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. New sequencing machines can swap sample labels. Reads then get assigned to the wrong sample. The scale and harm of this error were unclear.

The team used two plate-based data sets. About 2.5 percent of reads were mislabeled. That rate was lower than earlier reports suggested. Free barcode levels did not predict the swapped share. In droplet-based studies, swapping can create fake cell libraries. Such artefacts could mislead clustering and marker calls. The authors built an algorithm to remove swapped molecules. It targets data from 10x Genomics experiments. Readers get a way to keep using fast machines safely.
europmc-pmc6052888:
Angajala and co-authors review the many roles of mitochondria in immunity. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Mitochondria do far more than make energy. They help decide how immune cells develop and act. Metabolic shifts can therefore reshape immune responses.

Different fuel pathways mark different immune states. Some macrophages burn sugar in a broken cycle and inflame. Others burn fat and calm inflammation instead. Amino acid handling shapes T-cell fate as well. Mitochondria can also trigger alarm systems directly. Their DNA and reactive signals feed inflammation pathways. Splitting and joining of mitochondria matter too. Links with the cell's protein factory add another layer. Readers get an updated map of immuno-metabolism.
europmc-pmc6063888:
Manca and co-authors test whether milk exosomes survive feeding and spread through the body. Their research article appeared in Scientific Reports. Exosomes are tiny sacs that carry RNA and proteins between cells. Milk supplies them through the diet. Earlier work hinted they cross species lines.

Labeled exosomes from cow, pig, and mouse milk entered mice and pigs. They gathered in liver, spleen, and brain. Tracked microRNA cargos each showed distinct tissue patterns. Some reached the gut lining, heart, or brain. Milk exosomes failed to rescue mice unable to mature their own microRNAs. The authors blame low uptake or missing cargos. Readers get direct evidence on dietary exosome traffic.
europmc-pmc6099188:
Fiorucci and co-authors review how bile acid receptors tune innate immunity. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Bile acids were once seen as mere fat detergents. They also act as signals made with gut microbes. Two receptors, GPBAR1 and FXR, read those signals.

Both receptors sit on gut and liver immune cells. Macrophages, dendritic cells, and natural killer T cells carry them. Their signals keep these tissues in a tolerant state. That calm stops needless attacks on food and microbes. Receptor drugs show benefit in immune and metabolic disorders. Readers get a route from digestion chemistry to immune control.
europmc-pmc6132188:
Pollard and co-authors present a data article in Scientific Data on the eICU Collaborative Research Database. Intensive care units watch patients nonstop and log huge amounts of data. A telehealth system run by Philips collects such data from many hospitals. The team turned those records into a research resource.

The database holds records for more than 200,000 ICU stays across the United States. It includes vital signs, care plans, illness scores, diagnoses, and treatments. Names and direct identifiers were removed. Access is free after registration and a training course. Users must sign a data use agreement. The authors expect uses in machine learning and clinical research.
europmc-pmc6147588:
Liu and co-authors wrote a review in Aging and Disease on mitochondria in ischemic stroke. Stroke is a leading cause of death and adult disability worldwide. Most strokes are ischemic, meaning a blocked vessel starves brain tissue. Failure of mitochondria, the cell's power plants, is a hallmark of the damage that follows.

The review covers how mitochondria behave during blocked blood flow and its return. It focuses on quality control, the systems that repair or remove damaged mitochondria. New findings on mitochondria moving between cells also feature. Keeping these power plants working may help neurons survive. The authors highlight mitochondria as targets for future stroke treatment.
europmc-pmc6220188:
Niemeijer and co-authors used PET scans to measure immune markers in lung cancer. The markers are PD-1 and PD-L1. Standard tissue tests predict drug response only moderately. Small biopsies may miss varied marker levels. The study appeared in Nature Communications. It covered non-small-cell lung cancer patients.

The team gave patients a labelled tracer for PET-CT. Whole-body scans measured marker levels without surgery. Uptake varied greatly between patients. It also varied between tumours in one patient. That spread helps explain odd treatment responses. Some patients respond despite a negative tissue test. The authors say whole-body imaging gives a fuller picture. It may guide checkpoint drug use better than biopsy alone.
europmc-pmc6268288:
Sahigara and co-authors compare ways to set the safe use range of chemical prediction models. Their paper appeared in Molecules. Such models, called QSAR models, predict chemical behaviour from structure. Predictions hold only for chemicals much like the training set. The safe range is called the applicability domain. Rules for model checking require that range to be stated.

Several descriptor based methods can draw that range. Each draws the inner space of the training data in a different way. Cut off choices shift how many new chemicals count as inside. The team ran the methods on published, checked data sets. They compared model scores and where test chemicals fell. Results show that method choice changes the domain a lot. Careful choice matters when model output feeds safety law. The paper helps builders pick and defend a method.
europmc-pmc6269088:
Hosny and co-authors used deep learning on CT scans to forecast lung cancer outcomes. Their study appeared in PLOS Medicine. Patients with the same tumour stage often fare very differently. Scan features beyond size may hold clues to that split. The team gathered seven data sets from five centres. Together they held 1,194 patients with non-small-cell lung cancer.

A three dimensional network read scans of patients treated with radiation. Its forecasts tracked two year survival well. A transfer method then adapted the tool for surgery patients. It again tracked survival and split patients into risk groups. The network beat models built on age, sex, and stage alone. Its scores also held steady across repeat scans and readers. Maps of key scan regions are shown for review. Such tools could sharpen treatment planning.
europmc-pmc6324288:
Xu and co-authors track twenty years of ADHD diagnoses in United States children. Their study appeared in JAMA Network Open. ADHD is a childhood disorder of attention and impulse control. The team used the National Health Interview Survey. It is a yearly, nationwide household survey. Data covered 186,457 children aged 4 to 17.

The share with a diagnosis rose steadily over two decades. It climbed from 6.1 percent in 1997-1998 to 10.2 percent in 2015-2016. The rise held across the survey years studied. About one in ten children thus carried the diagnosis by the end. The authors say the trend matters for schools and clinics. It shapes demand for care, support, and trained staff. The paper gives a long baseline for child mental health planning.
europmc-pmc6345988:
Isobe and co-authors project microplastic levels in the Pacific from 1957 to 2066. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Lab tests show sea life can be harmed by microplastics. Whether test doses match real seas was unclear. The team paired computer models with ocean surveys. Ships sampled along a line from Antarctica to Japan.

The model treats microplastics as removable, not permanent. Removal in surface water takes about three years. Even so, amounts near the subtropical zone keep rising. Weight levels there may double by 2030. By 2060 they could reach four times current values. The North Pacific is a known hotspot for plastic. The forecast gives experiments a realistic dose range to use.
europmc-pmc6348388:
Wilson and co-authors review the super-donor idea in fecal microbiota transplantation. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology. Transplanting donor stool cures most repeat C. difficile infections. For chronic diseases tied to gut imbalance, results vary. Some donors seem to work far better than others. Those are the proposed super-donors.

The review gathers the evidence for their existence. Donor microbe diversity and makeup predict success in studies. Certain keystone species may drive the effect. Host genetics and diet can also sway results. They affect whether donor microbes settle and last. Finding true super-donors could sharpen treatment. It could also reveal how microbes drive chronic disease. The authors call for careful donor profiling in future trials.
europmc-pmc6387488:
Ackerman and co-authors forecast joint replacement demand in Australia, in BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders. They used the national joint registry for hip and knee replacements done for arthritis. Data ran from 2003 to 2013, with forecasts to 2030.

Population growth and aging drive the expected rise, the model shows. The authors also tested how obesity trends would change knee replacement counts. Cost figures came from national hospital data. Their forecast gives health planners a base for staffing and budgets. It warns that demand for these operations will keep climbing steeply. Private and public hospitals both face the surge.
europmc-pmc6400988:
Vilgelm and Richmond review chemokines in cancer, in Frontiers in Immunology. Chemokines are small proteins that guide immune cells to the right places. Inside tumors, they can help or harm the patient.

Some chemokines draw in cells that attack the tumor. Others help the tumor spread or shield it from attack. Their balance shapes whether a tumor looks inflamed and cell-rich. It also affects how well immune therapy works. The review closes with ways to block the harmful signals or boost the helpful ones. Drug trials are already testing some of them.
europmc-pmc6404988:
Spaide and co-authors review OCT angiography in Progress in Retinal and Eye Research. This imaging method shows blood flow in the retina and choroid in fine detail. It builds on OCT, a major advance in eye imaging.

No dye is needed, and the images split flow by tissue depth. That detail far exceeds older dye-based methods. The review traces how the method grew and how its machines work. It also covers faults in the images and the steep learning curve for readers. The method is barely a decade old, they note.
europmc-pmc6412088:
Justice and co-authors report a first-in-human pilot study in EBioMedicine. Senolytics are drugs that clear senescent cells, which drive many age-linked diseases. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is a fatal lung disease tied to such cells.

Fourteen patients took dasatinib plus quercetin in short bursts over three weeks. The main aim was to test if such a trial could run at all. Retention and completion of planned checks were the key measures. Early signs on physical function were also tracked. The authors present the study as a feasibility step, not proof of benefit.
europmc-pmc6412188:
Lee and Jun review silver nanoparticles for medicine in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Particles under one hundred nanometers across can kill germs and carry drugs. Their size and shape can be tuned during making, which changes how they act.

The review covers physical, chemical, and biological routes for making them. It explains the light-based traits that make silver particles useful as probes. Uses range from device coatings to imaging and diagnosis. Safety questions remain, the authors note. They close by weighing promise against the need for careful design.
europmc-pmc6428888:
Elovitz and co-authors study how vaginal microbes and local immune defenses together shape the risk of spontaneous preterm birth. From a cohort of 2,000 pregnant women, they compared 107 women who delivered early with 432 who delivered at term. Preterm birth remains a leading cause of newborn death, and prediction has been poor.

Bayesian modeling tied seven bacterial taxa to higher risk, with stronger effects in African American women. Higher levels of the immune peptide β-defensin-2 lowered that risk, though the pattern varied by group. Low β-defensin-2 raised risk even when protective Lactobacillus species dominated. Early screening and immune or microbiome therapies are the practical hopes raised.
europmc-pmc6478888:
Yoshii and co-authors review how B vitamins, made by plants, yeasts, and bacteria but never by mammals, mediate trade between diet, gut germs, and immunity. Some gut germs cannot make their own B vitamins either, so host and germs trade supplies. The mix of germs then decides how much of each vitamin the immune system truly sees.

Each member of the family has its own immune role: folate and riboflavin products, for instance, bind the MR1 protein and can switch MAIT cells on or hold them back on purpose. Shortage raises infection, allergy, and inflammation risk across the family. The review sorts a scattered field around that shared need for outside supply.
europmc-pmc6482288:
Lambertsen and co-authors ask whether post-stroke inflammation should be treated as a target or borrowed as a tool. Ischemic strokes make up about 90 percent of all strokes. In the hours after one, resident microglia activate and blood immune cells invade the damaged zone, where the response both widens the infarct and later clears it, enabling repair.

Cytokines carry both messages: tumor necrosis factor, interleukin-1, IL-6, and IL-10 each hold protective as well as harmful roles, so blunt neutralization risks collateral damage. Animal and early clinical studies still encourage the attempt. The review argues for next-generation therapies that silence only the destructive signaling while leaving recovery biology alone.
europmc-pmc6486588:
Chen and co-authors build a photodetector that senses circularly polarized light directly, with no filters or wave plates, by growing the detector from a chiral hybrid perovskite. Mantis shrimp do this trick in their retinas; silicon cannot, lacking handedness. Marrying chiral organic molecules to an inorganic lead iodide framework gave the material both polarization sensitivity and strong charge transport.

The device reached a responsivity of 797 milliamps per watt and detectivity of 7.1 × 10^11 Jones, answered at 150 hertz, and ran for a month. Flexible versions on plastic film performed comparably, thanks to solution processing. Direct polarization sensing suits drug screening, surveillance, and quantum optics where bolted-on optics are a burden.
europmc-pmc6550188:
Abràmoff and co-authors report the pivotal trial of an autonomous AI that spots diabetic eye disease in primary care offices, writing in NPJ Digital Medicine. Diabetic retinopathy is the top cause of blindness in working-age adults, yet under half of patients keep up with eye exams. The system reads retinal photos on the spot, with no specialist in the loop.

The trial enrolled 900 adults with diabetes at ten clinics. Trained office staff ran the camera, and results were judged against an expert reading center using photos plus cross-section scans. The AI caught 87.2% of cases beyond mild disease and cleared 90.7% of healthy eyes, beating both preset bars, with usable images in 96.1% of patients. On these results the FDA authorized it — the first autonomous AI diagnostic cleared in any branch of medicine.
europmc-pmc6595688:
Zhang and co-authors review PKM2, a glycolysis enzyme with an outsized role in cancer. Their review appears in Cell and Bioscience. Pyruvate kinase helps cells draw energy from glucose. The M2 form dominates in embryos and in tumors. PKM2 shifts between a four-part tetramer and a two-part dimer. The tetramer drives plain energy production. The dimer enters the nucleus and steers gene activity.

The shift between forms acts as a metabolic switch. It feeds the Warburg effect seen in tumor cells. It also affects invasion, spread, and growth. Chemical tweaks like phosphorylation move PKM2 around the cell. The review maps these controls and locations in detail. That map points to PKM2 as a cancer drug target.
europmc-pmc6696688:
Pang and co-authors review the interplay of ageing, genetics, and environment in Parkinson's disease. Their review appears in Translational Neurodegeneration. The disease kills dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra. Misfolded alpha-synuclein spreads in prion-like fashion. No single factor explains most cases. Ageing is the strongest risk factor alone. Genetic causes account for about five percent. Heritability overall sits near thirty percent. Environmental links remain causally unsettled. Recall bias and reverse causality cloud them.

Converging pathways unite the three domains. Mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired autophagy recur. Oxidative stress and neuroinflammation join them. Animal models should embody all three factors. Therapeutic targets may emerge from shared pathways. Prevention remains the long-term prize.
europmc-pmc6701588:
O'Cathain and co-authors give guidance on developing complex interventions to improve health and health care. Their guidance paper appears in BMJ Open. Intervention development was only briefly sketched before. The team built consensus from many evidence sources. Reviews of published approaches came first. Interviews with developers followed. Two e-Delphi studies and a workshop settled priorities. Development should be a dynamic, back-and-forth process. Stakeholder input runs through that whole process. Published evidence and existing theory both inform design. Programme theory needs stating plainly early on.

Direct data gathering grounds choices in context. Later real-world use deserves early attention. Refinement cycles with stakeholder input close the loop. Each action's relevance varies by context. Developers should revisit them as work proceeds.
europmc-pmc6723188:
Salehi and co-authors review alpha-lipoic acid and its medical uses. This sulfur compound occurs in plants, animals, and people. It works as a strong antioxidant and helps enzymes inside mitochondria. Doctors already use it for nerve pain linked to diabetes. Its benefit is capped by how poorly the body absorbs it.

Only about 30% reaches the blood, and it breaks down fast. The review covers new formulations that raise absorption, including liquid forms and special matrices. One mirror form of the molecule, the R form, performs better than the other. Better delivery could raise the compound's healing effect in several conditions.
europmc-pmc6751188:
Yuan and co-authors assessed inflammation markers across major mental disorders. Inflammation is suspected in many mental illnesses. For a marker to serve as a test, its changes must be repeatable and specific to one disorder. The team gathered 43 pooled reviews covering eight disorders, from schizophrenia and bipolar disorder to depression and autism.

The source set held 704 papers on 44 inflammation-related factors in total. Well-powered studies gave far more consistent results than small ones. After weak studies were removed, 30 of the 44 factors still showed changes. Some markers, such as sIL-2R, were raised steadily in bipolar disorder. The work shows which inflammation claims in this field can be trusted.
europmc-pmc6752088:
Fraze and co-authors measured how often U.S. medical providers screen patients for social needs. Health depends heavily on food, housing, transport, utilities, and safety from violence. The team used survey data from hospitals and physician practices. They asked whether screening covered all five needs at once.

About 24% of hospitals and 16% of practices reported screening for all five. Federally qualified health centers screened more than other practices. So did practices in bundled payment and Medicaid care programs. Academic medical centers screened more than other hospitals. Most providers, the study finds, do not screen for these needs at all. Practices serving poorer patients screened at higher rates.
europmc-pmc6778088:
Ozato and co-authors linked a gut microbe genus, Blautia, to visceral fat in Japanese adults. Visceral fat, packed around the organs, ties strongly to heart disease and death. Most microbe-obesity studies use body mass index, a crude stand-in. This population study of 1,001 adults aged 20 to 76 measured visceral fat directly and analyzed it by sex.

Patterns differed between women and men at the phylum level. One result held for both sexes. Blautia was the only genus significantly tied to visceral fat area, and the tie was inverse: more Blautia, less fat. In women, nine genera tracked with fat levels. The finding marks Blautia as a candidate for obesity research.
europmc-pmc6791888:
Cao and co-authors review immune cell apoptosis in sepsis and what it means for treatment. Sepsis is organ failure driven by a disordered response to infection. Early on, inflammation runs wild. Later, the immune system collapses into a paralyzed state, and patients die of secondary infections weeks afterward. Excess cell death, or apoptosis, is a prime suspect in that collapse.

Postmortem studies confirm sepsis-driven apoptosis in patients of all ages, from newborns to adults. Lymphocytes of both the innate and adaptive arms die off. Their loss raises the risk of new infections and poor outcomes. Neutrophils behave oddly too, dying late at first, then flooding out immature. Strategies that block apoptosis could rescue immune function, the authors argue.
europmc-pmc6800388:
HuBMAP Consortium describe the NIH Human Biomolecular Atlas Program, an effort to map the human body at cellular resolution. New technologies can chart tissues in three dimensions with fine molecular detail. Over seven years, HuBMAP aims to build an accessible framework for single-cell mapping. It will support technology development, data collection, and spatial mapping across organs.

Trillions of cells in many states make up the body, yet their detailed organization in tissues is largely unmapped. HuBMAP will register single-cell profiles onto tissue images. Protein location, cell type markers, and neighborhood states will be layered in. The program coordinates with other agencies and consortia toward one shared atlas. The goal is a reference for health and disease alike.
europmc-pmc6813288:
Korbecki and Bajdak-Rusinek present a review in Inflammation Research on palmitic acid and inflammation. Palmitic acid is a saturated fatty acid. Its blood level is high in people with obesity. The review centres on macrophages. These immune cells make many of the signals that drive swelling and pain.

Inside cells, the acid is changed into other fats such as ceramides. Those products switch on pathways linked to toll-like receptors. The authors cover ER stress, NF-kB, and the NLRP3 inflammasome. They also cover FABP4 and key cytokines. A final part links this response to insulin resistance.
europmc-pmc6883788:
Hashimoto and co-authors report a study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences on the immune cells of supercentenarians. People who pass 110 years tend to stay healthy for most of their lives. Their immune systems likely keep working when others fail. The team profiled thousands of circulating immune cells from such donors, one cell at a time.

They found an unusual expansion of CD4 T cells with killing ability. CD4 cells normally help other immune cells rather than attack targets directly. Receptor analysis showed these cells came from a narrowed set of clones. Nearly 60 percent of control donors' T cells sat in early, naive states, while supercentenarian cells skewed late and battle-worn.
europmc-pmc6898788:
Liu and co-authors model who responds to a melanoma drug, in Nature Medicine. Blocking the PD1 checkpoint frees the immune system against advanced melanoma, but only some patients benefit. Predictors of response remain incomplete. The team gathered a well-documented group of 144 patients treated with anti-PD1 therapy. Their tumours were sequenced before treatment, both the gene-coding regions and the full set of active genes.

Tumour mutation count predicted response less cleanly than hoped, because melanoma subtype clouded it. Features tied to antigen presentation, the MHC-I and MHC-II systems, did better. Prior treatment with anti-CTLA4 therapy changed which features mattered. The authors combine molecular and clinical measures into one predictive model.
europmc-pmc6901688:
Guo and co-authors build a death-risk score for viral pneumonia, in Frontiers in Microbiology. Viral pneumonia kills at widely different rates from patient to patient. Doctors lacked a score tuned to it for judging who is in danger. The team studied 528 patients treated at Ruijin Hospital in Shanghai between May 2015 and May 2019. Viruses were identified with a multiplex genetic test.

Within 90 days, 76 patients, 14.4 percent, had died. Weighing admission features, the authors built the MuLBSTA score. Its strongest item, infection spread across several lung lobes, carries 5 of the points; low lymphocyte counts and bacterial co-infection also score. The tool beat the standard CURB-65 score at predicting death in their data.
europmc-pmc6912988:
Kovaka and co-authors present StringTie2, in Genome Biology. RNA sequencing reads the messages active in a cell. New single-molecule machines return reads thousands of letters long, transforming what can be assembled. Rebuilding full transcripts from those reads is the task of an assembler. Long reads carry high error rates, which older assemblers handle badly.

StringTie2 is a reference-guided assembler built for both read kinds. New methods smooth over long-read errors, and it can also exploit super-reads pre-assembled from short reads. In the authors' tests it proved more accurate than every comparable tool, while running faster and using less memory. Intron-level checks, a strict test of transcript joins, favoured it on all datasets.
europmc-pmc6918388:
Martău and co-authors review three natural polymers for food and biomedical use. Their review appeared in Polymers. The polymers are chitosan, alginate, and pectin. All three are abundant and come from natural sources. Firms use them as stabilizers, thickeners, and capsule agents.

The authors weigh three traits for each polymer. They assess biocompatibility and biodegradability in depth. They also assess bioadhesiveness, the grip on body surfaces. Food packaging and drug coatings get detailed treatment. So do uses in biotechnology and medicine. The review closes with limits in the human gut. Those limits shape where each polymer can work well.
europmc-pmc6944088:
Spek explains how to read and answer checkCIF alerts, the warnings raised when crystal structures are validated. His paper appeared in Acta Crystallographica Section E. Modern instruments and software make collecting X-ray diffraction data fast and routine. Solving a structure is often a black-box step. The real bottleneck is final analysis, validation, and proper reporting.

Less trained authors can miss warning signs that seasoned crystallographers spot at once, such as oddly short contacts between molecules. Pitfalls include pseudo-symmetry, disorder, and twinning. Spek gives background on the validation procedure and details many specific alerts. For each, he sets out options for how to respond. The goal is simple: readers should be able to trust the chemistry a structure claims to show.
europmc-pmc7000688:
Sabatini and Chiocca review human papillomavirus as a cause of head and neck cancers. Their review appeared in the British Journal of Cancer. The virus family holds more than 170 types that infect surface tissues. High-risk types are proven causes of cervical cancer.

A clear role is now emerging in cancers of the throat, above all the oropharynx. Virus-driven tumours differ from tobacco- and alcohol-driven ones in spread patterns, clinical behaviour, and molecular makeup. Head and neck cancers overall exceed 650,000 new cases a year worldwide. The authors detail infection across racial and ethnic groups, and differences between women and men. An outlook on care closes the review, covering diagnostic markers and targeted therapies in development.
europmc-pmc7010688:
Cuomo and co-authors track how genes steer stem cells as they turn into gut-layer cells. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Early human development cannot be watched directly, so stem cells in dishes stand in. How a person's genetic makeup changes the journey was largely unknown.

The team grew induced pluripotent stem cells from 125 donors together in a pooled design, then read gene activity cell by cell as they became endoderm. Some cell lines differentiated well and others poorly, and the study found molecular markers that predict which way a line will go. Differences between donors' genomes let the team map hundreds of genetic variants that raise or lower gene expression. Many acted only at certain stages or in certain cell states, fading in and out as differentiation proceeded. The work shows development is not one fixed script: common genetic variation tunes it person by person.
europmc-pmc7082388:
Bousfiha and co-authors present the 2019 update of the IUIS phenotypical classification of inborn errors of immunity, in the Journal of Clinical Immunology. The International Union of Immunological Societies expert committee maintains this list. It sorts immune defects by the signs and lab results a clinician sees, not by gene alone.

The update covers 430 single-gene errors across ten broad groups. Sixty-five conditions are new in this edition. For each group, the authors give a diagnostic algorithm built from clinical and laboratory features. The defects can show up as infection, cancer, allergy, autoimmunity, or autoinflammation. Readers at the bedside get a user-friendly map from a patient's picture to a likely gene defect, in a field that grows harder to hold in mind each year.
europmc-pmc7091888:
Tai and co-authors characterised the receptor-binding domain of the new coronavirus spike protein, in Cellular and Molecular Immunology. The spike grips the ACE2 receptor to enter human cells, making its binding region a prime target for drugs and vaccines. The team made the binding-domain protein and tested how it behaves.

The SARS-CoV-2 binding domain attached to human and bat ACE2 more strongly than the older SARS virus version did. Added as a free protein, it blocked both viruses from latching onto cells. Antibodies raised against the SARS binding domain also reacted with the new one and could neutralise the new virus. The results support vaccines built on this protein piece.
europmc-pmc7113588:
Chen, Kroemer, and Kepp review mitophagy, the process that removes worn-out mitochondria, and its role in ageing, in Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology. Faulty mitochondria are a hallmark of ageing: they make less energy, leak reactive oxygen, and gather DNA mutations. Mitophagy clears damaged units and restores balance under stress.

The process appears weakened in many human diseases, including brain degeneration, heart and vessel disease, and cancer, as well as in ageing itself. The authors sum up the mechanisms that control mitophagy and where it fails. Treatments that switch mitophagy back on might ease these dysfunctions, they argue, making the pathway a target worth pursuing.
europmc-pmc7164388:
Maier and Brockmann explain why China's confirmed COVID-19 cases grew more slowly than a simple epidemic curve predicts, in Science. Cases rose from about 330 on 21 January 2020 to more than 17,000 by 2 February, yet the growth bent below exponential. Such bending can mean susceptibles are running out, but here something else was at work.

Their model attributes the slowdown to containment and the public response taking effect, even while headline case counts kept rising. By 28 March, Hubei's total had saturated at 67,800 cases with no new daily cases. The study is an early quantitative verdict that aggressive measures were working in China, offered while other governments chose their own strategies.
europmc-pmc7175788:
Abd-Alrazaq and co-authors study what Twitter users posted about COVID-19 in early 2020. Their study appeared in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. The team pulled English tweets with set search terms. The window ran from February 2 to March 15. About 2.8 million tweets were gathered at first. After screening, 167,073 unique tweets from 160,829 users remained.

Topic modeling sorted the tweets into 12 topics. These grouped into four broad themes. They covered the virus origin and its sources. They also covered impact on people, nations, and the economy. A fourth theme covered ways to cut infection risk. Sentiment was positive for most topics. Deaths and rising racism drew negative sentiment. The authors urge health agencies to watch social media in crises. They also call for a faster public health voice online against fake news.
europmc-pmc7195988:
Güner and co-authors lay out community prevention measures against COVID-19. Their article appeared in the Turkish Journal of Medical Sciences. The World Health Organization declared the outbreak an international emergency on January 30, 2020. By March it called the crisis a pandemic. No approved drug had yet been shown to work against the virus.

Prevention, the authors argue, is society's strongest weapon. Hand hygiene, social distancing, and quarantine form the core. Closing schools and offices and cancelling gatherings cut contact further. Crowded markets need entry limits or online alternatives. The article also covers protecting workplaces where distance is hard. Readers get a practical checklist for slowing spread while treatments were still missing.
europmc-pmc7258488:
Du and co-authors estimate the serial interval for COVID-19 from public case reports in China. Their short study appeared in Emerging Infectious Diseases. The serial interval is the time between symptom onset in a person who spreads the virus and onset in the person they infect. That gap is a key input for models of how fast an outbreak grows.

The team used 468 transmission events reported outside Hubei by February 8, 2020. They found a mean interval of 3.96 days. In 12.6 percent of pairs, the second person showed symptoms first. That pattern suggests spread before symptoms. Their estimate was far shorter than those for SARS and MERS.
europmc-pmc7280488:
Uribe-Querol and Rosales give an overview of phagocytosis, the way cells eat and kill particles. Their review covers cells that take in microbes, stray matter, and dead cells. The targets are larger than 0.5 micrometers. Almost all cells can do this, but a few types do it far better than the rest.

Those expert cells are macrophages, neutrophils, monocytes, dendritic cells, and osteoclasts. Their surfaces hold sensors that spot a target and start the eating process. The work runs in set steps: find the particle, take it in, form a pocket called a phagosome, and ripen that pocket into a phagolysosome that digests the load. The review lays out the cells, the sensors, and each step in turn.
europmc-pmc7283388:
Dexheimer and Cochella review microRNAs, short RNA molecules that turn genes down after their messages are made. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology. RNA silencing is older than multicellular life, and the microRNA toolkit expanded as plants and animals grew more complex. No higher animal lineage has managed to lose it.

Destroying the microRNA machinery causes severe embryo defects in every animal tested. The authors explain how cells control when and where microRNAs are produced, and how different silencing complexes produce different effects on their targets. Animal groups use that variety in specific cell types and compartments. The review ends with how microRNA families evolved and diversified, and what those sequence changes mean for development.
europmc-pmc7306788:
Zandalinas and co-authors show that plants handle combined stresses, such as heat with drought, through whole-plant signaling that differs from single-stress responses. Their study appeared in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Individual stresses are well studied, but real fields deliver combinations, and knowledge of how plants acclimate to them was thin.

Plants can integrate local and body-wide signals generated when two stresses strike at once. Which part of the plant senses each stress changes how fast and how well the whole plant acclimates. Signals travel systemically so distant tissues can prepare, a process tied to reactive oxygen species. The results matter for agriculture, where stress combinations can devastate yields, and for breeding crops that survive the mixtures a changing climate brings.
europmc-pmc7357988:
Hogan and co-authors present a modelling study in The Lancet Global Health. It asks what COVID-19 disruption could do to three other diseases. Those diseases are HIV, tuberculosis, and malaria. The setting is low-income and middle-income countries with high burdens.

The team ran four pandemic response scenarios through disease models they had already built. They estimate deaths over five years could rise by up to 10 percent for HIV. Tuberculosis deaths could rise by up to 20 percent, and malaria by up to 36 percent. Missed HIV treatment, late tuberculosis care, and halted net campaigns drove the harm. Keeping key services running would cut most of it, they argue. Readers get a warning that the pandemic's death toll runs beyond the virus itself.
europmc-pmc7518588:
Woodhouse and co-authors validate FoundationOne Liquid CDx, a blood-based genomic profiling test for solid tumors. The assay reads cell-free DNA shed into the blood. It promises a match to tissue testing as precision therapies expand.

Validation covered more than 7,500 tests and 30,000 unique variants. The panel spans 324 genes across more than 30 cancer types in the studies. The false positive variant rate was about 1 in 8,000 in the validation runs. Variant calling matched an orthogonal method closely overall. The test also gauges complex markers such as microsatellite instability and blood tumor mutational burden. The authors present clinical validity across multiple tumor types. They back the assay as a complement to tissue testing in the clinic.
europmc-pmc7539288:
Xie and co-authors review NAD+ metabolism and its role in health and disease. NAD+ helps cells handle energy and stress. Its levels shift with food, damage and infection.

The review explains how NAD+ drives redox reactions in cells. It also serves enzymes that modify DNA, RNA and proteins. Other enzymes use it to make messenger molecules. Long imbalance in NAD+ can disturb cell function. That imbalance links to metabolic disease and cancer. It also links to aging and brain disorders. The authors outline new treatment ideas from this work. Readers get a broad map of a central cell system.
europmc-pmc7666188:
Zietz and co-authors test whether blood type tracks with COVID-19 risk. They used health records from the New York Presbyterian hospital system. The set held 14,112 people tested for SARS-CoV-2 whose blood type was known. Outcomes were infection, intubation, and death.

Infection was a bit more common in non-O blood types than in type O. Risk of intubation fell for type A and rose for types AB and B. Death risk rose for type AB and fell for types A and B. Rh-negative type looked protective across all three outcomes. The authors add this to growing signs that blood type plays a role.
europmc-pmc7745388:
Smith and Pollak review how early life stress shapes child development. Harsh or chronic stress in childhood links to wide harms later. Yet children exposed to like events fare unlike ways. The mechanisms that carry risk from event to outcome are still unclear.

The authors trace effects on brain circuits that link the prefrontal cortex, amygdala, and stress hormone axis. Dopamine systems also shift after early stress. These changes flow in part through the stress hormone system. Most past work logged only which events a child faced. The authors urge measures of how the child reads those events, to explain why paths diverge.
europmc-pmc7763888:
Montalto and De Amicis review cyclin D1, a cell cycle driver with many roles in cancer. In normal cells, cyclin D1 levels are tightly held. In cancer, its activity surges in many ways. Its gene is amplified in several tumor types, a sign of poor outlook. The protein pushes cells from rest into DNA copying.

New work places cyclin D1 at the cell membrane, where it aids invasion and spread. It also governs select small RNAs. It shapes how tumor and support tissue interact, feeding most cancer hallmarks. The authors focus on breast cancer as the clearest case. They frame the protein as a bridge between growth control and invasion.
europmc-pmc7784288:
Zhang and Nie present scMC, a method for merging single-cell genomics datasets from different experiments. Merged data mix real biological differences with technical noise. Older methods often strip out both kinds of variation. Real signals can be lost that way.

scMC uses variance analysis to learn the biological variation. It then infers the technical part without supervision and subtracts it. Context-shared signals stay in place. Context-specific signals stay too. The authors tested scMC on simulated data. They also used real single-cell RNA-seq and ATAC-seq datasets. Results showed accurate alignment across datasets. The tool kept true biological signals that other methods tended to remove.
europmc-pmc7788688:
Arroyo-Hernández and co-authors review radiation-induced lung injury. Radiation and drug therapy work well for chest cancers. Lung damage is the dangerous side effect. Inflammation of the lung, called pneumonitis, can be life-threatening.

The injury unfolds in two phases. Early radiation pneumonitis is acute lung inflammation. Late radiation fibrosis is lasting tissue damage. Damage comes from direct cell killing, oxidative stress, and immune attack. Diagnosis rests on ruling out other causes with scans and clinical checks. Lung function tests help predict risk during treatment. Steroid drugs are the standard treatment for pneumonitis. The authors give practical advice on prevention, diagnosis, and care.
europmc-pmc7822488:
Uruén and co-authors review how biofilms help bacteria survive antibiotics. Drug-resistant bacteria threaten human and animal health. Biofilms are a second survival strategy. Bacteria in a biofilm sit inside a self-made matrix. That shelter changes how drugs reach them.

The biofilm blocks drug entry, so killing levels may never build up inside. Nutrient and oxygen levels fall off with depth. Cells in deep layers slow down and tolerate drugs. Some slip into a dormant, persistent state. Defense pumps switch on in spots, and mutation rates rise. Loose DNA and close contact speed gene sharing between cells. The authors argue that grasping these tricks is key to new infection treatments.
europmc-pmc7933288:
Huang and co-authors present a review of natural products in cancer therapy, past, present, and future. Natural products have rich chemical variety. They have been mined for anticancer power for more than half a century. That work brought several natural drugs into clinical use and opened new lines of attack. Yet hard problems remain in turning finds into treatments.

Cancer therapy itself has changed fast, and new tools have reshaped the search. The authors argue the field stands at a crossroads. Old strategies for finding and testing natural compounds need a fresh look. They call for systematic methods across the whole pipeline. New pharmacological models should judge candidates more like real tumours. Fresh directions opened by modern technology deserve a fair trial. The review aims to revive a rich source of cancer drugs.
europmc-pmc7938888:
Casarotto and co-authors report a research study on how antidepressant drugs work at the molecular level. How these drugs turn binding into mood recovery has long been unclear. The brain receptor TRKB is central to the story. It receives a growth factor that supports flexible connections between neurons. The team found the receptor also senses cholesterol in the cell membrane.

Both classic and fast-acting antidepressants bind directly to TRKB, they report. The binding helps the receptor move to synapses and answer its growth signal. Computer simulations mapped the binding site in fine detail. A mutation that broke the site also broke the drugs' effects in cells and animals. The authors propose this shared binding as the common root of antidepressant action. It may explain why standard drugs act so slowly.
europmc-pmc7961088:
Pang and co-authors present a review of the links between plant chemicals and plant microbiomes. Plants make secondary metabolites for defence against pests and germs. They also help the plant cope with stress and deal with neighbours. The microbes that live on and in a plant shape many of the same tasks. The two systems turn out to talk to each other, and the review maps that talk.

Plants can steer their microbiome by leaking chosen chemicals from their roots. In return, the microbes can shift the plant's own chemistry. The review sets out the patterns seen so far and the routes that may drive them. New lab methods for reading both sides at once get full cover. Most work rests on model plants so far. The authors argue the lessons can guide farm crops toward hardier, lower-input growth.
europmc-pmc8078488:
Wang and co-authors report a phase II trial of toripalimab in hard-to-treat nasopharyngeal cancer. No checkpoint inhibitor had been approved for this cancer. The patients' tumors had returned or spread despite standard chemotherapy. All 190 patients received the PD-1 blocker every two weeks. Response rate was the main measure of success.

The objective response rate reached 20.5% across the full cohort, with responses lasting a median of 12.8 months before fading. Median overall survival came to 17.4 months in this heavily treated group. Patients whose plasma EBV DNA fell by half or more by day 28 responded at 48.3%, a rate far above the 5.7% seen in those without such a drop. Tumor mutational burden did not predict response. Two genomic marks did point to poor response. Safety stayed manageable throughout the trial.
europmc-pmc8128288:
Davies and co-authors estimate how fast the UK coronavirus variant spread and what it would do. The variant, flagged as VOC 202012/01, rose during England's November lockdown. It carried 17 mutations, eight of them in the spike protein. Several changes plausibly sharpened binding to human cells. The team attacked the growth data with several models. Statistical and dynamic approaches were run in parallel.

All routes converged on a faster-spreading virus. The variant proved 43 to 90% more transmissible than earlier lineages in their estimates. No clear sign emerged that it made people sicker. Faster spread alone means more cases and more admissions. By late March it made up roughly 95% of new infections in England. The authors warn of large resurgences when controls ease. Vaccine rollout speed becomes the deciding variable. A fitter variant rewrites the whole control problem.
europmc-pmc8185188:
Meng and co-authors trace a recurring deletion in the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein. The deletion, called ΔH69/V70, arose in many lineages on its own. It often followed changes that help the virus bind ACE2 or escape antibodies.

Lab tests showed the deletion alone does not dodge antibodies. It does raise infectivity by packing more cleaved spike into virus particles. It can partly rescue escape mutants that had lost infectivity. In the Alpha variant, removing the deletion weakened the spike. The study explains why this deletion kept coming back. Tracking such repeats helps read how the virus evolves.
europmc-pmc8236488:
Zhu and co-authors survey how inflammation, epigenetics, and metabolism converge in cell senescence and ageing. Ageing research has moved fast in recent decades. Decline in body function often starts with senescent cells and ageing organs.

Epigenetic change and immune-metabolic rewiring reshape how cells answer signals. Those shifts also steer cell fate choices. The review gathers current findings on each control layer. It shows how the layers feed one another. Interventions that target senescent cells get a full hearing. So do drugs aimed at the control systems themselves. The review closes with gaps that still block firm therapies.
europmc-pmc8473088:
Uddin and Roni tackle the storage problems of mRNA-based COVID-19 vaccines. The Moderna and BioNTech/Pfizer shots proved the most effective early options. Their mRNA design allowed fast development. But both demand ultra-cold storage to stay potent.

Most poor countries lack the cold chains that mass vaccination needs. That gap limits fair access to these vaccines. The review gathers current research on making the delivery system tougher. Ideas aim to keep vaccines stable at higher temperatures. Success could change the fight against this pandemic and future waves. The authors sort the strategies and judge where each stands.
europmc-pmc8499488:
Peters and co-authors update the methods and uses of scoping reviews. These reviews map a field rather than test one tight question. Their use grows fast, and guidance for them grows too. The JBI method and the PRISMA scoping extension lead that guidance.

Some papers still call themselves scoping reviews without using the tools. The authors explain how scoping reviews differ from other review types. They set out when this design is the right choice. News on current method work and future steps is included. Clear terms and shared methods are the push. The piece serves as a short, firm source for review teams.
europmc-pmc9046088:
Ternes and co-authors show that formate, a metabolite from a gut bacterium, speeds colorectal cancer growth. The bacterium Fusobacterium nucleatum is tied to this cancer, but the chemical crosstalk was unclear. In lab cultures, the bacterium raised formate output and shifted cancer cell metabolism. Formate then triggered a signaling pathway that made tumors more invasive and more stem-like.

In mice, the bacterium or formate alone raised tumor numbers or size. Immune changes followed, with more inflammation-friendly T cells. The authors name formate a gut-derived oncometabolite: a small molecule from microbes that helps cancer progress.
europmc-pmc9098388:
Billingham and co-authors test what the NLRP3 inflammasome needs from mitochondria to switch on. This protein complex drives inflammation and is linked to many chronic diseases. Past work tied it to reactive oxygen species from mitochondria, but results clashed. The team used drug blockers and gene tools to settle the point.

Blockers of four parts of the mitochondrial electron transport chain all stopped activation. Substitute enzymes that restore energy flow without making reactive oxygen also restored activation. The key shared factor was phosphocreatine, which keeps ATP levels up. When it fell, ATP fell and activation failed. The authors conclude the chain supports activation through energy supply, not through reactive oxygen.
europmc-pmc9118588:
Tie and co-authors survey cells that suppress the immune system inside tumors. Such cells help cancers escape attack and resist modern immune therapies. They include myeloid-derived suppressor cells, certain macrophages and neutrophils, and regulatory T cells. Signals from the tumor and from these cells add to the block.

The survey gives the traits and jobs of each cell type in turn. It then sets out drug targets tied to those cells and signals. Some tactics worked in lab studies but disappointed in patients. The authors weigh those mixed results with care. Readers get a map of a key barrier to cancer immunotherapy and the main routes now tried to break it.
europmc-pmc9204188:
Germain and co-authors present scDblFinder, a method to spot doublets in single-cell sequencing data. Doublets form when two cells land in one droplet and get read as one. They can create fake cell types and false findings. About 10-20% of droplets in a typical run may be doublets.

The method builds on the strengths of earlier approaches and runs inside the Bioconductor framework. It proved fast, flexible, and accurate on RNA and ATAC data alike. Even in complex data sets it caught most doublets formed from unlike cells. An independent benchmark already ranked it above rival tools. The authors add notes on how doublets form and how they affect enrichment analysis.
europmc-pmc9244088:
Tangye and co-authors update the classification of human inborn errors of immunity for an international expert committee. These disorders stem from damaging variants in single genes. They can cause infection risk, autoimmunity, allergy, marrow failure, or cancer. Each is rare, but together they form a large burden.

The update documents 55 novel monogenic gene defects found since the prior update. One phenocopy caused by autoantibodies is also included. The total count of inborn errors of immunity now reaches 485. Only defects the committee judged to meet its threshold were added. The report serves immunologists and geneticists who diagnose these disorders. It also aids study of the mechanisms behind immune disease.
europmc-pmc9252788:
Holm reports upgrades to the Dali server for protein structure comparison and family unification. Structure comparison reveals deep evolutionary links that sequence alone can miss. Deep learning has now supplied accurate models for many families once unknown. Dali is widely used to relate new structures to known ones.

Two upgrades stand out in this update. The foldomes of key organisms in the AlphaFold Database are now searchable. Structural alignments also carry protein family annotations. With those tools, the author found a new diverse subgroup in the WRKY/GCM1 clan. It links several named families to a known member structure. The server is free, open to all, and needs no login.
europmc-pmc9308588:
Kari and co-authors compare methods for detecting programmed cell death. Cells can die by set programs such as apoptosis, necroptosis, and pyroptosis. Each leaves its own shape changes and marker molecules. Telling the programs apart is hard, yet it matters for cancer drug work.

The review sorts detection methods by the hallmarks and markers they read. Microscopy and blood-based tests are both covered. For each method, the team weighs the principle, uses, strengths, and limits. A side-by-side comparison aims to name the most reliable options. The authors close with ways detection could improve. Better staging of cell death, they argue, would sharpen both research and treatment design. Apoptosis, first named in 1972, remains the best-studied program.
europmc-pmc9373888:
Kauhanen and co-authors review whether youth mental health changed from before to during the COVID-19 pandemic. They kept only studies that measured the same groups over time or repeatedly. Four databases were searched for work on ages 0 to 24. The final set held 21 studies from 11 countries.

Together the studies covered more than 96,000 children and young people aged 3 to 24. Most found worse mental health in adolescents and young adults after the pandemic began. Depression, anxiety, and distress rose; loneliness grew and well-being fell. Social isolation, school closures, and family stress sit among the suspected drivers. The authors call for urgent, high-quality studies of risks and protective factors. Such work would ready services for future crises.
europmc-pmc9636688:
Liu and Panagiotakos give a brief review of real-world data, its methods, uses, and open problems. Digital tools now flood medicine with fresh data streams. Wearables, e-health services, and social media all add to the flow. Such data reach past the walls of classic trials and lab work.

The review sorts data types and sources first. Health records, claims, and registries are the classic wells. It then covers the models teams use on such data. Machine learning and causal inference tools lead that list. Real-world data can back proof for new trials, the authors note. It can also answer questions trials never reach. Scale and mess are the twin problems of the field. New methods must grow while rigor and ethics hold firm. The piece serves as a primer with source trails.
europmc-pmc9812788:
Moiseeva and co-authors map senescent cells in injured muscle and show they blunt its regeneration. Repair needs stem cells and niche neighbors in close talk. Senescent cells turn out to sit inside that repair niche. Their scarcity had kept them hard to study before.

The team paired single-cell reading with a sorting trick. That let them isolate senescent cells from young and old mice. Damaged muscle gained these cells early after injury. Two marks defined them across types and ages alike. Inflammation and fibrosis signals ran through all of them. The cells built an aged-like, inflamed pocket in the niche. That pocket froze stem cell growth and repair. Clearing senescent cells sped regeneration in the mice. Blocking their output through CD36 also sped repair. Adding senescent cells by transplant slowed repair instead.
french-chemists-essai-phlogistique-1788:
In 1788 the lead chemists of France took Kirwan's defense of phlogiston and turned it into French, with notes that hit back at each claim. The team held Guyton de Morveau, Lavoisier, Laplace, Monge, Berthollet, and Fourcroy. It was a joint strike by the new school in one book.

Page by page, their notes show where Kirwan's scheme fails the test of weight and trial. Kirwan read the notes, gave up his old scheme, and joined the new camp in time. French in tongue, the book is the death writ of the old chemistry.
frus-1861-d188:
On 29 April 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Mr. King as part of his first great round of orders. The letter is document 188 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The record heading gives King no post, so the letter stands on its date and its writer. April 1861 was the month Seward stocked the whole service with fresh orders. His note to King joins the first great round of direction that followed the fall of Sumter. April rounds like this one show the service being manned for war at full speed. Full speed in April set a pace the service kept through the whole year.
frus-1861-d288:
Mr. Morgan reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in a dispatch dated 6 April 1861. The printed record keeps it as Document 288 in the President's message volume for 1861. It was written in the month the Civil War began, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d88:
Charles Francis Adams sent a second dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 28 September 1861. It is document 88 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Two reports in one day suggest a post dealing with more than one live point. Adams kept his files as clean as Seward kept his. The second letter rounds out a dense month in the fullest correspondence of the 1861 record. The double report closes a month in which the London file grew by a third. A third more paper in one month shows the post at full wartime stretch.
frus-1862-d188:
The fourth Seward letter of 10 November 1862 closes the set as Document 188 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Like the other three, it went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London.

A four-letter mail shows how much business one legation could carry: talks with ministers, shipyard reports, press reaction, and cases of detained ships or men. No one letter tells that whole story. Preserved together, the set lets readers see the London post's full load in a single week of November 1862. Adams held the London post from 1861 to 1868, the longest run of any Union envoy in Europe.
frus-1862-d288:
Two Seward dispatches to Paris are dated 20 June 1862, and the first is Document 288 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Both went to William L. Dayton, the American minister to France.

Seward wrote a week before Lee's counterstroke drove McClellan from Richmond, at the last moment of the spring's optimism. His instructions in this pair carried the Department's line into a summer that would test it hard. Reading them now, with the sequel known, shows how much wartime policy was written in honest uncertainty. Dayton's French was limited, and he leaned on his staff and on careful written notes.
frus-1862-d388:
In Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Simon Cameron in St. Petersburg on 13 August 1862, in a dispatch printed as Document 388 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Mid-August 1862 brought the opening of the campaign that ended at Bull Run, though no one could know its result when Seward wrote. His letters to Russia that summer carried the Union's case to its friendliest hearing in Europe. This dispatch shows the Department cultivating that friendship deliberately, even while its attention was consumed by Britain and France. St. Petersburg's friendship later sent Russian fleets to American ports in 1863, to great cheers.
frus-1862-d488:
On 15 March 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands. The instruction is Document 488 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Mid-March found Union forces advancing on several fronts, and Seward's letters abroad pressed the theme that the rebellion was losing ground. At The Hague the practical questions were maritime: Dutch ports, Dutch colonies, and the rules belligerent ships must obey. Pike's value to Washington lay in his blunt, newsman's grasp of Dutch opinion. An instruction like this one set the points he was to make. It even set the order he was to make them in. He would use them at his next meeting with Dutch officials.
frus-1862-d588:
On 28 May 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Thomas Corwin, the American minister in Mexico. The instruction is Document 588 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

By late May the French were advancing into Mexico's interior and the question for Washington was how far protest could safely go. Seward's orders to Corwin kept the American position clear. The United States wished Mexico well. It opposed the European enterprise. It would not be drawn into a second war. Corwin's own instincts ran hotter, which made exact instructions necessary. The dispatch shows the leash and the trust between a secretary and a distinguished minister in the hemisphere's hardest post.
frus-1862-d688: A Mr. De Long dated this dispatch 27 February 1862 and sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It is document 688 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, one week after his letter printed just before it. The record gives his name and date but not his post or its place.
frus-1862-d88:
Secretary of State William H. Seward sent a dispatch to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 27 June 1862. The printed record keeps it as Document 88 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1863p1-d188: Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Charles Francis Adams, his minister in London, on 7 May 1863. It is document 188 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, within the orders that steered American policy toward Britain during the Civil War. Through such letters Washington told its man in London what to press, protest, or let pass.
frus-1863p1-d288:
The Secretary of State, William H. Seward, wrote to his minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, on 9 September 1863. The letter is document 288 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Orders crossed the Atlantic by steamship and took ten days or more to arrive. By the time Adams acted, events in London could already have moved on. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d388:
Washington's business with Britain on 10 February 1863 included this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. The paper is document 388 of the 1863 volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Lyons reported everything to London, so Seward wrote knowing his words would be read there too. Each note spoke to two audiences at once. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d488:
In the flow of wartime mail, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons on 2 May 1863. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d588:
Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington addressed a formal note to Secretary William H. Seward on 16 July 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d688:
Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this note to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington, on 11 November 1863. It appears as document 688 in Foreign Relations of the United States for 1863, the State Department's printed record of its wartime mail.

The day after his 10 November notes, Seward wrote again, which shows how fast matters could move. Union and British officials clashed at times over seized ships and Southern agents in British ports. Short notes like this one kept those clashes from growing. The reader gets a close look at the craft of calm words. Each line was meant to hold a line without giving offense.
frus-1863p1-d88:
Charles Francis Adams closed his mail day with this third dispatch of 19 February 1863 to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 88 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Three sheets in a day was no rare thing at the London post in 1863. The work spanned talks with Lord Russell, the temper of Parliament, and word on ships built for the South. This letter ends the day's set. Filed with the rest, it is part of the great run that makes this volume the chief printed source. That source tells the Union's fight to keep Britain neutral.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d188:
President Roosevelt wrote to Prime Minister Churchill on 4 November 1943 in telegram number 407, a short secret message sent from Washington. It settles the American position on Turkey just after the Moscow foreign ministers' conference, where the Soviet Union had pushed hard for Turkey to join the war.

Roosevelt agrees that the United States will join Britain and the Soviet Union in demanding Turkish air bases at once. He also agrees to press Turkey to enter the war before the end of the year. One condition is attached: no British or American forces needed for Overlord, the planned invasion of France, or for the fighting in Italy may be diverted to the eastern Mediterranean.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d288:
A United States delegation memorandum at Cairo on 23 November 1943 answers reports that Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek feared the Soviet Union meant to back the Chinese Communists against his regime. Preserved in the Hopkins Papers, the paper was probably written by Harry Hopkins, with a final sentence added by Ambassador Harriman.

Its reading of Moscow is reassuring. The Soviet government, it says, wants peace inside China under a strong central government. It knows that can come only through the Generalissimo. It holds no ambitions for Chinese territory in general, as its pullout from Sinkiang shows. It will press Chiang toward a more liberal policy, and toward some settlement with the Communists, as a party or inside his government. Korea might win independence under a four-power trusteeship.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d388:
President Roosevelt handed Marshal Stalin a secret paper at Tehran on 29 November 1943 on advance planning for air operations in the northwestern Pacific. Like its companion papers of that day, it looks past Germany's defeat to the war against Japan.

Bombing Japan from the Soviet Maritime Provinces, Roosevelt argues, would be of the utmost importance, Roosevelt argues. That importance would come once war between the Soviet Union and Japan began. Allied bombers could then destroy Japanese military and industrial centers.
