Born at Raab, Hungary, in 1849, he took his medical degree at the University of Vienna in 1874. A year later he was teaching anatomy at Utrecht as a privat-docent.

Vienna called him back as assistant professor in 1879, and Graz made him professor in 1882. From 1888 he held the Vienna chair of descriptive and topographical anatomy. His many journal studies cover the skull, glands, and the sense of smell. His largest book treats the normal and diseased anatomy of the nasal cavity and its air spaces.
judge-epitome-of-theosophy-1888:
William Q. Judge boiled his creed down to its bones in An Epitome of Theosophy, a brief tract of 1888. The word means a short sum of the whole. In a few pages he states what the creed holds on God, man, death, and the fate of the soul.

The tract is like a short creed card for the faith. New fans could learn it by heart. Groups gave it out at doors and talks. Judge had a gift for plain, brief speech. This tract is that gift at its most lean. Brief as it is, the tract packs in karma, planes, and Masters. A keen fan could grasp the whole creed's frame from these few pages.
kalevala-vol1-crawford-1888:
Elias Lonnrot, a Finnish doctor, built the Kalevala from the songs of the folk of Finland and Karelia. John Martin Crawford turned it into English in 1888, the first full English form of the epic. This book is the first part of his work; the second part stands in the library too.

The songs tell of Vainamoinen, the old singer sage, and of the forging of the Sampo, a mill of wealth. Charms, births of iron and fire, and quests fill the lines in the old runo metre. The epic gave Finland its voice as a nation, and Crawford gave it to English ears.
kingsford-dreams-and-dream-stories-1888:
Anna Kingsford kept a log of her dreams, and Dreams and Dream-Stories prints it in 1888. Her friend Edward Maitland set the notes in form past her death. In sleep she met guides, saw signs, and got creeds in tale form. She held these dreams bore true light.

Some dreams read as brief fables. Some gloss her war on cruel tests on beasts, a cause she led. The log is the chief source for her signs and lore. It shows how her creed grew from night sight, not books. Some dreams warn, some teach, and some read as pure signs. Maitland adds brief notes where a dream needs a key to grasp.
kipling-plain-tales-1888:
Rudyard Kipling was a teenage newspaper reporter in India when he wrote these stories. Plain Tales from the Hills, published in 1888, was his first book for a wide audience. He wrote it at Simla, the summer capital where British officials escaped the heat.

The forty short tales show Anglo-Indian society in miniature: flirtations, feuds, pranks, and sudden tragedies. Young officers and clever widows scheme through the season while disease and distance shadow everything. Kipling's style is quick, dry, and knowing far beyond his years. The book announced a major storyteller and remains a sharp picture of the British Raj at play.
knigge-philos-endliche-erklaerung-1788:
Adolph von Knigge gave the Illuminati its shape as a working order, recruiting members and building its grades. By 1788 his partnership with founder Adam Weishaupt had collapsed in anger and mistrust. Philo's endliche Erklärung und Antwort, printed at Hannover that year, is his final public word on the break.

Writing under his order name Philo, Knigge answers the charges and questions put to him about his role. He complains that private letters and small slips were dragged into print to ruin men in public. He gives his side of the quarrel and explains why he left. Students of the order read the pamphlet as the key record of its inner split.
lea-inquisition-middle-ages-vol-3-1888:
Henry Charles Lea closed his History of the Inquisition of the Middle Ages with this third volume in 1888. It turns from the map of the tribunal to special subjects that cross all lands. Lea's calm, record-based method made the set the standard work in English.

The Knights Templar and their fall, the trial of Joan of Arc, and the crimes of Gilles de Rais fill the great case studies. Lea then anatomizes the Inquisition itself: its books, its prisons, its money, and its men. He ends with the intellectual price the system charged the church. The three volumes together remain the base on which all later study builds.
lempriere-classical-dictionary-1788:
John Lemprière published his Bibliotheca Classica in 1788, a dictionary of the Greek and Roman world. Lemprière was a schoolmaster and clergyman who wanted classical learning within reach of readers without Latin and Greek. The book is better known by its short name, Lemprière's Classical Dictionary.

Thousands of entries explain gods, heroes, places, and stories from ancient myth and history. The dictionary gave poets a ready store of classical material: Keats, Byron, and Shelley all drew on it for their verse. For about a century it was the English reader's standard gateway to antiquity. Later classical dictionaries replaced it in schools, but its entries still show what educated readers of the Romantic age knew and loved.
library-of-the-world-s-best-literature-a:
Volume Two of Warner's anthology appeared in 1896, dated on its own title page. Charles Dudley Warner served as editor, with Mabie, Runkle, and George Henry Warner as associates. Professors from leading American universities formed the advisory council behind the selections. The series promised the world's best literature, ancient and modern, between its covers.

Like its companion volumes, this one collects excerpts and whole pieces across many centuries. The range runs from early classics toward the literature of Warner's own century. Short introductions and careful editing helped general readers approach famous names. The volume preserves a snapshot of the shared reading culture of its time. Harvard's Crawford Toy, a professor of Hebrew, headed the council list. Princeton's William Sloane represented history and political science there.
life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld-advo:
Chapter Four opens Motley's third volume on Barneveld and his times. An insurrection at Utrecht had just been subdued by the States' army. Dutch embassies hurried to England and France seeking support. Henry IV prepared for war and longed for Barneveld's presence in Paris.

Then came the king's murder, which transformed French politics overnight. Sully fell, and Spanish influence triumphed at the French court. Negotiations over the India trade added strain to Dutch diplomacy. The volume shows one assassination redirecting the fate of nations. Conversations between Henry and the Dutch commissioners fill long central passages. Henry's coronation preparations for his queen proceed alongside his war plans.
lives-of-alchemystical-philosophers-base:
Arthur Edward Waite revived these alchemists' lives in 1888. His materials were collected in 1815 by Francis Barrett. Recent researches supplement Barrett's older biographies here. The Boston Medical Library copy reached the Internet Archive in 2011.

Waite adds a demonstration of the magnum opus's true principles. Alchemical re-construction, he argues, works as spiritual chemistry. The adepts' lives illustrate that hidden doctrine across centuries. Waite had already written on the Rosicrucians and magic's mysteries. Waite also digested Éliphas Lévi's writings on magic. The real history of the Rosicrucians preceded this volume. Plain readers can follow the lives without knowing the old art first.
lives-of-alchemystical-philosophers-to-w:
Waite's 1888 London edition adds a list of books to the alchemists' lives. George Redway published it from York Street, Covent Garden. The preface traces the foundation to Barrett's earlier Lives. A full list of alchemy writers came with that first book.

Waite adds fresh research to the 1815 materials. His account explains the great work of alchemy remade. Soul-side chemistry, not mere metal-making, frames his case. The new list covers alchemy and hermetic thought broadly. A critical catalogue of alchemical writers followed Barrett's lives. Waite's preface directs readers to that foundation explicitly. The lives run from old adepts down to men of Barrett's own day.
maine-international-law-1888:
Henry Sumner Maine's International Law was published in 1888 from his Cambridge lectures of 1887. Maine, the author of Ancient Law, was the great master of the historical method in legal study. In these late lectures he turned that method on the law between nations.

Maine traces how states slowly learned to live under rules: the growth of diplomacy, the laws of war, and the treatment of neutral nations. He treats international law as a real growth from custom and treaty rather than a code handed down at once. His skepticism about grand schemes keeps the lectures grounded in practice. They were his last lectures, printed after his death in 1888. The book shows the Victorian jurist viewing world order through history's lens, and it still rewards readers who doubt easy theories of global law.
mathers-tarot-1888:
S. L. MacGregor Mathers wrote his tarot tract, Book T, in 1888. It was made for the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn. Mathers led that order and set its teach in print. The tract gives the sense the order laid on each card.

Hebrew marks, star signs, and grades of the order lock to the cards. Short fate senses for each card fill the last pages. The scheme in Book T lies at the root of the Waite-Smith pack. Most new occult packs since draw on its plan in some form.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-marie-antoinette:
Volume five of Campan's memoirs opens book two at chapter one. The oath of the States General at the Tennis Court starts it. A royal sitting on June 23 follows that famed oath.

The King orders the Orders to vote apart, and threats follow. The Queen counts Necker's absence that day as treachery or cowardice. Then come the risings of July 11, 12, and 14, 1789. The Bastille falls, and Flesselles and Launay are killed by the crowd. The people still cried love for the King that July, she notes. The Queen and the Comte d'Artois drew the crowd's hate instead.
molinos-spiritual-guide-1688:
Miguel de Molinos was a Spanish priest in Rome whose Spiritual Guide, Englished in 1688, taught the quiet way of prayer to eager readers. The book won praise across Europe and, for a time, papal approval in high places. Then Rome condemned its propositions, and Molinos died in prison.

Molinos tells the soul to lay aside effort, images, and even anxious self-examination, resting in God without grasping. Critics charged that such quiet kills moral effort and the church's sacraments alike. His fall shaped European mysticism by warning it where the line of suspicion lay. Its short chapters made it a handbook readers could carry and reread.
monluc-commentaries-cotton-1688:
Blaise de Monluc, a Gascon soldier, wrote his Commentaires in 1592 about the wars he fought under King Henri II of France. Charles Cotton's English translation, first made in 1674, appears here in the printing of 1688. Monluc rose from common soldier to marshal by wounds, daring, and a fierce will to be remembered.

His memoir is all camp and battlefield: sieges, charges, feuds, and the raw talk of men at war. King Henry IV is said to have called the book the soldier's breviary, the handbook every fighter should keep. Monluc spares no one, least of all himself, in telling how war really felt. The Commentaries remain a classic soldier's memoir of the 1500s.
morris-dream-john-ball-1888:
William Morris, the designer and poet, had become a committed socialist by the 1880s. He published A Dream of John Ball in 1888, pairing it with a shorter prose piece, A King's Lesson. The dream tale first ran in a socialist newspaper, Commonweal, which Morris helped run.

A modern socialist narrator dreams himself back to 1381, during the Peasants' Revolt led by Wat Tyler. He talks through the night with John Ball, the rebel priest who preached that things would never be well while some were masters and others servants. Morris uses the rising to ask what his own movement must learn. The book blends history, hope, and warning.
most-die-anarchie-1888:
Johann Joseph Most published Die Anarchie in 1888, as number ten of the Internationale Bibliothek. Most was the era's most notorious German-American anarchist editor. The pamphlet argues that the public misunderstands the word anarchy. Anarchy, he writes, does not mean confusion; it means the absence of rule, or freedom.

All rule, he argues, arose from the evil will of the strong to subjugate the weak. Property owners hold power in every age, against the propertyless. He lists three stages: ownership of men, of land, and of property generally. Such works were later barred from American mails, and their editors jailed or deported.
nutt-studies-holy-grail-1888:
Alfred Nutt published Studies on the Legend of the Holy Grail in 1888, and it helped found modern Grail scholarship. Nutt was a folklorist, and he asked a bold question about the famous cup. Was the Grail a Christian relic, or something older?

Nutt pointed to Celtic tales of cauldrons of plenty that feed every guest and never empty. Behind the holy cup, he argued, stood these pagan wonders from Welsh and Irish story. His Celtic-origin case set the terms of debate for decades. Scholars still argue with this book, which is a sign of how much it started.
olympiodorus-alchemist-art-sacre-berthel:
Olympiodorus of Thebes, a scholar of the sixth century, wrote a long commentary on Zosimos and on the sayings of the old alchemists. His work On the Sacred Art is given here in the French version of Berthelot and Ruelle, from their 1888 edition of the Greek alchemists. Olympiodorus read the art through Neoplatonic thought.

He treats the metals, the egg of the philosophers, and the work of turning base stuff toward gold as signs of a deeper order. His pages carried the alchemy of Alexandria into the Byzantine world. Without such bridges, the Greek art would not have reached the Arabs or the Latin West. The commentary is dense, learned, and strange.
openalex-w1582174288:
Jon Paul Rodríguez, Garry Peterson, and six co-authors wrote this paper. It appeared in Ecology and Society in the year 2006. Ecosystem services are benefits people gain from nature. Management choices can raise one service while cutting another. Such losses are called trade-offs in the paper.

Trade-offs vary by place, by timing, and by reversibility, they write. Some choices are explicit, others happen without awareness. Across global scenarios, provisioning services won most often. Cultural services were almost never counted in the models. Supporting services were often taken for granted, they found. Good policy must track long-term, slow changes too.
openalex-w1951965788:
Pete Smith and a large international team wrote this paper. It appeared in the journal SOIL in the year 2015. Soils drive major global cycles of carbon and water. They also host the largest diversity of land organisms. From those roles flow key services to people.

Managing soil to boost one service can harm another, they note. The paper examines how soil cycles and biodiversity interact. It asks how management shifts services for good or ill. Farms, climate policy, and nature protection all depend on soils. The authors urge care for soils as living systems. Their framework links soil science to ecosystem policy.
openalex-w2059874988:
Subhamoy Pal, Allison Dauner, Indrani Mitra and colleagues compared commercial tests for early dengue diagnosis. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2014. Early diagnosis improves care and follow-up. A dengue protein called NS1 marks early infection. Many rapid tests and lab kits target it.

The team tested seven products on stored patient samples. Samples came from South America. Lab kits proved more sensitive than rapid strip tests. All tests were highly specific overall. Most tests missed one dengue type more often. They also worked less well in repeat infections. Tests performed best on days three to four of illness. The data help clinics choose tests for early care.
openalex-w2067376788:
Liliana Porras-Hurtado, Yarimar Ruiz, Carla Santos and colleagues reviewed the STRUCTURE software for population genetics. Their paper appeared in Frontiers in Genetics in 2013. The program is one of the most used tools in the field. It sorts samples into genetic groups. Researchers needed up-to-date guidance on its use.

STRUCTURE detects allele frequency differences within data. It assigns each individual to likely subgroups. The review covers the program's main applications. It explains key parameter settings in plain terms. It also surveys extra software that supports STRUCTURE runs. Good settings matter for trustworthy group assignments. The guide serves both genetics and forensic users.
openalex-w2090628788:
Simon Delgado, Bobbie Erickson, Roberto Agudo and colleagues identified a new virus from a fatal fever case in Bolivia. Their paper appeared in PLoS Pathogens in 2008. A small cluster of haemorrhagic fever cases struck near Cochabamba. Samples survived from only one patient. That patient died after severe bleeding signs.

Lab teams grew the virus from patient serum. Tests showed it was an arenavirus. Full gene sequences of both segments were read. It was closest to the Sabia virus of Brazil. Differences were large enough to mark a new virus. They named it the Chapare virus. Bolivia thus faces two arenaviruses that cause severe fever.
openalex-w2102456788:
Marianne Sinka, Michael Bangs, Sylvie Manguin and colleagues produced a global map of dominant malaria mosquitoes. Their paper appeared in Parasites and Vectors in 2012. Maps help show where malaria can spread. Few past maps rested on full evidence. The team built theirs from predicted species ranges.

They combined distribution maps for each major vector. The result shows how complex the picture is regionally. In Africa, three species share dominance widely. In Asia and the Pacific, many species coexist. Dominance shifts from place to place there. A large occurrence database underlies the maps. The authors discuss where the method may mislead. Control programmes can plan around local vectors.
openalex-w2114260388:
Christophe Monnin, Valerie Chavagnac, Cedric Boulart and colleagues studied unusual underwater springs in Prony Bay, New Caledonia. Their paper appeared in Biogeosciences in 2014. The springs release highly alkaline water. Such systems have been known on land since the 1800s. A recent survey found many similar vents underwater.

A research cruise sampled water, gases and rock deposits. Divers collected samples at vents up to fifty metres deep. One spring sits exposed at low tide. The fluids differ sharply from normal seawater. Their chemistry reflects reactions with deep rock types. Microbes living there were also characterised. High-pH systems interest scientists studying early Earth conditions. They may resemble habitats on other worlds too.
openalex-w2125198788:
Amy Buck, Gillian Coakley, Fabio Simbari, and colleagues published this study in Nature Communications in 2014. They asked whether worm parasites can send small RNA messages into the cells of the animal they infect. In mammals, RNA is known to travel between cells inside tiny sacs called exosomes.

The team studied a gut worm that infects mice and is related to human hookworm. They showed the worm releases sacs packed with small RNAs and a worm Argonaute protein. Mouse cells took these sacs in. Giving the worm sacs to mice through the nose calmed type-two immune responses and reduced swelling signs triggered by an allergen.
openalex-w2135648488:
Cosme Damião Cruz published this software paper alone in Acta Scientiarum Agronomy in 2013. He presents GENES, a free program for data analysis in experimental statistics and quantitative genetics. Plant and animal breeders use such tools to estimate traits and judge whether a selection plan is likely to succeed.

GENES runs many biometric models for processing breeding data. It is available online in Portuguese, English, and Spanish, with guide literature and sample files. The program works with Word, Excel, and Paint for moving data and results in and out. It also links with the free tools R and Matlab through supplied scripts for extra analyses like genome-wide selection.
openalex-w2318568688:
Saskia Keesstra, Johan Bouma, Jakob Wallinga, and colleagues published this forum paper in SOIL in 2016. They argue soil science is essential to reaching the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. Soils quietly underpin food security, clean water, climate action, biodiversity, and health, yet soil experts often sit outside those debates.

The authors map soil functions and their ecosystem services onto several goals. Their advice to colleagues is direct. Embrace the goals as a platform proving the field's relevance. Show how modern soil information improves joint studies across disciplines. Lead whole-system analyses, spread the word on soil organic matter, and train knowledge brokers. The paper is a call for soil scientists to claim their seat at the policy table.
openalex-w2395026888:
Dorothée Bakker, Benjamin Pfeil, Camilla Landa, and colleagues published this data paper in Earth System Science Data in 2016. It presents version 3 of the Surface Ocean CO2 Atlas, the global collection of surface-ocean carbon dioxide measurements. These records anchor estimates of how much human carbon the ocean absorbs.

The atlas now holds over fourteen million quality-controlled values from more than thirty-six hundred datasets, spanning 1957 to 2014. This version adds over four million values and four recent years over its predecessor. Quality checks run automatically at upload, accuracy is defined for every quality grade, and a flag now marks data from newer sensors and platforms. An upgraded viewer and automated uploads promise faster future releases for climate researchers.
openalex-w2575837388:
The Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network reported this study in Nature in 2017. It gives an extensive molecular portrait of cervical cancer, a leading cause of cancer death worldwide. The team analyzed two hundred twenty-eight primary tumors with many kinds of genomic tests. Few studies of this cancer had ever been so large or so complete.

The analysis found strong patterns of APOBEC mutagenesis, a process that scars DNA in a distinctive way. It named several newly confirmed mutated genes, including ERBB3, CASP8, and TGFBR2. Some tumors amplified immune targets PD-L1 and PD-L2, which matter for modern immunotherapy. Human papillomavirus DNA was built into the tumor genome in most samples. That integration was linked to structural changes and higher activity of nearby genes. Together the results map new routes toward understanding and treating this cancer.
openalex-w2964004288:
Regina Medina-Sauza, Marycruz Álvarez-Jiménez, Alix Delhal, and colleagues wrote this systematic review in Frontiers in Environmental Science in 2019. It examines how earthworms shape the microbe communities of the soil. Earthworms work in tight soil spaces, yet their effects spread to the whole soil layer they inhabit.

Feeding is the main route of influence, since earthworms eat soil and the microbes in it. Digestion can cut microbe numbers, above all fungi. At the same time, worms can favor or stir up certain microbes that help them digest soil organic matter. The review pulls together this evidence on how worms, meal by meal, build up the living community of the soil.
openalex-w3086687188:
Carolina Sansaloni, Jorge Franco, Bruno Santos, and colleagues published this study in Nature Communications in 2020. It analyzes genetic diversity across eighty thousand wheat accessions held in seed collections. Wheat supplies about a fifth of the protein and calories in human diets worldwide.

Since farming began over ten thousand years ago, breeding raised yields but thinned the gene pool of elite wheat. That narrowing now limits the creation of new varieties for a changing world. By scanning the vast collection, the team traced the footprints that past selection left in the genome. Some footprints mark losses to repair; others mark chances to recover useful traits. The study turns a seed vault census into a breeding roadmap.
openalex-w3210397188:
Rosario Javier-Astete, Jorge Jiménez-Dávalos, and Gastón Zolla test a fast way to measure wood chemistry in two Amazonian trees. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2021. Capirona and Bolaina grow quickly and are in rising demand for timber. Breeders need the amounts of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin in young trees, but standard lab tests are slow.

The team scanned stem samples with infrared light, a method called FTIR, and built prediction models from the spectra. Wood makeup differed between the top and base of each stem, which helped the models learn. Lignin was predicted well in both species, and cellulose very well in Bolaina. The method could speed up breeding of better timber trees.
openalex-w4368363688:
Ahmed Osman, Eman Abd El-Monaem, Ahmed Elgarahy, and colleagues review how to prepare sorbents for cleaning water, in Environmental Chemistry Letters in 2023. Adsorption, trapping pollutants on a solid's surface, is a cheap and effective treatment. Classic adsorbents come from fossil fuels and can cause fresh pollution themselves. Sorbents made from living waste promise a cleaner alternative that also fits the circular economy.

The review covers biological sorbents, magnetic sorbents, and other low-cost options. Raw materials range from wood and farm waste to algae, bacteria, and animal waste. The authors explain preparation methods, the pollutants each type removes, and how the trapping works. They also cover how spent sorbents can be renewed, a key step for real-world use.
openalex-w4383105288:
A global team of seabird researchers maps where oceanic birds meet plastic pollution at sea, in Nature Communications in 2023. Plastic spreads unevenly across the oceans, and so do the birds at risk of eating it. Petrels, a wide-ranging seabird group, often swallow plastic and are already highly threatened. The team combined plastic density estimates with tracking data for more than seven thousand birds of seventy-seven petrel species.

High exposure areas emerged in the Mediterranean and Black seas and in parts of the Pacific, Atlantic, and Indian oceans. Threatened species faced disproportionately high risk. Risk peaked mostly on the high seas and in the waters of the United States, Japan, and the United Kingdom. The authors call for international cooperation, since birds breed in one country and feed in many.
openalex-w4407468688:
Oliver Cornely, Rosanne Sprute, Matteo Bassetti, and colleagues present a global guideline for candidiasis. It appeared in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2025. Candida fungi are the leading cause of fungal disease in hospital patients. They sicken and kill people worldwide.

Three international societies joined forces to write the guidance. The European Confederation of Medical Mycology led it, working with two partner societies. It covers how to diagnose this infection and how to treat it. It aims to give doctors everywhere one shared, evidence-based standard. Steady use of one standard should improve outcomes for a common and dangerous set of diseases.
openalex-w7129093688:
Naoya Murakami, a radiation oncologist at Juntendo University in Tokyo, wrote a 2026 review on treating lung cancer that is locally advanced and cannot be removed by surgery. This form of non-small cell lung cancer makes up a large share of cases and is hard to treat well.

Murakami traces three decades of change, from radiation alone to radiation combined with chemotherapy, and then to immune therapy or targeted drugs given afterward. A trial drug called durvalumab became standard care after combined treatment, and another drug helped patients whose tumors carry a specific gene change. He also warns that lung inflammation from radiation can be fatal, so dose limits and risk checks matter greatly.
openalex-w7137857988:
Leticia Pereira led a 2026 study in the Journal of Antibiotics proposing a new way to hunt for antibacterial drugs using Euglena gracilis, a single-celled organism with a plant-like chloroplast. Because that chloroplast keeps some bacterial features, antibiotics can bleach it white while the cell itself stays alive by eating organic carbon.

One test can therefore flag three things at once: antibacterial action, lack of poisoning to the cell, and whether a compound crosses several membranes. The team tuned the test and set simple light readings to sort results automatically. They tried it on a commercial compound library and on rare natural compounds from myxobacteria and fungi. The screen is cheap and broad, though some antibiotic classes will slip past it.
openalex-w7162264588:
Yu Takiguchi and Koji Nemoto published a 2026 mathematical study of two conflicting rumors spreading through the same population, such as fake news and its correction. Their model borrows from epidemic theory: people can catch and spread either rumor, lose interest, and become susceptible again. Unusually, each person's opinion feeds back on how easily each rumor infects them.

Working out every steady state and its stability, the authors find a surprising coexistence mechanism. Belief in one rumor can paradoxically help the opposing rumor spread, and a rumor with a lower infection rate can sometimes spread further. A majority advantage also emerges on its own, and a rumor dies out unless its starting share passes a critical threshold, which the authors derive.
openalex-w7204485688:
Ana Alice Gomes Damasceno and Débora Silva Santos released a Portuguese-language study in Brazil in 2026 on maker methodology in biology and chemistry teaching. Maker culture, learning by building, promises an exit from fragmented, lecture-only science classes. The research reads research papers on classroom applications of the approach, looking for convergences, successful experiences, and gaps in prior studies.

Maker work develops self-rule, creativity, critical thinking, and collaboration, the authors find. In biology, didactic model building, investigative experiments, and interdisciplinary projects stood out. In chemistry, experimentation in maker spaces, problem solving, and prototype creation led. The culture has great potential to improve science teaching, they conclude, though real adoption depends on infrastructure, teacher training, and deeper work.

Marivalda Brandão Ramos de Sousa led a Portuguese-language qualitative study, published in Brazil in 2026, on the difficulties teachers face working with autistic students in the municipal schools of Dom Inocêncio, Piauí. Autism diagnoses have risen sharply, and schools must be ready to include these students fully. Five early-years teachers answered a form sent through WhatsApp, and the team analyzed responses by categorical content analysis.

The teachers reported great difficulty working with autistic children and made clear they do not feel pedagogically prepared. Inclusion, on their account, does not happen in practice. The authors point to an urgent need for continuing training across the municipal network, so that legal inclusion becomes classroom reality for autistic students.
openalex-w7204947088: Ana Júlia Ribeiro Almeida and eleven co-authors in Brazil released a Portuguese-language review in 2026 on the psychosocial impact of acne vulgaris on adolescents and young adults. Acne is one of the most visible skin problems of youth. Appearing on the face at exactly the age when appearance weighs most heavily on self-image and social life. The review gathers the work on what that burden does to teenagers and young adults psychologically and socially. A dimension of the disease that purely medical treatment can overlook.
openalex-w7205006588:
Victoria Matos Carvalho led a Portuguese-language review, in Brazil in 2026, on implantable cardioverter-defibrillators for preventing sudden death in non-ischemic heart failure. These devices are used for primary prevention in selected patients, but their benefit, mainly on overall mortality, remains controversial. Using standard review guidelines, the team searched two sources in April 2026 for 2021 to early 2026 randomized and cohort studies, with two independent reviewers selecting and appraising the work.

Results were mixed, the authors report. Evidence generally favored the device for preventing sudden cardiac death and fatal arrhythmic events. Findings on death from all causes were not uniform, with some studies showing benefit and others no major reduction. Benefit magnitude seemed to vary with patient traits, making selection decisive.
openalex-w7205006988:
Pablo de Oliveira Lopes wrote a Portuguese-language review, published in Brazil in 2026, of Baby, a 2024 film by Marcelo Caetano about homosexual life in urban São Paulo. The film follows Wellington, a young man leaving a detention center, and Ronaldo, a sex worker, whose relationship mixes affection, desire, conflict, and protection. Reading through queer theory and concepts such as discursive smuggling, equity, and chemsex, Lopes examines how the film portrays homosexual lives marginalized by race, class, and dissident sexuality.

The film also reproduces subaltern positions, he argues, by tying its characters to clandestinity and illegality. Leaves underexplored themes such as married men living double lives and chemical sex among men who have sex with men. Despite its merits in exposing part of queer São Paulo, the review concludes, the film reinforces stereotypes that deserved more questioning.
openalex-w7211991188:
Leonardo Cristiano da Silva, writing alone, measures the shock that new rules for blended teacher-training degrees sent through Brazil's higher education market. His documentary study uses federal legislation from 2024 to 2026, national census microdata, and national exam results. Blended degrees mix online and in-person study, and the new regulation redrew what distance teacher training may look like.

Most teacher-training students were enrolled at a distance in 2024, well over a million of them, in a format the new rules then barred. Graduates of distance programs also performed far worse on the national exam than classroom-trained peers. In the first admission cycle under the new norm, demand for distance courses fell sharply at the big listed education groups while blended formats grew. The rules, Silva concludes, make physical campuses a competitive asset again, though towns served only at a distance risk losing access.
openalex-w7211997288:
Debora Lucia de Araujo Figueiredo leads a team asking people with depression how they experience care at a psychosocial care center in Crateus, Ceara, Brazil. These centers are the community backbone of Brazilian mental health care. The researchers interviewed thirty users with depression and mapped the themes in their answers with text analysis software. Three themes organize the findings: improvement tied to symptoms easing, help as emotional support alongside medicine, and everyday coping strategies.

Medication matters to users, above all because it reduces symptoms, and they say so clearly. But they also value what pills cannot do: being welcomed, being heard, psychotherapy, and the routines of daily life. Drug treatment alone, users report, does not meet their needs, yet the care model stays centered on medication. The authors call for strengthening the non-drug practices users themselves praise.
openalex-w7213870788:
Daniel Lemes da Costa Filho and colleagues examine suppressor immune cells in systemic lupus erythematosus. Their 2026 article, in English, begins from autoimmunity: the immune system attacks the body's own cells when it cannot tell self from non-self. Lupus symptoms can range from mild to severe.

Myeloid-derived suppressor cells normally help hold immune responses down. Under disease conditions, they may expand and stop working properly, the authors explain. The study set out to explore what these cells contribute to how lupus develops. That dual role, protector turned problem, makes the cells a candidate point for understanding and perhaps controlling the disease.
openalex-w7214054288:
Elizangela Cristina de Paula Donato and co-authors propose a digital training model for staff at the central animal facility of the Federal University of Minas Gerais. Their 2026 article designs an online, self-instructional in-service course aligned with open science. Rigid face-to-face routines currently limit the continuing training that national rules require.

An adult-learning approach for the public sector guides the model. The ADDIE instructional design frame and the Moodle platform structure the course. Removing place and time barriers should let learning fit around daily laboratory work. Expected results include smoother process management, higher legal compliance among researchers, standardized good practice, and a stronger institutional culture of animal welfare.
openalex-w7214500388:
Andréa Carla de Lima Melo, Maria de Fátima Calógeras, and Rozineide Iraci Pereira da Silva wrote a 2026 article on how learning is assessed in youth and adult education in Brazil. Students in this sector arrive with very different school, social, and work histories, so a single grading style fits poorly. The authors link formative assessment, meaning feedback that guides learning, with fairness in how students are judged.

Their critical review found grade-centered practice still common, beside approaches that use assessment to diagnose needs and replan teaching. They stress recognizing what students already know, stating criteria clearly, and gathering varied evidence. From this, they set out five principles, from recognition to equity. Fair assessment, they conclude, keeps academic rigor while giving students a real chance to learn and to show what they know.
openalex-w7214502088: Daniela Maysa de Souza led a nine-author article, published in a Brazilian journal in 2026, on the formative potential of the reflective portfolio in health teaching. A reflective portfolio is a collection in which teachers or students record work and think back over what it taught them. The evidence sample for this entry contains only the title page and author list, with no abstract or findings, so the study's conclusions are not described here.
openalex-w7214616288:
Danilo Lucateli Maria and Keila Aparecida de Lima reviewed the literature, in a 2026 article, on functional training to prevent falls in older adults. Falls can bring injuries, loss of the ability to live on one's own, and lower quality of life, so prevention matters as the number of older people grows. Functional training means exercises built around everyday movements, aimed at strength, balance, coordination, and mobility.

Across the studies reviewed, functional training improved exactly those capacities: muscle strength, balance, coordination, mobility, and overall functional ability. Those gains attack the main factors behind fall risk. The authors present regular functional training as a practical way to help older adults stay independent longer. The review is a summary of earlier research rather than a new trial, so its value lies in collecting findings that agree, for those who design exercise programs for seniors.
openalex-w7214706888:
Maria Socorro Vasconcelos led a 2026 article on the people who connect Brazil's inclusive special education policy to real schools: intersectoral coordinators. National policy and a new national network demand cooperation between levels of government and between education, health, social assistance, public management, schools, and families. The authors review studies and recent decrees to judge what these coordinators can actually do.

Coordination, the review indicates, can identify local needs, organize communication flows, train professionals, and follow up on actions. It does not remove the school's own responsibility for teaching its students. Permanent cooperation networks, the authors conclude, can bring national guidelines closer to local realities and strengthen access, permanence, participation, and learning for special education students. The article maps a role that is easy to overlook and hard to replace.
openalex-w7214719788:
Djanice Batista da Luz Azevêdo and Rozineide Iraci Pereira da Silva wrote a second 2026 article together, this one on health education by community health workers in Brazil. These workers live in the areas they serve and link families to primary care teams. The bibliographic review gathers scientific work and documents on their educational strategies inside the family health program.

Home visits, individual and group guidance, active searching for people who miss care, family follow-up, vaccination campaigns, preventive actions, and community mobilization form the core of the work. Living close to the territory helps workers spot health needs, build trust, and carry messages between residents and the wider care team. The authors conclude the role is strategic for health promotion, and they call for stronger initial training, continuing education, and better working conditions to widen its effect.
openalex-w7220674988:
Renata Burghausen Valença de Souza led a seven-author 2026 protocol for a scoping review on preventing obstetric violence, disrespectful or abusive treatment during childbirth care. Rather than giving results, the article lays out how the mapping will be done. It follows the Joanna Briggs Institute method and the scoping review reporting extension. It searches five databases, screens titles, abstracts, and full texts with two reviewers working apart, and extracts data with a standard instrument.

The review aims to name prevention strategies across institutions, education, and public policy, together with their implementation contexts, target audiences, barriers, and facilitators. The mapping, the authors conclude, can support respectful care practices, professional formation, and public policy that qualifies obstetric care. Protocols like this one make reviews reproducible before they begin, letting others check the plan against the finished product.
phrenology-as-a-science-microform-a-lect: The sample we host shows only the title pages of Phrenology as a Science, with no lecture text visible. They present a lecture delivered by Professor William Seymour, phrenologist and psychologist, in Shaftesbury Hall, Toronto, in July 1888. The catalogue record notes the work survives as a microform, the filming format in which many such small Canadian pamphlets of the period were preserved for libraries.
plos-pbio-0020288:
Steven D. Mason, Richard A. Howlett, Matthew J. Keske, and their team tested a muscle oxygen sensor in PLOS Biology in 2004. HIF-1α is a protein that reacts when oxygen runs low. The team removed it from mouse skeletal muscle and checked how the mice handled exercise.

Endurance changed when the sensor was missing, showing it helps set how muscle copes with hard work. Muscles must match blood flow and fuel use to demand, and oxygen sensing is part of that match. The study helps explain why training and altitude have the effects they do. It also warns that drugs targeting HIF pathways, now in wide study, will have real effects on exercise capacity.
plos-pone-0000088:
Yi Xing, Karen Kapur, and Wing Hung Wong addressed a data problem in gene chips in PLOS ONE in 2006. Affymetrix exon arrays measure gene activity piece by piece, exon by exon, using many small probes. Picking which probes to trust, and how to sum them into one score, decides whether the results mean anything.

The authors set out rules for probe selection and a method for computing the expression index. Faulty probes, which react to the wrong target, are a known trap in chip data. Cleaner inputs give cleaner biology. Methods papers like this one rarely make headlines, yet thousands of later studies stand on them. The exon arrays opened a window on splicing that careful math had to keep clear.
plos-pone-0000188:
Xuhua Xia published this molecular evolution paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Protein production starts when a ribosome lands at a start signal, and the Kozak consensus sequence around that signal was thought to fine-tune the start. The author tests the +4G site in that sequence and reports it is not related to how efficiently translation begins.

A claimed rule of translation falls under direct testing here. Negative results of this sort clean up the textbook picture of how genes are read. The paper matters for anyone designing gene sequences or predicting protein output from DNA, tasks where a false rule leads to false expectations.
plos-pone-0000288:
Vanina Vergoz, Edith Roussel, Jean-Christophe Sandoz, and colleagues published this bee learning study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Honeybees can be trained by smell using the sting extension reflex. In that reflex, a bee that senses a threat paired with an odor extends its sting. The authors reveal aversive learning in honeybees through this conditioning setup.

Bees were famous for learning rewards, learning which smells mean food. Showing they also learn aversively, which smells mean danger, completes the picture of their learning. The work gives bee neuroscience a second conditioning tool, useful for studying memory and its chemistry.
plos-pone-0000388:
Harish Babu and colleagues refined a way to grow brain precursor cells from adult mice, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Their source was the dentate gyrus, one of the few brain regions that keeps making new neurons in adulthood. They cut out the tiny region and grew its precursor cells as a clean, enriched layer in culture.

The cultured cells went on to produce working granule cell-like neurons, the main cell type of the dentate gyrus. A reliable culture system like this gives researchers a steady supply of adult-born neurons to study. That helps work on how the adult brain adds new cells, and what those cells do for learning and memory.
plos-pone-0000488:
Adrian B. Hehl and colleagues tested a cell-death protein in an unusual host, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Giardia lamblia is a primitive intestinal parasite that lacks mitochondria, the cell's power stations. Bax is a protein that normally triggers cell death by acting on mitochondria. The team studied Bax function in the absence of mitochondria in this protozoan.

If Bax still works in a cell with no mitochondria, its killing mechanism must reach beyond them. Odd organisms make good tests for claims about how basic machinery works, because they strip away the usual context. The study probes how ancient and how flexible the cell-death program is.
plos-pone-0000588:
Georgia Panagiotakos and colleagues measured radiation's long shadow over brain stem cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Radiation therapy saves lives but can harm the developing or adult brain. The team studied the long-term impact of radiation on two cell pools in the brain. One pool holds stem cells. The other holds oligodendrocyte precursors, the cells that renew tissue and make myelin, the insulation of nerve fibers.

If precursor pools are depleted for good, later cognitive and repair problems have a cellular explanation. Long-term studies matter because patients, especially children, live decades after treatment. Findings like these inform how radiation doses are planned to spare the brain's regenerative reserves.
plos-pone-0000688:
Erin K. Hanson and Jack Ballantyne built a sharper DNA typing system for forensic work, published in PLOS ONE in 2007. Forensic labs use Y chromosome short tandem repeats, markers called Y-STRs, to identify a male DNA donor. The method shines when male DNA hides in excess female DNA, as in many sexual assault investigations.

Commercial typing kits already existed, but each added marker raises the power to tell men apart. Their title promises ultra-high discrimination from one multiplex system, testing many markers at once. Better discrimination means fewer ambiguous matches in casework. For courts and labs, a stronger Y-STR panel is a practical advance, not just a technical one.
plos-pone-0000788:
Ricardo Núñez Miguel, Joyce Wong, Julian F. Westoll and colleagues modeled the working end of an immune alarm receptor, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Toll-like receptor 4, or TLR4, sits on the surface of immune cells. It is activated by lipopolysaccharides from the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria, forming part of the mammalian innate immune response. Its cytoplasmic domain, inside the cell, passes the signal onward.

Their title states that a dimer, two copies joined, of that domain provides a specific scaffold for recruiting signalling adaptor proteins. Shape explains specificity: only the paired platform fits the right adaptors. That geometry guides drug ideas for sepsis and inflammation.
plos-pone-0000888:
Yamina Seamari, Jose Narvaez, Francisco Vico and colleagues built methods to separate two states of brain cortex activity, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Cortex networks fall into a slow rhythm during deep sleep and anesthesia. Cells swing between up states, active and charged, and down states, quiet and resting, less than once a second.

Telling those states apart in recordings sounds simple but is easy to get wrong. The authors offer robust ways to do it both live, as data comes in, and later, offline. Clean state labels underpin many studies of sleep and memory. Their methods give other labs a firmer base for that work.
plos-pone-0000988:
Insuk Lee, Zhihua Li and Edward Marcotte built a cleaner probabilistic gene network for baker's yeast, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Gene networks merge millions of separate observations into one model of how a cell works. For yeast, such a network is a workhorse for predicting what unstudied genes do.

The catch is bias: well studied genes gather more links just because they are well studied. The authors present an improved network with that bias reduced. A fairer map gives unknown genes a better chance of being placed correctly. Yeast networks often prototype methods later used on human data, so the fix travels.
plos-pone-0001088:
Dietrich Gotzek, D. DeWayne Shoemaker and Kenneth Ross examined gene variation behind fire ant social form, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The fire ant Solenopsis invicta comes in two social forms. Some colonies have one egg laying queen; others have many. That difference reshapes colony life entirely.

A candidate gene had been implicated in regulating this social behavior. The team study molecular variation at that gene across forms. Few traits offer so direct a line from one gene region to a whole society's structure. The fire ant is also a major invasive pest, so its social genetics carry practical weight for control efforts in the southern United States.
plos-pone-0001188:
Leptospira interrogans is a corkscrew-shaped bacterium that spreads through the bloodstream and colonizes many tissues, causing leptospirosis. Brian Stevenson and colleagues examined proteins on its outer surface in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Infectious leptospires can resist killing by the complement system, part of the immune defense in blood.

The authors show that the bacterium's endostatin-like outer membrane proteins bind host fibronectin and laminin, two proteins of the tissue scaffold, plus regulators of complement. Grabbing scaffold proteins may help the bacterium attach and invade. Binding complement regulators may help it hide. Together these tricks explain part of its success as a pathogen.
plos-pone-0001288:
Animals must sense how much sugar is available and respond, and for years attention focused on glucose sensing inside cells. Emilie Stolarczyk and colleagues studied sensing outside cells instead, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They disabled GLUT2, a glucose transporter that also acts as a sugar sensor, in mice.

The authors report that loss of sugar detection by GLUT2 affects glucose homeostasis in the mice. Homeostasis is the body's balancing of blood sugar levels. Their work shows that detection at the cell surface is a real part of that balance, not a sideshow.
plos-pone-0001388:
Fredrik Vannberg and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a gene variant and tuberculosis. TB kills and sickens many people each year, most of all in sub Saharan Africa. A cell receptor coded by the gene CD209 can grab and take in the TB germ. Prior work had linked a variant near this gene to TB risk.

The team tested that link in their own groups of patients and controls. They asked whether the same variant raised or lowered the odds of disease. Firm checks like this sort true risk genes from false leads. The data help guide the search for host traits that shape who falls ill with TB.
plos-pone-0001488:
Yvonne Vallès, Kenneth Halanych, and Jeffrey Boore published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on mobile DNA in an animal genome. Group II introns are RNA pieces that cut themselves out of messages and can hop to new spots. They are common in germs and cell parts, but rare in animal nuclei. They are thought to be the kin of our own splicing parts.

The team found these introns in the genome of a two sided animal, a first of its kind. That find breaks the old bounds for where they can live. It hints they were once more common in animal lines. It also adds a data point to the tale of how gene splicing arose.
plos-pone-0001588:
Jeffrey Trimarchi, Michael Stadler, and Constance Cepko wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on single eye cells in mice. The retina grows from stem like cells that read cues from their world. The varied fates of those cells must in part stem from varied gene use. The team read gene use in single retinal stem cells, one by one.

Even cells of the same type and age showed wide spread in gene use. That spread may be the raw stuff from which distinct fates are picked. Single cell reads catch what pooled samples smear out. The work sets a base for how the eye builds its many cell types.
plos-pone-0001688:
Françoise Guinet, Patrick Avé, Louis Jones, and their co-authors traced the earliest events of plague infection in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Yersinia pestis, the plague bacterium, evolved recently from a gut pathogen, Yersinia pseudotuberculosis. In doing so it gained entry through the skin and extreme virulence. Which early events make it so deadly was the question.

The authors report two faults acting together. The innate immune cells that should attack first respond poorly, and the bacteria infiltrate lymph nodes in a distinctive way. The full text gives the infection time course, the cell counts, and the node pathology. These first hours decide whether plague takes hold, so they are also where new treatments would have to act fastest.
plos-pone-0001788:
Benjamin S. C. Uzochukwu and co-authors compared how mothers in town and countryside respond to childhood fever in south east Nigeria, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Childhood fevers from malaria remain a major cause of illness and death among under-five children in Nigeria. How dangerous a mother judges the fever to be shapes what care she seeks.

The team surveyed rural and urban mothers on their perceptions of severity and their patterns of health care use. The full text gives the survey results and the rural-urban contrasts. Fever care often starts at home or with drug sellers. Knowing those first steps is essential for programs trying to get sick children treated in time.
plos-pone-0001888:
Ada De Luigi and colleagues tested a family of common drugs against prion disease in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Prions are rogue proteins that cause fatal brain ills in animals and in people, such as Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. In past lab work, tetracycline drugs bound to the rogue protein and made it lose its tough, hard-to-break form.

The team asked whether that effect could slow real infection, both when prions enter the body and when they are placed in the brain. Past work had shown lower prion levels and longer life in hamsters dosed with these drugs. A cheap, known drug class that buys time would be a rare gain in a field with no cure.
plos-pone-0001988:
Paul Gilbert and co-authors tested a video counselor for HIV patients, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Cutting drug use and unsafe sex among people with HIV helps their own health and lowers the chance they pass the virus on. Guidelines tell providers to screen and counsel for these risks, yet busy clinics often skip it.

The program, called Video Doctor, gives interactive counseling by computer in the clinic. As the title states, it reduced drug and sexual risk acts among HIV-positive patients in diverse clinics. A tool that counsels without staff time could fill a gap that human clinics struggle to close.
plos-pone-0002088:
Douglas Bakkum, Zenas Chao, and Steve Potter studied slow shifts in how brain networks pass signals, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Precise timing of nerve spikes is essential to many brain functions. From one neuron's view, the timings of incoming spikes from its partners decide whether it fires, and when.

The team grew cortical networks in the lab. Over the long term, they tracked how activity changed both the delay of spike travel and spike size. As the title states, this long-term, activity-dependent plasticity reshapes propagation itself. Wiring that retimes its own signals adds a layer to how networks learn.
plos-pone-0002188:
Christiane Dolecek, Tran Thi Phi La, Nguyen Ngoc Rang, and co-authors compared two antibiotics for typhoid fever in Vietnam, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Drug-resistant typhoid is a growing clinical problem worldwide. Older fluoroquinolone drugs such as ciprofloxacin and ofloxacin, once first-line treatments, had begun to fail.

The team ran a randomized controlled trial in children and adults with uncomplicated typhoid. Patients received either gatifloxacin or azithromycin, and the researchers compared cure rates and safety. Head-to-head trials like this give doctors in high-burden regions evidence for which drug to reach for when the old standbys no longer work.
plos-pone-0002288:
Conrad Earnest and co-authors reported on six months of exercise training in inactive postmenopausal women. Their 2008 PLOS ONE paper covers how training changed heart rate variability. Heart rate variability, the small timing changes between beats, falls with age and low values predict higher mortality. Postmenopausal women have lower variability than younger women, and inactivity and obesity can push it lower still.

The data come from the DREW study, a controlled trial of exercise dose in this group. The team measured whether training raised variability over six months. Results from a large, careful trial help doctors prescribe exercise with clearer expectations for heart health.
plos-pone-0002388:
Attardo and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Alessio Attardo, Federico Calegari, Wulf Haubensak, and others. Its subject is live Imaging at the Onset of Cortical Neurogenesis Reveals Differential Appearance. The rest of the title points to the Neuronal Phenotype in Apical versus Basal Progenitor Progeny. The neurons of the mammal brain are made by progenitor cells that divide at one of two surfaces.

Some divide at the apical surface of the ventricular zone, and others divide at its basal side. What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002488:
Led by Swaddle, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from John P. Swaddle, Stavros E. Calos, and others. Its subject is increased Avian Diversity Is Associated with Lower Incidence of Human West Nile Infection: Observation of the Dilution Effect.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002588:
Research by Massacand and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Joanna C. Massacand, Patrick Kaiser, Bettina Ernst, and others. Its subject is intestinal Bacteria Condition Dendritic Cells to Promote IgA Production. Immunoglobulin (Ig) A represents the predominant antibody isotype produced at the intestinal mucosa.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002688:
Research from Abhay Kumar Thakur and co-authors, published in PLOS ONE in 2008, covers UV-Light exposed prion protein fails to form amyloid fibrils. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Abhay Kumar Thakur, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Amyloid fibril formation involves three steps; structural perturbation, nucleation and elongation. The authors add a further point. We have investigated amyloidogenesis using prion protein as a model system and UV-light as a structural perturbant. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002788:
Work by Kamaldeen Baba and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was adenosine deaminase activity is a sensitive marker for the diagnosis of tuberculous pleuritis in patients with very low CD4 counts. The catalog record names Kamaldeen Baba first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Adenosine Deaminase Activity (ADA) is a commonly used marker for the diagnosis of tuberculous pleural effusion. The authors add a further point. There has been concern about its usefulness in immunocompromised patients, especially HIV positive patients with very low CD4 counts. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002888:
Anne-Pierre Morel, Marjory Lièvre, Clémence Thomas and colleagues linked two big cancer ideas in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. One idea holds that cancer stem cells start tumors. The other holds that epithelial cells spread by first changing form, a shift called epithelial-mesenchymal transition, or EMT.

Working with a mammary tumor model, the team reports that forcing that shift can generate breast cancer stem cells. The title states that result directly. If the two processes are joined, a drug that blocks the shift might also curb the stem cells that regrow tumors after treatment.
plos-pone-0002988:
Naomi Willis, Thomas Cox, Syed Rahman-Casañs and co-authors named lamin A/C a risk marker in colorectal cancer in 2008. A-type lamins are structural proteins of the cell nucleus, coded by the LMNA gene. Faults in that gene cause several early-ageing and degenerative diseases.

Lamins also affect the retinoblastoma protein and cancer genes such as beta-catenin, both relevant to bowel cancer. The PLOS ONE study evaluates lamin A/C as a biomarker, a measurable sign of risk or outlook. A reliable marker could help sort patients by likely course and treatment need. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003088:
Marcel Kool, Jan Koster, Jens Bunt and co-authors split medulloblastoma into five subtypes by integrated genomics in 2008. Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in children. Cure rates had improved, but predicting outcome was still a major challenge and survivors suffer serious therapy side effects.

Combining genetics, pathway signatures, and clinical features yielded five subtypes with distinct profiles, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, finer subtypes let doctors spare low-risk children the harshest treatment. The classification also gives drug research defined targets instead of one mixed disease. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003188:
Alice Hadchouel, Fabrice Decobert, Marie-Laure Franco-Montoya and colleagues link gene variants to a preterm lung disease in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Building the air sacs of the lung requires coordinated remodeling of the matrix outside cells, in which matrix metalloproteinases, or MMPs, play an important role. The team postulated that variants in MMP genes might affect MMP function in preterm lungs and alter the risk of bronchopulmonary dysplasia.

Their title reports identification of MMP16 as a new player in lung development. Readers see a candidate gene for a serious disease of premature infants. Genetic risk clues may one day help target closer monitoring.
plos-pone-0003288:
Ming Yi and Robert M. Stephens present a pathway ranking method in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Analysis of microarray and other high throughput data often involves identification of genes consistently up or down-regulated across samples as the first step in extraction of biological meaning. This gene-level paradigm can be limited as a result of valid sample fluctuations and noise.

Their method, SLEPR, is a sample-level enrichment-based pathway ranking approach seeking biological themes through pathway-level consistency. Readers get a shift from single gene lists to whole pathway patterns. Pathway views often survive noise better and point more directly to disease processes.
plos-pone-0003388:
Chiara Begliomini and co-authors scanned human brains during grip tasks in this 2008 study. Grasping turns what the eyes see into precise hand movements. In monkeys, a known brain circuit handles that change. The team asked how the human version of the circuit behaves.

People grasped objects with the left hand or the right hand during scans. Brain activity shifted with the hand used and with the person's own handedness. Right-handed and left-handed people did not use the circuit in the same way. The study shows that hand choice shapes motor planning deep in the brain.
plos-pone-0003488:
Gita Ramjee and co-authors ran a trial of added STI protection for women in this 2008 paper. The test group used a diaphragm plus lubricant gel, with condoms. The control group used condoms alone. All women in the trial faced risk of HIV and other infections.

The trial tracked new cases of chlamydia and gonorrhea. Those are common sexually transmitted infections of the cervix. Results showed whether the added barrier gave extra protection. Such evidence guides prevention advice for women who cannot rely on condoms alone. Many women cannot count on partners to use condoms every time.
plos-pone-0003588:
A. Puppo and co-authors disturbed the egg cell's outer skeleton in this 2008 study. As eggs mature for fertilization, their inner calcium stores reorganize. That change yields a more efficient calcium response at fertilization. The actin cytoskeleton also remodels during maturation and fertilization.

Altering the cortical actin deregulated calcium signaling in the eggs. It also disrupted single-sperm fertilization and sperm entry. The skeleton is thus no passive frame but an active director. Its state helps decide whether fertilization proceeds normally. Egg quality sets the odds for in vitro fertilization in clinics worldwide. Calcium waves are one of the first signs doctors and lab staff watch for after sperm meets egg in the dish.
plos-pone-0003688:
Nyambayar Dashtsoodol, Hiroshi Watarai, Sakura Sakata, and colleagues published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Natural killer T cells are unusual immune cells that grow in the thymus. They were thought to come only from cells carrying both the CD4 and CD8 markers. The earliest steps of their growth stayed unclear.

The team identified precursor cells that carry neither marker, a double-negative stage. These precursors can develop into natural killer T cells as well. The extra path widens the known family tree of cells that bridge the body's fast and slow immune defenses.
plos-pone-0003788:
Annette Schneider, Dimitry Spitkovsky, Peter Riess, and colleagues published this stem cell methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. Many stem cell lines must first grow alongside feeder cells to stay undifferentiated and potent. Later, those feeder cells count as contamination and must be removed. The team built a way to sort the two apart.

Their technology frees stem cells from feeder cells cleanly. As the title's fairy tale puts it: the good into the pot, the bad into the crop. Pure stem cells make later experiments and therapies safer and easier to interpret.
plos-pone-0003888:
Jennifer Waldo and Michael Scherrer described a small protein from dividing yeast cells in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns Dad1p, part of the Dam1-DASH complex. That complex sits in the kinetochore, the structure linking chromosomes to the spindle. Good links let cells split their chromosomes evenly between daughter cells.

The authors produced Dad1p in the lab and gave its first detailed description. Early data on a single part helps map how the whole complex grips chromosomes. Faults in such parts can lead to cells with the wrong chromosome count. The work supports wider studies of cell division in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
plos-pone-0003988:
Thore Egeland and Antonio Salas addressed gaps in DNA haplotype databases in 2008. Forensic and disease studies often use haploid DNA, like mitochondrial DNA. Databases of normal size hold only a fraction of all haplotypes. Users still need reliable estimates for the missing types.

Their PLOS ONE article gives methods to estimate haplotype frequency and coverage. Coverage tells how much of a population a database captures. Better estimates strengthen forensic match statistics and population studies. The work helps labs state honestly what their databases miss. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal. Each claim in it can be checked in the full text that sits with this record. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004088:
Qing Chang, Wenxue Tang, Shoeb Ahmad, and co-authors studied ear gap junctions in mice in 2008. Connexin26 and connexin30 build gap junctions in the cochlea. Mutations in either are the top cause of inherited early deafness. How their loss damages hearing was not fully clear.

Their PLOS ONE article reports metabolite transfer fails without connexin30. Gap junctions pass small molecules between cochlear cells. Mice lacking connexin30 showed that transfer compromised. The finding links a hearing protein to the ear's chemical housekeeping. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004188:
Jennifer Serwanga and colleagues published this HIV study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Some people infected with HIV stay free of symptoms for long periods without any antiretroviral therapy. Viral control, CD4 cell loss, and HIV-specific immune responses all help decide how fast the disease moves.

The team studied therapy-naive Ugandans and their HLA-B genes, which shape which virus pieces the immune system attacks. They report that T-cell recognition of the viral Gag protein across several virus clades, tied to certain HLA-B types, correlates with slow disease progression. The link points to the kind of immune response a vaccine would want to copy.
plos-pone-0004288:
Fatemeh Malekzadeh and colleagues published this pilot study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The environmental risk factors behind Crohn's disease, a chronic inflammation of the gut, remain largely unknown. A recent suggestion blamed refrigerated food, on the theory that cold-loving bacteria could be involved.

The team ran a pilot case-control study exploring the link between Crohn's disease and early exposure to domestic refrigeration. Comparing patients' early home environments with those of controls tests whether the fridge hypothesis deserves a larger study. Unusual hypotheses need small, careful tests before big ones. The study was a pilot, meant to guide a bigger one.
plos-pone-0004388:
Radiation can cause tumors, including cancers of the colon. Yet inherited traits change how strong that effect is. Eiram Elahi, Nirosha Suraweera, Emmanouil Volikos, and co-authors hunted those traits in mice. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper used Apc Min mice, a strain prone to gut growths called adenomas. They crossed that line with BALB/c mice, known to be unusually sensitive to radiation tumors.

The team counted adenomas after radiation in the crossed mice. They then mapped the DNA regions tied to higher counts. Five regions, called quantitative trait loci, controlled the outcome. Each locus is a stretch of DNA that shifts the trait. Finding them helps separate inherited risk from radiation dose itself.
plos-pone-0004488:
Air pollution breathed in by a mother before birth may leave a mark on a gene tied to asthma. Frederica Perera, Wan-yee Tang, Julie Herbstman, and co-authors report on it in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their study follows a group of about seven hundred children in New York City. Asthma rates there are among the highest in the United States.

Traffic fumes contain polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, chemicals that cross the placenta. The team linked that exposure to DNA methylation, a chemical mark, on a gene called ACSL3 in the child. The mark is a candidate biomarker, a measurable sign of exposure. If such marks predict asthma, doctors could spot high-risk children early, and cities would have stronger evidence for cleaning traffic air.
plos-pone-0004588:
A mouse protein switched on by interferon helps resist the bacterium behind chlamydia by eating it from inside the cell. Munir Al-Zeer, Hesham Al-Younes, Peter Braun, and co-authors report on it in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is Irga6. Chlamydia infection triggers gamma interferon, a central immune protector in humans and mice. In mice, the primary defense involves the interferon-induced IRG protein family.

The precise mechanisms of that defense were unclear. The team shows Irga6 mediates host resistance against Chlamydia trachomatis via autophagy, the cell's self-eating process, which can digest invaders. Human chlamydia is a major sexually transmitted infection. Understanding how mice clear it naturally may suggest ways to strengthen human defenses.
plos-pone-0004688:
Brant Peterson and colleagues showed that large genomes can help find gene control parts, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Finding the short DNA stretches that switch genes on is still a hard task. One good trick compares DNA across species and looks for parts that stay much the same over time.

That trick has found many control parts in animals with backbones. The team asked if big genomes make the search sharper. Extra DNA can act as a clean backdrop that makes kept parts stand out. If so, species with large genomes become strong tools for gene control hunts.
plos-pone-0004788:
Tina Bianco-Miotto and colleagues showed that methylation of the ABO promoter underlies loss of ABO expression in many leukemia patients, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Loss of A, B, and H blood antigens from red cells is frequent in myeloid cancers. The group had earlier reported such changes in more than half of patients with myeloid malignancies they studied.

The team tested whether promoter methylation silences the ABO gene in those cases. They found methylation does underlie loss in a significant share. The mechanism explains a long noted blood bank puzzle. It may also serve as a disease marker.
plos-pone-0004888:
Marie Bourjade, Alice de Boyer des Roches, and Martine Hausberger showed adult young ratio regulates social behavior of young horses, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Adults play important roles regulating social behaviour of young individuals. Early studies suggest the share of adults in a group shapes how the young develop socially. The team tested if that share shapes aggression and bonding in young horses kept in groups of varied makeup.

More adults means calmer, better integrated youngsters. Group composition is a welfare lever in husbandry. Social learning needs adequate adult models. Horse management can apply ratios directly. These findings offer a firm starting point for the next round of testing.
plos-pone-0004988:
Whale sharks are the ocean's largest fish. The species is declining and poorly studied. Jennifer Schmidt and colleagues sampled their DNA across the oceans. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They compared three major ocean populations. Baseline data were badly needed for conservation planning.

They found low genetic differentiation across the three populations. The sharks mix more than their vast range suggests. Treating them as separate stocks would be a mistake. Conservation must view them as one connected population. The finding also raises questions about their migrations. These giants apparently travel far enough to keep their genes well mixed.
plos-pone-0005088:
Alzheimer's risk climbs with age. Women face higher risk than men. Lisa Placanica, Lei Zhu and Yue-Ming Li looked for a mechanism in mouse brain. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They measured gamma-secretase activity. That enzyme helps carve out the amyloid protein tied to Alzheimer's.

Activity shifted with both age and sex. The enzyme's behavior differed between male and female brains. It also changed across the lifespan. The pattern may explain part of the risk profile of sporadic Alzheimer's. Genetic mutations explain rare early cases, not the common form. This work points at an enzyme whose tuning changes with the two biggest risk factors.
plos-pone-0005188:
Interleukin-3 is a signal that tells blood-forming cells to grow and to take on set roles. It works by docking onto a receptor on those cells and starting a chain of signals inside. Dey and colleagues modeled that docking step in detail in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Their model shows that two interleukin-3 molecules also interact with each other as the larger complex assembles. That cytokine to cytokine contact helps switch the receptor on. The picture adds a step that drug designers must keep in mind when they try to boost or block blood cell growth signals.
plos-pone-0005288:
The human Y chromosome carries blocks of duplicated DNA, and one region holds a puzzling patchwork segment. Schmidt and colleagues traced a gene family related to DUX4 in that region in PLOS ONE in 2009, across humans and other hominoids.

The family sits in a transition zone between the Y chromosome's active and silent parts. Its evolution proved complex, with duplications reshaping the family over time. Mapping that history helps explain how the male chromosome is built and why parts of it vary so much. The Y chromosome is hard to read, with many near-copies of the same stretch, so a clean map of one gene family there is a prize for genome work.
plos-pone-0005388:
Mechanical loading can push stem cells toward becoming bone, a fact with promise for regenerative medicine. How force is converted into that fate choice was the question for Arnsdorf and colleagues in PLOS ONE in 2009. They focused on Wnt signaling, a key fate pathway.

Non-canonical Wnt signaling played a role in the mechanically induced bone fate. So did beta-catenin signaling related to N-cadherin, a cell adhesion protein.
