This cholesterol, carried in high-density particles, had already been linked to spine wear, but its value for judging outcomes was unknown. The team reviewed patients who had a common fusion operation over five years.

Nearly a thousand patients were included, and their recovery was scored by function and cost measures. Statistical screening kept cholesterol level among the factors tied to outcome. A cut point emerged: patients in the normal range recovered better than those with abnormal levels. In patients without brain or vessel disease, the pattern bent into a U shape, with a middle band of levels looking best. The authors caution that the link was modest and uneven across groups. Still, a routine blood value might one day help surgeons set expectations before operating.
plos-pone-0351988:
Broken ribs are easy to miss on chest scans of older patients, whose bones carry extra growths and thinning. Shan Xiong and co-authors tested whether a computer helper improves detection in emergency care, in a 2026 PLOS One study covering more than one thousand chest injury patients.

Six radiologists read scans alone and again with the helper, and a senior panel set the true answers. Reading alone, the doctors caught fewer fresh breaks in patients over sixty than in younger ones. With computer help, their catch rate for older patients rose to match the younger group. False alarms also fell, suggesting real value for busy emergency teams.
plos-pone-0352088:
Malalaniaina Rakotobe and colleagues examined how young brain cells connect in the developing cerebellum of mice. Older microscope work had spotted unusual links between cells in a layer where new neurons are born. The team wanted to know what those links really are, since several kinds of cell bridges can look alike under the microscope.

Using dyes, genetic labels, and live imaging in week-old pups, they separated bridges left over from cell division from other connections. Some dividing-cell bridges were present, while a second bridge type was absent. They also found thin membrane protrusions joining cells, related or not, hinting at a little-studied way cells may talk during brain growth. More work is needed to learn what those links do.
plos-pone-0352188:
Hussen Ebrahim and seven colleagues document what Ethiopian highland farmers know about local forage plants. Their 2026 study surveys three hundred twenty-three smallholders in two districts of the northeastern highlands. Livestock there feed mainly on natural pasture. Scientists have catalogued these herbaceous forages before, but implementation ignored farmers' own knowledge and failed. Interviews and rankings captured how farmers see the resource, its decline, and the obstacles to using it better.

Farmers confirmed the pasture is shrinking alarmingly. Forestland expansion took the largest share of blame, then cropland growth and resettlement. For using local forages, land shortage ranked as the top challenge. Lack of awareness and spreading eucalyptus plantations followed. Farmers had already cut animal numbers in response. The study argues that grazing science starting from this knowledge stands a chance of working. Restoration plans drawn without the people who read these pastures daily have a long record of quietly failing.
plos-pone-0352588:
Erin Wertz and six colleagues fight false claims by adding facts. Their 2026 study ran forty-eight field experiments inside Instagram ads. The targets were people who rarely read news. Short verified videos addressed climate change, vaccines, judging news, and election integrity. The ads reached nearly two and a half million accounts. Over forty thousand viewers completed follow-up assessments.

The intervention worked. Forty-six of the forty-eight tests moved results in the right direction. Forty reached statistical significance. Belief accuracy improved, and so did democratic attitudes and media literacy. Vaccination intentions budged somewhat as well. Effects did not depend on special persuasive tricks or formats. Some climate effects persisted over time. For platforms and public agencies, the study demonstrates a scalable, positive route to resilience: put good information where non-readers already scroll.
plos-pone-0352688:
Rongkang Pei, Zeyu Lyu, and Guolong Wang build an artificial intelligence model for reading social media storms. Their 2026 study tackles narrative structure in posts about public events. Such posts carry opinion, emotion, and fast-moving themes. Older tools treated sentiment, topic, and time separately. The authors fuse all three inside a transformer model built on a RoBERTa language backbone.

The combined model beat four kinds of baseline systems. It recognised narrative structure more accurately. It also classified sentiment and topics better. Performance held up across different events and in noisy, messy text. Those are exactly the conditions of real public opinion monitoring. The authors close with ethics: privacy, anonymisation, and bias all need care. The tool could help officials follow public reaction during crises, provided those safeguards hold.
plos-pone-0352788:
Lucas Souza and seven colleagues build a new blood test for cattle brucellosis in this 2026 study. Brucellosis spreads from animals to people and hurts herds worldwide. Current tests use crude bacterial extracts. Those can react falsely to other germs. The team instead predicted small protein fragments, called epitopes, that the immune system recognises. Synthetic copies became the test's targets.

Two peptides survived screening against known positive and negative cattle sera. Built into a standard laboratory test, they caught eighty-four percent of positive animals. They correctly cleared about eighty-three percent of negatives. A combined multi-epitope protein performed notably worse on both measures. The authors call the work preliminary. Still, defined synthetic targets could eventually replace messy bacterial extracts, giving veterinarians cleaner and more consistent brucellosis screening.
plos-pone-0352888:
Belachew Getnet Eneyew and Workiyie Worie Assefa investigate this 2026 PLOS One study of why wetlands in two districts of northwestern Ethiopia are being turned into farmland. The team combined satellite land-cover records spanning thirty-six years with household surveys and interviews with local experts, then modeled what shapes attitudes toward converting wetlands.

Nearly half the wetland area had become farmland over the study period. Most households and even officials favored conversion despite recognizing wetlands' benefits, and local government had handed wetlands to unemployed graduates and landless families as a jobs measure. Age, land and livestock holdings, and livelihood type all shaped the appetite to convert. The authors urge ecological checks before conversion and wider job creation so families are not forced onto wetlands.
plos-pone-0352988:
Yibo Chen and three colleagues ask, in this 2026 PLOS One study, whether large language models predict people's behavior better when they first predict emotions. The setting is deliberately narrow: personnel in high-pressure, high-stakes roles, drawn from a single cultural background so the data stay consistent. The team built a dataset linking scenarios, emotions, and behaviors, then fine-tuned a language model on it.

The emotion-first model beat both a plain baseline model and a model trained to predict behavior directly, across several accuracy measures. The authors connect this to decision theories that treat emotion as a step in choosing actions. They present the work as a bridge between artificial intelligence and behavioral science, with lessons for forecasting behavior where mistakes are costly.
plos-pone-0353288:
Yang, Wu, and Mo built a classifier for indoor radio positioning in a 2026 study. Ultra-wideband signals locate people and goods indoors, but walls block direct paths and warp the signal. Telling a blocked path from a clear one is the key first step.

Their method combines several fast tree models in parallel and reads signal patches at multiple scales across time and frequency. Tests on a public data set beat deep learning and single-tree rivals on accuracy and held up on new data, with workable computing cost. Reliable blocked-path detection could steady indoor navigation in warehouses, hospitals, and malls where satellite signals fail.
plos-pone-0353388:
Mar Riera-Pagespetit and seven colleagues ask whether sugar control still protects the kidneys after age eighty, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study from Spain. Doctors often relax targets in the very old to avoid dangerous low-sugar episodes, leaving the kidney question open. The team followed more than a thousand patients over eighty with type 2 diabetes and initially healthy kidneys, across five years of records.

Kidney disease appeared in over half of both groups, but clearly more often — and sooner — in those with poor sugar control. Statistical adjustment left the link standing on its own. The authors do not demand strict targets for everyone; they argue sugar control deserves a real place in individualised decisions for the oldest patients.
plos-pone-0353488:
Unahalekhaka and colleagues tracked a drug-resistant hospital germ across Thailand in a 2026 study. The germ resists a last-resort antibiotic family and causes dangerous blood infections with few treatment options. Gene sequencing covered dozens of isolates collected from hospitals nationwide between 2020 and 2024.

One global clone dominated and appeared in region after region. Resistance came mainly from one gene, with a second powerful resistance gene riding on moving DNA pieces in a subset of isolates. That moving piece matched a known carrier found in two clones. Steady gene tracking, the authors argue, is essential to catch spread early and guide hospital infection control.
plos-pone-0353688:
Dejan Mihajlovic and seven colleagues translate a questionnaire about period pain into Serbian and check that it still measures what it should, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The scale asks how much menstrual pain interferes with daily life, a burden most women experience but medicine often underrates. Three hundred and fifty female health-science students with period pain in the past year completed the Serbian version plus a standard stress questionnaire.

The translation held together excellently: items hung on a single factor, consistency scores were high, and scores rose alongside depression, anxiety, and stress scores as expected. Serbian clinicians and researchers now have a validated tool for a complaint long dismissed as normal.
plos-pone-0353788:
Rezapour compared two popular tools for finding genes that switch on or off in a 2026 study. Gene studies guide disease research, yet the tool chosen can change the gene list a team reports. Tests used real and partly simulated data from virus, bacteria, and scarring conditions, with repeated sampling at many sizes.

One tool found more changed genes when samples were few, while the two tools agreed more as samples grew. Genes found only by the other tool, though fewer, predicted outcomes better in fresh data from separate virus studies. The author advises judging tools by whether their gene lists hold up elsewhere, not by list length alone.
plos-pone-0353888:
Yanhua Xiao and six colleagues build a neural network that spots changes between satellite images taken at different times, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Their data are hyperspectral images, which record many narrow colour bands and reveal changes invisible to ordinary cameras. Standard methods compare the two images too crudely and blur fine detail.

Their design extracts deep differences layer by layer, then uses fine interpolation to recover changes smaller than a single pixel. The network is aimed at mixed-resolution image pairs, a common real-world headache. Better change detection feeds land-use monitoring, disaster assessment, and environmental watch-keeping, where missing a small change can mean missing the start of a much bigger one.
plos-pone-0354088:
Madhawi Altaib and three co-authors asked what new speech-language pathologists actually need to succeed at work, in this 2026 PLOS ONE interview study. University training is meant to prepare graduates, yet employers still report gaps. Fifteen people took part in focus groups: former students, teachers, practising clinicians, and employers who hire them.

Four themes ran through the discussions: personal qualities, working independently, solid academic grounding, and day-to-day clinical skill. Attitude, flexibility, and clear decision-making mattered as much as book knowledge. Participants wanted broader hands-on placements and more specialised teaching. Their message is that degree programmes must keep evolving if graduates are to handle varied clinics confidently from day one.
plos-pone-0354288:
Momeni Javad and colleagues map in 2026 where wind is most likely to strip soil in eastern and northeastern Iran, a dry region hit by dust storms. Ten learning models were trained on climate, soil, land shape, and rock data. Two models, a forest based one and a combined ensemble, scored best on standard accuracy checks.

Their maps put roughly a quarter to a third of the area at moderate or high risk. Sandy soil, seasonal temperature and rain patterns, height, and a wetness measure drove the pattern most. The maps can help officials target tree planting, grazing control, and other defences before land degrades further.
plos-pone-0354488:
Kangbien Park, a single author, published this 2026 paper proposing a rulebook for steering evolution in the lab. Directed evolution of creatures that reproduce without sex promises useful microbes and molecules, but experiments stumble at known points. Park sets out ten formal logics meant to handle those difficulties, then tests them in a simulation where an imaginary limb evolves toward a wing.

Simulated populations using the logics reached the target trait about two and a half times faster and with good accuracy, while those without them lagged. Park discusses what would make the approach rigorous in real experiments.
plos-pone-0354588:
Wang and colleagues, in a 2026 laboratory study, examine how a medical collagen sponge made from cow tissue affects macrophages, key immune cells that guide healing. Such sponges are widely used to stop bleeding and fill tissue, and they break down safely in the body. Their effect on immune behavior, though, was largely untested.

In cell cultures, the sponge made macrophages grow faster and eat particles more actively, and it raised their output of a signal that grows new blood vessels. Fluid from those cells then helped vessel cells form tube-like structures. The sponge mildly stirred resting immune cells, yet it calmed cells that had been provoked by a bacterial toxin, cutting their output of inflammatory signals. This two-way action, the authors suggest, helps explain how the sponge supports tissue repair: lively when healing starts, restraining when inflammation runs hot.
plos-pone-0354688:
Vera Sorin and five colleagues published this 2026 study on language models drafting the summary section of chest scan reports. Impressions guide care, but machine drafts can drift into generic wording. Using nearly twelve thousand CT lung artery reports, the team let two large models write summaries with no examples, random examples, or examples retrieved to match each case.

Matched examples won every comparison, and giving more examples at calmer settings helped further. Scores still landed in the middle range, so Sorin insists radiologists must check drafts before any clinical use. The trick is retrieval, not just model size.
plos-pone-0354888:
Liang Xu and Xiao Wu published this 2026 study of how Korean speakers and Chinese learners of Korean handle requests and refusals in conversation. Using written dialogue tasks built around twenty-four linked scenarios, they compared native speakers with intermediate and advanced learners, counting which politeness strategies each group chose and how scenario factors changed those choices.

Native speakers used a wider range of strategies than learners, though advanced learners closed much of the gap. Choices also shifted when several social factors combined. Xu and Wu propose their scenario design as a template for teaching the delicate art of saying no politely.
plos-pone-0355188:
Chaoyang Luo and Jing Bi study in 2026 heat treated coal waste in cement. They ask if it can replace part of the cement in building mixes. Two helpers were added to boost the waste. One was red mud, and the other was a silicate solution. Tests varied the mix in a set grid. Heat flow and microscope tools tracked how the paste set.

The silicate slowed the main setting stage. It also kept water being used at later stages. That points to a longer curing process. Red mud partly made up for strength lost with the waste. Using both helpers gave lower strength than silicate alone. Its inner structure was also looser and less even.
plos-pone-0355288:
Ruo-qiao Wen and colleagues compare in 2026 three ways to extract DNA from blood for finding very faint malaria infections after treatment. Finding hidden low level infections matters where malaria has been nearly wiped out, since missed cases can restart spread. The methods used a spin column, a red cell bursting route, and magnetic beads.

The bead method gave far more DNA, kept long pieces intact, and found more positive cases among faint clinical samples. It also detected the parasite at lower dilutions than the column method. The authors recommend bead extraction for surveillance screening where missing a case carries high risk.
plos-pone-0355488:
Charlotte Goodrose-Flores and Linda Björkhem-Bergman compared quality of life in Swedish women living with lipedema, a painful fat disorder. Lipedema causes abnormal fat build-up, usually in the legs, and is often missed or dismissed. Their 2026 study set women with lipedema beside healthy women and an exploratory group with advanced cancer.

Women with lipedema scored worse than healthy women on every quality-of-life dimension measured. On pain, physical function, and emotional problems, their scores matched the cancer group's. Their general health scores were lower still, and body image worries were markedly higher. They also reported more pain, fatigue, depression, and anxiety. The authors argue lipedema deserves recognition as a heavy burden, not a minor condition.
plos-pone-0355688:
Madalitso Chelenga and colleagues lay out a protocol, published in 2026, for the first global tally of Tritrichomonas foetus. This single-celled parasite has a split reputation. In cattle it is a serious cause of infertility and lost calves. In cats it causes stubborn diarrhea. In pigs it is a harmless gut passenger.

The planned review will search five databases without language limits for prevalence studies in the three hosts. It will pool the numbers by species and region. It will probe how diagnostic method and farm management shift the estimates. Duplicate screening and bias checks are built in. A trustworthy world map of this parasite would show surveillance programs where to look harder. It would also show where control efforts are actually keeping herds clean.
plos-pone-0355988:
Seyed Houtan Shahidi and three colleagues settle a practical question for runners in this 2026 study: does the standard one percent treadmill incline really reproduce outdoor running? Twelve trained male endurance runners completed identical staged workouts indoors on a treadmill and outdoors on a track, with breath-by-breath gas measurement throughout. The team compared running economy, the oxygen cost of covering a kilometer, and total energy cost across intensities.

Outdoor running cost more on every measure. Oxygen cost per kilometer was higher outside at all intensities, and the economy gap widened as effort approached the second ventilatory threshold; carbohydrate burning also rose outdoors near that intensity. The authors conclude the customary one percent grade under-corrects for the road. Athletes and coaches should not treat treadmill numbers as a perfect mirror of outdoor performance when planning training or testing.
plos-pone-0356088:
Igor Loncaric and an international team screened the mouths of Pacific marine mammals along Southern California. They hunted a group of staphylococci better known from dogs and cats. Their 2026 study sampled 452 animals across eight species. The set ran from California sea lions and elephant seals to dolphins and a pygmy sperm whale. Every isolate was then characterized with susceptibility tests and several layers of genetic typing.

They recovered forty-six isolates, mostly one species. Some were resistant to penicillin and tetracycline. A string of brand-new genetic types appeared, alongside fresh virulence genes. The diversity suggests these bacteria are established, evolving residents of marine mammals. They are not stray contaminants. The authors call for long-term monitoring of a potential bridge between wildlife, pets, and people.
plos-pone-0356388:
Benjamin Hägglund and four colleagues validate a cheap way to test pointing accuracy in clinic, in this 2026 study. Reaching precisely to a target is basic to arm function, and disorders of movement control degrade it, yet clinics lack a standardized, affordable test. Their protocol uses a small consumer hand-tracking camera and measures the average error across ten pointing attempts, with each hand, eyes open and closed.

Twenty adults performed the tests while a laboratory-grade multi-camera system recorded the same movements as a reference. With eyes closed, the cheap device's scores lined up moderately to very strongly with the reference system. With eyes open, agreement was weaker, though the average bias stayed small. The authors call the validity acceptable for clinical use and outline the further checks, reliability and sensitivity to change, still needed before routine adoption.
plos-pone-0356488:
Nhan Hien Phan and colleagues reviewed fifty patients aged eighty and over treated for bile duct stones. The treatment was a through-the-liver endoscopic laser procedure at their center in 2023 and 2024. Their 2026 retrospective study chose this route because open surgery is perilous at such ages. A scope is threaded through the liver to shatter stones with a holmium laser. The team graded clearance, complications, and hospital stay.

Every patient finished with complete or near-complete clearance. Most needed a single session, and nobody died from the procedure. About a quarter had adverse events, nearly all minor. Stones lodged both inside and outside the liver, plus active bile duct infection, predicted incomplete clearance and longer stays. The authors present the technique as a feasible lifeline for the very old.
plos-pone-0356688:
Wei Xu and Zhuxin Mao grade the feeding quality of common vetch, a legume forage. It was grown across three climate zones of western China. The zones run from cold alpine plateau to dry loess hills. Forage quality shifts with weather, and farmers need guidance on where and what to plant. Four cultivars grew in replicated plots for one season. The team measured sugars, protein, fat, and fatty acids. Then they blended the traits into a single quality score. The score was built from the data's main patterns.

Place beat cultivar: ecological zone moved most traits more than variety did. Alpine and transitional zones outscored the dry loess zone, with alpine vetch richer in sugars and healthy fats while warm dry conditions capped quality. Xu and Mao advise matching vetch planting to zone strengths when building high-quality forage supplies.
plos-pone-0356788:
Ayesha Liaqat and colleagues designed a candidate tuberculosis vaccine entirely on the computer, stitching together parts of four proteins the TB bacterium uses at different stages of infection. Their 2026 study follows the reverse vaccinology route: predicting which pieces the immune system can see, checking the stitched molecule for safety signals, and simulating how it docks onto an immune sensor.

The construct, named TetraFuVac11, passed the standard computational screens: predicted to be stable, non-allergenic, and non-toxic, and it held its grip on the immune receptor in motion simulations. The team also mapped how to build it in bacteria for laboratory production. None of this proves protection; it produces a well-vetted blueprint that now needs animal and cell experiments.
plos-pone-0356888:
Jingyi Hou and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE hunting for anti-aging compound combinations hidden inside a traditional Chinese herbal formula, Dengzhan Shengmai. Such formulas are synergistic by design, but finding which chemicals cooperate is a needle-in-haystack problem. The team built a deep learning system that fuses molecular properties, safety predictions, and network embeddings of protein interactions, then ranks pairs by whether their joint effect should exceed their separate ones.

The system scored near the top of standard accuracy measures, beating conventional baselines; protein network features carried most weight in its judgments. From thirty profiled chemicals, the three top combinations were tested in artificially aged nerve-like cells, restoring viability, calming oxidative stress, and cutting senescent cells substantially. Gene profiling showed roughly a thousand aging-related gene changes reversed across shared longevity pathways. The framework is offered as a general synergy hunter for complex traditional formulas.
plos-pone-0356988:
Fei Tong and Yinxi Cai examined whether city growth in China's Yangtze River Delta counties keeps people and land in step. They used satellite night lights, population grids, and land cover data from 2013 onward. Their 2026 study trained a deep learning model to extract urban land and population patterns. It scored how coordinated the two were in each county. It also probed which forces drove coordination in each period.

Land urbanized faster than population nearly everywhere, leaving a region-wide mismatch. Yet coordination improved steadily. It spread outward from core cities toward the east. The leading driver changed by era, with foreign investment dominating the earliest period. County-level diagnosis like this helps officials see whether new districts are filling with people or merely with pavement.
plos-pone-0357088:
Xiaoming Li and a large team studied road asphalt blended with very high shares of recycled tire rubber. The rubber made up from three tenths to half of the mix. The team also studied how heat and oxygen age such blends. Their 2026 study baked samples in laboratory aging ovens. It then probed stiffness, cold cracking behavior, and chemistry. It also tracked vapor emissions across the material's simulated life.

The richest rubber blend behaved unexpectedly well at first. Aging made its rubber network swell and cross-link. That fought the separation that plagues such mixes. It also shielded the asphalt beneath from hardening, a sacrificial protection. The trade-off arrived in deep cold, where the dense skeleton relaxed stress poorly. Late life brought peeling at the rubber and asphalt boundary. The work maps both the promise and the expiry date of tire-heavy roads.
plos-pone-0357288:
Katherine Young is first author on a 2026 PLOS ONE subgroup analysis of a trial in severe lung infection caught during hospital care. Such infections increasingly involve germs that resist carbapenems, a last-line drug class, leaving few options. The study drug adds relebactam to imipenem to shield it from bacterial enzymes.

Within the RESTORE-IMI 2 trial, the authors compared patients whose lung germs resisted imipenem but stayed sensitive to the pairing against those with sensitive germs. Death rates by day twenty-eight were similar in the two groups. New resistance to the pairing emerged during treatment in only three patients. Lab checks described the resistant isolates in detail.
plos-pone-0357388:
Julia Reddy leads a team of eight following substance exposed newborns who went home without a child protection report, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Hospitals may discharge such infants when no safety concern is apparent, but what happens over the following years was unknown. The study linked California births from 2018 to protection records, comparing exposed children with unexposed ones across their first five years.

Fewer than fourteen percent of exposed children were ever reported for maltreatment harm in that window. Still, exposed children were modestly more likely to be reported, and to have a report confirmed, than unexposed children, by roughly three percentage points. The same small elevation appeared even when the only exposure was cannabis. The authors suggest that families judged safe at birth may still benefit from voluntary support, rather than surveillance alone, to keep risk low.
plos-pone-0357488:
Hung-Chih Yeh and co-authors test whether lifting straps change scores on a standard full-body strength test. The test asks athletes to pull hard against a fixed bar at thigh height while standing on a force plate. Thirty men took part, half trained judo players and half students who lift weights for fitness, and each man pulled both with straps and bare-handed in random order.

Straps raised peak force, speed of force build-up, and total push across both groups, with no special extra gain for either group. Judo players still showed stronger grips in a separate squeeze test. Yeh and colleagues argue that straps let the test measure whole-body strength rather than grip limits, so labs should state clearly which way they test.
plos-pone-0357588: Starek and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on catheters steered by magnets inside the body. Doctors guide these soft tubes with outside magnets during heart procedures. In lab tests, the team measured how much force the catheter tips apply. They compared different catheters and settings head to head. The right force matters: too little fails to treat, too much can harm tissue.
plos-pone-0357788: Rico-Bolívar and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on why people living with HIV end up in hospital. The records came from a large specialist hospital in Bogotá, Colombia, covering 2018 through 2024. Sorting the causes over those years shows how needs shifted, including through the pandemic. Hospitals can use such counts to plan beds, clinics, and support for this patient group.
plos-pone-0357888:
Olivia Young led a team of seven authors testing loving-kindness meditation in a randomized trial, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. This practice involves wishing well to oneself and others. The team asked whether it can ease pain and improve social well-being, two things that often worsen together in chronic illness.

Young's trial used random assignment and a control comparison, the strongest design for such a question. If a gentle, low-cost practice delivers measurable relief, it could sit beside standard care without drugs or side effects. The social side matters too: pain isolates people, and a practice aimed at connection may help on both fronts. Careful trials are how ancient practices earn, or fail to earn, a place in modern care.
plos-pone-0357988:
Abdushukur I Rakhmatullaev led a team of five authors screening Uzbek apple varieties for disease resistance, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Local apples face apple scab, powdery mildew, and fire blight, three costly orchard diseases. Instead of waiting for symptoms, the team used genetic markers to hunt resistance in local varieties.

Rakhmatullaev's marker-assisted screening speeds up the search for hardy trees adapted to Central Asian conditions. Varieties that already grow well locally, and carry resistance, are gold for breeding programs. Importing foreign varieties can fail on climate or taste; improving local stock avoids both traps. The markers found here let breeders select resistant seedlings early, cutting years from orchard development.
plos-pone-0358588:
Kunmiao Xu led a team of six authors redesigning highway guardrails, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Guardrails must stop speeding cars without becoming hazards themselves. The team designed an extra-high grade rail from a strong steel grade called 700L, aiming for a lighter rail that still holds firm after impact.

Xu's work covers both the lightweight design and how stable the rail leaves a vehicle after a hit. Stronger steel means less material for the same protection, saving cost and transport weight. Road agencies replacing aging rails need designs proven in analysis before roadside use. The study speaks to a quiet truth of road safety: the barrier beside the road saves as many lives as the brakes in the car.
plos-pone-0358688:
Karen A Sullivan and Keeley Lappin survey how the public experiences concussion coverage inside live sports broadcasts, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Broadcasts reach millions during games, and what commentators say in the moments after a head knock shapes how families and junior coaches treat the injury. One hundred sixty-three respondents rated thirty statements about the portrayal and twelve proposals for improving it.

Agreement clustered on a clear message: the portrayal should improve. A majority endorsed twelve of the thirty perception statements, and ten of the twelve recommendations won agreement, led by the demand that coverage prioritize player health over spectacle. Perceptions did not split by personal background or concussion history; the appetite for better coverage was shared. The authors argue broadcasters hold an underused public health channel, and that audiences are ready for it to carry accurate, health first information.
plos-pone-0358788:
Shi Chen leads a team of eight estimating a hidden population, gay and bisexual male students at colleges in China's Hainan Province, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The group faces elevated HIV and syphilis risk, and student infections are rising, yet no one knew the population's size, which prevention planning requires. The team harvested user data from Blued, the main gay social network app, over ten days in May 2023, and combined it with a questionnaire for a multiplier estimate.

Nearly nine in ten surveyed students used the app, and three quarters of them used it to seek partners. The multiplier method put the college population at roughly three and a half thousand men, concentrated in the cities of Haikou and Sanya. Two smaller cities showed unusually high shares of active users. The authors direct sexual health outreach first to these hotspots and active networks.
plos-pone-0359288: Kirts and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper that builds a new tool for music research. The tool, called MEEM, asks listeners about the feelings a piece of music stirs in them, in modular sections. The team then ran checks on how well the tool holds up as a measure. A sound tool helps researchers compare, across studies, how songs move listeners.
pmc-13197388:
Saul González-Hilario and colleagues review the arms race between antiviral proteins and viruses in 2026. IFIT proteins are part of the body's first-line defense. They spot viral RNA, the virus's genetic code, by odd features at its tip and block its use.

Viruses fight back with tricks that make their RNA look like host RNA. Some add the same chemical marks, some steal caps from host messages, and some borrow host enzymes. Two less-studied IFIT members steady the defense complex and tune its grip on RNA. The authors propose future drugs that strip viral disguises, so the innate immune system, the body's built-in first defense, can spot the virus again.
pmc-13198888:
Ivan Bivolarski and colleagues present a 2026 case report on mixed treatment signals in spread prostate cancer. Doctors track this cancer with scans and PSA, a blood marker. When scans improve while the marker rises, teams face a hard call on whether therapy works.

Their patient was a 72-year-old man with high-risk prostate cancer spread widely to bone. After systemic therapy, targeted scans showed partial response, yet PSA kept climbing. Inflammation markers in blood rose too. Standard scans still showed mixed bone lesions, part hardened and part eaten away. The authors read the clash as uneven tumor behavior and early resistance. They urge combined tracking of scans, markers, and inflammation.
pmc-13199188:
Hani Belhadj and colleagues profiled a microbe from bee pollen for new antibiotics in a 2026 study. Drug resistance is dulling current antibiotics, and soil microbes of the Streptomyces group make most natural ones. The team isolated a new strain from pollen gathered by Algerian bees and probed its chemistry.

The strain strongly curbed three test microbes, including a staph germ and a yeast. Gene and microscope checks confirmed its group. Chemical profiling found a rich mix: fatty compounds, scent-like volatiles, and more than forty nonvolatile bioactive compounds. Known antibiotics sat among them, plus other drug-like classes. The strain's rich output makes it a strong lead for natural product hunting.
pmc-13202188:
Teens may know which foods carry key vitamins yet still not eat them, and a 2026 survey headed by Tripti Shrestha checks that gap in Nepal. The cross-sectional study assessed knowledge, attitudes, and practices about micronutrients among teens in Madhyabindu Municipality, using a school-based sample.

Surveys went to 755 teens between October and December 2022, selected through multistage random sampling. About half showed adequate knowledge of micronutrient-rich foods, fewer held positive attitudes, and fewer still noted good eating practices in daily life. Maternal education, family income, parents' occupations, and nutrition content in the school curriculum all shaped the results, prompting calls for family-inclusive education.
pmc-13214188:
Elysse Bautista-González and colleagues reconstruct in 2026 the long road lung cancer patients travel to treatment at Mexico's national cancer institute. Fragmented services and weak referrals stretch the journey and deepen inequality in a disease where delay kills.

Records for 2,645 suspected cases admitted between 2004 and 2021 were combined with structured interviews with forty-six patients. Four diagnostic pathways emerged, and the median time from first symptom to treatment ran between five and eight months depending on route. Interviews exposed late symptom recognition, wrong first diagnoses, scattered referrals, money worries, and long travel. Most patients had bounced between several public and private providers before arriving.
pmc-13217188:
Hadi and colleagues report a case of Menkes disease where a child lived far longer than the usual course. Menkes disease is an X-linked disorder of copper handling, caused by faults in the ATP7A gene. It damages the brain and nerves, weakens connective tissue, and marks the hair and bones in ways doctors can recognise.

Most children with the classic form die by about age three. This patient's new gene variant came with a milder, prolonged path, which the team documents in detail. Single cases like this stretch what is known about a disease. They also hint that some variants may leave enough copper transport working to change the outlook.
pmc-13218188:
Sharon L. Cadogan and co-authors test whether common acute infections raise the risk of severe mental illness, in a 2026 matched cohort study using United Kingdom health records. Infections trigger body-wide inflammation, and inflammation has been suspected in the origins of psychosis and bipolar disorder, but data on everyday infections were thin. The team ran six matched cohort studies from primary care records spanning 2007 to 2024.

Adults with gastroenteritis, chest, skin, or urinary infections, sepsis, or meningitis and encephalitis were matched with up to five uninfected people. Follow-up tracked new diagnoses of schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, or another psychosis. Every infection carried a higher risk after adjustment, rising from a modest increase for skin infections to more than triple the risk after meningitis or encephalitis, with sepsis high. The authors suggest that prompt infection treatment, mental health support after severe infections, and vaccination where relevant could help limit this risk.
pmc-13223888:
Ureej Akram and co-authors review photoresponsive microgels, soft polymer particles that swell or shrink under light, in a 2026 article. Light-sensitive groups built into the gel network drive the quick response. The review gathers synthesis and design schemes, explains how the light response works, and surveys testing methods for these materials.

Uses range from drug delivery and tissue scaffolds to soft robotic parts, sensors, smart coatings, catalysis, water cleanup, and photonic devices. The gels are described as biocompatible, functional, and fairly low in toxicity. Recent work and future directions close the survey, which maps a small material with an outsized range of possible jobs.
pmc-13225288:
Luwen Hu and colleagues develop a 2026 eye-drop formulation for fungal keratitis, a sight-threatening corneal infection. The standard drug, natamycin, dissolves poorly in water and irritates the eye surface. The team packed it into fatty bubbles called liposomes and decorated them with apo-transferrin, a protein that starves microbes of iron while also fighting them directly.

Laboratory checks confirmed the decorated particles formed evenly and carried the drug as intended. Early results showed the formulation loaded and released natamycin in a controlled way, and safety testing in corneal cells and mice followed. The design aims to keep the drug on the eye longer while adding the protein's own antifungal and calming effects.
pmc-13226788:
Zhongya Gu and colleagues test a 2026 light-based therapy in mice bred to develop Alzheimer's-like disease, asking whether the brightness of flickering light changes its benefit. Flicker at forty flashes per second has attracted attention as a gentle way to nudge brain rhythms, but intensity had not been compared directly. Young adult bred mice received either bright or dim visual flicker.

Bright flicker improved the animals' cognitive performance and cut amyloid deposits in both the visual cortex and the hippocampus, a memory centre. Dim flicker changed molecules only in the visual cortex, with little effect elsewhere. Blocking autophagy, the cell's cleanup system, weakened the bright-light benefits, tying the effect to that cleanup pathway.
pmc-13226988:
Marco Oltrecolli and co-authors review a 2026 treatment landscape for male germ cell cancers that stop responding to platinum chemotherapy. These tumours, the commonest cancers in younger men, are usually highly curable thanks to platinum sensitivity. Trouble begins at second or later relapse, where expected survival drops below a year and standard options narrow sharply.

At first relapse, salvage chemotherapy still cures about half of patients, and high-dose regimens repeatedly outperform standard doses in large retrospective series, though proof from prospective trials is pending. Beyond that, ordinary cytotoxic drugs remain the mainstay because targeted agents have yet to show real activity. Approaches aimed at a surface protein called Claudin-6 look most promising among the emerging options surveyed.
pmc-13230288:
Yingdi Liao and colleagues gather in 2026 animal studies that tried boosting the immune receptor TREM2 in Alzheimer disease models. TREM2 guides how brain immune cells respond to amyloid plaques and tau tangles, two hallmarks of the disease. The team searched three databases and combined results from twelve studies.

Raising TREM2 levels in one common mouse model cut plaque counts and plaque area, with stronger gains in younger animals. Antibodies that activate the receptor also lowered plaque numbers in several models. Effects on tau and on soluble amyloid forms were less steady across studies. Memory problems eased in treated animals. Benefits depended on disease stage, model type, and how the receptor was targeted.
pmc-13232588:
Wei Sun and colleagues design in 2026 a layered magnet whose spin pattern can be set to six states by sliding its sheets. Altermagnets split electron spins without overall magnetism, a trait wanted for low-power spin electronics. Electric control of that splitting has been the missing piece for real devices.

Calculations on a two-layer manganese phosphorus sulfur crystal show sliding along three distinct paths flips the electric polarization. Each path also turns the spin pattern by a fixed step, giving six stable, switchable states instead of the usual two. Each state leaves a distinct fingerprint in a sideways voltage response, so states can be read electrically. Multi-state memory built this way could pack more logic into one cell.
pmc-13233188:
Jingkang Xia and colleagues published a 2026 systematic review of video studies on hamstring strain injuries in soccer. Watching match footage lets researchers see the exact movement and body position at the moment a hamstring tears, detail that medical records rarely capture. The team searched seven databases and gathered seven studies covering 342 injuries in eleven-a-side football.

Non-contact injuries were reported far more often than injuries involving indirect contact, and sprint-type injuries more often than mixed-type ones. Comparisons of sprinting against stretching, attacking against defending, and first half against second half showed no clear differences. Pooled figures pointed to sprinting and running actions as the typical setting. Extra analyses of posture and sex differences were treated as exploratory.
pmc-13233888:
Dominik Tschimmel, Tim Hucho, and Steffen Waldherr published a 2026 mathematical study of antibody staining curves used across biology laboratories. Staining strength is usually read from dose-response curves, and the classic Langmuir model assumes binding reaches equilibrium. Real staining protocols break that assumption, because antibodies accumulate permanently while the free supply in solution drains away.

For a uniform field of binding sites, the authors solve the depletion model exactly and derive inequalities ordering it against simpler models. For patchy, realistic binding landscapes, where exact solutions seem impossible, they prove a well-behaved solution exists and bracket it between bounds. Those bounds let experimentalists estimate how much antibody depletion bends their curves, improving how staining protocols are designed and interpreted.
pmc-13234288:
Carolin Haas and colleagues presented in 2026 a short questionnaire for judging suicide risk in primary care. The ten-item tool, called SuPr-10, was built for patients who already show depressive symptoms. Existing screening often misses protective factors, such as reasons for living and sources of support. The team tested the questionnaire in several groups of German-speaking patients.

Validation work covered more than five hundred participants whose depression scores met a set threshold. Statistical checks found two parts, one covering protection and one covering risk. Scores lined up well with established measures of suicidality and depression. The tool separated people with a past attempt history at a modest level. The authors stress that broader testing is needed before wider use.
pmc-13234988:
Anna-Lena Wetterteg, Jacques Riad, and Per Nordin piloted in 2026 a simple graded test for recovery after a torn Achilles tendon. Thompson's test squeezes the calf and watches whether the foot moves, signalling tendon connection. Their four-point scale grades movement of the injured foot against the healthy side. Twenty-four patients treated without surgery were tested repeatedly during the first twelve weeks.

Two physiotherapists graded movement visually while a three-dimensional motion system measured the same motion. Agreement within and between the visual examiners was high in the pilot results. Agreement between the visual scale and the motion system was only moderate, though. Average foot movement rose over follow-up in both measurement approaches. The authors judge the scale reliable for clinicians, while its accuracy against instrumented measurement needs further study with a refined setup.
pmc-13235088:
Joseph Roux de Bezieux and colleagues searched in 2026 for a blood marker that predicts bleeding during heart bypass surgery. Patients often take two antiplatelet drugs together until surgery, which raises bleeding concern. Four platelet-related proteins were measured in one hundred forty-three patients before their operations. Standard platelet function tests and later blood loss from chest drains provided comparisons.

Two proteins, called PF4 and NAP-2, ran much lower in patients on dual therapy than on aspirin alone. Their levels matched several laboratory measures of platelet reactivity in the study. Levels of both proteins also related independently to blood lost during the first day after surgery. The other two proteins showed no useful links to outcomes or test results. The authors name PF4 as the most platelet-specific candidate for guiding care around surgery.
pmc-13236988:
Gaber and colleagues tailor a family of borate glasses for two jobs at once: bending light and blocking gamma rays. The glasses mix borate with a ceramic compound known as BCZT, made by the standard melt and quench route. Tests confirmed every sample stayed glassy, with no crystals, while density rose as the mix changed.

The team measured how the glasses handle light, including nonlinear effects prized in photonics, and how well they shield radiation. A cheap, lead-free glass that blocks gamma rays could serve in medical and nuclear settings. Showing that one recipe can be tuned for both optics and shielding widens where such glasses might be used.
pmc-13238688:
Zijie Xiang and a large team reviewed in 2026 how failing mitochondria drive aging-related disease, and what stands in the way of treating them. Mitochondria, the cell's energy plants, falter with age both from internal damage and from breakdowns in the systems that recycle, split, merge, and rebuild them. Escaped mitochondrial DNA can also trigger inflammation through an alarm pathway.

The review connects these failures to muscle, bone, brain, heart, and metabolic diseases. Candidate treatments range from metabolic tuning to transplanting healthy mitochondria and editing mitochondrial DNA directly. Tissue-to-tissue differences in mitochondria remain a major obstacle to clinical use. The authors aim to move mitochondrial medicine from mechanism toward precise intervention.
pmc-13238788:
Mitu Rani Sarker and colleagues enriched gluten-free noodles in 2026 with tomato powder and defatted soybean flour, then measured nutrition, cooking behavior, texture, and taste. Tomato levels ran from five to twenty percent, with soy flour fixed at ten percent. Rising tomato content steadily lifted phenolics, flavonoids, and antioxidant capacity across several assays.

Fiber, protein, and minerals such as calcium and magnesium also climbed, and the noodles absorbed more water and yielded more when cooked. Texture turned softer, though cohesiveness and springiness held steady. Tasters preferred the batch with fifteen percent tomato powder, rating its flavor and overall acceptability highest. The authors present the pairing as a practical route to functional noodles for people avoiding gluten.
pmc-13239288:
Anastasios Koulaouzidis, Wojciech Marlicz, and Ervin Toth wrote a 2026 letter challenging claims for hybrid endoscopy in Crohn's disease, where a capsule camera examination is paired with colonoscopy on the same day. The original article credited standard colonoscopy preparation for better capsule images in patients in remission. The letter writers say the claims outrun the data on several fronts.

The preparation regimen itself was never fully specified. Both groups shared the same median cleansing score despite a claimed difference. The relapse analysis rested on tiny subgroups shaped by doctors' discretionary choices. More purgative, they note, does not reliably mean more diagnostic yield in the wider literature. Timing may matter more than intensity. They ask for distributions, justified protocols, and proof of benefit beyond the capsule alone.
pmc-13239388:
Janis Timsans and co-authors describe a 2026 case of stubborn inflammatory muscle disease linked to the anti-Jo-1 antibody. A middle-aged woman had severe muscle weakness and pain from 2019 onward, and every standard immune-suppressing treatment failed to control her condition.

Clinicians then tried tofacitinib, a Janus kinase inhibitor normally approved for joint diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis. Her strength improved markedly, a muscle enzyme in her blood returned to normal, and steroid treatment could be stopped. The authors say this is the first reported success for this drug class in anti-Jo-1 myopathy without lung involvement, and they suggest it deserves study in similar resistant cases.
pmc-13239788:
Emi Watanabe and team built a short form for gauging teamwork that crosses job lines in a 2026 study. Such work asks mental health staff to let go of parts of their own role and share one frame with peers. No form in use caught that skill, so the team set out to make one.

They drew on past work, expert review, and data from staff in a Japanese training course. The final form has ten items in two groups. One group covers working across lines, and the other covers use of that skill in patient care. Scores held steady across jobs and sexes. Scores also rose with note after a year of training. The form is offered for judging team-based care.
pmc-13240088:
Anthony K Dah and colleagues report a hidden cause of infertility in Ghana in a 2026 case paper. Tuberculosis of the female genital tract often produces no clear symptoms, quietly damaging the womb and tubes, and standard tests miss it because very few bacteria are present in genital samples.

A camera inspection of the womb combined with tissue analysis confirmed the diagnosis even though a molecular test was negative. The authors believe this is Ghana's first published case confirmed that way, and they urge doctors in endemic regions to keep suspicion high.
pmc-13240188:
Huang and colleagues build a screening platform that makes prime editing, a precise DNA rewriting tool, fast enough to test many gene variants. Their platform, EvoPRIME, sharpens the process and enriches for cells that took the edit.

The team reports efficiency matching the best current systems, without needing to disable the cell's repair guards. Sharp screens like this can finally sort harmful variants from harmless ones at scale.
pmc-13240388:

A gradient boosting model beat two traditional statistical models and an established nomogram at separating patients by risk. It found a group with under three percent ten-year recurrence risk. Applying its strata could trim follow-up imaging by roughly a tenth, pending outside validation.
pmc-13240988:
Berding's team in Georgia dissected the language of surgeons' posts sharing research on the platform formerly called Twitter. Eighty-four posts came from 17 of the most-followed surgeon accounts. The posts skewed highly analytic but low in warmth and authenticity. Formal, analytic wording tracked with fewer readers and citations, not more. Confident clout helped readership, and a negative tone surprisingly raised impact. Whether the linked article was open access made no significant difference.
pmc-13241488:
Sharkawy's team at Cairo built hybrid-mode cruise control for electric cars. Their smart controller switches among cruising, spacing, and braking modes. One software platform tunes settings and gains online in real time. A real electric vehicle on a test rig faced a lidar-spotted virtual leader.

The car held speed and gap through harsh test runs. Cruising tracked at 98 percent accuracy, spacing control close behind. Braking lagged at 55 percent, limited to coasting-only slowing. Sharkawy offers the unified scheme as relief from driveline math headaches. All three modes ran in one scheme.
pmc-13241888:
Jia Wang and a large team report a 2026 nanoparticle study for triple-negative breast cancer, a type that responds poorly to immunotherapy. pmc-13242588:
Yao Zhang and co-authors mapped how colorectal tumors build an immune-suppressing neighborhood, using single-cell data and large public datasets. Their study appeared in Cancer Informatics in 2026. pmc-13245788:
Heirani Moghaddam, Cressman, and Manson tested how people adapt their reaching when vision is distorted, in this 2026 PLOS One experiment. For half, the cursor was rotated slightly; for the others, it was mirror-flipped across the body's midline.

Under the mirror flip, only about half learned at all, and none showed that unconscious learning. The contrast suggests mirror reversals force a different, more deliberate strategy than rotations, a point that matters for rehabilitation and training design.
pmc-13246488:
Yilmaz and co-authors review a new direction for farm sensing in this 2026 Global Challenges article. Smart farming already uses buried probes to track soil moisture, temperature, acidity, and nutrients, but rigid probes cover little ground and can be fragile. The authors ask whether geotextiles, the fabric sheets already spread over fields, could carry flexible sensors across whole plots.

Their conclusion is that fabric-based, large-area sensing is plausible and could adapt as conditions change. Such platforms, they argue, would give precision agriculture denser, cheaper soil data for healthier soil management.
pmc-13246688:
Issa Abuiram, Noor Hassline Mohamed, and Praneetha Palasuberniam measure exam anxiety among Palestinian university students in a 2026 survey. Exam anxiety blends worry and body arousal around tests and can drag down grades. War strain and money pressure may deepen it for Palestinian students.

Heavy study load, low family income, smoking, and illness predicted worse anxiety. Strong family support and high grades guarded against it. Students who exercised rarely fared worse than regular movers. The model explained about a fifth of the spread in scores.
pmc-13247588:
van der Coelen, Sas, and Richter-Unruh followed hormone patterns in girls with Turner syndrome to foresee ovarian failure, in this 2026 Journal of the Endocrine Society study. Turner syndrome, a missing or altered X chromosome, often shuts the ovaries down early, and predicting which girls keep ovarian function matters for fertility counseling. Girls who entered puberty spontaneously had shown lower FSH and higher AMH, the hormone marking egg reserve, already before age eight. In a joint statistical model, lower AMH significantly predicted earlier ovarian insufficiency, while FSH did not. Individual predictions stayed very uncertain, however. The authors say AMH informs counseling but a dependable personal prediction model needs more data.
pmc-13247788:
Ho, Chan, Lo, and co-authors asked whether diabetes medicines protect against depression, in this 2026 Psychological Medicine cohort study. Depression diagnoses were compared between patients exposed to each glucose-lowering drug and those not exposed.

Exposure to any antidiabetes agent was linked to substantially lower risk of a first depression diagnosis. Several individual drugs, starting with metformin, showed the same direction. Sensitivity analyses, including longer exposure windows and single-drug use, supported the pattern. The authors are careful: records cannot prove the drugs prevent depression, and mechanisms need dedicated research.
pmc-13248488:
Chen and Feng studied whether China's bulk drug-buying policy changed how drug firms innovate, reported in 2026. Firms covered by the policy raised research spending intensity by about a fifth relative to its average, and gained more patents each year. Gains grew over the first four years and were strongest in large, private, and chemical drug firms. The authors read this as firms shifting money from marketing toward real research.
pmc-13248788:
Enshi Lu and co-authors build learning models to diagnose a traditional Chinese syndrome in sleeplessness and stomach pain in a 2026 study. The syndrome, liver-spleen disharmony, guides herbal care, yet its criteria vary by doctor. A data-driven rule could steady diagnosis.

A decision tree method won clearly on accuracy and balance of errors. Low mood or irritability ranked as the top clue, ahead of belly fullness and rib-side pain. The model offers clinics a shared yardstick for this syndrome.
pmc-13249188: Boucher, Shamma, and Boubenec issued this correction in PLOS Biology in 2026. It concerns their paper on blood flow responses in the premotor cortex, the brain area that helps plan movement, during decision making. Some supporting figures were wrong: in one, the spots labeled T and R were swapped, and panels showing how brain positions were matched across images needed fixing. The notice supplies the corrected figures. The paper's main claim, that these responses track what the animal perceives more than how it moves, stands unchanged.
pmc-13250388: Awan writes a 2026 letter in Clinical Case Reports about watching children whose duodenum is blocked after seatbelt injuries. The blockage can come from a blood collection behind the abdominal lining, and careful non-surgical care may suit stable children. Awan argues that monitoring should not rest on stomach tube output alone. Teams should set escalation triggers in advance, combining tube output, the child's overall condition, inflammation markers, nutrition, and selective imaging, so worsening cases move to stronger treatment without delay.
pmc-13251188:

pmc-13253188:

pmc-13253288:
Martyna Cieślik and colleagues review what happens when therapeutic bacteriophages meet macrophages in the human body in a 2026 article. Once inside a patient, however, they are foreign particles, and the immune system treats them accordingly.

Macrophages, the immune system's large scavenger cells, are central to that encounter. They clear circulating phages from blood and tissue, which can shorten treatment and blunt its antibacterial effect. Understanding them may let clinicians dose phages around immune clearance and may even turn phage-immune effects into treatments themselves.
pmc-13253788:
Prabesh Ojha and colleagues run computer tests on tiny silver wires in a 2026 study. After cooling, the wires were pulled in virtual tensile tests at varied strain rates.

Wires fused at lower heat with faster heating kept higher yield strength, since limited atom movement preserved twin boundaries. Faster pulling also raised strength. pmc-13253888:

pmc-13253988:

pmc-13254988:

pmc-13255388:

pmc-13255988:

pmc-13256088:

pmc-13256488:

pmc-13256988:

pmc-13257588:

pmc-13258888:

pmc-13259188:

pmc-13259288:

Botanists gain a rare look at dual secretion logistics.
pmc-13259388:

pmc-13259488:

pmc-13259688:
Chengqian Chen and coauthors review Hodgkin lymphoma care shifting from cure at any cost toward functional cure in a 2026 article. pmc-13260688:

pmc-13260788:

pmc-13260888:

pmc-13261088:

pmc-13261988:

pmc-13262888:

Tracking error combines sideways drift and heading angle, held within preset limits. The team built a joint simulation platform with human drivers in the loop. pmc-13263188:

The gap between methods was largest for zone I fractures and shrank across zones II and III. Small movements at the break fell as the fracture line neared the midline, suggesting a better fit there.
pmc-13263288:

pmc-13263488:

A previous calf strain came with about two and a half times the odds of later rupture, and most paired injuries hit the same leg, on average about two years apart. Three quarters of injured players returned, but efficiency, wins, and playing time all fell sharply afterward. Video showed a consistent false-step mechanism in nearly all cases with footage.
pmc-13263888:

pmc-13264088:

Educators and policy makers can use the dataset to design support that matches student concerns.
pmc-13264288:

pmc-13264588:

pmc-13264888:

Death rates were high, especially with solid cancers and liver cirrhosis. Drug-related cases and blood cancers fared better. The findings support care tailored to the underlying cause, planned by several specialists together.
pmc-13264988:

Disease was uncontrolled in 72.5 percent of patients, yet in 43.7 percent of those cases no treatment change was made. Inertia linked to traits like former smoking, fewer past flare-ups, and patient satisfaction with treatment. Doctors judged disease controlled in over two thirds of uncontrolled cases, a sharp perception gap, while the mismatch was small in truly controlled cases. Treatment satisfaction and lack of recent flare-ups most swayed doctors' views. The authors urge standard, structured follow-up for severe COPD.
pmc-13265888:

They removed the stone, cut out the pouch, and repaired the urethra. Tissue examination completed the assessment. The case adds guidance for similar rare presentations.
pmc-13266188:

pmc-13266988:

pmc-13267488:

pmc-13268488:

pmc-13269088:
Fanny Sandberg and co-authors track in 2026 how donor DNA fragments in blood and urine fluctuate in kidney and liver transplant patients over the first two years. The authors advise reading each patient's own trend alongside cutoffs, and weighing the absolute measure more in liver and urine testing.
pmc-13269888:

Training is shared across devices without moving private data.

pmc-13270288:
Christian W Schmitt and co-authors age in 2026 a family of sulfur-rich plastics called inverse vulcanised polymers, testing how sunlight, heat, moisture, acidity, and microbes wear them down. The team exposed common versions to real and simulated environments and tracked the changes.

The results give designers a rule of thumb: pick stubborn chemistry for long outdoor life, or degradable chemistry where controlled disappearance is the goal.
pmc-13270888:
Ricarda S. Schulz led a 2026 cohort study on whether cognitive decline, a drop in thinking and memory performance, raises stroke risk in older women. Past work linked poor thinking scores to stroke, but change over time had rarely been studied as a moving process.

The analysis used 5,093 United States women health workers, average age 66, from the Women's Health Study, followed for an average of 11.6 years. In that time, 302 strokes occurred. Women were grouped by their four-year change in thinking scores, from most improved to most declined. Stroke risk did not rise in a clear pattern across those groups, with the greatest-decline group close to the most-improved group.
pmc-13272388:
Nagaraj Segar and Vijayarajan Vijayan present in 2026 CITADEL, a blockchain system for health records built to resist quantum-era attacks while letting hospitals learn from shared data. Medical records hold very private facts, and future quantum machines could break today's codes. No past design joined privacy, quantum-safe security, and shared learning in one frame.

Hospitals train shared models in time slices, each weighted on its own. On made-up records for five thousand patients at ten sites, the system beat nine rival methods at predicting return visits within thirty days.
pmc-13272488:
Susannah Waxman and Adriana Di Polo reviewed blood vessel damage and repair in glaucoma for a 2026 article. Glaucoma damages the optic nerve and is a leading cause of blindness that cannot be reversed. Most care lowers eye pressure, yet the authors focus on the vessels that feed the retina.

The review explains how healthy eye vessels are built and controlled, then sets out how flow fails in glaucoma. Weak blood supply can starve retinal ganglion cells, the nerve cells that carry visual signals. Since vessels can regrow and reshape more readily than neurons, repair may protect those cells. The authors list open questions and research paths for vessel based treatments.
pmc-13272688:

They said they remembered 35.1 percent, but half of the repeats were caught and 20.2 percent of new films were wrongly claimed. Only 1.3 percent of all films yielded a correct name code or case position, so memory alone rarely identified anyone.
pmc-13273188:

C-Fos switched on another enzyme that makes the molecule from glutamate instead, a backup route. C-Fos also raised genes that push tumors toward a hard to treat nerve like form. The authors suggest blocking these enzymes could weaken tumors and expose them to cell death.
pmc-13273888:
Aishwarya N and co-authors created DriveNet, a dataset for recognizing driver posture, in a 2026 data article. Poor seating posture strains the neck and shoulders of people who drive for work. An alert system that spots bad posture could prompt correction, but training one needs many labeled images.

Three volunteers performed each posture in turn while a smartphone camera recorded video, and frames were sampled to build equal class sets. The images are meant for training and testing machine learning classifiers that judge seating posture. The authors offer the dataset to support ergonomic monitoring research aimed at cutting musculoskeletal risk for occupational drivers.
pmc-13273988:
Daniel Pfeifer, Markus Graf, and Clas Rurik introduce a 2026 journal article describing Genestrip, a computer tool for sorting DNA reads. Such tools match short DNA fragments, called reads, against reference genomes to name the organism they came from. Older tools need huge amounts of computer memory to do this.

Genestrip instead builds small databases for chosen groups of organisms, from a dozen to a few thousand species. The authors report results on par with a leading tool while using only a fraction of the memory. Example databases were built on a normal personal computer within hours. Uses they name include tick surveillance, medical testing, and farming.
pmc-13274588:

pmc-13274888:

Pole walking, brisk walking with ski-like poles, can build balance and strength in older adults. Balance, leg strength, and self-rated physical function all improved over the twelve weeks.
pmc-13275188:

pmc-13275288:

Three things balance at once around that line: clear sky reflection, cloud effect, and open ocean share. High clouds in the east offset low clouds in the west. pmc-13275988:

pmc-13276588:

pmc-13276888:

pmc-13276988:

pmc-13277188:

pmc-13277388:

pmc-13278388:

pmc-13278788:

pmc-13279288:

pmc-13279488:

pmc-13279688:

pmc-13280588:

pmc-13280688:

pmc-13280788:

pmc-13281288:

pmc-13281888:

pmc-13282088:

pmc-13282288:

pmc-13282688:

pmc-13283388:

pmc-13283488:

pmc-13283788:

pmc-13283888:

pmc-13283988:

pmc-13284388:

pmc-13284488:
