The one-day course used team simulations, skills stations, and talks based on a prior needs survey.

From 2022 to 2024, 98 residents from nine programs attended, and most who replied felt better prepared to manage child patients, steady airways, and do key procedures. At nine-month follow-up, most respondents said the day eased their move to solo practice. Breathing distress care and spotting heart disease were themes they planned to carry into practice.
pmc-13284888:
Andreea-Ramona Treteanu and co-authors survey telemedicine views among Romanian medical students in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Remote care now shapes access and workflow, yet student readiness in Romania was little known. A nationwide online survey ran in late 2024 across all university centers, with 608 students replying to 21 questions.

Most students knew the term telemedicine, but few had used it themselves and most had no formal training, the authors report. Large shares backed its place in medical schooling and felt it lifts care quality. Time saving and specialist access topped the gains, while limits on physical exams and weaker personal contact topped concerns. The authors link uptake to training and confidence.
pmc-13284988:
Clemens Rieder and co-authors report a 2026 project to extend a common health data model for life support research. Extracorporeal life support creates dense data, yet shared standards to store them across centers are lacking. Experts tested whether the OMOP common data model could hold circuit and treatment details for this care.

The standard model lacked many fitting concepts for circuit data, the team found. They built custom tables and new concepts, cutting needed database entries by up to ninety percent for test cases. The expansion, called the ECLS common data model, was released as open source in the public domain. The authors say shared structure should lift data quality and multi-center research.
pmc-13285088:
Svenja Jung and co-authors test a new 3D printed template system for skull surgery in a 2026 preclinical study. The retrosigmoid route reaches tumors and vessel lesions near the ear, but closing the bone gap afterward can be hard, above all if the opening must grow mid-surgery. The concept uses a printed stencil to mark implant edges on the skull first.

Nine senior surgeons tested the system on a printed model of the rear skull space, doing openings on both sides. The implant gap with the new concept was far smaller than with the standard method in the trials reported here. Timing for prep and closure was also logged. The authors call the fit gain promising, pending patient tests.
pmc-13285388:
Thinking skills nine months after intensive care lag for Spanish-speaking survivors next to English-speaking peers, Ana Lucia Fuentes and co-authors show in a 2026 study. Patients with weak English are often left out of big recovery studies, even though language gaps may shape delirium care. The team enrolled adults from two mixed intensive care units in 2024 and 2025.

Phone testing found lower scores for Spanish speakers, with over half classed as impaired versus about a third of English speakers in this small group. The gap shrank a bit once delirium and deep sedation entered the math. The authors point to care gaps, such as missed delirium and deeper sedation, as one path behind the split.
pmc-13285588:
A new gene-based family tree for bone marrow failure syndromes holds up in real-world data, Giulia Maggioni and co-authors test in a 2026 study. The taxonomy sorts myelodysplastic syndrome patients into sixteen groups by gene faults, chromosome quirks, and gene loss marks. The team checked it on 5,136 past cases plus RNA data from 477 fresh cases.

Groups showed clear gaps in traits and disease course, and RNA reads backed their biological separateness. Yet folding group links into a top risk score did not sharpen forecasts. Apart from one grim group, the labels failed to predict drug or transplant response, though they tracked survival. Non-gene factors may steer treatment response more.
pmc-13285688:
Necibe Tugce Goktas, Sirin Guven, and Ener Cagri Dinleyici ran a trial of two probiotic strains in young children with sudden infectious diarrhea. Published in 2026, the trial took place at a children's emergency department. Probiotics are often suggested to shorten such illness, yet evidence for specific strain pairs has been incomplete.

Children aged one to six were assigned to standard fluids alone or fluids plus five days of the two bacteria. Among 145 children, diarrhea lasted about 46 hours with probiotics against about 82 hours without. Far more treated children were diarrhea-free by three days, and no side effects appeared. Gut microbe profiles shifted modestly by day thirty, while overall diversity stayed unchanged.
pmc-13285988:
Gabriela Lipošćak and co-authors recount a rare valve clot case in a 2026 report from cardiology care. A 67-year-old man arrived with a heart attack, and imaging showed a floating clot in the main left coronary artery with no major plaque to blame. Doctors suspected a clot had formed on his own stiff aortic valve and broken loose into the heart's blood supply.

Suction tools cleared the clot twice after chest pain returned the next day, and ultrasound inside the artery ruled out hidden plaque. A heart valve narrowed by calcium, plus a rhythm problem found later, fit the suspected source well. After three months of blood thinners, surgeons replaced the valve with a tissue one. Later scans found a small new channel between two heart chambers, a rare surgical side effect, but tests showed it carried little flow, so watchful care was chosen.
pmc-13286088:
Haochen Zhou and colleagues report scope surgery to free a fish bone buried in the food pipe wall in a case report published in 2026. The patient, a 63-year-old woman, came in four days after swallowing the bone by accident, and a scan showed it lodged upright deep in the wall. The scope alone showed only swelling and a sore patch, with no bone in sight to grab.

Sound imaging through the scope pinpointed bright traces of the bone under the surface lining. Doctors then cut along the sore with a fine electric knife, a tuned version of a tumor removal method, and lifted the bone out with small forceps under direct view. Clips closed the cut, and a scan one week later showed no leftover bone or harm. A month on she ate normally with no complaints, spared the open chest surgery such cases can demand.
pmc-13287088:
Shohei Udagawa and a large team compare the safety of two orders for delivering total neoadjuvant therapy, the full course of treatment given before surgery for locally advanced rectal cancer. Their 2026 study reviews ninety-three patients treated at one cancer center between 2020 and 2023. One strategy starts with chemotherapy, the other with radiation-based treatment followed by chemotherapy.

Severe chemotherapy side effects struck about half of the radiation-first patients but under a fifth of the chemotherapy-first group. Full chemotherapy doses were also completed far more often when chemotherapy came first. A few patients in each group stopped chemotherapy because of side effects, more in the radiation-first arm. Tolerability, the authors conclude, favors starting with chemotherapy.
pmc-13287288:
Jinglong Chen and co-authors fed a chromium supplement in 2026 to yellow-feathered chickens kept under repeated daily heat for two weeks. One hundred eighty birds were split into a cool control group, a heated group on plain feed, and a heated group given the supplement in feed.

Heated birds grew more slowly and converted feed poorly. Supplemented birds partly recovered that loss. Heat shortened the gut and raised stress hormone and toxin levels in blood, while the supplement eased those changes and strengthened gut lining genes. Gut microbe patterns also shifted back toward the cool group. The authors link protection mainly to a healthier intestine.
pmc-13287588:
Xianmang Xu and co-authors introduce in 2026 a special issue gathering nine studies on cleaning heavy metal pollution with living systems instead of harsh chemical methods. Metals reach food, tap water, and daily products, and older clean-up routes can be costly and rough on ecosystems.

Collected work spans microbe-based cleaning, plant and microbe pairings, metal recovery by leaching, and soil additives. One strand weighs the toxic effects of tiny particles themselves. The editors frame the set as a step from lab proof toward field use. They argue that living clean-up must prove itself at scale before it can guide real sites.
pmc-13287688:
Yasemin Utkueri and colleagues present a method in 2026 for aligning whole-body magnetic resonance scans from different UK Biobank volunteers onto a common frame. Alignment used fat and muscle outline maps, drawn by an automated tool, on top of standard brightness matching, with men and women handled separately.

On 4000 volunteers the mask-guided method folded tissue far less often than brightness-only alignment. Overlap scores for body regions rose by several points against three rival methods. Age maps for fat and tissue volume also came out cleaner and better aligned. The authors say standardised scans will sharpen studies linking body measures to health records at population scale.
pmc-13287888:
Robin Kate Kelley and co-authors report a halted drug combination trial in bile duct cancer, published in 2026. The cancer carried a mutation in the IDH1 gene, which the drug ivosidenib targets. Two immune therapy drugs, nivolumab and ipilimumab, were added in hope of a stronger joint effect. The phase 1/2 study enrolled patients whose cancer had grown after one or two earlier treatments.

Only seven patients entered the safety lead-in phase before problems stopped the trial. Every patient developed immune-related side effects, most often rashes that appeared within about twelve days. Lowering the ivosidenib dose did not prevent the reactions in the next three patients. Several rashes were serious, and no patient showed a clear tumor response on scans. The sponsors closed recruitment, and other studies are testing different partners for ivosidenib instead.
pmc-13288288:
Le Zhang and colleagues describe a combined scope and tube treatment for stomach stones in a child, in a 2026 case report. A bezoar is a hard mass of swallowed material that can block the gut. A nine-year-old boy arrived with five days of belly pain and vomiting after eating hawthorn snacks on an empty stomach. Scans showed several large stomach stones and a stone lodged in his small bowel.

Doctors first softened the stomach stones with cola drinks given through a nose tube. A gastroscope then cut and crushed the largest stone, near six centimeters wide, and removed the pieces. For the bowel blockage, they placed a long drainage tube through the scope into the small intestine. Suction plus cola, bicarbonate, and oil cleared the lodged stone within ten hours. The boy's bowel function returned, and he went home eating a normal diet.
pmc-13288388:
Adam J Devall and co-authors set out a Cochrane review plan in 2026. The plan covers the diabetes drug metformin for women with polycystic ovary syndrome. The drug would start before pregnancy and continue through the first three months. The condition raises risks of infertility and pregnancy loss, and metformin is already widely used around conception.

As a plan, the document states the question, the comparison against dummy pills or no drug, and the outcomes the finished review will weigh for benefit and harm. No results are reported yet. The authors frame the review as a check on a common practice whose balance of gain and risk in early pregnancy remains unsettled.
pmc-13288888:
Karl-Hermann S Kamgang and colleagues track antipsychotic use in Swedish youth in 2026. Their register study covers everyone under age 18. It follows first prescriptions from 2008 to 2021. It also guesses the likely reason for each drug. Most use was off label, the team reports.

Use rose from 0.48 to 1.28 per 1,000 youths. The rise was steepest in teen girls. Quetiapine and aripiprazole grew the most. Autism was the top likely reason. ADHD and anxiety came next. Among cases with a clear reason, 81 percent were off label. The authors urge long-term safety checks. They also urge care with first prescriptions.
pmc-13289188:
Afifah Rahman-Shepherd and colleagues issue a 2026 call to action for public health schools. The first such school opened in 1916. Now over 150 exist worldwide. Health systems face deep reform calls. The authors ask what role schools should play.

Forty deans and leaders met in Bangkok. They were pressed to name their role. Four pillars frame the new mandate. One is close ties with policy bodies. Such ties can guide long-term choices. Short-term politics often harms health, they warn. Other pillars ground teaching and service locally. Schools must act as stewards, not bystanders.
pmc-13289788:
Michael P. Moghadasnia and colleagues report a 2026 breakthrough: a halogen-bonded organic framework that stays porous after drying. Halogen bonds can order light molecular solids by design, yet no such solid had proven lasting pores before. A threefold-symmetric building block ending in iodine-bearing rings assembled itself into a low-density crystal held by stacked layers and helical bond chains.

Gas uptake tests at very low temperature confirmed lasting pores after full solvent removal, and X-ray checks tracked the open structure. Slight twisting disorder inside the chains could still be resolved in the crystal data. A hydrogen-bonded twin solid collapsed on solvent exchange instead, showing the halogen version holds together better. New porous materials may follow.
pmc-13289888:
Ahmad Rifai Sarraj and coauthors ran a 2026 randomized trial on adding brain stimulation to a recruitment therapy for chronic paraplegia after spinal cord injury. Recovery is usually seen as limited once early spontaneous gains end. The base method pairs motor imagery with intense peripheral sensory input, and the add-on uses gentle direct current stimulation to the head, called tDCS.

Fifty participants with injury averaging 15.4 months earlier were split into standard care, base therapy, or combined therapy over ten days. Standard care showed no clear recovery in the trial. Both active groups gained sensory function equally, suggesting peripheral input alone restores feeling. Motor scores rose more with stimulation added, at 18 points versus 14 points as reported.
pmc-13290088:
Writing in 2026, Nolan Dvorak and Jeffrey Noebels describe a signaling pathway that makes brain cells overactive early in Alzheimer's disease. Their study links the protein complex mTORC2 to the sodium channel Nav1.2 in a mouse model of the disease.

The authors show that overactive mTOR signaling boosts Nav1.2 channel function, and that this effect needs mTORC2 and does not extend to other major brain sodium channels. In the mouse model, cortical pyramidal neurons showed the same raised channel activity and excess firing. Because overactivity appears before heavy damage and speeds later decline, the mTORC2 and Nav1.2 pairing is put forward as a drug target for early treatment.
pmc-13290388:
Family empowerment is widely preached for preventing stunting in babies and toddlers, yet the idea itself stays fuzzy, Titin Sutini and colleagues argue in a 2026 concept analysis. Stunting in children aged 0 to 2 years carries lasting effects on growth and development, especially in poorer countries.

Using the Walker and Avant framework, the authors searched PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar and synthesized 27 studies. Across the literature, empowerment came out as a process with five linked attributes: families deciding reflectively, confidence in their own ability, active participation, putting health knowledge to use, and pulling resources together. Families appear as active agents who monitor growth, provide stimulation, and act early in the first 1000 days. Sutini and colleagues propose measuring empowerment alongside growth so programs can target it directly.
pmc-13290588:
More than a third of young children in vulnerable Yemeni communities had acute watery diarrhea recently, Mansour Abdu Al-Taj reports in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Diarrhea still kills large numbers of small children, and what mothers know shapes how an episode ends.

Al-Taj interviewed 895 mothers from displaced and host communities face-to-face. The share of children with diarrhea was 36.4%, yet good knowledge of spread and prevention reached only 39.3% of mothers, and just 15.9% gave oral rehydration solution in the last episode. Older mothers and those with secondary schooling knew more, and knowledgeable mothers were nearly twice as likely to use the solution. The author calls for targeted teaching in these communities.
pmc-13290688:
Adding blood-flow restriction to electrical muscle stimulation helps over weeks but hurts acutely, Xin Shu and colleagues find in a systematic review from 2026. The review compares the combined method against stimulation alone for building muscle size and strength in healthy adults.

Seven studies with 124 adults met the criteria. In single-session studies, the combined method caused bigger immediate strength drops and fatigue, plus more swelling, favoring plain stimulation. In longer programs the pattern flipped, with trends favoring the combination for strength and muscle growth. Pooled numbers, though, showed no significant overall difference, and the authors note a confound: long studies all used fixed pressure while acute ones individualized it. Shu and colleagues read duration, not just the method, as the real divider and ask for cleaner trials.
pmc-13290788:
Laser and needling finish in a near tie for acne scar repair, Asia Batool and colleagues conclude in a systematic review and meta-analysis from 2026. Fractional CO₂ laser and microneedling are both standard for atrophic facial scars, yet direct comparisons have been scattered across small trials.

Seventeen head-to-head studies in adults were pooled under PRISMA rules. Average scar-score improvement did not differ significantly between the approaches, though categorical treatment success tilted modestly toward the laser. Safety split by comparison: laser carried about triple the risk of post-treatment darkening versus plain microneedling, yet hurt less than radiofrequency microneedling. Redness, crusting, and swelling were alike. Batool and colleagues advise matching the tool to skin type and scar type rather than declaring a universal winner.
pmc-13291288:
Many Pakistani children miss shots despite clinic visits. Areesh Fatmee leads a 2026 study of these missed chances. Mothers bring children in for other care needs. Staff fail to give due vaccines at that same visit.

Data came from a huge national household survey. It covered 195,000 homes and over 100,000 children. About one quarter of young children missed a dose. Miss rates were alike for first and later doses. Rural homes and uneducated mothers saw more misses. Private clinic visits linked to more missed shots, above all in cities. Maps showed sharp district gaps. Simple visit checks could close much of this loss.
pmc-13292388:
Fotini Mitropoulou and co-authors follow a 2026 cohort of 150 atrial fibrillation patients through recovery after cryoablation, asking who bounces back fastest. Quality of life was measured with the SF-36 survey before the procedure and at three and six months after it. The team looked for age and sex patterns in physical and mental component scores.

Overall scores climbed from a baseline of 57.5 to reach 77.1 at three months and 80.1 at six months in the group's results. Patients aged 65 and younger gained more function than older adults at both check-ins. Men seemed to improve a touch faster, but that sex gap faded after statistical correction. Younger age stood as the strongest independent predictor of recovery, ahead of paroxysmal AF type and starting ejection fraction. The authors advise tailoring follow-up talks to demographic recovery profiles.
pmc-13292588:
Qijun Liang and co-authors show heat stress killing duck heart cells through an iron-driven route, in a 2026 study. Jiaji ducks endured three hours of severe heat and humidity, while heart cells faced heat in dishes. Survival fell as exposure lengthened, and blood markers of heart damage climbed. Heart fibers looked disorganized under the microscope, and mitochondria shrank with lost inner folds. Protein profiling found over a thousand changed proteins.

Ferroptosis, a death program fueled by iron and fat oxidation, stood out in the changed pathways. Tissues held more reactive oxygen, more fat damage products, and more ferrous iron, while the protective glutathione system ran dry. Key proteins shifted in the directions ferroptosis predicts, and an energy-sensing pathway switched on alongside. Dish-grown cells mirrored the pattern, proving a direct cell response. The authors name targets for shielding poultry hearts during heat waves.
pmc-13292688:
Zhongcheng Sun and co-authors investigate a 2026 duck farm scourge in China: red skin and bristle feather syndrome, which reddens backs and wrecks feather growth in meat ducks. They collected 300 samples from sick and healthy birds across eight major producing provinces between February and July 2025. Quantitative PCR screened multiple pathogens, followed by family-tree analysis of the main hits.

Duck circovirus led detections at 66.44 percent of tested samples, then novel duck reovirus at 32.33 percent and waterfowl parvovirus at 19.18 percent in the screening. Solo parvovirus infection, mostly the novel goose type, carried nearly tenfold odds of the syndrome. Neither other virus hurt alone, but pairing either with parvovirus sharply worsened disease. pmc-13292788:
Minho Kim, Walid G Al Hakeem, and Michael J Rothrock used machine learning in a 2026 study of Campylobacter in pastured chickens. This gut bacterium is a food safety risk, yet what drives its spread from farm to final product is unclear.

Data came from 11 farms in the US southeast, gathered between 2014 and 2017, with 1,942 broiler samples of soil, feces, gut contents, and rinsed carcasses. Random forest models pointed to the farm itself as the strongest guide to whether the bacterium was present. Bird age and season also mattered, with summer peaks noted. Weather played a role too, as strong wind and rain on sampling day linked to lower levels in feces.
pmc-13293388:
Han Gong and colleagues trace cell lineages, in a 2026 study, to watch how the fruit fly gut ages from the inside. Stem cell upkeep shapes tissue aging, and the team followed gut clones across adult life with an improved labeling system.

Across days 3 to 33 of adult life, clone variety peaked right after emergence from the pupa, then fell sooner than expected. Later tracking to day 63 showed steady loss in the rear gut. Lineages born in the first 10 days lasted best, with one clone passing 63% of sampled cells by day 63, a share the authors report. Models could forecast which clones would endure.
pmc-13293788:
Ananda L. Roy, Ranjan Sen, and Dinah S. Singer introduce, in a 2026 editorial, a research collection on gene control in lymphocyte growth and response. Lymphocytes, the B and T cells of adaptive immunity, must switch genes on and off precisely as they mature and meet germs.

The editors frame the stakes: innate defenses act fast and broadly, while adaptive cells give slower, targeted clearance, with some cells bridging both arms. Gene control needs hundreds of factors meeting at one gene in the right cell at the right moment. The collection gathers work on those pathways in B and T cells, aiming to deepen a still incomplete picture of immune regulation.
pmc-13293988:
Midhun Krishnan Vasanthakrishnan, Marion Hogg, and Kif Liakath-Ali review RNA detection methods in 2026 through the lens of reproducibility. Offerings now span hybridization, amplification, imaging, and sequencing, and each rests on a different core principle. The authors trace growth from basic assays through PCR variants, microarrays, and single-molecule imaging to spatial and sequencing approaches.

Later parts cover bulk, single-cell, long-read, direct RNA, and spatial transcriptomics, plus CRISPR tests and metabolic labeling for RNA dynamics. Mature tools benefit from shared standards, while newer ones still need study-specific controls. Choosing well means matching the question, resolution, sample limits, and method maturity.
pmc-13295788:
Philipp Sewerin and colleagues compare heart tracings in psoriatic arthritis in a 2026 study. The joint and skin disease raises heart risk, including rhythm problems, yet structured tracing-based screening was missing. Records from 2014 to 2022 supplied patients and a matched comparison group.

Each group held 725 people of similar age and sex mix. Simple heart block rates matched between groups overall, at roughly one person in ten. Signs of atrial strain and a stretched heart recovery interval ran clearly higher in the arthritis group. Among patients, male sex and longer illness tied to conduction delay, supporting routine tracing checks.
pmc-13295988:
Daniel Orzechowski and colleagues review how to use amikacin safely in adults, in a 2026 narrative review. The antibiotic still kills most Gram-negative bacteria, among them drug-proof strains, and rarely triggers a gut infection that haunts other drugs. Its use is capped by harm to kidneys and ears. The team drew on fifty-six works to weigh dosing, drug level checks, and safety.

How best to watch drug levels stays unsettled, and guide targets vary widely on thin proof. Lower trough levels tied to less kidney harm, yet no firm safe line emerged. Illness severity, kidney swings, and partner drugs such as vancomycin all shift the risk, and ear harm stays a live worry. The authors call for dosing shaped to each patient and for trials that test watch plans head to head.
pmc-13296188:
Raisa Chowdhury and colleagues survey Canadian ear, nose, and throat doctors on how they handle vestibular migraine, in a 2026 study. The condition is a common yet often missed cause of dizziness. A fourteen-item survey went to members of the national society between February and April 2025, asking about training, diagnosis, treatments, referral habits, and blocks to care.

Forty-four doctors replied. Nearly all said they diagnose or treat the condition, and most felt at home with its ruling criteria, yet few had deep training in it during residency. Lifestyle and diet change led the treatments, with supplements and older antidepressants next, while vestibular therapy and newer migraine drugs were rare. Time pressure, thin training, and tricky diagnosis topped the blocks to good care.
pmc-13296688:
Yapeng Shi and colleagues teach a seven-jointed humanoid arm to choose natural postures while it moves, in a 2026 robotics paper. Extra joints give the arm many ways to reach the same hand position, and most look robotic rather than human. Operators first guided the arm through a wearable exoskeleton, recording the postures people actually prefer.

A small neural network learned to predict a key elbow-angle measure from each target hand pose. That prediction steers the solver toward human-like configurations without losing tracking accuracy. Tests in simulation and on a real robot showed better posture quality and lower energy use than fixed strategies. Prediction was fast enough for real-time control loops.
pmc-13297188:
Tuba Dilay Kökenek Ünal and colleagues measure, in 2026, a gene family tied to stem cells in bladder lining cancers from eighty-four patients. Ten family genes were read in tumour tissue split by grade and invasiveness, against normal lining controls.

Five genes ran higher in tumours and three ran lower. Low levels of five genes, including some raised overall, tracked with poorer survival. The authors say the family had not been charted in this cancer before. Their pattern hints at both forecasting value and possible treatment targets, pending wider study.
pmc-13297488:
Two rival maps of the developing hypothalamus get a head-to-head comparison in a 2026 review by Marika Kapsimali. One map, the prosomeric model, treats the region as an anterior unit split into two prosomeres. The newer tripartite model, built from gene expression, single-cell sequencing, fate mapping, and functional tests, places most of the hypothalamus within the diencephalon and sets its rear boundary at the retromammillary area. Kapsimali weighs the molecular evidence behind both and argues the tripartite scheme better fits vertebrate development.
pmc-13297588:
Elif Ozan, Mehmet Cudi Tuncer, and İlhan Özdemir test a plant compound as a partner for a standard cancer drug in ovarian cancer cells, in a 2026 study. The compound, quercetin, is a common plant pigment that steers stress and cell-death pathways. Pairs of the drug doxorubicin and quercetin were tried on OVCAR3 cancer cells, with normal skin cells as a safety check.

The pair killed cancer cells more than either agent alone, a true synergy by the maths used. Cell death programmes switched on strongly, execution enzymes rose, and reactive oxygen inside the cells climbed nearly sevenfold. Two growth-linked genes quieted. Normal skin cells withstood both agents better, hinting at a safety margin, though the authors call that hint early and unproven in animals.
pmc-13298288:
Sihui Chen and others review modelling and simulation of mass transfer in food processing, in a 2026 survey. Foods are porous, multiphase, and changing during treatment, so experiments alone cannot capture how moisture or solutes move over space and time. The review links governing equations to simulation workflow and real applications.

Formulations covered range from simple diffusion to coupled heat and mass flow, multicomponent transfer, and flow through porous media, each with stated assumptions. A unified workflow runs from transport identification through checking and transferability checks. Drying and multilayer foods serve as examples. The authors call for structure-aware, experimentally validated frameworks that engineers can actually reuse.
pmc-13298588:
Lelde Tiltina and Tiago Pereira report treatment of bleeding varices around a urinary stoma, in a 2026 case report. Portal hypertension from chronic liver disease and liver cancer forced blood through fragile collateral vessels where an ileal conduit meets the abdominal wall. Even slight injury from a stoma appliance can set off heavy, life-threatening bleeding there.

The bluish swelling at the stoma, sometimes called a caput medusae of the stoma, signals these high-pressure vessels. Management options range from conservative care to surgery and minimally invasive procedures. The chosen route used a percutaneous transhepatic approach, reaching the vessels through the liver to block them by embolisation.
pmc-13298988:
Speakers adjust their pronunciation after hearing their own voice distorted, even when the distorted voice arrives on a trial where they never actually spoke. Benjamin Parrell and colleagues demonstrate that result in a 2026 speech experiment testing what drives motor learning.

Participants were cued to say a word or, on some trials, to stop themselves. On stop trials they heard a recording of their earlier speech with its first formant shifted, timed as if live. They still adapted their vowels on later trials, countering the shift. Passive listening without intent to speak produced no adaptation. The authors conclude prediction errors, not corrective commands, drive speech adaptation.
pmc-13299488:
Specks small past sight can find a tumor, show it on a scan, and treat it in one trip. Junaid Ali and his team review such specks in a 2026 paper. They set three kinds side by side: zinc oxide, iron oxide, and gold.

Each kind brings its own gift. Zinc oxide wakes up in acid and can haul drugs. Iron oxide answers to magnets, fits MRI scans, and can heat a tumor. Gold gives a firm base to fix hot atoms and adds heat and ray boosts of its own. The team weigh how each is made, coated, and tagged with a hot atom. Most sets prove scan strength well. Proof on cure, long-run harm, and how the body clears the specks lags far back.
pmc-13299888:
Plans that let nurses pull urine tubes by their own call stall on pecking rank and sheer load in Saudi top-tier wards. Nader E Alotaibi and Ahmed S Alsadoun found why in a 2026 talk study. They spoke with 23 nurses, germ-guard nurses, and nurse chiefs at two big Riyadh care sites.

Talk across trades, years on the job, and pride in the work all helped the plans land. Load and short staff hurt them. So did the sway of doctors, which made nurses hold back. Thin know-how, shaky notes, and plain lack of note that a tube was still in hurt too. The team urge more say for nurses, tight notes, and fresh rounds of school for staff, so the plans stick and sick folks stay safe.
pmc-13301088:
M Lo and co-authors analyze a phrenic safe low voltage setting for a balloon in basket pulsed field system in a 2026 post hoc study. The right sided veins sit close to the phrenic nerve, so a gentler voltage option was built for spots where nerve capture cannot be avoided. Pooling two trials, the analysis compared 166 patients who received some low voltage work against those treated at nominal voltage only, split by paroxysmal and persistent disease.

Acute success nearly matched across every pairing, sitting in the high nineties. Twelve month effectiveness also tied for paroxysmal disease and leaned, without reaching significance, toward the low voltage group in persistent disease. Early safety events were uncommon everywhere, and no phrenic nerve event appeared in any group. Vein reconnection at repeat procedures looked similar between settings. The authors endorse the lower voltage as nerve protection that costs nothing in performance.
pmc-13301788:
In a 2026 screening study, Sung-Hoon Jung and colleagues test whether belly size changes how well an eye-based risk score reflects calcium build-up in heart arteries. The score, called Reti-CVD, comes from deep learning applied to photographs of the retina. Participants were symptom-free Korean adults having routine health checks.

The analysis covered 237 adults who had both retinal photographs and heart scans that measure calcium. People with any calcium had clearly higher retinal scores than those with none, and the link held after accounting for metabolic and lifestyle factors. Waist size, unlike body mass index, significantly altered the strength of that link. The score also separated cases better in people with abdominal obesity, suggesting waist measures should shape how such eye scores are read.
pmc-13301988:
G Szeplaki and co-authors report one-year lesion durability from the FARADISE registry in a 2026 analysis of pulsed field ablation for atrial fibrillation. This newer energy source uses brief electric pulses rather than heat or cold to scar the vein openings. A small share of patients return for a second procedure, offering a chance to inspect the original lesions.

Sixty-seven returning patients had three-dimensional mapping at the second session, letting doctors check each vein. pmc-13302188:

pmc-13303988:

pmc-13304188:

pmc-13306188:

pmc-13306288:

pmc-13308088:

pmc-13308388:

pmc-13309088:

pmc-13309388:

Corrected here is panel E of figure 3: the method text and scoring math did not match, so the team reran the analysis with the stated product method and replaced the panel. pmc-13310488:

pmc-13310788:

pmc-13310988:

pmc-13311088:

pmc-13311788:

pmc-13312488:

The authors conclude ultrasound gives a practical, measurable way to track swallowing recovery and guide therapy after stroke.
pmc-13319388:
Lucas Silva Mantovanelli and co-authors follow older adults for nine months in a 2026 study of steady exercise after a fourth COVID vaccine dose. Brazil based groups split by habit, with one group active on a regular basis and the other group far less active. Blood defense signs, swelling balance, body function, and walking load were tracked over time.

The active group showed shifts in key defense proteins and a better swelling balance, with one helpful signal rising while a harm linked ratio fell. Their strength and walking also improved by the last check. The less active group showed no such steady gains, and one helpful signal fell. Steady habits may help older bodies get more from a vaccine.
pmc-13319488:
Zhenhao Lin and co-authors build risk scores for muscle loss in inactive adults in a 2026 study drawn from British and American health data. Muscle mass and strength fade with age in this illness, raising risks of falls, hospital stays, and death. People who move little lose muscle faster, yet risk tools built for the wider public may not fit them well.

Past tools were often built from one data set and gave little clue about why a score came out high or low. Clear models that show their reasons were trained here for inactive middle aged and older adults as a group of their own. Checking whether the same key risks hold in both countries was a core aim of the work.
pmc-13319888:
Zeynab Pirayesh and co-authors teach software to guess how pleasing a face profile looks from jaw X-ray measures in a 2026 study. Braces and jaw care must weigh looks as well as bite, yet looks are hard to score in a steady way. Photos and side X-rays from 400 patients were rated for looks, then models learned to match those ratings.

Twenty six raters, most of them lay people plus a few experts, scored each photo on a short scale. Experts tended to rate looks higher than lay people, and rater sex shaped scores too. Among five models, a forest type model guessed best on held out cases. Soft tissue traits, above all face curve and jaw set, drove the scores most.
pmc-13320288:
Susana Banerjee and co-authors chart real world outcomes in advanced womb cancer by repair gene status in a 2026 study from England. A gene repair test sorts these cancers into groups that answer immune drugs in unlike ways, yet routine outcome data by that status were scarce. National registry records covered people treated from 2019 to 2021 who fit the entry rules of a major immune drug trial.

Among 1452 people who fit those rules, only about half had a repair test on file, which itself flags a care gap. Those with faulty repair were younger and far more often had one tumor type than those with sound repair. Their survival and gap to next care had not yet hit the median at last check, while sound repair groups showed shorter spans.
pmc-13320388:
Herui Yao and co-authors report an early phase dose trial of a guided missile drug for advanced breast cancer and other solid tumors in a 2026 study. The drug joins a protein seeker aimed at a growth mark on tumor cells with a strong cell poison on a snip away link. People whose tumors had spread or could not be cut out, after past drug care, took rising doses to find a safe level.

A total of 253 people were treated across dose steps given every three weeks. Dose limits hit at the top step from blood cell harm in two people. Tumor shrink rates ran high in the breast groups, topping four in five in the mark rich group in the counts reported, with time without growth past a year in two groups. A mid dose was picked for the next phase.
pmc-13320488:
Onyedikachi Ubani and Veronica M Ngole-Jeme share a 2026 data set on germs living in polluted fresh water wetlands in South Africa. Water came from five sites shaped by factory waste, sewage overflow, household waste water, runoff from informal housing, and landfill leakage. Long-read gene sequencing was used to capture the full mix of microbes at each site.

Sequencing on a PacBio platform gave high quality reads and tens of thousands of predicted protein coding genes per sample. Almost all matched known bacterial groups, led by Pseudomonadota, with smaller shares of Bacillota and Bacteroidota. The data give other teams a base for tracking how pollution reshapes wetland life and water safety.
pmc-13322188:
Caroleen Drachenberg and colleagues measure the burden of idiopathic hypersomnia in United States adults in a 2026 survey analysis. The condition causes severe daytime sleepiness without a clear cause, and real world burden data were limited. Data from national health and wellness surveys in 2021 and 2023 matched 163 affected adults with 326 similar adults without the condition.

Affected adults carried far more other illnesses, with a comorbidity score of 1.43 against 0.34 for matched peers in the study. Depression, anxiety, and quality of life scores were all worse. Care use was much higher too, with about 13 provider visits on average against about 3 for the comparison group in the past period.
pmc-13322488:
Victor Goiris Calderaro and co-authors follow new hearing aid users through their first year in a 2026 study. The group included 24 adults with moderate or severe sensorineural hearing loss. Brain response tests, speech sentence tests, and handicap questionnaires were run before fitting and again at six and twelve months.

Brain wave timing and size did not shift across the year for either tone or speech stimuli. Speech understanding still improved across the three stages, above all in moderate loss, and fitted thresholds opened access to speech sounds. Users also reported fewer social and emotional limits. Benefit in daily life can thus grow even when lab brain measures stay flat.
pmc-13322888:
Linfei Yu and co-authors show that the enzyme OTUD7B worsens atherosclerosis by driving a form of cell death, in a 2026 mouse and cell study. They built artery disease in mice with a high-fat diet and partial carotid tying, then studied human aortic smooth muscle cells in culture.

OTUD7B rose in plaques alongside necroptosis markers RIPK1, RIPK3 and phosphorylated MLKL, with more inflammation present. Lowering OTUD7B eased cell injury, cut inflammatory signals and reduced plaque build-up and fat deposits in animals. Restoring RIPK1 reversed that protection, which places the effect on the RIPK1 path. The authors nominate OTUD7B as a possible treatment target for artery disease.
pmc-13323088:
Patricia Paracuellos and a large team resolve, in 2026, how a bacterial injection machine loads one of its toxic cargoes. Type VI secretion systems are spear-like devices that fire effector proteins into rival bacteria and other cells. How cargo is recruited into the tube rings that form the spear shaft was poorly understood.

Using cryo-electron microscopy, the team pictured a cargo protein called Tce1 inside rings of the tube protein Hcp3 from Pseudomonas aeruginosa. A single cargo molecule sits asymmetrically, enclosed by two stacked rings and touching key residues on their inner surfaces. The images suggest loading begins with a simple paired complex before rings close around the cargo. Modelling indicates a second antifungal cargo loads the same way, supporting coordinated delivery of mixed payloads.
pmc-13323488:
Ni Luh Suriani and co-authors test black turmeric extract on male fertility in mice, in a 2026 study of Curcuma caesia. This traditional medicinal plant carries antioxidant and anti-inflammatory compounds, yet its effects on male reproduction were poorly documented.

Twenty-four male mice split into four groups received extract at three doses or none, in a randomised design. Chemical analysis found flavonoids, phenolics, tannins and alkaloids. The top dose raised sperm concentration sharply against controls in their measures, while the middle dose gave the best sperm viability, movement and normal shape, plus healthier testicle tissue structure. Testosterone levels were tracked by blood assay, and the authors judge the middle dose most balanced overall.
pmc-13323688:
Xin Wan and co-authors compare two antibody-based chemotherapy backbones in slow-growing B-cell lymphoma with heavy tumour burden, in a 2026 real-world study at the First Hospital of Jilin University. They reviewed 186 untreated follicular or marginal zone lymphoma patients treated between 2016 and 2025.

Complete response after induction ran far higher with obinutuzumab than with rituximab in the weighted comparison, and three-year survival without progression and overall survival also favoured obinutuzumab. Early progression within two years was less common in that group. Side effect profiles looked similar across arms. The authors used overlap weighting to balance the groups, and they present obinutuzumab as the stronger option for this high-risk set.
pmc-13325088:
Margherita Gazzotti and colleagues compute the acid strength of a new family of chiral phosphoric acid catalysts in a 2026 chemistry study. These acids steer many mirror-selective reactions, and their power depends on fine scaffold details.

The family rests on a decahydroquinoxaline frame with two-fold symmetry, and 34 new members were modeled with density functional theory. Two calculation routes estimated acidity in DMSO and acetonitrile, first checked against known BINOL-based acids. Substituent effects on the scaffold shifted acidity in clear trends. Bench titration then confirmed the forecasts, mostly within 1 pKa unit of measured values. The map gives catalyst designers a guide for picking acid strength before synthesis.
pmc-13325388:
Bruna Cristina Corcino Carneiro and colleagues simulate a water pair under an electric field in a 2026 study. Two linked water molecules form the smallest test case for the hydrogen bond quirks behind liquid water behavior.

Density functional runs raised the field step by step until the dimer snapped into a new shape. Past a threshold strength, the pair swung into a cis-like layout as the donor hydrogen shifted to one side. Vibration checks confirmed the new form sits at a stable energy dip. The switched shape kept a high dipole even after the field was removed, showing memory of the push. A simple dipole and torque picture explains the flip.
pmc-13325488:
Qigang Wu and team examine the delayed rise of extra Antarctic warming, the idea that Antarctica should warm faster than the global average. Their 2026 paper notes a puzzle: the Antarctic Peninsula warmed rapidly in the late twentieth century, yet the landmass showed weak warming or even cooling, with mean temperature cooling about 0.47 degrees per decade from 1990 to 2014, while sea ice grew weakly over 1979 to 2014.

The authors put the delay partly down to strong Southern Ocean upflow and ocean heat uptake carried away from the continent by northward surface waters. Flow followed a quasi-fixed wave-3 pattern, with winter trends with a weak Amundsen Sea Low and cyclonic anomalies over the Weddell and Ross Seas. Warming regions generally sit under anomalous northerly flow, cooling regions under southerly flow, while sea surface patterns projected onto negative Pacific and positive Atlantic decadal modes, likely contributing via tropical-polar links.
pmc-13325688:
Mahsa Ahankoob Nezhad, Akbar Esmaeili, and Maryam Beladi made two natural gel nanocomposites aimed at skin rejuvenation and slowing aging. Their 2026 study built the first from hyaluronic acid, starch, vitamin C, and selenium-rich algae with chitosan and polyethylene glycol. The second came from chitosan, collagen, and oregano extract, both known for healing and anti-aging effects. Polymer concentration, temperature, pH, and germ-killing power were optimized with response surface modeling.

Both mixes took in moisture strongly, at 85% and 75%, and showed strong germ-killing power against gram-positive bacteria, at 90% and 85%. Advanced statistical models showed promising physicochemical traits, and the authors highlight clinical potential for skin renewal products. Future work, they suggest, could extend the composites to other topical forms such as serums, lotions, and sunscreens, where natural, body-safe materials are prized.
pmc-13327788:
Tadeg Quillien offers a causal account of luck and intentional action in a 2026 article. People often deny that a lucky success was done on purpose, as when a poor shot hits a target by chance. Quillien argues that judgments hinge on how strongly a person's desire caused the outcome.

When chance dominates, desire looks like a weak cause, so purpose ratings fall. Experiments back the link: where purpose is denied, people also refuse to credit the agent's desire as the cause. Purpose judgments tracked cause judgments more closely than rival factors offered before. A firm desire-to-outcome link thus sits at the heart of the everyday idea of acting on purpose.
pmc-13327888:
Nabil Mohammad Azmi, Mohd Firdaus Mohd Hayati, and Zairul Azwan Mohd Azwan write a 2026 letter on botulinum toxin shots for urge fecal incontinence. They comment on a study of injections into the rectal wall for patients who had failed sacral nerve stimulation, a group with few gentle options left. The study reported durable score gains over a median 22.5 months with no adverse events.

The letter praises the work, then raises points needing care: a backward-looking, single-center design, a small sample, and reinjection left to physician judgment could all sway results. Only women were included, though anatomy and rectal behavior differ by sex. Repeat outpatient treatment still looks attractive before major diversion surgery, the writers agree.
pmc-13328188:
Xiaoxu Li and co-authors chart auxin hormone rewiring during bacterial wilt in a 2026 article. Ralstonia solanacearum clogs plant water pipes and devastates solanaceous crops, and auxin, a growth hormone, keeps surfacing as a regulator of the infection. The authors gather findings across model plants and crops over space and time.

Infected roots shift hormone patterns, raise indole-3-acetic acid, and switch on auxin programs in set tissues, while primary roots shorten, root hairs surge, and side roots grow late in infection. Root hair formation needs working auxin signaling, and susceptible plant types fire the pathway harder than resistant ones, while blocking auxin sensing raises resistance. Breeding or treating for calmer auxin responses may slow wilt.
pmc-13328488:
Yoon Sang Cho and co-authors test scan-based forecasting of inherited BRCA mutations in breast cancer in a 2026 multicenter study. Gene testing guides personal treatment but costs money, so flagging likely carriers from MRI could focus spending. High-risk patients from two centers who had both scans and gene tests supplied the data.

Three predictor families were tried alone and combined: clinic and pathology facts, radiologist-read scan traits, and computer-extracted radiomics from tumor outlines. Six learning models were checked by repeated splits inside one center and by cross-center validation. The multimodal design tests whether images add real signal beyond the chart, a question the authors put to strict outside checking before any clinic use.
pmc-13328788:
Namsu Kim, Sam-Jun Lee, and Jinseok Lee study memory and thinking problems in older women living at home in South Korea in a 2026 report. The group included 1,065 women aged 65 or older from 13 cities. Thinking was screened with a standard dementia test, while mood, muscle weakness, frailty, and long-term illness were also recorded.

Women with impaired thinking showed more depression, weaker muscles, more frailty, and more chronic illness than peers with normal scores. After adjusting for age and other factors, depression, diabetes, arthritis, weak muscles, and frailty each stayed linked to impairment. The authors argue that care should tackle mood, strength, and frailty together, since each may be open to change.
pmc-13329388:
Wei Yao and co-authors review materials that could keep brain implants working longer in a 2026 article. Electrodes placed in the brain lose stability over time as the body reacts to a foreign object. That reaction changes across phases, from early swelling to lasting scar tissue and fouling.

The review gathers bio-inspired and active material designs matched to each phase. Some calm early immune attack and limit scar growth. Others form barriers against fouling and infection, or resist wear from tiny movements and breakdown. By sorting designs by phase and by how they act, the authors map a path toward tougher brain-computer electrodes. Lasting, stable contact is the goal for clinical use.
pmc-13330688:
Zeng-Jin Huang and colleagues design a gel that eats wound glucose and returns oxygen for diabetic wounds in a 2026 study. Starving microbes of glucose can aid healing, yet the reaction drains oxygen and worsens low-oxygen stalls. The gel holds glucose oxidase plus a copper peptide, GHK-Cu, in a linked cascade.

The enzyme first turns glucose into peroxide while lowering local sugar. Copper then splits peroxide in a catalase-like step, freeing oxygen back into the wound. The peptide also supports skin repair on its own. Tests showed germ killing, tissue repair support, antioxidant action, and new vessel growth in the reported checks. The gel tackles sugar, oxygen, and repair at once.
pmc-13330788:
Musbahu Adam Ahmad and colleagues test coated carbon dots against breathing viruses in a 2026 study. Influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, and human metapneumovirus burden health systems, while current drugs face toxicity and resistance limits. Tiny carbon dots with tunable surfaces offer a fresh scaffold, building on earlier work against HIV entry.

The team made dots by heating, covering them densely with boronic acid and boroxine groups. The dots proved non-toxic and showed strong action against all three viruses in lab tests in the reported results. Blocking tests and docking models point to binding at sugar-rich virus surfaces, though firm proof awaits direct checks. The platform merits further study, the authors conclude.
pmc-13331988:
Christopher Hayes and Victoria Kucinski compare 2026 outcomes for two drugs used to ripen the cervix before induced labor at a community hospital. Cervix ripening strongly shapes how smoothly induction goes, yet everyday data from community hospitals remain thin. The team looked back at inductions from 2022 through 2023 that used only drug ripening, with 188 patients given misoprostol and 477 given dinoprostone. Cases using balloons, both drugs, or other complicating features were left out.

The main measures were time until birth and total hospital stay, with cesarean birth and newborn intensive care admission as secondary measures. Results were also split by whether patients had given birth before, since parity can change how induction unfolds. The study gives community clinicians practical timing data for choosing between the two drugs. Its single-hospital, look-back design means the numbers describe local practice rather than proving one drug superior everywhere.
pmc-13333088:
Priyanka Hembram and colleagues compare 2026 air-dried Pap smears with standard wet-fixed smears for cervix screening in low-resource settings. Cervical cancer remains a major public health problem, notably in low- and middle-income countries. Rehydration of air-dried smears was developed to overcome limits of standard wet fixation. The hospital-based cross-sectional study enrolled 282 women undergoing cervical cytology, preparing three smears per sample: one wet-fixed and two air-dried.

All smears were stained by the standard Pap method and judged for adequacy, cell counts, background, cytolysis, artifacts, nuclear and cell-body features, and matching diagnoses under the Bethesda system. The comparison asks whether the cheaper, simpler air-dried method matches wet fixation where labs lack full resources. If agreement holds, screening programs could extend reliable cervical cytology to settings that currently go without it.
pmc-13333388:
Chiara Martinello and colleagues updated the numbers on a scan finding in a systematic review and meta-analysis from 2026: unexpected tracer uptake in the prostate during PET/CT scans done for other reasons. Such incidental uptake is turning up more often as molecular imaging spreads, and teams must decide who needs a prostate workup.

Twenty-four studies met the criteria, 23 using the FDG tracer and one using somatostatin-style tracers. Pooled prevalence was 1.7 percent of FDG scans in men, while the other-tracer study saw 4.5 percent. Among uptake cases that went on to checks or biopsy, malignancy rates were 21.3 percent for FDG and 59.7 percent for the evaluated subset in the other study, with no cancers found in the somatostatin study itself. Cancer cases skewed older, with hotter uptake values, and uptake at the gland's edge predicted malignancy. The authors advise individual follow-up, above all for focal, edge-located uptake.
pmc-13333588:
Quang Tam Nguyen and colleagues overturn a suspicion in a 2026 melanoma study: nitric oxide, long blamed for poor outcomes, turns out to be required for anti-PD-1 immunotherapy to work. The gas, made by the enzyme iNOS, had a split reputation, harmful in some settings and immune-friendly in others, and the team tested its role directly.

In mice carrying melanoma tumors, animals lacking iNOS grew tumors faster and gained nothing from anti-PD-1 treatment, while normal mice responded. Nitric oxide donors in dishes slowed melanoma growth and pushed cells into death, and gene profiling showed the drug switched on interferon pathways, STAT1, IRF1, IFNB1, only when iNOS was present. In blood from 27 treated patients, a nitric-oxide-producing dendritic cell subset tracked with longer progression-free survival, at a hazard ratio of 0.453. The authors propose iNOS activity as both a response biomarker and a treatment partner worth developing.
pmc-13333688:
Oluwatosin Babasola and co-authors built a 2026 math model of a hypothetical human outbreak of H5Nx, a highly pathogenic avian influenza. Their model asks how vaccine timing and how the public acts shape an epidemic curve.

Unlike simpler models, theirs builds in three delays: incubation, vaccine rollout, and the lag before vaccination protects. The population splits into vaccine-accepting and vaccine-hesitant groups, and non-drug measures enter as well. Simulations showed that slow rollout and slow immune protection blunted vaccination's effect on peak infections, while earlier delivery cut early growth. Reproduction number and stability analyses frame the conditions for control. The results warn planners that speed of rollout matters as much as eventual coverage.
pmc-13334388:
Qian Shi and co-authors identified the fungus behind sugarcane white rash disease in coastal Guangxi, China, and screened fungicides against it in a 2026 plant pathology study. The disease has become endemic in the region's cane fields.

A fungus repeatedly isolated from diseased leaves reproduced the field symptoms in inoculation tests and was identified as Elsinoë sacchari from host range, symptoms, and form. It grew fastest on potato dextrose agar at pH 6.0 and 25 degrees Celsius, favoring oat as a carbon source. Lab assays found difenoconazole best at stopping mycelial growth and a pyraclostrobin-boscalid mix best against spore germination. Field trials singled out a trifloxystrobin-tebuconazole product for lowest disease severity and top cane yield.
pmc-13334788:
Jideofor K Ndulue and colleagues report a 2026 case of chronic low back pain masking inner-kidney calcium disease diagnosed by point-of-care scans. Low back pain is a major cause of harm worldwide, usually blamed on muscle-bone causes, yet non-muscle-bone causes should be weighed with lasting or unusual symptoms. Inner-kidney calcium disease is a rare renal calcium disease marked by calcium deposition in inner kidney tissue and tubules.

The patient was a 46-year-old woman with a three-year history of chronic low back pain without urinary tract symptoms, managed without surgery as muscle-bone pain without improvement. Bedside point-of-care scans showed two-sided bright inner-kidney cones pointing to inner-kidney calcium disease. Follow-up CT showed calcium buildup of the inner-kidney cones and multiple two-sided renal inner-kidney cysts, matching inner-kidney calcium disease.
pmc-13334888:
Başak Günay, Narmin Soylu, and Merve Bayram compared two stainless steel crown systems for children's molars in a 2026 retrospective cohort study. These crowns restore badly decayed baby teeth, but head-to-head evidence between commercial systems is scarce.

The study covered 65 children aged 2 to 8 who received at least one crown under general anesthesia. They were followed for at least six months, totaling 246 crowns from Kids Crown and NuSmile. A single calibrated examiner scored retention, fit, bite, contact, gum health, and complications, while parents rated satisfaction on a five-point scale. Both systems succeeded well, with retention above 97 percent overall and good marginal adaptation in 98.3 percent of crowns, slightly favoring Kids Crown on that measure.
pmc-13336388:
Ziwen Gan and co-authors made an underwater sound-absorbing material whose performance is set chemically rather than carved in shape in a 2026 study. Acoustic metamaterials usually obey a shape-sets-performance rule, which narrows bandwidth and complicates making them.

MXene nanosheets were coaxed to self-assemble with polyvinyl alcohol into a film of nano-thin layered structure, then laminated with styrene-butadiene rubber. Stable cross-links plus dynamic hydrogen bonds form a tunable constraint network. Raising or lowering crosslinker levels works like chemical scissors, sliding the local resonance bands without steps. At only 10 mm thick, deep below the wavelength, the material absorbed an average coefficient of 0.90 across 1000 to 4000 hertz in testing. Film thickness and layer count add physical tuning on top.
pmc-13336888:
Ronglong Chen and a large team overload tumor power units with calcium in a 2026 nanomedicine study. Flooding mitochondria with calcium can destroy tumors, but cancer cells pump and gate calcium tightly to protect themselves. Their metal-phenolic nanocluster, TCMH, packs calcium plus two gate modulators inside a polyphenol shell.

Acid inside tumor cells breaks the cluster open. Released signals suppress mitochondrial fusion and add hydrogen sulfide, jointly forcing the calcium gate open. Calcium surge and rising harmful oxygen species then feed each other, driving cell suicide from the power unit outward. The therapy worked strongly in mouth cancer models, including patient-derived grafts. Rewiring calcium self-control could sharpen this treatment class.
pmc-13337388:
Zesong Jiang and colleagues review testis macrophages, immune cells that guard sperm making, in a 2026 article on sperm production disorders. The testis is shielded from normal immune attack, and its macrophages keep that calm, tame swelling, and support hormone balance, all of which help sperm form. When sperm making fails, their numbers, placement, and behavior shift.

Wrongly switched-on macrophages feed lasting low-grade swelling that wrecks the sperm-forming setting. New single-cell gene tools have sharpened the picture of these cells' types and origins. The review pulls scattered work into one account, from how the cells arise to their roles across male infertility types. It closes by weighing treatments aimed at these cells, a target long missed in male fertility care.
pmc-13338688:
Areum Shin and colleagues surveyed COVID-19 vaccination among children with cancer and their parents in Korea, in a 2026 single-center study. Children with weak immune systems face high risk from severe COVID-19, yet earlier Korean data showed cancer patients vaccinated less often than other high-risk children. Surveys ran during the pandemic in July 2022 and again after it in late 2023 and early 2024.

In the first survey of 111 patients, only 28.8 percent had two doses, below the 40.7 percent rate in the general pediatric population. Fathers reached 90.1 percent and mothers 85.6 percent, also below the general adult rate of 96.4 percent. The team also probed why parents held back, giving clinics targets for counseling families of children with cancer.
pmc-13338988:
Emily D Duckworth and colleagues presented a psychiatric case in 2026 where stroke related speech loss complicated mental health care. Clear communication anchors psychiatric assessment, yet patients with aphasia after stroke face higher risk of misdiagnosis, delayed care, and poor treatment. The team describes a 49 year old woman with depression, anxiety, post traumatic stress, and functional neurological symptoms.

A left middle cerebral artery stroke left her with non fluent aphasia, and she was admitted to inpatient psychiatry for suicidal thoughts. The case exposes pitfalls in assessing mood, psychosis, and risk when speech is impaired. It urges adapted interviews, collateral history, and patience so mental health care does not fail patients who cannot speak for themselves.
pmc-13339588:
Alex Lloyd and colleagues map social and emotional profiles in at-risk teenagers in a 2026 study. Early adolescence is when many mental health problems start or worsen. Risk factors that cross diagnosis lines may matter more than single-disorder signs.

A total of 559 youths aged 12 to 14 at higher risk took part as reported, with average age 13.26 years. Questionnaires and tasks covered emotion reading, control, body sensing, and peer and family ties. A neural network projected profiles onto a flat map, and clustering found zones of similar functioning. Zones linked differently to broad symptoms, suggesting tailored support by profile rather than label.
pmc-13339688:
Ayla Yildiz, Süleyman Yazici, and Zülfiye Yildiz test a mitochondrion regulator as a heart ischemia marker in bypass surgery in a 2026 study. PGC-1 alpha was measured around aortic clamping in 44 adults having open-heart surgery between June and December 2024. Diabetes links received special attention.

Levels before and after surgery did not differ clearly, at 2.06 versus 1.43 in the reported means, while troponin rose sharply as expected. Starting levels tracked moderately with diabetes at r equal to 0.366 as reported. Diabetes and intensive care stay independently tied to the marker in adjusted models. The regulator looks more like a metabolic signal than an ischemia gauge.
pmc-13339788:
Hong Wang Fung and Wai Tong Chien talked in 2026 about how trauma linked dissociation can look like psychosis and shift treatment. Some psychosis like signs fit trauma linked dissociation better, yet they are often treated as true psychosis. The paper sets out five key facts on the overlap, drawn from recent clinical work.

People with dissociative identity disorder report more positive psychosis signs than people with schizophrenia, and hearing voices is common in complex dissociative disorders. To mistake dissociation for psychosis risks wrong drugs and missed trauma care. The talk urges doctors to check trauma and dissociation before they settle on a psychosis label.
pmc-13339888:
Zeliang Yang and colleagues optimize tongue swab culture for tuberculosis diagnosis in a 2026 study. Many patients cannot produce sputum, and tongue swabs offer a painless alternative. Swab samples spiked with a vaccine strain tested digestion times in growth tubes.

A 10-minute treatment with 4 percent sodium hydroxide gave the best balance of low contamination and growth as reported. Among 119 people with suspected tuberculosis, tongue culture matched sputum culture with sensitivity near 81.43 percent in the reported estimate. Against a combined standard, specificity reached 94.12 percent as reported. The method could widen testing for patients without sputum.
pmc-13340288:
Two bacterial strains that lock up cadmium are examined in a 2026 study by Yu Tao and colleagues. Achromobacter insuavis SL8 tolerated cadmium up to 600 mg/L and Enterobacter cancerogenus SL12 up to 400 mg/L, and each removed about 70% of the metal from a 100 mg/L solution.

Grown together, the pair reached 80.9% removal, forming cadmium sulfide particles and shifting surface chemical groups. Spectroscopy, metabolomics, and proteomics showed raised activity in metal transport, binding, energy production, and antioxidant defense. Pot trials removed 13% of cadmium from soil and 20% from Chinese cabbage, pointing toward farm use of such consortia.
pmc-1334188:
Hellens, Allan, Friel, and co-authors describe new plasmid vectors for quick gene tests in plants. Their method uses Agrobacterium bacteria to slip genes into leaves of a tobacco relative for short-term expression. The team built a series of pGreenII cloning vectors suited to that job.

They removed parts of older standard vectors that got in the way, making the new set cleaner to use. With them, researchers can measure how active a gene switch is and test gene silencing in days rather than months. Faster plant tests speed work on crops, resistance, and basic gene function.
pmc-13342188:
Lab-grown human microglia respond to a brain protein, in a 2026 study by Daniel Navin Olschewski and colleagues. Rodent microglia and cell lines translate poorly to humans, so the team grew microglia from induced pluripotent stem cells of two healthy donors.

Cells were challenged for 24 hours with osteopontin, a matrix protein tied to immune balance, bacterial lipopolysaccharide, or both. Identity and the phagocytic marker CD68 were checked by staining, viability by dye exclusion, shape change by branching analysis, and inflammatory genes by PCR. Showing these cells react physiologically to a context-relevant signal validates them as a human-first testbed for brain immune drugs.
pmc-13342688:
Munazza Shaikh and colleagues told of late postpartum eclampsia in 2026 on day seven after planned caesarean in a 21 year old first time mother with low thyroid. Late postpartum eclampsia, past 48 hours after birth, makes up about 15 percent of eclampsia cases. It often strikes women with no recorded high blood pressure before birth.

The patient had a planned caesarean for a mismatch between baby size and pelvis, with no high readings before or just after birth, yet eclampsia struck a week later. The case adds to scant reports on risk factors and urges high suspicion after birth even with no prior high pressure. Early spotting after discharge can save lives.
pmc-13343088:
Kaushalendra Mani and colleagues surveyed rheumatoid arthritis drug use in 2026 at a tertiary care hospital in a prospective study of 95 patients. Rheumatoid arthritis is a long term, disabling, body wide inflammation, and drug prescribing is among its most common treatments. Age, sex, and consultant drug orders were gathered and studied.

Most patients were aged 41 to 60, about two thirds of the group, with women in the majority at about three fifths. Common co illnesses were high blood pressure, diabetes, and anaemia, while disease span was mainly three to five years. Disease modifying drugs led prescribing at about nine in ten, followed by anti inflammatory drugs at about two thirds and steroids at about half, with biologics at under one in ten. Methotrexate led at about three quarters.
pmc-13343488:
Jill Ashey and co-authors catalog noncoding RNAs in reef-building corals in 2026, the first broad survey of its kind. pmc-13351888:

pmc-13353088:

pmc-13354488:

pmc-13355788:

pmc-13357088:

pmc-13358488:

pmc-13361688:

pmc-13362988:

pmc-13387688:

pmc-13394888:

pmc-13398188:

Xiaocheng Pan and co-authors review food packaging built around three natural pigment families, in a 2026 article on preservation and freshness sensing. Turmeric's curcumin fights microbes and oxidation and can kill germs under light when carried well. Anthocyanins, the reds and purples of berries, change color with acidity and so can signal spoiling food.

Carotenoids mainly guard fatty foods by soaking up damaging radicals. The review surveys films, coatings, gels, and tiny carriers that now hold these pigments, noting gains in stability and slow release. Weak points remain: the pigments fade, dissolve poorly, and behave differently in each food, which still limits shelf-ready products.
pmc-13466288:
Gema Torrijos-Gómez and colleagues examine how jaw joint disorders cluster with migraine and with mental strain, in a 2026 cross-sectional study of 120 people. Forty participants had no headaches, forty had episodic migraine, and forty had chronic migraine. Structured interviews and examinations sorted jaw disorder status for everyone.

Jaw problems appeared in nearly four fifths of migraine patients but only one fifth of controls, a roughly fourfold higher rate. Questionnaires measured headache impact, anxiety, depression traits, and sleep quality. Among patients, those with jaw disorders were compared on attack frequency, medicine use, and those same mental health scores, testing whether a sore jaw marks a heavier overall migraine burden.
pmc-13466488:
Ghayas and colleagues built a questionnaire in 2026 that measures how prone university students feel to violence and conflict in hot weather. Heat is linked to aggression in many studies, yet no dedicated scale existed. The team drafted items from the literature and from student interviews. Experts trimmed the pool to 25 items. A first sample of 1,000 students then shaped the scale's structure.

Sixteen items survived, forming a single dimension. Together they explained about 80 percent of the differences between students. The scale's internal consistency was near perfect, with an alpha of 0.98, a statistic where 1.0 means flawless agreement. A second sample of 350 students confirmed the single-factor shape. A third sample of 440 tested meaning. Scores rose strongly alongside a standard aggression measure. They showed no link with eating behavior, as expected for an unrelated trait. The authors present the tool as ready for heat-and-aggression research.
pmc-13467188:
Kuru and co-authors isolate a kneecap groove measurement tied to instability, controlling for kneecap height. Their 2026 retrospective MRI case-control study includes 123 knees. Forty-three had objective patellar instability and 43 were normal-height controls. Another 37 controls share the high kneecap, patella alta, that often accompanies instability, yet are stable. Nine shape parameters were measured, with the alta-positive group as the key comparison.

The trochlear facet asymmetry ratio compares the groove's two slopes. It graded cleanly across the groups. Values ran about 43 percent in unstable knees, 59 percent in alta controls, and 70 percent in normal controls. It discriminated instability best among the measures, and stayed associated after adjustment for kneecap height and age, each extra point of symmetry cutting odds by about ten percent. Two expert readers agreed almost perfectly. The authors propose the ratio as a morphology marker separable from kneecap height.
pmc-13467388:
Artur Szajna and co-authors investigate in 2026 how drilling and enlarging holes in 3D-printed ABS plastic parts affects size accuracy and surface roughness. Printed parts often need machining to reach tight tolerances, yet the print settings and cutting choices interact in ways that are poorly mapped. The team printed specimens in two orientations and machined them on a five-axis center at varied speeds and feeds.

Holes were either drilled fresh into solid material or enlarged from printed pilot holes with different amounts of stock left to remove. The smallest allowance, 0.062 millimeters per side, failed to clear the ridged print texture, leaving roughness high and uneven. Larger allowances behaved more predictably. The study gives hybrid print-and-machine shops concrete guidance on how much stock to leave for a clean finish.
pmc-13467788:
Kamila Lewandowska and co-authors feed pregnant ewes extra oils in 2026 to see whether the fat makeup of their milk improves. Thirty-two Olkuska ewes were split into four groups of eight: a plain diet, flaxseed oil, oil from black soldier fly larvae, or a two-to-one mix of the two oils. Supplements were given before lambing, and both transitional and mature milk were analyzed in detail.

The oils made no significant difference to transitional milk. In mature milk, though, the insect oil group reached a fat content of 6.09 percent, against 4.70 percent in the control group. Every oil treatment lowered total saturated fatty acids, and the insect oil and mix raised the monounsaturated share. The findings suggest insect oil, a novel feed fat, can shift sheep milk toward a profile many buyers consider healthier.
pmc-13468388:
Mutiara Saragih, Ewa Szczepańska, and Teresa Olejniczak review in 2026 how microbes can remodel coumarins, a common plant compound family that calms swelling, kills bacteria and parasites, and thins the blood. Editing these molecules with chemistry is hard to aim precisely, while microbes do the same edits with ease. Microbe enzymes add or remove small chemical groups on coumarins at set spots, changing solubility and potency in the process.

One edit gets special focus: swapping a methoxy group for a hydroxyl group can flip what a coumarin does in the body. The review weighs the drug promise of microbe-made coumarin variants against the practical hurdles, such as scaling brews and purifying products. For drug makers, microbe workshops offer a green way to build variants that bench chemistry struggles to reach. That widens the search for better medicines from familiar plant compounds.
pmc-13468588:
Tudor Andrei Rusu and Rusu Tiberiu present in 2026 a dry process that converts dirty, mixed plastic waste into a certified composite material. It skips the washing stage that keeps such waste out of recycling. The patented Romanian process feeds contaminated plastic into continuous single-screw extrusion with no water at all. The waste carries metal, paper, cardboard, and organic residues. Accredited laboratories then certified the product mechanical and thermal behavior.

The composite reached a tensile strength of 9.22 megapascals. It stretched a long way, elongating 112.8 percent before breaking. Its compressive strength was 14.5 megapascals. Across four batches, raising the polypropylene share shifted the properties predictably. The authors also quantified the carbon balance, crediting the process for the washing and drying energy it never spends. Hard-to-recycle waste is the largest untouched plastic stream, so a washing-free route with honest certification could matter at scale.
pmc-13468788:
Ruifang Xie and colleagues report a cancer study, published in 2026. It tests bufothionine against colorectal cancer. Bufothionine is an active compound from dried toad skin. The team used cell cultures and mouse tumours. Computer modelling of drug targets was also used. They asked whether the compound slows this cancer. They also asked through which pathways it acts.

Bufothionine reduced cancer cell growth and migration. It shrank mouse tumours. No obvious liver or spleen harm appeared. It triggered ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death. It acted through the STAT3 and p53 proteins. A protective pathway in the cells was switched off. A ferroptosis blocker partly reversed its effects. This supports the proposed mechanism.
pmc-13469288:
Michael D. Shapiro signs off in 2026 with his final President Page for the American Society for Preventive Cardiology, choosing reflection over an accounting of his two-year term. He writes that professional societies are not truly sustained by their codes of conduct, structures, or strategic plans. They endure because people volunteer time and energy for a shared purpose.
