That purpose shows in committee work, educational programs, mentorship of trainees, and manuscript review. It also shows in partnership building, and in the willingness to raise concerns when the society can do better.

Shapiro says he saw that quiet, unrecognized work repeatedly throughout his presidency, and that serving reinforced his sense of fortune in belonging to the ASPC community. The piece is a valedictory letter to colleagues rather than a scientific article. It closes his term by crediting the membership, not the office, for whatever the society achieved.
pmc-13469688:
Yueran Xu, Hanbo Gong, Qing Chen, and Mengjiao Shen introduce MSD-GasNet in 2026, a compact neural network that identifies gases from electronic nose readings. Smell sensors serve environmental monitoring and factory safety, yet their one dimensional response curves are hard to classify with small models. The team first converts each response curve into a two dimensional image that preserves how readings relate over time.

Two parallel branches then read the image at different scales, catching fine detail and broader shape while sharing work to stay small. On a five gas test set the model scored close to 97 percent accuracy with under eight hundred thousand parameters. Answers came in a few milliseconds per reading. A second dataset checked later in time still scored about 95 percent.
pmc-13470888:
İpekci and colleagues developed in 2026 a cinnamon oil microemulsion, a stable mix of oil and water droplets, to carry the blood pressure drug nadolol by mouth. Nadolol absorbs poorly, so a better carrier could raise its effect. The chosen mix used cinnamon oil, a common surfactant, and alcohol-based helpers, loaded with the drug. The team measured droplet size, charge, acidity, and stability, then tested the mix on gut cells and in rat intestines.

İpekci found the droplets were extremely small and the mix stayed stable in heat and storage tests. In the rat intestine test, the drug crossed the gut wall nearly six times faster from the microemulsion than from plain drug solution. The estimated share absorbed in humans was about four in ten. Cell tests showed the carrier was gentle on gut lining cells. The authors present it as a promising oral delivery route for this drug.
pmc-13471288:
Teng and colleagues published a 2026 study on wrapping a plant compound for better gut uptake. Dihydromyricetin, from a Chinese vine tea plant, fights oxidation but dissolves poorly. Bodies absorb little of it when swallowed in plain form. The team tucked it into fat bubbles coated with chitosan, a shell-derived polymer.

Coated bubbles trapped 54 percent of the compound, beating uncoated ones clearly. The coat also boosted the compound's antioxidant punch beyond the bubbles alone. Release slowed and steadied, holding up best at gut-like acidity levels. Through simulated digestion, the wrapped form survived far better than free compound. Gut access ended about three times higher than the free form. Storage stability also favored the chitosan-coated bubbles in tests.
pmc-13471388:
Huang and Li survey the behavioral tests used to study brain disease in mammals, from standard rodent mazes to newer assays for pigs, dogs, and primates. Their 2026 narrative review weighs what each test measures, where it works well, and where it falls short. Species covered range from tree shrews and rodents to pigs, carnivores, and non-human primates.

Rodent tests dominate the field, yet the authors stress a caution: over 99% of mouse genes have human counterparts, but that genetic closeness does not guarantee the same behavior or drug response. Large mammals offer brains closer to ours in structure and chemistry, which makes their slower, costlier testing worthwhile for some questions. The review closes by matching test choices to research goals rather than habit.
pmc-13471588:
Jinwei Tang and co-authors pool in 2026 published studies on social frailty among older Chinese adults living at home. Social frailty, shrinking social contact and support, is tracked less often than its physical cousin. The team searched eight Chinese and international databases through November 2025, with two reviewers screening and grading studies independently.

Twenty four studies covering more than two hundred forty thousand people survived screening. About a quarter of community dwelling older adults met the bar for social frailty, and about forty two percent sat in the pre frail band. Being female, very old age, depression, physical frailty, housing satisfaction, and marital status each showed significant links. The authors caution that studies differed enormously from each other, so the pooled figures are guides rather than exact national rates.
pmc-13472288:
Shuting Wang leads a large team demonstrating in 2026 continuous factory style production of piezoelectric films grown from glycine, the simplest amino acid. Glycine crystals generate charge under pressure and are body friendly, and a polymer directed method can grow them from water. The team adapted commercial polymer film equipment to run the growth without stopping, keeping a stable crystallization front by tuning feed rate and drying.

The films came out with a uniform sandwich structure, even thickness and grain size, and a steady piezoelectric coefficient over tens of centimeters, matching their kinetic model. Fifty six energy harvesting devices were built on a single sheet, all from the same run. The authors present the line as industrially viable for mass producing biocompatible sensors, harvesters, and therapeutic devices.
pmc-13473088:
Marcelo Cordeiro de Abreu and four colleagues tested in 2026 whether leaf sprays of helpful bacteria could cut wheat's need for factory-made nitrogen in Brazil's Cerrado. The Cerrado's harsh climate and nitrogen losses from feeds make wheat growing costly and wasteful, while microbes capturing nitrogen from air offer a cleaner path. In a 2024 field trial, wheat received either no urea, urea with a loss-reducing additive, one of two bacterial products, or both bacteria together.

Spraying both bacteria at once raised leaf nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and boron against the no-urea plot. One bacterium alone gave the largest boron gain of all, while urea excelled only for one leaf pigment. Stress-defence enzyme activity fell sharply under every fertilised treatment, most of all under the pair. The authors present combined leaf bacteria as a workable way to feed Cerrado wheat with less factory-made nitrogen.
pmc-13474388:
Nolan Kline and co-authors survey Florida parents in 2026 after the state announced plans to drop school vaccine mandates. Just over five hundred parents of school-age children answered online in late 2025. About four in ten said they were more likely to vaccinate after the news, while two in ten said they were less likely. The rest reported no change in plans.

Vaccine hesitancy, meaning doubt or delay despite access, was the sole factor tied to change on its own. Doubtful parents far more often moved away from vaccination, while confident parents more often moved toward it. Traits such as party ties did not explain the split once hesitancy was counted. Policy shifts may widen gaps that attitudes already set.
pmc-13474488:
Adeleke and co-authors surveyed 2,264 caregivers of young infants at 18 immunization clinics in Ogbomoso, southwestern Nigeria, to measure whether insecticide-treated bed nets actually get used against malaria. Their 2026 cross-sectional study combined questionnaires with regression analysis of the ownership-to-use pathway.

Ownership outran use: 62.6% of households owned a treated net, yet only 55.2% of infants had slept under one the previous night. Both parents' education levels tracked significantly with use, at p values of 0.006 for mothers and 0.002 for fathers among the chi-square tests. The strongest signal was belief: caregivers aware that nets prevent malaria showed an odds ratio of 174.4 for using one, an enormous association the authors read as misconceptions, not supply, being the binding constraint.
pmc-13474688:
Maheshwari and colleagues described in 2026 a method for finding bacteria that fight several plant diseases at once. Soybean seedlings face several soil-borne fungi together, so single-target control often falls short. Their Serial Knockout Isolation Technique combines enrichment culture, a sugar-iron test, and a cyanide assay, then a dual assay. Strains are screened against the main target fungi from strongest down, knocking out failures step by step.

The method recovered more bacteria able to fight several fungi than standard screening. It also lowered the chance of pulling out Enterobacteriaceae, a family including human pathogens, making workflows safer. The sought bacteria produce siderophores, iron-gathering compounds that starve fungi, among other weapons. The authors offer the technique as a targeted pipeline for hunting control strains in complex crop diseases.
pmc-13474888:
Yuxuan Zhang and three colleagues mapped in 2026 how short video addiction and inattention symptoms link in nursing students. They surveyed 456 undergraduates at four Chinese colleges between August and December 2025, building a symptom network and simulating interventions on each node.

Compulsive use and withdrawal sat at the network centre, while interpersonal and health problems bridged the two symptom groups. Simulated easing of compulsive use and withdrawal cut overall network activation most, while worsening "does not listen" raised it most. The authors point to those symptoms as targets for prevention and support.
pmc-13476988:
Benjamin Hambright and nine colleagues built in 2026 a tool to predict which lung resection patients will need home oxygen after discharge. They studied 1,875 adults at one institution, operated on between 2013 and 2023, excluding those already on home oxygen or missing lung function tests.

Only 6.4 percent of the cohort needed new home oxygen after discharge. Four factors raised the odds: obesity, current smoking, and two lung function measures, diffusion capacity and expiratory volume, below half of predicted. The resulting nomogram, validated by resampling, aims to guide counselling, prehabilitation, and surgical planning before the operation.
pmc-13477088:
Awad and co-authors followed 308 patients who had pulmonary endarterectomy between 2008 and 2022, an operation that clears chronic clots from lung arteries to relieve severe pressure strain. Their 2026 report asks what predicts survival years later, with a median follow-up of 4.5 years at their center. Half the patients had moderate or worse weakness of the right heart chamber before surgery, and average lung artery pressure started at 43 millimeters of mercury.

Operations killed 2.3 percent of patients, and average lung pressure fell to 26 millimeters of mercury after surgery in the cohort. Survival reached 97 percent at one year, 90.4 percent at five years, and 79 percent at eight years after the operation. Surprisingly, the degree of right heart weakness before surgery did not predict survival. Higher pressure remaining after surgery did, and higher filling pressure and greater oxygen needs each independently raised the risk of later death.
pmc-13477588:
Zixuan Zhao and coauthors published a 2026 computer simulation study of clear aligner treatment for pulling back upper front teeth after premolar removal. Aligners alone often tip front teeth and lose root control in such extraction cases. The team built finite element models of the upper jaw, teeth, ligaments, and aligners to test help from small palatal implants.

Four setups were compared, ranging from aligner force alone to elastic pulls from the implant to different attachment points, plus one rigid wire option. Elastic forces ran from 100 to 250 grams. Pulling from the implant to a traction button moved incisors farther back with better vertical control than aligner force alone. The simulations let orthodontists weigh anchorage strategies before applying them to patients.
pmc-13478388:
Prabha and Suganthi present a lightweight vision framework in 2026 for spotting foreign objects on roads, a safety task for self-driving cars. Anomalies come in two kinds: familiar objects in the wrong place, and wholly new objects the system never trained on. Their framework checks a scene-object compatibility table for the first kind and fuses novelty and uncertainty signals for the second, all inside a model of only 4.33 million parameters.

Trained on two street-scene datasets, the system scored 0.9506 on the Road Anomaly benchmark, where one means perfect separation of normal and abnormal scenes. On the harder Lost and Found benchmark it scored 0.6158, still competitive given its small size in the reported comparison. Removing parts showed the compatibility module added about 1.1 percentage points and the novelty head about 0.4, confirming both halves of the hybrid design earn their place.
pmc-13478488:
Luo and co-authors trained a deep learning system in 2026 to diagnose cutaneous vasculitis, inflammation of small skin blood vessels, from microscope slides of skin biopsies. The diagnosis is tricky because several look-alike conditions overlap, and human calls vary. Using slides from two centers collected between 2018 and 2024, the system learned from whole-slide images labeled only by the final pathology report, avoiding costly pixel-level tracing.

The training set held 378 vasculitis slides plus 285 slides of swollen-skin dermatitis, 286 of granulomatous inflammation, and 247 of fat-layer inflammation as the mimics. Across these four classes the model scored an area under the curve of 98.39 percent, a near-perfect separation mark on the standard diagnostic scale. It returns predictions within milliseconds and highlights the slide regions driving its call, which the authors pitch as a consistency aid for pathologists.
pmc-13478588:
Riemersma and colleagues validated a transplant symptom questionnaire in Brazilian Portuguese in 2026 and used it to map symptom burden in kidney transplant recipients. The 59-item scale asks both whether a symptom occurs and how much distress it causes, covering effects of anti-rejection medicines. They enrolled 485 recipients, 42.2 percent women, averaging 50.2 years old and a median of 7.4 years past their transplant, plus an expert panel to judge the scale's content.

Experts gave the scale a content validity index of only 0.49, a weak score suggesting it captures general symptom burden better than drug-specific side effects. Its internal structure and group comparisons still held up, and the commonest symptoms were anxiety, tiredness, and trouble seeing well in the recipient group. The most distressing were menstrual problems, seeing difficulty, and genital warts, with women and younger recipients reporting more psychological and appearance-related symptoms.
pmc-13479888:
Omar Al-Qaisi and coauthors published a 2026 scoping review of cancer care in regions torn by armed conflict. Wars destroy cancer centers, scatter specialists, and sever supply chains, yet knowledge of what breaks and what adapts stays in pieces. Four data banks were searched for studies from January 2020 to August 2025.

Cases span Palestine, Sudan, Syria, Iraq, Ukraine, and Afghanistan. Chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and surgery all suffered interruptions, alongside shortages of imaging staff, records, and affordable medicines. Services adapted through cross-border referrals, simplified protocols, and remote consultation where possible. The review sorts care challenges, system workarounds, and policy lessons so planners can prepare cancer services before the next crisis rather than improvising during it.
pmc-13479988:
Sidra Altaf and co-authors present a 2026 study of tiny coated particles designed to mop up a farm poison called profenofos. Profenofos blocks a key enzyme and can kill, yet current drugs have clear limits. The team wrapped plastic-based particles in membranes taken from red blood cells, so the particles act like decoy cells that soak up the poison.

In lab tests the coated particles removed close to ninety percent of the poison at the highest dose tried. In rabbits, treated animals lived at higher rates than untreated ones. Enzyme activity in red cells returned to normal by day four, with no major harm to liver or kidney tests. The study offers an early proof that decoy particles could help treat this type of poisoning, though much more testing lies ahead.
pmc-13480088:
Muhammad Nouman Javed and colleagues offer a 2026 updated pooled review of remote rehab for people with lasting symptoms after COVID. The team searched three databases for trials from spring 2024 to mid-2025 and kept 28 trials with about 1,400 people in total. Rehab reached patients at home through video and phone tools, with set exercise and breathing plans.

Remote care lifted scores on a sit-to-stand test and added a clear gain in six-minute walking distance. Breathlessness and fatigue scores both eased. Mood scores for anxiety and low mood did not shift in a clear way, and lung gains showed in only one measure. No serious harms were reported, though few trials tracked safety as a main aim. The review supports remote rehab for strength and stamina while noting that mood and lung care may need added help.
pmc-13480188:
Nimya Krishnan and co-authors describe a 2026 route to making melanin pigments from cheap industrial leftovers. Melanin, the dark pigment in skin and ink, sells for uses from coatings to electronics, yet standard microbe methods need a costly starting chemical. The team fitted bacteria with an enzyme called MelC tyrosinase and fed them thirteen cheaper phenol-type starters, several drawn from farm and factory waste streams.

Two starters worked best, giving pigment yields in grams per litre. Lab checks showed the products matched natural eumelanin in broad structure while staying partly soluble, which eases handling. The pigments held up under extreme heat and showed strong antioxidant power, with one form beating standard eumelanin many times over. Turning waste feedstocks into high-value pigment could link pollution cleanup with manufacturing.
pmc-13481388:
Rodrigo Garcia-Santisteban and co-authors describe a 2026 case of leukaemia returning as a lone tumour in an odd brain spot. An 88-year-old woman with a blood disorder turned leukaemia, long in remission, reported a month of vivid visual hallucinations, memory slips, and personality change. Scans found a small growth in the septum pellucidum, a thin wall between the front cavities of the brain.

Fluid drawn from around the spine held a blast population matching half the cells counted, with the same surface marks as her past leukaemia. Growths of this type usually sit in skin, nodes, or soft tissue, so a lone brain relapse is vanishingly rare. The case warns teams to weigh blood cancer return when past patients show new mind or mood symptoms, even after years of quiet remission.
pmc-13482588:
Xuefang Zheng and co-authors present a 2026 lean detector for spotting objects in near-dark photos, built on a recent YOLO model. Dim scenes crush contrast and bury small targets in noise, while brightening photos first eats computing power. Their design adds a self-tuning brightness step, a context module that links distant parts of the frame, and a slim detection head that hunts weak traces.

On a standard dark-photo dataset the model scored higher than its parent design by over two points on the main accuracy scale. Computing load dropped at the same time, from the parent level to a leaner figure. A second face dataset in the dark gave competitive results as well. Night driving, watch cameras, and drone checks all need this balance of sharp eyes and light maths.
pmc-13482988:
Shi and co-authors built a vision system to spot tender tea shoots on machine-picked leaves, so sorting machines can grade them without human eyes. Their 2026 study improved the YOLOv11 detector, a fast image-recognition model, with three add-ons that sharpen leaf edges, blend texture cues, and focus attention on key spots. The task is hard because shoots are small and leaves overlap each other.

The improved model, called YOLOv11-MSC, reached a mean average precision score of 90.1 percent on the test images used. It stayed small, with under three million parameters and modest computing needs, so it can run in real time on sorting equipment. Tests against rival detectors and stripped-down versions of itself showed each add-on helped. Shi presents the system as ready for practical tea grading lines.
pmc-13483188:
Lingyi Xu and co-authors report a 2026 two-part language model system that flags kidney injury a day ahead and explains its reasoning. Sudden kidney injury kills many hospital patients, and older alert tools cry wolf so often that staff tune them out. Records from 140,637 admissions at four Chinese hospitals trained the predictor, while a second model sorts each flag's drivers into fixable and fixed factors with tailored advice.

The predictor scored high on internal checks and held up at outside hospitals after light adaptation, with far fewer false alarms than the field's norm. Six kidney specialists graded the explainer on 200 cases across four hospitals, awarding high marks on eight quality scales with fair agreement. Pairing a sharp forecast with plain reasons may finally make early warnings usable on busy wards.
pmc-13483488:
Andrew Max Abaasa and Sylvia Kusemererwa examine a 2026 question from HIV prevention: can cheap checks stand in for lab tests when tracking use of a drug-releasing vaginal ring? Their data come from a trial in southwestern Uganda where 197 women used dapivirine or dummy rings, checked monthly for two years. Lab measures read drug left in returned rings and drug in blood, while cheap checks relied on self-report and ring colour change.

Agreement between measure types ran moderate in women under twenty-five and strong in older women. Cheap checks predicted true ring use well in the older group yet poorly in the younger one. Two thirds of the women were twenty-five or older, and most finished the two years. In cash-strapped programs, combining cheap checks may serve for older users, the authors conclude, while young women still need lab confirmation.
pmc-13484488:
Agal built a public practice dataset of more than 100,000 invented student records so researchers can develop early-warning prediction models without touching real student files. Privacy law rightly locks real records away, which has stalled progress in educational data mining. The 2026 dataset carries 28 attributes per student, from entrance exam scores to family income indicators, with realistic missing values and uneven class sizes deliberately built in.

Two prediction tasks anchor the framework: placing students into four academic levels and assigning them to four divisions from remedial to honors. Ensemble methods, which combine many models, clearly beat simpler approaches across the experiments reported. The best model reached balanced F-scores above 0.84 on the level task in Agal's testing. Feature explanations accompany the predictions so teachers can see why a student was flagged. Agal offers the dataset as shared ground for fair model comparisons.
pmc-13487288:
Romero and co-authors ran a 2026 proof of concept study using gene activity profiles to explain why some commercial broiler chicken flocks grow better than others. Subtle health or nutrition problems drag performance down without obvious signs. Gut and liver tissue from farms with historically different feed efficiency were compared.

Birds came from four farms in one production system, two classed high performing and two low performing at cycle end. Low performers had deeper gut crypts and a lower villus to crypt ratio, signs of poorer gut condition, Romero reports. Two pathway analysis methods agreed that low performers showed immune activation and suppressed nutrient metabolism in gut and liver. One method pinned their cell stress to low oxygen and oxidative stress tied directly to lower final body weight.
pmc-13487388:
Carola and colleagues report whether a standard breast cancer combination works in women over seventy. Their 2026 PalomAGE study is a French prospective observational study. It covers first-line endocrine therapy plus palbociclib, a cell-cycle drug. The 382 treated women were aged seventy and older with hormone-sensitive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer. Older patients are scarce in trials, so real-world feasibility was the primary question.

At eighteen months the permanent discontinuation rate was 41 percent. Median time to treatment failure was 23 months and median real-world progression-free survival about 30 months. A third of patients needed a dose reduction, and 11 percent stopped for adverse events, with no new safety signals and quality of life holding stable. A poor baseline geriatric screening score independently predicted stopping the drug. The authors conclude the regimen is feasible and tolerable in this age group, matching general adult results.
pmc-13487988:
Aishwarya Bhaskaran and co-authors propose a statistical method for survival data in a 2026 methods paper. Accelerated failure time models link patient traits directly to how long until an event, which can be easier to interpret than hazard models. Their setting is harder than usual because event times are known only within intervals and one predictor changes over time, a mix no ready software handled.

The team built a penalized likelihood approach, which adds a stabilizing penalty during fitting, and tested it in wide simulations. A melanoma brain metastasis trial, where scans every few months leave event times interval-censored, served as the worked example. The authors report the method performs well and fills a practical gap for trial analysts.
pmc-13488088:
Zainab Ajoke Abdulkadir and co-authors run a pilot trial of a combined approach to blood pressure control during pregnancy across Ghana and Nigeria in a 2026 study. Sixty women with chronic hypertension in pregnancy were assigned at two teaching hospitals to usual care or to a package with several supporting components. The main aim was feasibility, meaning whether the package could be delivered and women kept in care, alongside blood pressure change and safety outcomes.

Retention was high at both sites, reaching above ninety percent in Ghana. Systolic and diastolic pressures fell more clearly in the intervention group over follow-up in the reported comparisons. Rates reaching target pressure were similar between groups, and the authors present the pilot as groundwork for a larger trial.
pmc-13488588:
Kavita Vinekar and colleagues talk with patients who had a pregnancy of unknown location, in a 2026 study in the United States. The term means an early pregnancy test is positive, yet a scan shows no pregnancy inside or outside the womb, leaving miscarriage, normal early pregnancy, and dangerous ectopic pregnancy all possible. Twenty patients followed through a tracking list, most of them on public insurance, described care received in clinic and emergency settings between late 2023 and early 2024.

Patients valued a resident-staffed phone line for questions and results. Gaps appeared in how the not-knowing was explained, how mental health support was offered, and how quickly follow-up care arrived. A devoted pregnancy emergency unit was proposed. The authors call for clearer talk with patients and faster pathways.
pmc-13491688:
Karita Koskinen leads a four-person team laying out in 2026 the protocol for the Finnish GLAMP trial, a randomized test of two gentle surgical treatments for pilonidal sinus disease. The condition, an infected tract near the tailbone, burdens many working-age adults. Solid trials of newer small-incision techniques are scarce.

Patients whom the treating surgeon judges fit for either method are assigned at random on the day of surgery. Healing rate early on and recurrence over the longer term are the main outcomes, with treatment costs also compared. Quality-of-life surveys are filled in before surgery and two months later, plus questions on pain and healing. The protocol was registered after the fact in April 2025, and results are not yet reported.
pmc-13491788:
Adams and colleagues report a 2026 pilot trial called eTHOS, which tested a health screening clinic for staff in four English NHS hospitals. Nurses used an electronic system to screen employees for muscle and joint problems, mental health difficulties, and heart disease risk factors. Staff who screened positive received advice or a referral to services, following national guidelines. The team wanted to learn whether a larger trial of the clinic could work in practice.

Only 314 of 3,788 invited staff consented to join, a recruitment rate the authors describe as lower than expected, and 236 people were randomised between the clinic and usual care. Among 118 people sent to the clinic, screening found 57 who needed a referral, and about a third of them accepted it. The oversight committee judged recruitment poor but referral strong, and recommended a full trial with changes to reach underserved staff groups.
pmc-13492288:
Rillig argued in 2026 that global environmental change may soon gain a driver that is not human at all. Change on this scale, from land conversion to climate shifts, has always traced back to human acts, wanted or not. Rillig points to AI agents, software systems that sense, plan, learn, and act on multi step goals with little human steer. As such agents spread, their choices could shape ecosystems on their own.

Unlike chatbots that answer prompts, these agents pursue set goals on their own and can even spawn more agents. Their direct footprint, in land, water, and power for data centers, is well known. Rillig stresses a deeper shift: acts with world scale effects could flow from machine choices, not human ones. He urges the field to name artificial agency as its own force, and to track its direct and side effects with care.
pmc-13493188:
Camponeschi and colleagues search the blood of women with lupus for chemical marks on DNA that track pain, fatigue, and poor health, symptoms that linger even when the disease sleeps. Lupus in this cohort was quiet: the forty eight women showed near zero activity and damage scores. Their 2026 study scans over seven hundred thousand methylation sites, the tags that dim or brighten genes, and matches patterns to each woman's self reported scores.

Hundreds of sites tied to each symptom, hundreds for pain, fatigue, and health alike. Pain linked sites sat in genes for nerve signal tuning, a surprise against the usual inflammation story. Fatigue sites enriched for nerve growth and synapse pathways. Nine genes, including BDNF, a nerve support factor, carried marks shared across all three scores, hinting at one root. Symptom burden in quiet lupus, the authors argue, may be written in the nervous system, not in flares.
pmc-13493788:
Md Jisan Ahmed leads a fourteen-author team tracking in 2026 how foot-and-mouth disease moved through Bangladesh between 2017 and 2023, and whether weather can foretell its next wave. The viral disease devastates cloven-hoofed livestock and farm incomes across the country. Case records from the livestock department were matched with meteorological data, mapped for clusters, and fed to three forecasting algorithms.

Cases crested in March, with stubborn hotspots in the southeast and fresh clusters emerging in the north. Humidity and temperature rose alongside incidence, and wind speed also carried weight in regression models. Among the forecasters, the gradient-boosted XGBoost model predicted most accurately, ahead of random forest and the classical ARIMA approach. Risk maps flagged the south, especially before the monsoon, giving veterinary services a seasonal targeting tool.
pmc-13493988:
Abdi and colleagues tested whether immersive virtual reality can calm women during vaginal examinations in labour, a necessary check of the cervix that often brings fear and pain. In their 2026 randomised trial at a teaching hospital in Mashhad, Iran, 70 pregnant women in early or active labour were split evenly. Half wore a headset showing a relaxing virtual scene while trainees examined them, and half received standard care. Anxiety was scored before and after, and pain with recognised rating tools.

After the examination, the virtual reality group's average anxiety score sat far below the control group's, a gap rated highly significant, while the groups had started out alike. Pain ratings also favoured the headset group across every dimension of the McGill questionnaire, from sensory to emotional aspects. The authors call the approach promising for patient comfort and trainee teaching, but preliminary, since one hospital and seventy women cannot settle the question.
pmc-13495288:
Emre Övsay, Ayfer Atav, and Duygu Mustafa Pamuk test, in a 2026 study, whether light-activated disinfection cuts pain after root canal treatment by dental students. Pain after root work is common and peaks in the first days. The add-on therapy, called photodynamic therapy, uses a dye lit by light to kill germs inside the tooth. The study covered 92 patients treated for lower back teeth in a student clinic.

Patients split between standard final rinsing and rinsing plus the light therapy. Pain fell over a week in both groups. At three days, the light group reported clearly lower pain. They also used fewer pain tablets, and none needed antibiotics, while the standard group used more of both. The authors judge the add-on a useful extra for student-treated cases, within the limits of a backward-looking comparison.
pmc-13495388:
Xiaoxia Wu, Bingliang Li, and Hongxia Ren present a 2026 case report of a newborn with two birth defects fixed in one keyhole operation. The baby boy had esophageal atresia with a fistula, meaning the food pipe ended blindly while joining the windpipe, plus a rare duplication cyst on the food pipe wall. Only twenty such pairings have been reported since 1956, all handled by open chest surgery.

At three days old and over two kilograms, he had chest keyhole surgery. The team found a one-centimeter cyst, shelled it out while sparing the pipe's lining, tied off the fistula, and joined the pipe ends. The road after was rough, with pneumonia, a suspected leak, and a narrowing that needed three stretchings. By ten months he was growing back toward the charts, with no return of fistula or cyst. The authors call the one-stage approach feasible for chosen babies.
pmc-13495488:
Siyu Li and colleagues sort, in a 2026 study, patients with type 2 diabetes into hidden profiles of diabetes distress, the emotional weight of living with the disease. Average scores can hide groups in real trouble. The team surveyed 155 patients at a hospital in Heilongjiang, China, with a distress scale and a measure of self-regulation fatigue, then let a profile method find natural groupings.

Three profiles emerged: a low group near two fifths of patients, a small middle group, and a high group covering over two fifths. Belonging to the harder profiles tied to being female, older age, more illnesses at once, longer disease, worse blood sugar control, and deeper self-regulation fatigue. The authors urge care teams to spot the middle and high groups and aim support at easing mental burden and restoring self-control strength.
pmc-13498588:
Mhairi J McCormack and colleagues ask in 2026 whether worm infections weaken antibody responses to COVID-19 vaccination in Malawi. Long-lasting worm infections reshape the immune system, which could blunt vaccine effects in regions where such infections are common. Samples came from rural Karonga and urban Lilongwe, with stool and urine tests for several worm species and blood tests for virus antibodies.

People with a current worm infection showed lower neutralising antibody levels after vaccination, and lower levels of another antibody aimed at the virus spike protein. That link did not appear for antibodies left by natural infection, a contrast the statistical models supported after accounting for other factors. The authors suggest testing whether deworming before vaccination improves responses in areas where worms are widespread.
pmc-13499388:
Min Liu and co-authors build in 2026 a cancer nanomedicine that needs no separate carrier material. The recipe assembles the drug doxorubicin with copper ions and a small RNA that silences a protective gene in tumour cells. Carrier complexity has slowed similar products before. A natural sugar coating on the particles guides them toward tumours, and acidity at the tumour site triggers drug release.

In a breast cancer model, the combined particles shrank tumours more effectively than the plain drug solution while causing fewer side effects. Treatment raised damaging oxygen species at tumour sites, lowered the protective gene's protein, and depleted a defence molecule. The result is a self-reinforcing cycle pairing standard chemotherapy with a chemical attack driven by metal reactions inside the tumour.
pmc-13501488:
Eileen M. Condon leads a four-author team with a 2026 study of what helps or hinders steady family patterns for preschool children. Regular bedtimes, wake times, and shared meals support child health and behaviour, yet what shapes them is poorly mapped. The study recruited 130 caregivers, 107 mothers and 23 fathers, of children aged three to five from community settings. Caregivers reported their patterns plus risk factors, namely their childhood maltreatment history and mental health symptoms, and factors such as happy childhoods and social support.

Regression analysis tied a maltreatment history and mental health symptoms to less steady patterns, while happy childhoods and social support were tied to steadier ones. The maltreatment link survived adjustment for mental health symptoms. Social support changed the picture further: the maltreatment effect appeared only among caregivers with low emotional and practical support. The authors suggest such help should target caregivers carrying these histories.
pmc-13501588:
Hiroaki Fukui leads a ten-author team reporting a 2026 retrospective study of treatment retention among outpatients with gambling disorder in Japan. Records came from Tarumi Hospital for patients first seen between April 2019 and December 2023, with follow-up to December 2024. A structured cognitive behavioural therapy group programme, 24 sessions across a year, was offered alongside usual care. Eighty-two patients started it within 30 days of their first visit, and 55 did not take part. Retention meant staying in treatment rather than dropping out.

By day 30, retention stood at 89.0 percent in the programme group against 45.5 percent outside it. The estimated hazard of discontinuation was lower for participants, with a hazard ratio of 0.64. Even so, the rough estimate remained compatible with there being no difference. Among patients who stayed past day 30, later retention did not differ between groups. The authors suggest that strengthening contact in the first month may matter most.
pmc-13501688:
Adéla Krajčová leads an eight-author team reporting a 2026 prospective study of muscle stem cells in critically ill patients, run under the name SATELLITE. Weakness after intensive care can linger for years, and failed muscle regeneration is a suspect. The team biopsied the thigh muscle of 33 ventilated adults within 72 hours of admission, again at day 7, and again at day 180, comparing them with 20 healthy controls. Isolated satellite cells were tested for growth, differentiation, fusion, and mitochondrial behaviour.

Patients grew profoundly weak within a week and developed insulin resistance, yet satellite cell numbers per fibre matched controls at admission and day 7. Differentiation was briefly impaired at the start, with a fusion index of 68.9 percent against 74.0 percent in control cells on that measure. Fragmented mitochondria tracked with poorer cell growth and strength. By day 180, cell numbers had recovered but proliferation stayed near half of normal in the few survivors who returned.
pmc-13501788:
Kei Takahashi-Yamashiro leads a ten-author team reporting a 2026 laboratory study of what makes pancreatic cancer cells spread. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma kills most patients, and nearly half already have metastases at diagnosis. The team grew mouse Panc02 tumour cells in the pancreas of matched mice, harvested the tumours, and repeated the cycle three times. The resulting Panc02-3P line grew and spread more aggressively and had shifted toward a mesenchymal, mobile character, without changes in the classic switch genes.

RNA sequencing singled out the lysyl oxidase family, enzymes that cross-link the tissue scaffold: LOX, LOXL1, and LOXL3 were all raised in the metastatic line. Silencing LOX or LOXL1 with targeted RNA snippets blunted the cells' ability to migrate in dishes. The authors link this enzyme family to the invasive phenotype and float its members as targets for a cancer with almost no effective drugs.
pmc-13503288:
Jian Li leads a sixteen-author team with a 2026 study of a gene switch that strips endometrial cancer cells of their androgen receptor and sends them spreading. Advanced endometrioid endometrial cancer lacks good targets, and loss of the androgen receptor tracks with worse spread for reasons nobody had pinned down. Tumours with too much of the factor KLF12, or lacking the receptor, sat at later stages and carried worse outcomes. Raising KLF12 in tests suppressed the receptor and sped spread in dishes and animals alike.

The mechanism is direct silencing. Prediction tools and CUT&Tag mapping placed KLF12 on the receptor gene's promoter and intron regions, and a battery of binding tests confirmed it represses the gene. Freed from the receptor, cells underwent epithelial-mesenchymal transition, the identity loosening that enables invasion. The authors name the KLF12-androgen receptor axis as a prognostic marker and a candidate treatment entry point.
pmc-13503388:
Xinyan Liu leads an eleven-author team reporting a 2026 real-world safety and effectiveness study of the etonogestrel contraceptive implant in China. Across 31 centres between March 2016 and July 2021, 1,901 women aged eighteen or older received the radiopaque implant as routine care and were followed for up to three years; 45.5 percent completed the full study. Mean age was 32.1 years, and average exposure ran about 784 days. Drug-related adverse events touched 47.9 percent of women, serious events 1.1 percent, and insertion-site reactions 10.4 percent.

Irregular vaginal bleeding was the commonest complaint, affecting 15.6 percent, matching the known profile with no unexpected signals. Satisfaction stayed high: most women rated themselves satisfied or very satisfied at thirty-six months, and physicians were near-unanimous after removals. Exactly one pregnancy occurred during treatment, a rate of 0.05 percent of participants on the reported figures. The authors conclude the implant performs in Chinese practice exactly as its trial record promised.
pmc-13503788:
Sirin Apichonbancha leads a team that tested three vision-capable chatbots on wound photos, in a 2026 study. Judging wounds from photos is now common in remote care, yet doctors vary a great deal in their calls. Chatbots are being used for this task with little proof that they are safe.

From 1,200 wound photos, the team picked 450 across acute, chronic, and surgical types. Three experts set the agreed answers. Each chatbot got the same prompts, framed by two standard wound scoring tools. One model led on naming the wound type and on care advice, while a second led on size and urgency calls. The third often failed to reply at all. The authors warn that none is ready for unsupervised clinic use.
pmc-13503888:
Tanja Gosseling, Bartholomeus G H Latten, and Jan Peter van Zandwijk test whether smartwatch data can pin down when a person died, in a 2026 study. Death investigators now rely mostly on body cooling, which works only for a short window and is swayed by many unknowns. Watches record heart and motion data up to the end of life.

The team gathered watches from 27 people who died at a set time during a planned medical procedure. Data from three watch brands showed clear changes near death. In most cases the watch-based estimate landed within about half an hour of the doctor's stated time. Some records had unexplained gaps, so the authors urge caution. Still, watch data may add a useful check beside older methods.
pmc-13504788:
Merter Güçlü and Hatice Selin Güçlü compare child-oriented toothbrushing videos on YouTube in Turkish and English. In 2026, the one-time study assesses fifty-one instructional videos, twenty-seven Turkish and twenty-four English, with two independent reviewers scoring quality, reliability, and guideline adherence, plus engagement metrics. Early childhood caries remains a major public health concern, and families increasingly turn to online video.

English videos scored higher on quality, reliability, and guideline compliance, with median quality three point two five versus one point five and compliance five point five versus three. Animation channels scored clearly lower than educational and health channels. Popularity did not correlate with quality. The authors urge dental professionals to produce evidence-based, age-appropriate videos and guide families toward reliable content.
pmc-13505088:
Wang Chunmao, Han Ming, and Wang Zitong report seven cases where chemo plus immune therapy wiped out visible tumor before surgery in small cell lung cancer, in a 2026 study. This cancer grows fast and spreads early, and surgery plays a small role in its care. Strong pre-surgery treatment could change that for limited-stage disease.

Patients got a median of three cycles of chemo with an immune drug, then radical surgery and more treatment after. Scans showed three partial and three complete responses before surgery. Tissue checks after surgery found no living cancer in any of the seven, a complete pathological response. All had clean-margin removals with few complications. At a median of forty-two months, six stayed disease-free; one relapsed in nodes and brain and died. Side effects were mostly mild.
pmc-13507088:
Xin Li and colleagues report 2026 findings on a tissue-resident natural killer cell group in non-small cell lung cancer, the most common lung cancer type. Natural killer cells normally kill tumor cells, yet this group, marked by CD49a, behaved in a suppressive way. The team studied surgical samples with single-cell gene readings.

Tumors rich in these cells responded poorly to therapy given before surgery and held fewer tertiary lymphoid structures, small immune hubs linked to better outcomes. The cells showed high checkpoint genes, low killing genes, and high CSF-1 output. That signal pushed macrophages toward a healing M2 state that favors tumors. Blocking this group could improve pre-surgery therapy.
pmc-13507688:
Anjali Shinde and four co-authors report a severe drug reaction in a 58-year-old woman in India who had started the gout drug allopurinol, in 2026 work. About 35 days after starting the drug, she developed widespread itchy red skin lesions across her face, trunk, and limbs. Blood tests showed very high levels of a white cell type tied to allergy, plus kidney and liver strain. A standard scoring system gave a score of 7, which marks a definite case of this syndrome, called DRESS.

Doctors stopped the drug at once and treated her with fluids, steroids, antihistamines, and close support care. The steroid dose was then lowered slowly over time. She recovered fully, with no return of symptoms. The case also reviews Indian published reports and stresses early spotting, quick drug withdrawal, and reporting of harmful drug reactions.
pmc-13508288:
Natalia Rutkowska, Bartosz Sekuła, and Olga Marchut-Mikołajczyk screen bacteria living inside a common plant for compounds that grab heavy metals, in 2026 work. The team studied ten bacteria from the medicinal plant Galium aparine, drawn from three genera. They tested which growth conditions switch production on, and which metals the compounds can bind beyond iron. Genome reading mapped the gene clusters that build these compounds, and their spread across known genomes.

All ten strains made the compounds at moderate to high levels. One strain, a Priestia, bound a wide set of metals including cobalt, manganese, zinc, nickel, and copper. Another, a Peribacillus, grabbed the highly toxic lead, mercury, and cadmium with notable strength. Similar gene clusters turned up in many stored genomes, hinting at wide conservation. The authors propose these strains as candidates for farm and cleanup uses where metals contaminate ground.
pmc-13508388:
Yusuke Misumi leads a fourteen-author team studying what happens to a mildly leaking heart valve when a neighboring valve is replaced and the leak is left alone, in 2026 work. Patients had severe narrowing of the aortic valve and mild to moderate leakage of the mitral valve. All 430 patients had isolated aortic valve surgery between 2016 and 2021, with the mitral leak untreated. The main question was how many showed a meaningful mitral leak one year later.

Only twenty-two patients, about one in twenty, had a significant mitral leak at one year. Three baseline traits predicted that outcome: how fast blood crossed the aortic valve, the starting grade of the mitral leak, and the size of the left upper heart chamber. Patients stacking several risk traits fared worse on death and readmission. The authors advise weighing these traits when deciding whether to fix both valves at once.
pmc-13508588:
Tang and colleagues reviewed the protein PACS2, a trafficking adapter stationed where the cell's endoplasmic reticulum touches its mitochondria, and its role across cardiovascular and metabolic diseases. Their 2026 review argues these contact zones, called mitochondria-linked membranes, act as control hubs for calcium signals, fat handling, and cell death choices. PACS2 sits at the center of their control.

Tang details how PACS2 governs membrane trafficking and influences cell death, the self-cleaning process autophagy, and ferroptosis, a form of iron-driven cell death. The review assembles evidence tying PACS2 malfunction to metabolic disorders and heart and vessel conditions alike. The protein's effects flip between harmful and helpful based on cell type and disease setting. That duality slows drug work but multiplies entry points, such as blocking its binding to partners that promote death. They name PACS2 as a marker candidate and a treatment target that needs testing in patients.
pmc-13509388:
Jao and colleagues test a soft MRI coil designed for children's bodies. Their 2026 paper evaluates a thirty-channel high-density posterior cushion coil built into a padded cushion, against the rigid table coils standard in scanners. Adult-sized rigid arrays sit far from small patients, weakening the signal; a conforming cushion closes that distance. Twenty-five children were scanned with the prototype and twenty-five comparable patients with standard coils.

Every cushion-coil image was judged diagnostic, averaging about 4.1 on a five-point quality scale across two radiologists. Signal strength in the superficial back muscles ran about 34 percent higher than with standard coils, while the deeper liver signal was statistically similar between systems. Tests on phantoms agreed with the patient findings. The authors conclude the shape-conforming design improves signal where distance matters most, without sacrificing deeper imaging.
pmc-13509988:
Maria Vogt, Elke Rohmann, Hans-Werner Bierhoff, and Phillip Ozimek examine how LinkedIn use relates to changing career goals, in 2026 work. Professional platforms expose users to a steady stream of other people's progress, which can invite comparison. Data from 188 LinkedIn users were tested with correlation and pathway analyses built around comparison habits and the felt gap between current and hoped-for careers.

Heavier LinkedIn use went with more career comparison, which went with a larger felt gap, which in turn went with stronger goal revision. That full chain explained downward revision, where people lowered their aims. Upward revision, where people raised their aims, tied to LinkedIn use directly and not through the chain. How central a career felt to a person raised comparison frequency yet did not change the pathways. The authors frame the platform as a setting for self-checking and goal control.
pmc-13510188:
Zhang and colleagues reported in 2026 that a calming fat-based pathway in the brain fades when manganese builds up, and that this loss tracks with brain swelling and poor memory. Too much manganese, a metal met in mining and smelting, harms the brain, but the role of the body's own calming signals was unclear. The team paired worker blood data with mouse and cell tests.

In exposed workers, levels of the calming compound 15d-PGJ2 and its maker enzyme were lower than normal. In mice and cultured brain cells, manganese raised two drivers of swelling, C/EBPβ and MMP9, pushed immune cells toward an attack state, and hurt neurons. Silencing either driver eased the damage. Giving 15d-PGJ2 back lowered both drivers and partly restored memory in exposed mice. The results point to a possible treatment route.
pmc-13510388:
Ka and colleagues review in 2026 the case for DCTPP1 as a drug target in liver cancer. DCTPP1 is a house-cleaning enzyme that destroys abnormal building blocks of DNA, keeping the nucleotide pool clean for accurate copying. When its levels go wrong, cells suffer replication stress and genome instability. Recent studies find the enzyme turned up across many cancers, where it supports tumor growth, stress tolerance, and resistance to chemotherapy.

In hepatocellular carcinoma, the most common liver cancer, researchers have reported a feedback loop between DCTPP1 and MYC, a powerful cancer-driving protein, that rewires how tumor cells handle pyrimidine building blocks. The review gathers what is known about the enzyme's biology, its role in this cancer, and the prospects for blocking it therapeutically. The authors present DCTPP1 inhibition as a promising route that still needs drug development and testing.
pmc-13511188:
Norbert Farago and co-authors report a sports science study, published in 2026, tracking the physical demands placed on under-19 basketball players across a season in the Hungarian junior league. Fifteen players wore a local positioning system during eight home games, and the team compared external load between game quarters and playing positions.

Most measures, including total player load and hard accelerations, did not differ significantly by quarter or position. Jumps did vary, with centres showing clear differences between the middle and later quarters, and hard decelerations differed between guards and forwards in the second quarter. The authors suggest position-specific drills, while cautioning that one team's data cannot be generalised.
pmc-13512488:
Tayyaba Kazmi and six co-authors study a gene change and DNA methylation patterns in uterine fibroids among women in Karachi, Pakistan, in 2026 work. The study recruited 200 women with fibroids and 50 controls at hospitals. Blood hormone levels were measured. DNA from fibroid and normal womb tissue was typed for a variant in the MED12 gene and profiled for methylation, a chemical layer that tunes gene use.

Cases clustered between ages thirty-one and fifty, with much overweight and central weight gain. Hormone levels ran higher in cases across cycle phases. One genotype of the variant carried a sharply higher fibroid risk, and the top genotype multiplied odds many times over. Excess methylation was the most common epigenetic finding, present in about seven in ten fibroid samples. Age and body mass also fed the risk model. The authors link the gene variant to skewed methylation in these tumors.
pmc-13513388:
Gomes and colleagues report a 2026 study of sex differences in flight-related body structures in a paper wasp, Polistes simillimus.  The team measured body traits linked to flight in one hundred mated pairs and compared size and proportions between females and males.

Females were larger overall, as expected for the sex that founds nests and forages. The sexes also differed in body proportions, not just scale: wing and body part ratios shifted in ways that suit their different flight tasks. Proportion shifts can change speed, load carrying, and agility. The authors frame the measurements as testable hypotheses about how flight performance evolved in each sex, a step toward linking body shape to what wasps actually do on the wing.
pmc-13514488:
Pereira and colleagues evaluated two commercial gene-amplification tests for fast diagnosis of invasive fungal infections in at-risk patients in Paraguay. Their 2026 clinical study is the first of its kind in Latin America. One test detects Candida yeasts that invade the bloodstream. The other detects Aspergillus molds that invade the lungs and beyond, both notorious killers of immunocompromised patients when diagnosis comes late.

Pereira found the Candida test agreed strongly with blood culture, the slow standard method, in detecting bloodstream infection. The Aspergillus test matched closely with the standard fungal antigen test, especially in lung wash fluid samples. Because molecular tests return answers far faster than culture, the authors argue adding them to conventional workflows helps clinicians start targeted antifungal therapy earlier. They position the assays as complements to, not replacements for, culture and antigen testing in routine fungal diagnostics.
pmc-13514788:
Abramavičius and colleagues reviewed in 2026 two decades of studies on drug treatment for Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a tough germ that infects lungs, blood, and wounds in hospital patients. The germ resists many antibiotics, so doctors need clear proof of which drug plans work best. The team searched two large medical databases for studies published between 2000 and early 2026, and screened what they found.

Of nearly a thousand records, 249 studies met the review rules, and 34 had data clean enough to pool. No single drug or drug pair beat the rest across all cases. Results hinged on infection site, drug resistance, and how the drug moves through the body. Two antibody and vaccine ideas failed to help patients, while one lab-made antibody showed promise. The authors call for more uniform trials.
pmc-13514988:
Seyed Sina Ziaee and Katie Ovens survey, in a 2026 review, methods for measuring uncertainty in artificial intelligence systems that outline structures in medical scans. Modern neural networks segment tumours and organs impressively, yet they hand back a single answer with no hint of doubt, which can breed overconfidence where an image is ambiguous. Their survey sorts the field into Bayesian methods, ensembles of models, deterministic approaches, test-time augmentation, and hybrids. Foundation-model techniques are treated as a cross-cutting theme.

Standard tools receive close treatment, including Monte Carlo dropout and Bayesian neural networks. Other methods separate uncertainty from noise in the data itself from uncertainty born of limited knowledge. Applications span brain tumour scans, heart imaging, and lung nodule detection, while evaluation turns on calibration and how well uncertainty tracks actual errors.
pmc-13515088:
Shufan Li and six colleagues present a flexible electromagnetic actuator built around liquid metal circuits in a 2026 engineering study. Such soft actuators suit robots and wearable interfaces, yet liquid metal tends to peel away from polymer supports, degrading performance over repeated cycles. Their fix writes circuits of a gallium-indium alloy directly onto a spun nanofibre membrane blending graphene oxide with a stretchy polyurethane, betting that the oxide's chemistry grips the metal's surface layer.

The bet paid off. The actuator bent a full ninety degrees under a modest driving current and kept working through two thousand cycles with negligible decline. Hydrogen bonding between the graphene oxide and the metal's oxide skin, reinforced by the fibrous texture, explains the durability in the team's account. A soft gripper built on the design lifted objects up to seven times its own weight.
pmc-13515888:
Stavros Bashiardes and six colleagues review the case linking Epstein-Barr virus with multiple sclerosis in a 2026 article. Nearly every person with MS carries this common virus, and long-term studies show infection comes before the disease starts. The virus lives quietly in B cells for life and steers the immune system in lasting ways. The authors gather the population evidence, then turn to mechanism.

One candidate route is mistaken identity: immune replies to a viral protein called EBNA1 may cross-react with proteins of the brain and spinal cord. MS patients also handle the virus oddly, with skewed antibody and T-cell responses. Infected immune cells have been reported inside MS brain tissue, though their exact role is unsettled. Bashiardes's team closes by listing the open questions that must be answered before the viral link can be turned into prevention or treatment.
pmc-13516888:
Wang and colleagues reviewed in 2026 delayed diarrhoea caused by irinotecan, a first-line drug for advanced colorectal cancer. The side effect appears days after dosing and can be severe enough to derail treatment. The authors trace how the drug's active form, SN-38, is moved and recycled through the liver and gut. That exposure holds it against the gut wall, disturbing gut bacteria, immune balance, and the gut barrier.

Wang notes that current care leans on dose cuts and drug combinations, which often work poorly and risk weakening the cancer treatment itself. Herbal medicines and plant chemicals look promising as add-on options because they act on many targets at once, matching a problem with many links. The review maps the full pathway of the side effect and lists candidate agents, with special weight on traditional Chinese medicine and on ideas for more precise future drugs.
pmc-13517888:
Mengyang Ni and co-authors study in 2026 how cobalt-doped pyrite particles activate persulfate chemicals to destroy 4-chlorophenol, a toxic pollutant found in groundwater. Such oxidation treatment is injected underground, so knowing exactly how it works helps engineers dose it well.

The doped particles broke the pollutant down with both common persulfate types, but through different mixes of attacking species. One system showed an odd three-stage speed pattern: slow at first, then a sudden burst after about three minutes. Calculations traced the burst to a high-powered iron form whose creation became easier as sulfate built up on the surface. Dissolved iron leaking from the particles also helped, to different degrees in each system. The findings refine how cleanup crews might choose oxidants.
pmc-13518088:
Rayner and colleagues analyzed infection outcomes in 2026 from the FLOW trial of once-weekly semaglutide in people with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease. The main trial had shown the drug cuts kidney, heart, and death outcomes in this group, who also suffer heavy infection burdens. This prespecified analysis asked whether serious infections, hospitalizations for infection, and COVID-19 events also fell on the drug.

Semaglutide lowered the combined risk of a first serious infection event, infection hospitalization, or death by about a fifth against placebo. Infection serious events, COVID-19 events, and infection hospitalizations each ran lower on the drug. The benefit was larger in patients who started with poorer blood sugar control and in those with the heaviest urine protein, markers of higher risk. The authors say the drug's value in this population may extend beyond its proven kidney and heart gains.
pmc-13518988:
Krishnan K Mahadevan and a large team find in 2026 that pancreatic cancer drugs targeting mutant Kras open a specific window for one immunotherapy partner. Kras inhibitors alone recruit T cells into tumors, but responses fade. Testing combinations in mouse pancreatic tumors, only anti-CTLA4 blockade, not five other immune agents, synergized strongly.

Kras targeting flooded the tumor with mixed T cells: effectors, exhausted cells, and regulatory cells. Anti-CTLA4 then reprogrammed the regulatory cells toward a naive state by dialing down AP-1 factors at the IL-35 gene, revived exhausted killers, and drew in organized lymphoid structures. Two Kras drugs, MRTX1133 and daraxonrasib, showed the effect. The team calls the pairing immediately relevant for trials.
pmc-13520288:
Fatmah Ahmed Alamoudi and three others asked nurses in 2026 about running Enhanced Recovery After Surgery protocols after emergency laparotomy, one of the riskiest abdominal operations. Recovery bundles were built for planned surgery, and their fit with unstable emergency patients is unclear. Twenty nurses from wards, intensive care, and post-op units at two Saudi teaching hospitals shared what they saw.

Four themes emerged. The protocol served as a clear roadmap with set steps. Nurses kept balancing its rules against patient instability, and their advocacy and judgment were the real go-betweens for delivery. Staffing gaps and site-to-site variation hurt consistency. The team built an Adaptive ERAS Implementation Model: recovery care as dynamic and nurse-led, not checklist work.
pmc-13520388:
Simon Kayembe and colleagues check in 2026 two rapid tests for African sleeping sickness in Kasai-Oriental province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, where cases have fallen toward elimination levels. In low-prevalence settings, false results matter greatly, so stored blood samples were tested against a strict reference method.

The set held 447 samples, with 227 confirmed cases and 220 controls. One test caught about 85 percent of cases with about 72 percent correct negatives, while the other caught about 90 percent of cases. Full specificity and paired comparisons follow in the results. Programme managers gain head-to-head accuracy figures for surveillance choices.
pmc-13520488:
Indiris Abdu, Anchiye Getachew and Abayeneh Girma pool in 2026 studies of hard tick infestation in Ethiopian camels, animals central to livelihoods across East Africa. Ticks drain blood, spread disease and cut productivity, yet a national pooled figure was missing.

Eleven cross-sectional studies covering 4,895 camels in six regions met quality checks. Pooled infestation reached about 86 percent, with Tigray, Dire Dawa and Afar highest in regional breakdowns. Consistency, bias and sensitivity checks accompany the headline figure. Such a high pooled rate argues for coordinated tick control, since single-farm efforts alone are unlikely to hold gains.
pmc-13522488:
Anju Kanjirakandi Ashokan leads a 2026 study of a bacterium, Serratia strain CS01, that makes both a protein-cutting enzyme and a red pigment. Genetic sequencing identified the isolate, while chemical analyses confirmed an enzyme of about sixty kilodaltons and a pigment resembling prodigiosin. Tests measured protection of red blood cells, antioxidant activity, and antibacterial effects in the lab.

The pigment protected red cell membranes at levels close to a standard anti-inflammatory drug and showed strong antioxidant activity at the highest dose tested. The pigment also inhibited three bacterial species more strongly than the crude extract did. Because one strain yields an enzyme and a pigment with several useful actions, the authors present it as a promising source for new drugs and products.
pmc-13523188:
Paolizzi and co-authors ran a 2026 study on how social cues boost learning in preschool children, including autistic children. Associative learning means linking two events that occur together, and social sights usually strengthen such links. Whether that boost holds for autistic children who speak very little was unknown.

Seventy-two children aged two to four took part, split among typical children, speaking autistic children, and minimally speaking autistic children. In an eye tracking task, neutral cues were paired with social or non-social pictures on screen. Typical and speaking autistic children later looked longer toward where the social picture had appeared, showing the boost. Minimally speaking children showed no such difference, which Paolizzi reads as a distinct learning profile.
pmc-13523288:
Ying Yang, Tianji Gao, Shaonan Xu, and Bei Xu evaluate an added biologic drug in children with lupus in a 2026 single-center retrospective study. Forty children with active systemic lupus erythematosus were split evenly between standard therapy alone and standard therapy plus belimumab, given by infusion on a tapering schedule. Kidney and skin remission, disease activity scores, steroid doses, and side effects were compared over six and twelve months.

Remission rates and laboratory improvements were broadly similar between groups at both time points, with no statistically clear advantage on most outcomes. Steroid doses, however, fell much further in the added-drug group by the later checks reported. One child had reversible drops in protective antibodies and B cells, and no severe infections or infusion reactions occurred. The authors call for larger prospective studies to confirm a steroid-sparing benefit.
pmc-13523388:
Nan Jia and co-authors compare two ovarian stimulation protocols ahead of fresh transfer in younger patients whose outlook is poor, in a 2026 retrospective study. Women under thirty-five with low ovarian reserve marker levels were drawn from fertility treatment records spanning 2016 to 2024. Nearly five thousand cycles were compared, then matched one to one to balance the groups before further analysis.

After matching, the agonist protocol produced a higher clinical pregnancy rate and a notably higher live birth rate than the antagonist protocol. Ectopic pregnancy, early miscarriage, and preterm birth did not differ clearly. The agonist group also had fewer cancelled fresh transfers and fewer cycles ending in freezing all embryos. Adjusted analysis confirmed both advantages, supporting the agonist approach for this specific patient group.
pmc-13523688:
Tripathi and Milner built an atomistic simulation framework that models a discharging lithium-ion battery from molecular interactions upward, in a 2026 computational study. Standard battery models need more than thirty parameters measured from experiments on working cells, which is invasive and gives no insight into why the numbers take their values. The authors instead derive the needed behavior from simulated motion of the electrolyte's ions and solvent.

Tripathi unified four simulation types: mobility runs that watch fluxes respond to steady forces, susceptibility runs that watch concentrations respond to applied potentials, bulk modulus runs under pressure. A discharge run where one electrode steadily absorbs lithium ions while the other releases them. In the discharge run the ion flux settles to a steady current driven jointly by electric force, concentration gradients, and compression. Linking the calibration runs to the discharge through mobility coefficients produces a self-consistent molecular description of ion transport.
pmc-13523788:
Santos and Blitzkow described a 2026 case report of a sixty-five-year-old man whose pancreas became severely inflamed six years after stomach removal surgery. His whole stomach had been taken out for cancer and rebuilt in a Roux-en-Y pattern, which reroutes food and digestive juices along separate limbs. He arrived with severe upper belly pain and vomiting.

Blood tests showed very high pancreatic enzymes, and scans revealed a blocked afferent limb, the limb carrying bile and pancreatic juices. A repeat scan three days later confirmed tissue death in the pancreas, called necrotizing pancreatitis. Emergency surgery found a scar band strangling that limb, and cutting it restored flow. Santos reports he recovered smoothly and stayed symptom free at six months.
pmc-13524188:
Zhihan Hu and colleagues review, in 2026, the role of neutrophil extracellular traps in diabetic wounds that fail to heal. These traps are webs of DNA and proteins cast out by neutrophils, a frontline immune cell. Diabetic wounds often stall in chronic inflammation, and trap activity is increasingly blamed.

The review sorts trap formation into vital and lytic forms. It then refines the lytic route into a classical subtype driven by an enzyme called NOX2 and a rapid subtype driven by mitochondrial reactive oxygen species. Evidence on how traps behave in the diabetic wound environment is gathered, including both defense and damage. Treatments that block formation, break traps down, or neutralize them look promising before clinical testing. The authors call for standard markers and local delivery to limit immune suppression.
pmc-13524788:
Jun Chen and others report a 2026 study linking a gut bacterium's toxin to gall bladder cancer. Enterotoxigenic Bacteroides fragilis, already tied to colorectal cancer, was found enriched in gall bladder tumors. Whether the bacterium actively drives this aggressive biliary cancer was unknown.

Patient samples confirmed enrichment, and mouse work showed the bacterium colonizes the gall bladder and speeds tumor cell growth in culture and in patient-derived organoids. Tumor growth in a mouse graft model depended on the bacterial toxin. Mechanistically, a bacterial surface protein engaged a host receptor, switching on JAK2-STAT3 signaling, while toxin-driven NF-kB signaling raised a chemokine that recruited suppressive immune cells and promoted blood vessel growth. The authors nominate these steps as treatment targets.
pmc-13526488:
Al Shabaan and colleagues reported a 2026 case report on kidney stone surgery in one fifty-year-old woman. She had stones low in both ureters, the tubes carrying urine to the bladder, plus pain, fever, and raised kidney markers. Tubes placed through her back into the kidneys, called nephrostomy tubes, first drained the blocked urine.

Two weeks later Al Shabaan broke up the stones with a laser passed through a rigid scope while salt water flowed down through those back tubes. The forward flow pushed fragments toward the bladder instead of letting them bounce back up, and kept the view clear. Every fragment was basketed out and stents were placed, and a scan four weeks later showed no leftover stones. No problems from the irrigation were seen.
pmc-13526788:
Jichao Li and colleagues tested a rumen yeast that could cut methane from dairy cows without hurting milk output. Published in 2026, the study screened 73 rumen strains in the lab, picking Pichia membranifaciens M12, which cut methane by about one sixth. A randomized trial then fed 36 cows either plain feed or M12 at two doses.

The high dose cut methane per unit of feed eaten by nearly one fifth, with no cost to milk performance or animal health. Multi-omics work showed M12 suppressing methane-making microbes and hydrogen producers while boosting other rumen residents, and gene data showed methane-making genes falling as propionate-making genes rose. The authors read this as energy rerouted from methane toward useful products. Readers get a sustainable farming lead with field-scale testing still ahead.
pmc-13527088:
Ammaji Rajala and colleagues define, in a 2026 mouse study, the role of the metabolic enzyme PKM2 in keeping the retina alive. PKM2 both drives a sugar-burning step and helps switch genes on, coordinating energy and survival. The team mapped when and where each PKM form appears, then deleted PKM2 in specific retinal layers.

PKM2 appears by the second day after birth, before its sibling form, and concentrates in light-sensing photoreceptors, while PKM1 dominates in ganglion cells. Removing PKM2 from retina, rods, or the pigment epithelium weakened sugar metabolism, cut energy production, and caused disorganization and degeneration. In the pigment layer it also lowered a key visual-cycle protein and disturbed cone arrangement across the retina. Rod deletion worsened early degeneration in a disease model, underscoring metabolic interdependence.
pmc-13527688:
SM Sabrina Yesmin leads a large team in a 2026 study estimating sales of antimicrobials for food-producing animals in Bangladesh during 2023, evidence meant to steer national policy on drug resistance. Data were collected and calculated with a World Organisation for Animal Health tool, broken down by drug class, molecule, and route of administration.

Total sales reached 475,750 kilograms across 301 products and thirty-eight molecules. Oral dosing accounted for nearly ninety-six percent of volume. Tetracyclines were the top class at about a third of sales, followed by aminoglycosides near a fifth, and eight molecules made up almost four fifths of all sales. Just over a fifth of volume belonged to classes ranked as highest-priority critically important for human medicine. The authors call the pattern overuse requiring stewardship action.
pmc-13528088:
Kiran Shahzadi and five colleagues report pancreatic tuberculosis posing as cancer in a 2026 case from Pakistan. A 24-year-old man had five to six months of right-sided belly pain. Jaundice and a five-kilo weight loss followed. Scans found a mass in the head of the pancreas. The picture strongly suggested pancreatic cancer.

An ultrasound-guided needle biopsy told a different story. Tissue showed the cheese-like granulomas typical of tuberculosis. A rapid gene test confirmed the TB germ. Drug treatment for tuberculosis brought clear clinical and scan improvement. The authors stress geography: where TB is common, it belongs on the list for pancreatic masses. Biopsy before big surgery can spare patients needless operations. Their case adds to a small but growing set of reports.
pmc-13529588:
Yingyin Gao and a large team report in 2026 on why advanced prostate cancer stops responding to the drug abiraterone. They focus on super enhancers, clusters of DNA switches that strongly turn genes on, and on how these switches rewire cancer cells.

By mapping enhancer activity and gene expression, the team found overactive enhancers driving two regulator genes, ELF3 and JUNB. That pair pushed cancer cells toward a nerve-like state through a signal called WNT11, which helped them resist the drug. The changed cells also raised protective genes that block ferroptosis, a form of cell death tied to iron. Breaking this chain in lab and animal tests restored drug sensitivity and triggered that cell death.
pmc-13530188:
William A Liguore and colleagues show in 2026 that aging monkeys develop the same enlarged fluid channels around brain vessels seen in older humans. These perivascular spaces may signal how well the brain clears waste, yet mice never form the visible kind. Scans covered 94 rhesus macaques aged 5 to 28 years.

Automated counting found channel number and volume rising steeply with age, spread across the brain in a human-like pattern. Microscope checks on removed tissue confirmed a scanned tube truly was such a channel. The monkey therefore offers a bridge between mouse experiments and human brain aging studies.
pmc-13531088:
Abdul Rasheed Bahar, Yasemin Bahar, and Frank Alexander Baciewicz report in 2026 a hidden aortic tear found mid-operation in an 86-year-old woman.
