She had severe valve narrowing, widespread coronary disease, and chest pain that resisted a full day of medical therapy. Surgeons planned valve replacement plus bypass grafting.

During surgery the upper aorta looked abnormal, and ultrasound confirmed an acute type A dissection, a tear in the rising aorta. Because the tear began high, a focused patch repair replaced the standard full replacement. She recovered and remained alive three years later.
pmc-13531888:
Daisong Jiang and co-authors settle in 2026 how to measure valve calcium on contrast scans by weighing real calcium from removed valves. Past checks leaned on another scan estimate as truth. Fifty surgical patients had their excised leaflets burned and weighed precisely, giving an absolute reference for two brightness cutoffs and a learning model.

The deep learning model tracked weighed calcium most closely, with the smallest error and bias. The higher fixed cutoff came second, while the lower cutoff overestimated and skewed with size. The authors back learning-based measurement for planning valve replacement.
pmc-13533188:
Shannon L Edmed and colleagues review in 2026 obstructive sleep apnea among Indigenous peoples worldwide. The disorder blocks the upper airway during sleep and links to heart disease, diabetes, and poor daytime function. Early signs suggest Indigenous groups carry a higher burden, yet global proof had not been gathered.

From 599 records the team kept 41 studies from six countries. Reported rates varied widely by sample type, and strong population estimates were rare. Care proof covered only airway pressure therapy, with low use over time. Readers see a clear call for screening and care shaped with local communities.
pmc-13534188:
Shouxiang Yang and colleagues study in 2026 a long non-coding RNA named TLX1NB in periodontitis, a long-term gum disease driven by bacterial films. Gene scans found TLX1NB raised in gum tissue from patients, and a lab model with stimulated gum cells showed the same rise. The RNA sits mostly in the cell nucleus.

Lowering TLX1NB cut key swelling signals, eased cell death, and boosted cell growth in the model. Tests showed TLX1NB binds MMP8, an enzyme that breaks down collagen, and both act together on swelling paths. Readers see a fresh target for calming gum tissue harm.
pmc-13534388:
Cristina A Munoz de Leon-Lopez, Irene Navarro-Lobato, and Zafar U Khan review in 2026 chemical tags that control AMPA receptors, the main carriers of fast signals between brain cells. Tags added after a protein is built steer receptors into or out of synapses, shaping learning strength. The review covers seven tag types and how they interact.

Strengthening a connection adds tags that insert receptors, while weakening favours tags that pull them inside. Faults at tag sites disrupt memory in lab models, and faulty tag control links to aging, Alzheimer disease, and schizophrenia. Readers get a map of targets for memory research.
pmc-13534588:
Eunice Tan and colleagues build in 2026 a machine learning ranking model to predict long-term survival for donor and recipient pairs in liver transplant. Organ shortage makes each match count, and older scores predict pair outcomes poorly. Records from a national registry covered transplants from 2009 to 2019.

Their score beat standard survival models at six months, one year, and three years after transplant. Performance was strongest for the sickest recipients with high severity scores. Readers see a tool that could support allocation choices, though live clinical testing must come before routine adoption.
pmc-13535888:
Lorena Morton and colleagues study brain immune cells during remission in a mouse model of relapsing gut inflammation that mimics ulcerative colitis. Patients often keep anxiety and low mood during remission, yet brain changes then were unstudied. Mice went through three cycles of gut inflammation and recovery before brain checks.

The blood-brain barrier leak seen during flares healed in remission, yet cortical immune cells stayed in a pro-inflammatory state linked to unbalanced synapses. Hippocampal cells shifted to a repair mode that guarded circuits. Gut remission thus does not fully restore brain immune balance.
pmc-13536788:
Chunhua Xi and co-authors study low blood sodium before hip fracture surgery in older adults in a 2026 review of 1,901 patients aged 60 years or older treated between 2015 and 2021. Low sodium was split into mild and stronger levels. Models linked each level to complications and to death at one month and one year, with extra checks on whether later sodium problems and complications carried the risk.

About one in eight patients arrived with low sodium. Mild low sodium raised complication risk without a clear link to early death. Stronger low sodium raised both complication risk and early death risk sharply. Later complications and later low sodium together explained a large share of the early death link. The authors urge prevention of complications and careful sodium correction.
pmc-13538488:
Walter N Harrington and co-authors test whether broadly binding human antibodies to an internal flu protein protect mice in a 2026 study. Surface protein antibodies anchor most flu vaccines, while internal nucleoprotein antibodies remain puzzling despite wide strain coverage. Three human antibodies isolated after natural infection in the 2018 to 2019 season were given to mice before flu exposure. Binding, neutralization, and cell defense activation were also checked in dishes.

All three antibodies bound nucleoprotein strongly across many strains, yet none limited weight loss or death in mice. None neutralized infection in dishes either. Surface binding to infected cells occurred without triggering cellular antiviral responses. The authors caution that vaccine plans chasing similar antibodies must first boost potency or clarify any helpful role.
pmc-13538688:
Loreto Lancia and colleagues track the long-term burden of heart failure in an Italian province in a 2026 population cohort study. All 5,883 residents discharged alive after a first heart failure hospital stay between 2014 and 2022 were followed through 2023. Survival curves charted death and readmission at set points up to nine years, and models hunted predictors of the combined outcome.

By five years, about seven in ten patients had died or returned to hospital, rising to roughly six in seven by nine years. Nearly half of all readmissions landed in the first year. Male sex, older age, longer first stays, and earlier discharge years predicted worse outcomes. The authors stress ongoing care, with nurses central to improving results.
pmc-13540888:
Chuchu Zhao and Guiying Zhang build a prediction model in a 2026 study. The model forecasts survival in endometrial cancer. That is the commonest cancer of the female reproductive system. The model rests on genes tied to palmitoylation. Palmitoylation is a fat-tagging process that alters protein behaviour.

The team worked from a large public cancer database. They distilled six signature genes from the data. Lab checks in cells and patient samples matched the patterns. A risk score built on those genes split patients into two groups. The high-risk group fared worse than the low-risk group. Immune cell mixes also differed between the groups. Clustering found two molecular subtypes of the cancer.
pmc-13542288:
Lu Yang and colleagues published a 2026 habitat study of Saunders's Gull, a globally endangered waterbird whose largest breeding population gathers in China's Liao River Estuary National Nature Reserve. Field surveys at 53 points supplied breeding records, which were combined with 24 environmental variables in a MaxEnt model, a method that predicts where conditions suit a species. Geographic analysis then mapped the most promising breeding ground inside the reserve.

Wet grassland dominated the study area. Four factors together explained about 71 percent of habitat suitability: elevation, wind speed, soil acidity, and soil electrical conductivity, each favouring a fairly narrow band of values. Worryingly, only about two percent of the area counted as highly suitable breeding habitat. The maps give reserve managers exact places to protect and show how field observation plus modelling can guide care of a scarce breeding bird.
pmc-13543388:
Anne Katrine Normann and colleagues published a 2026 scoping review of screening for intimate partner violence during pregnancy and after birth across Europe. Violence in this window harms mother and child, yet practice varies and the scale is likely undercounted. Following recognised scoping methods, the team searched seven databases for screening tools used in European antenatal and postpartum care, judged study quality, and asked representatives of forty-six countries about their programmes.

Twenty-four studies were included, with quality ranging widely, and thirteen tools were identified, most often the Abuse Assessment Screen and the Woman Abuse Screening Tool. No tool covered stalking or digital abuse. Replies came from twenty-two countries: seventeen had screening programmes, five had none, and most programmes recommended asking everyone rather than only those judged at risk. Practice remains far from uniform, the authors say.
pmc-13543788:
Ana Quiles Rocher and colleagues published a 2026 case report of repairing a carotid artery aneurysm in the neck using the patient's own jugular vein, a conduit surgeons rarely choose. A 69-year-old man had a steadily enlarging neck mass that imaging showed to be a 22-by-31 millimetre aneurysm of the internal carotid artery, a type needing difficult high exposure. His leg veins, the usual graft source, proved too narrow on mapping.

Surgeons removed the aneurysm, temporarily shunting blood to the brain, and sewed in a reversed segment of the internal jugular vein taken through the same incision. Recovery was smooth apart from a temporary vocal cord weakness, and no congestion followed from closing the vein. Scans at one year confirmed an open, unst narrowed graft. The jugular's calibre match and same-incision harvest, the authors argue, earn it a place on the options list.
pmc-13543988:
Xiao Gong and colleagues published a 2026 review of making wine from fruits other than grapes, from berries and stone fruit to citrus, pome, and tropical harvests. Fermenting surplus or blemished fruit into wine can cut the heavy post-harvest losses these crops suffer and add value, yet most producers borrow grape methods wholesale. The review walks the whole production chain, from juice preparation through fermentation to keeping the finished wine stable.

Non-grape wines fail in their own ways: raw materials lack the sugar-acid balance grapes provide, fermentations need targeted control, and haze, browning, and safety faults threaten the bottle. Quality, the authors argue, comes from deliberately compensating for each fruit's deficiencies rather than imitating Bordeaux habits. Standardised, fruit-specific processes would let country wines become a deliberate industry instead of an improvisation.
pmc-13544088:
Gao and colleagues traced a 2025 outbreak of acute gastroenteritis at a boarding high school in Anhui Province, China to rotavirus C, a less common cousin of the main childhood diarrhea virus. Rotavirus C causes only about one percent of human rotavirus cases and rarely erupts in outbreaks, so a school-wide event was a rare tracing chance. The team joined field work with rapid multiplex testing and full genome sequencing.

Thirteen complete rotavirus C genomes came from this single outbreak, an unusually rich haul, and comparison with global sequences let the team place the strain's origin and spread. The investigation confirmed the virus as the outbreak's cause among final-year students in close quarters. The authors highlight multiplex PCR testing, which checks several viruses in one run, as the tool that let managers act in time. Offer the genomic record as a reference for future events.
pmc-13545588:
Mingming Pang, Chu Yang, and Yanlong Luo proposed in 2026 a new neural network design for outlining organs and tumors in medical scans, a step that guides diagnosis and treatment planning. Their design, AFFUNet, changes how features from different depths of the network are blended, letting the model learn the blend rather than fixing it. Two added training penalties push the model to work harder on difficult pixels and on exact boundaries.

Tested on a multi-organ CT benchmark and a heart MRI benchmark, the design edged past a strong recent rival on overlap scores while adding almost no computing cost. Tests that removed one piece at a time confirmed each change helped, especially for small organs. Clinical evaluation still lies ahead, the authors note.
pmc-13547288:
Laurène Fenwarth and a large French team reported in 2026 on acute myeloid leukemia carrying TP53 mutations, a subgroup with notoriously poor outcomes, focusing on patients strong enough to receive intensive chemotherapy. Gentler drug combinations are the usual choice for this group, yet patients whose mutation burden is low might still gain from the intensive route. The team screened patients enrolled in three prospective ALFA trials between 2008 and 2016.

Of 978 screened patients, 83 carried at least one TP53 mutation, and most of those met the formal threshold for TP53-mutated disease. The mutated group arrived with lower white blood cell counts and fewer blasts in the marrow than other patients, while age and rates of secondary leukemia matched. The study sets up a direct look at intensive treatment results in this hard-to-treat group.
pmc-13547388:
Mohammed A Alhartomi and co-authors designed in 2026 a scheduling brain for factory sensors that harvest wireless power and can offload heavy computing to nearby edge servers. Batteries on such devices are tiny, so the scheduler must trade energy against delay in real time without knowing the future. Their approach blends a queue-based control method with deep reinforcement learning that also adjusts processor speed.

A virtual energy queue softens the hard battery limits, letting decisions run online without forecasts. Simulations showed energy efficiency gains of fifteen to twenty percent over a fixed-power baseline, with device batteries hovering in a healthy middle range. Queues stayed stable and response deadlines were respected, which the authors offer as a path to sustainable industrial sensing.
pmc-13547988:
Gong Yang and colleagues measured in 2026 a urinary marker of fat oxidation damage to test a counterintuitive idea. The idea: lower oxidative stress in the body might precede higher colorectal cancer risk near diagnosis. Their nested study drew on two Shanghai cohorts with 1,938 cases and a United States cohort with 285 cases for replication. The key marker was one specific isoprostane made only by free-radical attack on fats.

Low marker levels predicted higher risk, and the pattern held in both populations. For cancers diagnosed within five years of enrollment, people at the low end faced roughly two to four times the risk of those at the high end, depending on the measure. Beyond five years the link vanished. The authors caution that high-dose antioxidant supplements might carry unintended risk for some people.
pmc-13550788:
Mohamad Watfa and colleagues probed how often prostate needle samples miss aggressive hidden patterns. Published in 2026, the study drew on 1,167 in-a-row prostate-removal patients from 2023 to 2025 with paired needle and surgery tissue data. Large cribriform glands and duct cancer mark lethal prostate cancer, yet biopsy spotting stays weak even with MRI targeting.

Past work found every spread or lethal event after surgery in patients with the cribriform pattern, and a cribriform-based model flagged spread and death with full hit rate. Edge-case pattern 4 and odd duct growth may signal missed aggressive disease, but their trust is open. The study aims to measure needle-to-surgery miss rates, test biopsy scores, and trace the harms of missed patterns. Readers get the study's design and context for judging biopsy limits.
pmc-13551788:
Ghulam Muhammad Sami Ullah Asif, leading thirteen colleagues, published a 2026 genomic analysis of Brucella suis, a bacterium that causes brucellosis in pigs and people. Many genomes were public, yet no single study had combined the species' full gene pool, evolution, and vaccine targets. The team analyzed 91 genomes, reconstructing family trees from shared genes and from gene presence patterns.

The pan-genome remained open, meaning new strains keep adding genes, with 2,146 core genes shared by all. Chromosome organization was largely conserved with local rearrangements, and distinct evolutionary clades emerged. Screening the core proteins found 64 candidate antigens sitting on the cell surface, which the authors offer as starting points for rational vaccine design after laboratory validation.
pmc-13551988:
Zhijian Chen, with thirteen colleagues, published a 2026 study of air pollution in pregnancy and newborn health scores. The setting was a birth cohort in Shenzhen, China, with 20,894 women. Six pollutants were estimated from each woman's home address. Exposure was split by pregnancy trimester. The Apgar score rates a newborn's health at birth. Models tested single pollutants and the full mix together.

Mid-pregnancy exposure to three pollutants tied to higher risk of a low one-minute Apgar score. The three were fine particles, coarse particles, and nitrogen dioxide. Mix models agreed that each step up in total pollution raised the risk. Fine particles and nitrogen dioxide gave the largest shares by both methods. The team calls for more work and more public health focus on pregnancy exposure.
pmc-13554088:
Guowei Zhang and colleagues traced how stress damages neurons in the brain's hypothalamus through failing mitochondrial quality control, publishing the study in 2026. The hypothalamus coordinates hormonal and bodily stress responses, and its injury is linked to many diseases, yet the molecular chain was unclear. Using rat models of short and long stress, the team examined mitochondrial shape, turnover, and the signalling that governs them.

Stress pushed mitochondria toward excess splitting and away from fusion, while stress hormones, acting through their receptor, switched off a protein kinase gene and cut a key phosphorylation step. Short and long stress also triggered different clean-up pathways, depleting mitochondria, and prolonged stress shifted cell death from one form to another. The findings name a candidate mechanism for stress-linked brain injury and future treatment research.
pmc-13554188:
Mauro Pettorruso leads a large team asking whether psychedelic drugs can heal minds without the trip in a 2026 perspective. Trials show promise for depression and anxiety, yet the intense inner journeys these drugs cause need heavy staff support. Such care is costly and shuts out people with certain mental health risks. The team weighs lab and clinic proof on splitting benefit from experience.

One route blocks the main serotonin switch the drugs flip, testing whether gains survive. Another crafts biased cousins of the drugs with little or no trip built in. Early animal work hints that healing signals downstream may act on their own. Whether they can fully replace the lived experience stays open, the authors say, but success would widen access greatly.
pmc-13554388:
Wu and colleagues tackle a timing dilemma after one of cardiology's deadliest complications. Their 2026 retrospective study covers 138 patients at Beijing Anzhen Hospital between 2008 and 2025. All had surgery for ventricular septal rupture, a tear through the heart wall following a heart attack. Operating early risks fragile tissue; waiting risks death before surgery, and safe delay strategies are poorly evidenced.

One in six patients died around the operation, a perioperative mortality of about 17 percent. Surgery performed on or after the eighth day after rupture was associated with lower mortality. Two factors independently protected patients: an opened infarct-related artery, cleared by catheter treatment, and reaching that eight-day threshold. An opened artery also made surviving to day eight more likely, whenever it was done. The authors support bridging patients toward later surgery when their condition allows.
pmc-13555188:
Akimichi Morita leads a seven-author team studying cream-only treatment patterns in Japanese psoriasis care in a 2026 study. Guidelines reserve whole-body drugs for wide disease, high-impact sites, or failed creams. Claims data covered 6,361 patients who began with creams alone. A survey arm applied expert criteria for when whole-body treatment becomes due.

Fewer than one patient in ten moved to whole-body drugs during follow-up, after about two years on average. Most cycled through several cream classes first, nearly four on average. In the survey group, more than nine in ten cream-only patients already met at least one expert criterion for whole-body therapy. The authors call this undertreatment and urge clinics to apply the eligibility rules in daily practice.
pmc-13555988:
Youseef Alotaibi and Surendran Rajendran presented in 2026 a system that pairs detection of cognitive impairment with adaptive game therapy. Their design reads brain scans and tries to catch decline early in conditions such as Alzheimer's disease. A game component then adjusts its difficulty to each patient, aiming to keep therapy matched to ability.

The detection side combines an improved vision transformer with a recurrent network, so spatial detail and change across scan slices both inform the result. A reinforcement learning method, driven by an iterative hiking search, tunes game difficulty as the patient plays. Reported test scores were very high across accuracy, recall, and related measures. The authors present the pairing as a way to join diagnosis with engaging, personalised treatment.
pmc-13556088:
Wenzhu Wang and ten colleagues studied in 2026 how temperature and salty, alkaline conditions affect maize protoplasts, the wall-less plant cells used as a test bed for gene work. Protoplasts are versatile but fragile, and their handling rules are still being worked out. The team exposed the cells to cold, room, and warm temperatures and to a strong saline-alkali mix, then measured survival, membrane damage, and the chemistry of oxidative stress.

Cells kept cold stayed stable and kept their antioxidant defences up for at least sixteen hours, preserving both viability and internal proteins. Warm storage near body temperature damaged them badly, while room temperature caused little harm over the same span. Salt-alkali stress likewise cut production and survival. Practical guidance follows for labs: keep protoplasts cold, work within a safe time window, and expect stress chemistry to shift with conditions.
pmc-13558588:
Sen Yan and six colleagues build FMTdb, a dataset on fecal transplants for functional gut disorders. Gut disorders burden many patients, yet gut therapies lag for lack of large datasets. Their 2026 paper gathers patient, clinical, and multi-omic microbiota data. It covers 15 screened long-term donors, 370 recipients, and 2,008 healthy controls.

Records track donors and recipients before and after treatment across time points. By linking microbes with host response, FMTdb supports marker discovery and mechanism study. It also aids tailored gut treatments for gut disorders. The resource thus connects gut microbes to treatment response.
pmc-13558688:
Maria Doughan and eight colleagues asked in 2026 whether the circumstances of a person's birth echo in their mouth six decades later. Using the long-running ARIC cohort in the United States, they analysed more than six thousand adults. The group averaged about sixty-two years of age. Each person received a full gum examination in the late 1990s and reported their own birth history. Models adjusted for social, behavioural, and cardiovascular factors that could muddy the link.

Adults born early or at low weight carried roughly half again higher odds of gum disease than peers born on time at normal weight, though their tooth loss was no greater. Heavy babies showed the mirror pattern: no extra gum disease, yet higher odds of having lost teeth. The authors frame oral health as a life-course outcome and suggest that birth history belongs in dental risk assessment.
pmc-13558888:
Sri DR Syarief and colleagues tested whether lean scheduling could cut waiting times for gynaecologic cancer surgery in an Indonesian referral hospital, publishing the interrupted time-series study in 2026. Long waits for cancer surgery risk disease progression and death, yet operating capacity often sits underused. At Dr. Hasan Sadikin Hospital in Bandung, the team reserved one operating room and nine weekly elective slots for gynaecologic oncology.

Across 24 monthly points, mean waiting time fell from 8.16 weeks before the change to 3.64 weeks after, with an immediate drop of nearly three weeks once the slots began. A slight upward drift followed as throughput rose, but waits stayed far below baseline. Waste analysis showed less waiting, overprocessing, and coordination friction. The study backs dedicated slots and lean scheduling for time-sensitive cancer surgery.
pmc-13560188:
Mehmet Özer and colleagues measure tissue stiffness in the placenta, fetal lung, and fetal liver of women with intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, a liver disorder specific to pregnancy. Their 2026 prospective case-control study enrolled 120 women with singleton pregnancies at thirty-six weeks, half with the disorder and half matched healthy controls. Point shear wave elastography supplied the stiffness readings in a single session.

Every tissue measured stiffer in the cholestasis group. Peripheral placenta averaged 9.29 kilopascals against 4.92 in controls in the reported values, with the same direction at the placental center, the fetal lung, and the fetal liver. Stiffness climbed alongside liver enzymes and bile acid levels at diagnosis. It fell as the gestational week at diagnosis grew later. The authors suggest the ultrasound technique may mirror tissue-level changes of the disease and could add a noninvasive diagnostic angle beyond blood tests.
pmc-13560288:
Tat and colleagues report a 2026 study of life quality in adults living with severe hemophilia A. Thirty-six men took part. The team scored joint health, pain, and dynamic balance with a computerized platform test, recorded falls over the past year, and measured quality of life with a hemophilia-specific questionnaire.

Joint health, pain, and balance each showed a moderate link with quality of life: worse joints, worse pain, and worse balance went with poorer scores. Fall history showed no clear link. When the three factors were combined in one model, none stood alone as a significant predictor, which suggests they overlap heavily. The authors argue that care checks should include balance testing, not just joints and pain, so therapy can target the mix that drags quality of life down.
pmc-13560588:
Rashawn Ray and Keon Gilbert argue that the criminal justice system itself damages public health, in a 2026 perspective piece. The United States jails more people per head than any comparable nation, and policing, incarceration, and carceral health crises fall hardest on Black, Indigenous, and other communities of colour. Drawing on peer-reviewed studies, national data, and policy analysis, the authors trace how carceral practices generate illness.

Police violence spills into community rates of chronic disease and mental illness, while crowded facilities bred infection at rates many times the outside population during COVID-19. Barriers such as qualified immunity and union contracts shield misconduct and divert funds from health-promoting services. The authors back co-responder teams, diversion, violence interruption, and Medicaid enrolment before release, urging a shift from punishment toward upstream investment.
pmc-13562588:
Ali Hasan and colleagues designed new benzofuran compounds as reversible, selective blockers of the enzyme MAO-B for Parkinson's disease, publishing the study in 2026. In Parkinson's, dopamine falls as brain cells are lost, and MAO-B breaks dopamine down, so blocking it should ease motor symptoms. The team synthesised ten halogenated benzofuran derivatives and tested them against both monoamine oxidase forms.

All ten favoured MAO-B, and the best, BF2, blocked it potently with a selectivity index above 1,000, acting competitively and reversibly like the reference drug safinamide. BF2 and a runner-up were non-toxic to test cells and moderately crossed a lab blood-brain barrier model, with docking and simulations showing stable binding. BF2 emerges as a candidate worth advancing toward Parkinson's treatment.
pmc-13562688:
Hatti and co-authors reported a 2026 engineering study on a modified ring oscillator PUF, a circuit that turns tiny manufacturing differences into a device specific secret. Such functions help prove a chip is genuine, but older designs offer few challenge and response pairs. Attackers can then learn those pairs with machine learning.

Hatti added configurable delay units built from logic gates that reroute signals according to each challenge, greatly expanding the pair space. Extra steps scrambled challenges and used repeated voting over time to steady the answers. Built on two Xilinx FPGA boards, the design produced near ideal uniqueness and uniformity scores. Reliability stayed above ninety-nine percent on one board and near that level on the other.
pmc-13563788:
Masahide Hagiri and four colleagues turn an office flatbed scanner into a water-testing lab for fluoride. Too little fluoride harms teeth; too much stains and damages them, so supplies need cheap checks. Standard methods demand dedicated instruments. Their 2026 method develops colour with Alfusone reagent in a 96-well plate, scans the plate, and reads the colour numerically in five colour systems at once. Many samples and standards run together on a single scan.

One channel, the hue value, proved most sensitive, detecting fluoride down to 0.086 milligrams per litre and quantifying from 0.29, comfortably below the World Health Organization guideline and Japan's drinking water standard. Spiked bottled and tap water came back near the true value on the red and one colour-opponent channel. The authors offer the attachment-free setup, built from shop-bought reagents and office gear, for small labs and field teams that cannot house a spectrometer.
pmc-13563888:
Bo Dou and four colleagues characterise a new hyaluronidase, an enzyme that chews through the gel-like hyaluronic acid armouring many tumours. Market enzymes come from animal tissue, with contamination risks, or are recombinant and weak. Their 2026 study pulled a previously unstudied version, Ph-HAase, from the bacterium Pedobacter heparinus. Purification recovered 43.08 percent of activity at 47.5-fold purity, yielding an enzyme of 79.6 kilodaltons. It stayed stable below 30 degrees and near neutral acidity, preferred hyaluronic acid, yet also cut two related tissue sugars.

The surprise was direct anticancer action. On melanoma cells in culture, the enzyme collapsed mitochondrial membrane potential, piled up reactive oxygen, and switched on the mitochondrial route to programmed cell death, shifting the relevant gene and protein signals. Animal studies confirmed an anti-melanoma effect. The authors claim the first report of this enzyme source doing double duty: softening tumour defences for other drugs while attacking melanoma itself.
pmc-13572188:
Weiyun Zhang and co-authors silence, in a 2026 cell study, the vitamin D receptor in gut lining cells taken from young broiler chickens to prove how active vitamin D boosts phosphorus absorption. Earlier work in whole birds hinted that the receptor drives both absorption and the gene for a phosphate transporter called NaPi-IIb.

Raising vitamin D doses lifted absorption and switched both genes on more strongly, with a middle dose working best. With the receptor silenced by targeted RNA, the vitamin's boost to absorption and transporter expression was blunted, confirming the receptor's central role. Poultry nutritionists gain a firmer mechanism for setting vitamin D levels that build strong bones without wasting phosphorus.
pmc-13572388:
You Zhou, with eight colleagues, reports a 2026 cell study of how a protein called Nrf2 helps switch on a danger sensor in immune cells. The sensor, the NLRP3 inflammasome, drives swelling when it assembles. Nrf2 is best known for guarding cells against damage, yet it also seemed to aid this sensor, for reasons that were unclear.

Work in two kinds of macrophage, the immune cells that eat germs, showed that blocking Nrf2 cut sensor activity. Nrf2 raised levels of a second protein, Klf9, by binding its gene switch. Klf9 then kept a third protein, TXNIP, stable, and TXNIP helped the sensor parts join up. Mice lacking Nrf2 fared better in models of gut swelling and gout. The chain marks a fresh drug target for diseases the sensor drives.
pmc-13572488:
Meng Dang, with three colleagues, presents a 2026 control system for electric vehicles that drive each wheel with its own motor. Such cars promise sharp control, yet staying stable front-to-back under hard starts, stops, or slick roads is hard. Past methods react late and switch modes in jolts.

The system first gauges the car's state by fusing laser scans with motion sensors and a tuned filter. A bank of predictive controllers then splits driving into scenes and blends their commands by weight, which smooths each shift. In simulations and hardware tests, the yaw rate error fell to 0.111 degrees per second. Control accuracy rose by 21.7 percent over a standard predictive method. The authors aim the design at complex, mixed road conditions.
pmc-13573488:
Zijuan Wang, with eight colleagues, reports a 2026 trial of home preparation for frail older men facing prostate removal. Frailty shrinks the reserve a body needs to weather surgery, and the wait before this operation is short. The team tested whether a brief, many-sided home program could lift fitness in that window.

Eighty men aged 60 and up who were prefrail or frail were assigned at random to the program plus usual care or to usual care alone. The program joined exercise built into daily life, food tuning, mind support, pelvic floor drills, and breathing work, for a median of 12 days. On the six-minute walk, the program group gained near 28 metres while the usual group slipped slightly. Gains held across the recovery path, with hints of faster first walks and gut recovery. No harm was tied to the program.
pmc-13574788:
Alejo A Morales, with six colleagues, reports a 2026 test of a common blood-pressure drug in lab models of a rare bone disorder. Geleophysic dysplasia stunts growth, stiffens joints, and strains the heart and lungs, often killing young. Faults in three genes tangle the tissue mesh and may overdrive a growth signal the drug is known to calm.

Losartan blocks a hormone receptor and has eased similar signal-driven disease in other settings. The team gave it in preclinical models of this dysplasia to judge benefit before any human use. Rare-disease drugs often jump from such models straight to small trials, so a clear lab verdict matters. The title states the outcome plainly: benefit was limited in these models. The work steers the field away from a tempting shortcut and toward targets with firmer ground.
pmc-13574888:
Tiantian Hu and co-authors describe a 2026 case of a child with a rare inherited risk for blood cancer. An eight-year-old girl had high-risk myelodysplastic syndrome, a bone marrow disorder, linked to a germline change in the DDX41 gene. Such gene changes usually cause disease much later in life, so cases in children are scarce.

Care began with azacitidine and venetoclax, which brought the marrow into remission. She then received a stem cell transplant from an unrelated cord blood donor. Complications included a viral brain infection and graft-versus-host disease of skin and gut, both controlled. At 13 months she stayed in full remission, and the authors stress screening donors for the same gene change.
pmc-13576888:
Sinem Coşkun-Albayrak and three colleagues compare how visible dental filling materials are on X-rays, in a 2026 study. Fillings must stand out from tooth on radiographs so dentists can spot new decay and check edges. New 3D-printed resins, permanent and temporary, may not match older materials on that visibility, called radiopacity.

Eight materials were made into small blocks at 1 and 2 millimetre thicknesses, ten of each, and imaged beside tooth slices and an aluminium step wedge. Clear differences appeared across materials. Printed temporary resins were the least visible, conventional composites the most, and printed permanent resins sat between. Thicker blocks were more visible for every material. Some printed temporaries fell below dentine and enamel in visibility. The authors warn that faint materials can hide problems and should be chosen with care.
pmc-13578088:
Tolulope Bella-Awusah leads a 2026 systematic review of mental illness rates among young people who live in city slums across low- and middle-income countries. Slum conditions stack poverty, crowding, and violence onto the years when many disorders first appear. The review screened nearly four thousand records across seven databases, with the search updated to March 2026.

Twenty-four studies covering 26,794 young people were pooled. Depression affected 31 percent, anxiety disorders 35 percent, post-traumatic stress 24 percent, and alcohol use disorders 23 percent in the pooled estimates, though studies varied enormously. Food insecurity and exposure to violence were the risk factors named most often. Support from adults and feeling connected to the neighbourhood protected against illness in the studies that looked. The authors call for policies shaped to slum realities and for better routes into care.
pmc-13581488:
Babiker Mohamed Rahamtalla and colleagues systematically reviewed sixty-five studies on climate-sensitive health effects published between 2000 and 2025. Rising emissions are driving heatwaves, wildfires, extreme rain, and sea-level rise, and the review weighs deaths, illness, and economic costs together. Non-optimal temperatures alone were tied to 5.08 million deaths each year from 2000 to 2019.

Heat raised all-cause mortality by 3.3 percent per degree above each locality's optimum, while wildfire smoke contributed roughly 339,000 premature deaths yearly. Heat-related labor losses reached about 5.3 percent of global work hours in 2020. Early warning systems and deep emissions cuts could prevent up to 42 percent of these deaths, the authors conclude, with low-resource settings bearing the heaviest burden.
pmc-13583388:
Zhiqiang Pang and Peng Yu wrote this 2026 commentary on a study by Xu and colleagues about how rice plants recruit helpful soil microbes. Plants leak sugars and acids from their roots, yet those foods could feed almost any microbe. The puzzle is how a plant draws in just the microbes it needs when a nutrient runs short.

Xu's team traced a full chain that starts with a rice gene called OsA1. When phosphorus is low, the gene's protein pushes roots to release malate, a root acid, which draws in a bacterium named Bacillus cereus FU2. That bacterium frees phosphorus locked in soil matter, so the plant can take it up. Pang and Yu hold the work up as a model for building farm microbiomes by design.
pmc-13584288:
Gunjan Kumar and colleagues exposed a wide know-do gap in oral health under India's national program in rural Odisha. Knowledge of the National Oral Health Programme was low, yet attitudes were favourable and service use was minimal. Their community study surveyed 417 adults in Satyabadi Block, Puri District, in mid-2024, using a validated questionnaire and clinical exams, and modelled pathways from knowledge to behaviour.

Only 6.7 percent knew the program, while 75 to 85 percent held favourable attitudes, yet just 2.4 percent used services. Average decayed-missing-filled teeth stood at 3.69, and the knowledge-to-practice pathway explained about a third of behaviour variation. The authors blame structural barriers, distance, cost, and weak infrastructure, and call for mobile units, health-worker training, and behaviour-change communication.
pmc-13584388:
Wenqi Zhong and colleagues build a smarter image tool for finding gut polyps during colonoscopy in this 2026 paper. Polyps can turn into bowel cancer, so software that outlines them helps doctors act early. The catch is that models trained on images from one hospital often stumble on scans from other machines, and polyps range from tiny flat spots to large lumps.

Their system, named FD-MSP, splits what it learns into features that stay the same across machines and features tied to each device. It also keeps model patterns at three size scales and blends them through a gated output stage. Tested on three public colonoscopy datasets, the tool beat earlier cross-domain methods on the new sets. The authors frame the design as a fix for both the machine gap and the size spread at once.
pmc-13586488:
Hyejin Noh and colleagues looked back at thirty-three years of kidney graft disease at Seoul St. Mary's Hospital. From 1991 to 2023, 4,188 graft hosts had a needle test or graft removal, with 7,229 proven diagnoses in all. Graft attack, known as rejection, topped the list at 37.7 percent, with tube and tissue disease next at 25.4 percent.

In needle tests, T-cell attack led at all ages, while drug harm rose with age and ball-filter disease peaked in hosts under twenty. IgA-linked disease led the ball-filter group. In graft removals, attack also led but fell with time. This long view helps doctors guess which graft fault fits which age.
pmc-13587288:
Edson Serván-Mori and a large team study early motherhood across Mexico over two decades. Teen and very young motherhood remains tangled with poverty and lost schooling in much of Latin America. Their 2026 work joined census records from 2000, 2010, and 2020, covering more than three million women aged 12 to 24. Household income was filled in with a machine learning method trained on spending surveys.

Early motherhood eased only slightly across the twenty years and stayed thick in poorer homes. Marital status, age, and household shape predicted it best, while income ranked far down the list. The income link bent in an odd curve, rising a little at the bottom before flattening and falling. In the time-based models it worked mostly through schooling delays and early unions rather than directly. Place itself kept a stubborn effect, which points the authors toward local fixes.
pmc-13591788:
Lorena Garcia-Castillo leads a 2026 study of a fasting mimicking diet in mice bred to model Lynch syndrome, an inherited fault that raises colon cancer risk. The syndrome stems from broken DNA repair genes, while diet and gut microbes also shape cancer growth. Mice ate cycles of a plant based, low calorie diet that mimics fasting, over ten months. Gut microbes were read by deep gene sequencing.

The diet held down weight gain in males only, a split by sex the team notes. More telling, it blunted the drift toward a harmful microbe mix as cancer neared. Helpful species such as Lactobacillus johnsonii held on, while E coli fell back. Garcia-Castillo and the team also saw blocked rises in pathways that feed tumor growth.
pmc-13591888:
Ying Wang leads a 2026 study of a new infant formula built to copy key parts of human milk. The formula adds a whey concentrate rich in alpha-lactalbumin and milk fat globule membrane, plus a fat form found in breast milk. Chinese infants aged under a month were enrolled by feeding style: 60 formula fed and 60 breastfed, each followed for six weeks. Gut comfort was the main score.

Formula fed babies scored close to breastfed ones on a gut symptom index, meeting the preset bar for equal standing. Helpful Bifidobacteria levels, growth, and most immune and gut barrier markers also matched. One marker ran higher in breastfed babies, and total gut acids ran higher in the formula group. Wang and the team call tolerance good overall.
pmc-13594388:
Mehmet Gokcin, Yasemen Yanar, and Cigdem Dikel turned European sea bass skin, a fish-processing by-product, into gelatin and then into edible packaging films. Their study extracted the gelatin and benchmarked it against commercial bovine and fish gelatins using microscopy, chemical analysis, and spectroscopy.

The sea bass gelatin was almost pure protein with very little fat or ash, a glycine-rich amino acid profile much like other gelatins, and a respectable gel strength. Films softened with glycerol stretched to nearly double their length before breaking and carried a fair tensile load at a thin gauge. The films dissolved readily in water, which suits edible uses. The authors conclude that fish skin waste can stand in for mammal-derived gelatin in food packaging, matching international commercial standards on the measures they tested.
pmc-13595488:
Chaofu Yue and a team of co-authors investigated how sphingosine-1-phosphate, a signaling lipid that steers immune and cardiovascular responses, protects the heart during the inflammatory injury caused by bacterial endotoxin. Gene and single-cell analyses first flagged RASGRP1, a macrophage-rich gene, as a hub in the injury response, and the study followed that lead in rats and cultured macrophages.

In rats given the toxin, six weeks of the lipid treatment lessened heart muscle inflammation and scarring, improved pumping measures, and lowered injury, oxidative, and inflammatory markers. In macrophages it calmed inflammatory output, restored energy metabolism, and cut levels of a signaling chain running through RASGRP1, S100A9, and the NLRP3 inflammasome. Binding experiments supported direct engagement between the lipid and RASGRP1. The authors present the pathway as a mechanistic handle on endotoxin-driven heart injury.
pmc-13602888:
Emily L. Trew and three colleagues report in 2026 a family of rhodium and iridium complexes built around an unusual nitrogen-rich ligand. The ligand, an azidophosphonamide, grips a metal through different nitrogen atoms, and light can flip which grip it uses: linkage isomerism. The team prepared complexes carrying bulky adamantyl or mesityl groups, paired with cyclooctadiene, cyclooctene, or carbon monoxide, then probed for stability.

In the cyclooctadiene complexes, the ligand bound through its first two nitrogens in an extended shape. Ultraviolet light at 365 nanometers flipped them to the alternative pairing without shedding nitrogen gas. Swapping in carbon monoxide kept the extended shape in the solid state. One rhodium cyclooctene complex instead held the ligand in a folded shape, the first stable folded phosphazide seen on a group 9 metal. Light made it expel nitrogen gas to form a new compound. Structures were confirmed by NMR and X-ray crystallography.
pmc-13613688:
İbrahim Halil Demir and colleagues report a 2026 comparison of hydatid disease in bone against the same disease in soft tissue. The study covers 64 patients treated in a region where the illness is common. Hydatid disease comes from a parasite that forms cysts in the body, and in muscle or bone it is rare and often looks like a tumour on scans. The team reviewed patients who had surgery between 2010 and 2024 with lab-confirmed disease.

Twenty-six patients had bone involvement and 38 had soft tissue involvement. The groups were alike in age, sex, blood inflammation marks, and antibody test results at the start. The authors compared cyst shape, complications, spread to liver or lungs, and return of disease after surgery. Their findings help surgeons plan for two forms of one disease that behave in distinct ways.
pmc-13615488:
Rebecca Danning, Zheng Tracy Ke, Xihong Lin, and Rong Ma present a 2026 method, called SEEK-VFI, for picking the genes that matter most when tracing how single cells develop over time. Studies of single cells often follow a branching path of cell change, and the first step is choosing highly variable genes. Standard picks can confuse genes that vary because of the growth path with genes that vary for no useful reason.

Their method blends topic models, a tool borrowed from text analysis, with a scoring system that needs no preset number of groups. In tests it beat current methods and found key genes that sharpened the rebuilt growth paths, cleaned the visual maps, and strengthened later analysis. For biologists charting how stem cells turn into tissues, a better gene shortlist means a truer map of development.
pmc-13616288:
Kai Wu and colleagues report a do-it-all liquid salt additive that fixes two faults of pure-iodide wide-bandgap perovskite solar cells, the top layer in stacked tandem panels. Mixed-halide versions split apart under light, while pure-iodide versions suffer uneven crystal growth because their building blocks dissolve and set at different speeds. Lead content adds a safety worry on top.

The additive grabs each player in turn: it helps caesium iodide dissolve, holds two organic cations steady with hydrogen bonds, and latches onto loose lead ions. The mix stays smooth in solution and sets at a lower temperature into a more even film. Tackling mixing, growth, and stray lead with one ingredient brings tough, split-proof top cells closer to real tandem production.
pmc-13616388:
Shouqiang Zhu and colleagues study a helper protein, 14-3-3γ, that may protect thinking after surgery, a problem called postoperative cognitive dysfunction that clouds memory in many older patients. Spinal fluid screening in a large Alzheimer's research cohort of 237 people flagged the protein as a marker of brains at higher risk. Blood levels in a separate group of 213 surgical patients then tracked with who developed thinking problems or delirium after their operations.

In mice, anaesthesia and surgery lowered the protein in the hippocampus, the memory centre, while boosting a harmful chemical tag on the tau protein at one specific site and damaging synapses. Raising the protein back up protected those connections. A blood marker that flags risk, tied to a mechanism that can be defended, gives surgical teams two gifts at once: warning and a target.
pmc-13617588:
Paula Johanna Filser and five colleagues review telehealth for people who use mechanical ventilation at home, a growing group for whom hospital follow-up trips are exhausting and costly. Their systematic review, registered in advance, searched three major databases for studies comparing telehealth-supported home ventilation with standard care on clinical or economic outcomes.

From three hundred fifty-six records, eleven studies qualified, mostly European trials totaling one thousand four hundred fifty-eight patients. Their conditions included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and obesity hypoventilation syndrome. Carbon dioxide control and quality of life matched standard care, while results for hospitalizations and flare-ups were mixed, and survival trends hinted at benefit without proving it. Starting ventilation at home saved money, though long-term cost results varied. The authors call for standardized outcomes and longer follow-up to guide lasting adoption.
pmc-13618888:
Abubakar Aji and seven colleagues grow zinc oxide nanoparticles with help from the leaves of Vitex doniana, a West African tree, and test them against wax buildup in crude oil pipelines. Wax crystallizing out of cooling crude chokes flow, and current inhibitors raise toxicity concerns. Six analytical methods characterized the plant extract and the resulting nanocrystals, which proved to be a pure hexagonal wurtzite phase of about thirty-six nanometers.

At a dose of just a few hundredths of a percent by weight, the particles cut crude viscosity by up to about fifty-six percent at room temperature. Microscopy showed the wax reorganizing into clustered crystals, evidence the particles co-crystallize with the wax and disrupt its network. Thermal analysis showed the material itself barely loses mass even at high temperatures. The authors propose the green-made nanoparticles as a sustainable flow assurance option for waxy crude production.
pmc-13623988:
Aneta Łukaszek-Chmielewska leads a paired study of how burning coal concentrates natural radioactivity into ash. Coal holds small amounts of radioactive potassium, radium, and thorium from the ground. Regulators and builders who reuse ash need to know how much those levels jump when the carbon burns away, and direct before-and-after measurements were scarce.

Nine hard coals from Poland and abroad were burned under controlled conditions, and both coal and matching ash were measured with gamma-ray spectrometry, which counts radiation by energy. The coals all sat below world average radioactivity. In the ashes, activity and every hazard index rose about six-fold on average, with enrichment ranging roughly four- to ten-fold. The external radiation dose rate passed the reference level in every ash sample. Most ashes still sat within recommended limits. The authors urge treating ash as a radiologically distinct material in reuse rules.
pmc-13629288:
Suganya Ramalingam and four colleagues present three cases of cemento-osseous dysplasia in Indian women, a benign jaw condition in which normal bone is gradually replaced by fibrous tissue and mineralised material. The condition usually appears by chance on dental imaging and affects women far more often than men.

Each woman showed a different face of the disease, which falls into periapical, focal, and florid forms defined by location and spread. The varied appearances easily mimic tooth-root cysts and other jaw lesions on scans, which is why the authors stress combining the clinical picture, imaging, and tissue examination before settling on a diagnosis. Their series adds uncommon Indian case material, particularly for the rare florid form, to a literature dominated by other populations.
pmc-13632088:
Karthik Chinnaswamy, Archisha Marya, and Anand Pillai reviewed studies of joint replacement for a stiff, arthritic big toe. The condition, called hallux rigidus, is often treated by fusing the joint solid, which stops pain but ends movement. A replacement joint promises to keep motion. The team gathered studies reporting scores for pain and function before and after total replacement of the first toe joint.

Across the pooled studies, function scores improved a lot and pain scores fell sharply. Joint movement also improved on average, though gains varied widely between studies and sometimes vanished in prediction ranges. About one in ten feet later needed revision surgery, and X-ray failure appeared in a larger share. Longer follow-up hinted that implants wear out over time. The authors present replacement as a choice for selected patients, not a sure substitute for fusion.
pmc-13633888:
Yan Luo and nine colleagues published this 2026 survey study on how much benefit people demand before they will take a statin. The smallest worthwhile difference is the least gain a person finds worth a treatment's burdens. The question matters because statins prevent heart attacks in healthy people, yet many decline them. More than twelve hundred adults in the United States and Japan weighed three risk scenarios using a structured trade-off method.

Across every scenario, the typical demanded benefit was larger than what statins usually deliver. People who saw their own risk as higher asked for less benefit in return. Current statin users and people with a high cholesterol history also settled for less. Prior education about cholesterol lowered the demanded benefit in both countries. The authors argue that honest conversations about personal risk and real benefit size could bring patient choices closer to what studies show.
pmc-13635488:
Ajmina Hasan Flabe and three colleagues studied glucose swings in young people with diabetes in Bangladesh. Swings matter: wild variation raises complication risk even when average sugar looks acceptable. The team fitted ninety-seven patients aged one to twenty-five with hidden glucose monitors for fourteen days at a Dhaka center. Sixty-eight had type 1 diabetes and the rest type 2. A fasting blood test measured C-peptide, a marker of how much insulin the body still makes.

Variation ran far above international targets in most participants, worse in type 1 than type 2. Young people with lower own insulin output swung more, in a graded pattern holding after accounting for age and treatment. The marker test existed for under half the group, so the authors label the link a hypothesis. If larger studies confirm it, a cheap blood test could flag children at highest risk where glucose monitors are scarce.
pmc-13638988:
Tessa S. Canoy and nine colleagues describe a 2026 attempt to enrich fermented foods with lysine, an amino acid often scarce in plant-based diets. Bacteria in the Bacillus and Priestia groups make lysine naturally, but a genetic switch called a riboswitch limits how much they produce.

Using a lysine-like chemical to select mutants, the team found strains with changes in that switch and in related genes. One mutant made over 150 times more free lysine than its parent strain in test media and three times more in oat fermentation. The non-engineered approach could raise the protein quality of fermented plant foods.
pmc-13639088:
Xiaokang Lv and three colleagues review in 2026 what is known about L-citrulline, a supplement amino acid, for muscle performance and protein balance. Interest centers on whether it can slow the muscle loss that comes with aging, known as sarcopenia.

The review gathers rodent and human studies on muscle function, protein building, and the pathways behind them. Evidence suggests citrulline can support muscle protein synthesis and exercise capacity, though key questions remain. The authors point to dosing strategy, transport in the body, energy-producing mitochondria, and gut microbes as priorities. Their map aims to guide nutrition research for aging muscle.
pmc-13641588:
Konrad Kubiński and nine colleagues present a study of boron-cluster compounds called metallacarboranes and how they fight the yeast Candida albicans. These compounds kill fungi, but the proteins they act on inside the cell were unknown.

Using beads coated with one compound to fish proteins out of yeast extract, the team found seventy-two binding partners, including fourteen known antifungal targets. The chaperone protein Hsp90 bound most strongly, and direct tests confirmed the compounds attach to it and change its activity in a dose-dependent way. The authors say this gives boron-cluster drug design a clear mechanistic foothold.
pmc-13643288:
Alika K. Maunakea and ten colleagues present a study of lasting metal exposure after the 2023 Maui wildfires, a disaster where fire burned homes and infrastructure, not only vegetation. Such events can mobilize old contaminants that ordinary smoke monitoring misses.

The community cohort enrolled 1,400 adults six to eighteen months after the fire and measured twenty-four metals in urine alongside breathing tests. Several metals ran well above national reference levels, with antimony about forty times higher, and the worst values clustered in the hardest-hit areas. Across three mixture models, higher combined metal load tracked with abnormal lung function, led by arsenic, cadmium, and copper.
pmc-13644188:
Hsin-Hao Lai and five colleagues present a 2026 validation of a Traditional Chinese questionnaire measuring HIV stigma inside health facilities in Taiwan. Existing local tools captured personal attitudes but missed the policies and habits of whole facilities.

After expert review and a pretest, the main sample of 619 health workers split into halves for exploratory and confirmatory analysis. Seven factors emerged, from fear and extra precautions to facility policies and willingness to treat key populations. Scores matched a related provider stigma scale where expected and stayed distinct where the new tool adds structural ground. The authors offer it for routine monitoring.
pmc-13645588:
Adelaida Hernaiz and seven colleagues study sheep cells exposed to scrapie, a fatal prion disease, to catch the earliest gene changes after exposure. Prions are misfolded proteins that damage the brain. The team grew neuron-like cells from sheep stem cells and dosed them with scrapie-infected brain material. Gene activity was read at two and four days after dosing.

Dozens of genes changed at each time point, with little overlap between the two days, which shows the response keeps shifting. Early changes centered on signaling and immune-linked genes, while later changes leaned toward broad gene shutdown. Follow-up tests confirmed most of the shifts the main analysis found. The work offers an early map of how a naturally at-risk species reacts to prion exposure, which may help researchers choose targets for later studies.
pmc-13645888:
Irene Quiliconi writes a 2026 philosophy article arguing that human flourishing grows out of vulnerability rather than despite it. Flourishing is often treated as an abstract ideal in well-being studies. She instead roots it in the lived reality of fragility and mutual dependence. Her main guide is Alasdair MacIntyre, who tied moral life to our animal nature and our need for others.

The second half of the article brings in phenomenology, the study of lived experience, to ground virtue in the body. Three features of vulnerability serve as compass points: embodiment, living alongside others, and lived time. Quiliconi argues that an environment stays truly habitable only when these are protected, even under extreme fragility. The piece speaks to ethics, care work, and any field weighing what people need in order to thrive.
pmc-13646388:
Oonjee Oh and ten colleagues explore the ethical strains nurses feel when family members take part in a patient's care, in a 2026 study. Family-centered care is widely praised, yet its daily practice raises hard questions. The team analyzed eighty-two interviews with practicing nurses across four US states. Three themes organize what the nurses described.

First, nurses walked a fine line between supporting families and keeping professional boundaries, and family advocacy could help or complicate care. Second, disagreements inside families pulled nurses into conflicts not of their making. Third, clashing ethical, legal, and family expectations left many nurses feeling helpless and morally distressed. The nurses stayed committed to involving families, the authors note. Their conclusion is that health systems must actively address these tensions rather than leave each nurse to absorb them alone.
pmc-13649388:
Guo-long Dong and seven colleagues built a deep learning tool to grade face aging in Chinese women. The tool also shows its work, so users can see which face traits drive each grade. Three hundred women aged 18 to 60 took part, and their face photos were scored on tone, shape, texture, and one more trait.

The model sorted faces into six age stages with good scores, and most errors fell between stages next to each other. A clear order emerged from the scores. Skin tone changed first in early aging. Face shape changed next, and texture broke down last. The team says this order can guide skin care plans made for each stage of life.
pmc-13649988:
Yuhang Wang and two colleagues check whether a routine liver blood test can flag children with Crohn's disease who are unlikely to respond to infliximab, a standard injected treatment. A low reading on the test, called ALT, sometimes signals poor nutrition and heavy inflammation rather than a healthy liver. That raised the question of a link to treatment failure.

The team reviewed 116 children who received the drug on a set schedule and were judged for response a few months later by two specialists who did not know the blood values. Half of the children had low ALT, and failure to respond was much more common in that group even after disease severity and other treatments were counted. The test alone sorted patients only modestly well, so the authors present the link as exploratory and warn against using the cutoff on its own.
pmc-13650788:
Kimberly R Bennett and seven colleagues, publishing in 2026, build a laboratory model of the barrier that shields diffuse midline glioma, a lethal childhood brain tumor, from drugs. No flow-capable model of this blood-brain-tumor barrier existed, so the team grew one inside a microfluidic chip.

Patient-derived tumor cells were embedded in a gel matrix together with brain vessel cells, support cells, and pericytes, and the mixture self-assembled into perfusable microvascular networks at several tumor densities. Flowing tracer through the vessels showed tumor presence did not significantly change leakiness. Single-cell gene sequencing then compared barrier devices, tumor-bearing devices, and inflammation-stimulated controls. Tumor-bearing vessels carried a distinct gene signature rather than a generic inflammatory one, tumor cells adopted a wandering, mesenchymal-like character, and predicted signaling between tumor and vessel walls was extensive. The model mirrors patient vessel features for future drug testing.
pmc-13651488:
José Laerte Boechat and thirty-nine colleagues survey food allergy in older Brazilians, a group allergy research usually skips in favor of children. Six hundred thirty-two people aged sixty and over, recruited through their own doctors across all five regions of Brazil, answered a standardized questionnaire about lifetime reactions.

Just under a fifth reported having had an allergic reaction to food at some point, while only about half that share reported an actual medical diagnosis. A smaller fraction described the immediate, repeated pattern that suggests true allergy. Shellfish, milk, and fresh fruits led the culprit list, and hives and gut symptoms were the commonest complaints. The sample skewed female with an average age around seventy. Analysis linked self-reported allergy to several social and clinical characteristics. The authors underline the gap between perceived and diagnosed allergy in old age, and the need for confirmatory testing in this population.
pmc-13652288:
Nicholas Derrico and six colleagues present two surgical cases of brain aneurysms at the tip of the basilar artery that came back after coil treatment. Such recurrences are hard to fix, since further endovascular work risks complex hardware, incomplete closure, and worse pressure symptoms. Instead, the surgeons disconnected the aneurysms by interrupting the basilar artery just below its apex, a direct approach that settles the problem at once.

Two details made the operation workable: imaging that confirmed a connecting artery able to support blood flow. A perforator-free zone found during surgery where the vessel could be closed safely. Both cases are described with their imaging and operative findings. For neurosurgeons facing aneurysms that keep returning after endovascular repair, the report offers a durable fallback with clearly stated conditions for when it can be used.
pmc-2631488:
Langfelder and Horvath present WGCNA, an R package for weighted correlation network analysis. Correlation networks were becoming a common tool in bioinformatics when they wrote. Their method groups genes that rise and fall together across samples into related modules.

Inside the package, weighted analysis builds networks from microarray and similar data in a principled way. Modules can then be tied to traits such as disease state or tissue type. WGCNA gave systems biology a shared, documented toolkit, and its gene modules are now a routine starting point for hunting disease genes.
pmc-2892488:
Darling, Mau, and Perna present progressiveMauve, a method for aligning multiple whole genomes at once. Aligning genomes remains hard because related organisms differ by rearranged blocks, duplicated segments, and genes gained or lost. Those changes create a mosaic of matching and non-matching regions, even between close relatives.

ProgressiveMauve was designed to align two or more genomes while allowing for that shuffling. It finds conserved blocks and shows how their order changed. Such alignments let researchers trace how pathogens evolve, which parts of a genome stay stable, and where new genes enter.
pmc-2945788:
Goecks, Nekrutenko, Taylor, and co-authors present Galaxy, a web platform for computational research in the life sciences. As biology came to rely on computation, worries grew about whether results could be reached and repeated by others. Galaxy was built as an open, web-based home for genomic research.

The platform addresses access, reproducibility, and transparency together. Researchers can run analyses through a browser, share exact workflows, and let others rerun them. That openness helps small labs do serious genomic work and lets reviewers check how a published result was actually produced.
pmc-4202688:
Vidarsson, Dekkers, and Rispens reviewed IgG antibodies in 2014, covering their subclasses and allotypes. IgG is the most abundant antibody type in human blood serum. It comes in four subclasses that are much alike but differ in parts of their constant region, above all near the hinge.

Those small structural differences change how each subclass triggers effector functions, the actions that clear germs and infected cells. Allotypes, the inherited variants of these antibodies, add a further layer of variety. The review links structure to function across all forms. That knowledge matters for vaccines, antibody drugs, and tests that read immune responses.
pmc-5446088:
Bowden, Del Greco, Minelli, and their team wrote in 2016 on how to judge gene-based causal tests that use summary data. A method called MR-Egger had just been put forward for such tests. It can work even when some gene variants used as tools are not valid, and it can flag bias.

The paper centers on a statistic that shows how much the variant-level results vary. That value tells the user how far the MR-Egger results can be trusted for a given dataset. When the spread is too low, the bias test loses its power. The guidance helps analysts pick the right method and read its output with care.
pmc-5889788:
Andrea Cipriani, Toshi Furukawa, Georgia Salanti, and a large team compared antidepressant drugs in 2018. Major depression is common, costly, and a heavy burden worldwide. Drugs are used more often than talking therapy because services are scarce.

The team pooled hundreds of trials to compare many antidepressants head to head, even where no direct trial existed. All the drugs beat a placebo for short-term response, but they differed in side effects and dropouts. The rankings give doctors and patients a firmer base for choosing a first drug. The study is widely cited in treatment guidelines.
pmc-6912988:
Sam Kovaka, Aleksey Zimin, Geo Pertea, and coauthors presented StringTie2 for long-read RNA assembly in 2019. New sequencers read RNA in stretches thousands of letters long. Long reads can reveal full transcripts that short reads piece together poorly.

StringTie2 assembles those long reads against a reference genome with better handling of their error patterns. It also works in a mixed mode that pairs long reads with accurate short ones. Tests show cleaner transcript models and fewer false joins. Transcript studies of complex genes rely on such tools to get isoforms right.
pmc-8128288:
Nicholas Davies and colleagues modeled in 2021 how transmissible the B.1.1.7 variant of SARS-CoV-2 was in England, and what its spread would mean. This variant, first flagged in the United Kingdom, carried many mutations affecting how the virus attaches to and enters human cells. Using several kinds of statistical models and data streams, the team estimated its growth advantage over earlier forms of the virus.

Their results indicated the variant spread substantially faster, which raised the level of control measures needed to hold it back. The findings landed while the variant was sweeping England, and they informed urgent policy choices. The study also became a model for how to size up a new variant quickly.
proudhon-system-economical-contradiction:
Benjamin R Tucker published his translation of Proudhon's System of Economical Contradictions in 1888. Proudhon had issued the work in 1846 with the subtitle The Philosophy of Misery. Tucker, Proudhon's chief American champion, spread his books through his journal Liberty and its press.

Proudhon marched through the ideas of political economy, division of labor, machinery, competition, and monopoly, finding each both good and harmful. That method of paired contradictions drove Karl Marx to answer with The Poverty of Philosophy, a famous attack. The quarrel split the young socialist movement. Tucker's translation lets English readers judge Proudhon's dense, daring critique of political economy in the form that provoked Marx.
psellos-de-operatione-daemonum-greek-lat:
Michael Psellos, the brilliant Byzantine courtier of the eleventh century, wrote a dialogue on the operation of demons. This edition of 1688 prints the Greek with Latin alongside. The Renaissance had met Psellos through Ficino's Latin translation of 1497, which made Byzantine demon lore a Western classic.

In dialogue, Psellos explains how demons act on bodies and minds in the Eastern church's teaching. Their kinds, powers, and limits receive orderly treatment. The tone is curious rather than frightened. Greek and Latin on facing pages served the scholars of 1688. The book is the demon lore of Byzantium, elegantly imported westward, and it coloured occult writing for centuries.
pseudo-democritus-physica-mystica-berthe:
The Physica et Mystica, questions on nature and secret things, claims the name of Democritus, the laughing philosopher of atoms. In fact it comes from Bolos of Mendes, writing in Egypt in the first or second century. It is the oldest layer of Greek alchemy. Berthelot and Ruelle printed it in 1888, in French translation.

Recipes for making gold, silver, purple dye, and gems fill the book, mixed with spells and the lore of like acting on like. A letter to Leucippe travels with the text. The work shows alchemy at its birth, half craft and half mystery. All the later art, Greek and Arab, grows from these pages.
queiros-os-maias-1888:
Eça de Queirós published Os Maias in Portugal in 1888, and the text here is the Portuguese original. Carlos da Maia, last hope of a great Lisbon family, is raised by his grandfather Afonso after family tragedy. Carlos studies medicine, idles in high society, and falls in love with a married stranger, Maria Eduarda.

A buried secret about Maria's birth turns love into horror for them both. Around the pair, Eça paints Lisbon's politics, salons, and newspapers with amused disgust. The novel tracks the Maia family's slow decline across three generations. Portuguese readers rank Os Maias as their greatest novel. Its English translation of 1925 exists but could not be staged here.
reid-essays-active-powers-1788:
Reid's Essays on the Active Powers of Man, from 1788, turn Thomas Reid from the mind's knowing to its doing. Five essays, complete here, treat the powers that move a person to act. Will stands first, then the springs of action: appetite, desire, and affection, summed up as motives.

Morals close the work, as Reid grounds right and wrong in a moral sense open to reason. The book is his moral philosophy entire, the partner of his Essays on the Intellectual Powers of 1785. Against theories that made humans mere bundles of feeling, Reid defends free, rational agency. His calm system shaped moral teaching in Scotland and America for a century.
rhys-celtic-heathendom-1888:
John Rhys gave these talks as the Hibbert Lectures in 1888, on how faith grew among the Celtic peoples. Rhys held the chair of Celtic studies at Oxford. His theme was the old faith of Britain and Ireland before the church age. The talks drew crowds who wanted hard proof, not just old tales.

He traced gods, rites, and hero tales through Welsh and Irish texts and folk use. Druid belief holds a key place, weighed with care from the old proof. The talks stand as the first sound school study of Celtic pagan faith, still cited today.
schiller-revolt-of-the-netherlands-1788:
Schiller turned from plays to history with his History of the Revolt of the Netherlands, published in 1788. Edward Backhouse Eastwick translated the work into English in the nineteenth century. The book tells how the Dutch provinces rose against Spanish rule in the 1500s.

Schiller traces the clash of faith, taxes, and foreign rule that drove the revolt. William of Orange and the Duke of Alva stand out as the great opposed figures. The narrative gave Schiller the ground from which Don Carlos had grown. It also won him respect as a historian, not only a playwright. Readers still value its clear story of a small people's fight for its liberties.
scientific-american-supplement-no-633-fe:
Scientific American Supplement No. 633 came out in New York on February 18, 1888, within Volume XXV. Like other weekly numbers, it sold for five dollars a year alone or seven dollars with the parent paper, founded in 1845. Architecture leads the contents, and the list then moves through the sky, biography, chemistry, and electricity.

H. H. Statham opens a lecture run on building design, first heard at the London Society of Arts, with thirty-four pictures tracing how styles grew. An astronomy piece argues that sunlight may have split one comet into five. C. S. Hallberg profiles the botanist Linnaeus, while chemistry pieces cover gas making gear, the placing of atoms, and fluorine. L. Weber closes the list with notes on electricity in the air.
scientific-american-supplement-no-643-ap: The subterranean temples of India lead the archaeology contents of Supplement No. 643, dated New York, April 28, 1888, in Volume XXV. Those temples are described and illustrated as wonderful works of the ancient dwellers in Hindostan, in three illustrations. Biography gives General F. Perrier, with a portrait and life of the French geodesian. It also gives his triangulations in Algiers and Corsica. The Crown Prince of Germany, Prince William and his son, as heir to the German throne, follows.
stevenson-black-arrow-1888:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote The Black Arrow as a serial for a boys' magazine, using a pen name. It appeared in book form in 1888, after Treasure Island had made him famous. Stevenson himself thought it rather careless work, but young readers loved it.

During the Wars of the Roses, young Dick Shelton finds his father was murdered by his own guardian. He joins the outlaws of Tunstall Forest, who sign their revenge with black arrows. Battles, escapes, and a rescue-romance follow as Dick shifts sides in England's civil war. Richard of Gloucester, the future Richard III, appears as a chilling young fighter. The novel is a fast, rousing adventure of the fifteenth century.
storm-rider-white-horse-1888:
Theodor Storm published The Rider on the White Horse in 1888, a German novella set on the Frisian coast. Hauke Haien is a bright farm boy who rises to become dike master. He dreams of a new, safer dike against the North Sea. Villagers mock his plans and fear his pride and ambition.
